manifest.instructions: cint 0.2.0 (MCP-P.1): deterministic, capability-free integer programming language. No floating point (use scaled integers or muldiv(R, a, b, c, mode)), no implicit type promotions (use `x as T`), conditions require parentheses and Bool type (`if (x != 0) { ... }`), scalar variables require initializers (`I64 x = 0;`), and entry programs use `void main() { ... }`. Read `cint://cheat-sheet` or call `cint_get_recipe` before writing `.ci` code.

resources.cint://from-c: # cint for C programmers This page is part of CU-000.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *Read this before [201](201/README.md) if you know C. It lists what carries over, what changes and the lesson that shows each change running.* ## what carries over Much of cint reads like C. Functions are declared with the return type first, statements end with a semicolon and blocks are in braces. `if`, `else`, `while`, `break`, `continue` and `return` keep their meaning, and so does the C form of `for`. `switch` looks the same and differs in the ways listed below. Comments are written with `//`. Integer types say their width in the name: `I8` to `I1024` are signed and `U8` to `U512` are unsigned. `I32` is C's `int32_t` and `U8` is `uint8_t`. cint compiles a program to C17, and [201-00](201/00-start-here.md) shows the C it makes. ## what changes | In C | In cint | Shown in | |---|---|---| | Signed overflow is undefined behavior. | Every plain operator is checked. A result that does not fit stops the program with a fault that names the operation, the operands and the exact result. | [201-01](201/01-numbers-that-hold.md) | | Unsigned arithmetic wraps without a sign of it. | Plain unsigned operators are checked too. Wrapping is written as an operator of its own, such as `+%`, and saturating as `+|`. | [201-03](201/03-operators-at-the-edge.md) | | A shift by the width of the type or more is undefined. | A shift that loses bits faults. | [201-03](201/03-operators-at-the-edge.md) | | Integer promotion and implicit conversions happen everywhere. | No conversion happens on its own, not even to a wider type. `as` converts and faults if the value does not fit. `as%` keeps the low bits and `as?` hands the failure to the program. | [201-02](201/02-types-and-conversions.md) | | `/` rounds toward zero, and `%` takes the sign of the dividend. | `/` rounds toward negative infinity, and `%` takes the sign of the divisor, as in Python. `div_trunc` and `rem_trunc` give C's results. | [201-04](201/04-division-and-rounding.md) | | A rounding rule is set somewhere else, or implied. | Each rounded division names its rule, such as `div_round(a, b, half_even)`. | [201-04](201/04-division-and-rounding.md) | | An array index is not checked. | Every index is checked, and one past the end faults with `E_BOUNDS`. | [101-12](101/12-lists.md) | | A function takes a pointer and a length. | A function takes a view of an array, `in I64[n]` to read it or `inout I64[n]` to change it, and the length travels with it. | [201-07](201/07-debugging-by-comparison.md), [201-09](201/09-functions.md) | | A deep recursion can crash when the stack runs out, unless the compiler turns it into a loop. The depth depends on the machine. | At most 256 calls can be in progress at once, counting `main`, and one more faults with `E_DEPTH` on every machine. | [201-09](201/09-functions.md) | | A `case` without `break` falls into the next. | A case ends at the next `case`. Falling through is written as `fallthrough;`. | [201-08](201/08-control-flow.md) | | `if (x = 5)` assigns and tests. | An assignment is a statement, so this is error C1041. | [201-08](201/08-control-flow.md) | | Braces around a body of one statement are optional. | Every body needs its braces. | [201-08](201/08-control-flow.md) | | `i++` is an expression with a value. | `i++` is a statement, and it is checked. | [201-08](201/08-control-flow.md) | | C uses `#include` and `#define`. | There is no preprocessor. `const` names a constant. | [401-02](401/02-hunting-an-overflow.md) | | C has `float` and `double`. | There is no floating-point type. Every value in these courses is an integer. | | ## the same program on every compiler A C program that overflows can print one thing at `-O0` and another at `-O2`, and [301-01](301/01-when-64-bits-are-not-enough.md) shows one doing exactly that. A cint program prints the same bytes on GCC, Clang, MSVC and Apple Clang. When it faults, it prints the same fault record on each of them, field for field. So one saved output checks a run on any of those compilers, as [201-05](201/05-tests-and-goldens.md) shows. ## where to start Start with [201-00](201/00-start-here.md). It sets up cint and shows the four commands and the C that a small program becomes.
resources.cint://from-python: # cint for Python and NumPy programmers This page is part of CU-000.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *Read this before [201](201/README.md) if you know Python. It lists what carries over, what changes and the lesson that shows each change running.* ## what carries over `for i in 0..n` counts from 0 to n - 1, as `for i in range(n)` does. `/` on integers rounds toward negative infinity and `%` takes the sign of the divisor, which is Python's rule for `//` and `%`. A string with `{name}` inside prints the value of `name`, much as an f-string does. Tests can live in the same file as the code, and `cint test` runs them. ## what changes | In Python or NumPy | In cint | Shown in | |---|---|---| | `int` grows to any size. | Every integer has a fixed width, from `I8` to `I1024`. A result that does not fit stops the program with a fault that names the operation, the operands and the exact result. | [201-01](201/01-numbers-that-hold.md), [301-01](301/01-when-64-bits-are-not-enough.md) | | A NumPy `int64` array wraps without a warning, and an `int64` scalar warns and carries on with the wrapped value. | Arrays and single values are checked the same way. Wrapping is written as an operator of its own, such as `+%`. | [201-01](201/01-numbers-that-hold.md), [201-03](201/03-operators-at-the-edge.md) | | `astype(np.int16)` keeps the low bits of a value that does not fit. | `as I16` faults when the value does not fit. `as% I16` keeps the low bits when that is the intent. | [201-02](201/02-types-and-conversions.md) | | A variable takes whatever type is assigned to it. | Each variable is declared with its type, and no value changes type on its own. | [201-02](201/02-types-and-conversions.md) | | `round` rounds ties to even, without saying so at the call. | Each rounded division names its rule, such as `div_round(a, b, half_even)`. | [201-04](201/04-division-and-rounding.md) | | `float` is the default for fractions. | There is no floating-point type. Every value in these courses is an integer. | | | Indentation marks a block. | Braces mark a block, and every body needs them. | [201-08](201/08-control-flow.md) | | A deep recursion stops with `RecursionError`. | At most 256 calls can be in progress at once, counting `main`, and one more faults with `E_DEPTH`. | [201-09](201/09-functions.md) | | A list grows and shrinks. | An array has a fixed length, and every index is checked. | [101-12](101/12-lists.md) | | A function can change a list it is given. | A function says what it may do with an array: `in` to read it, `inout` to change it. | [201-09](201/09-functions.md) | | The interpreter runs the source. | cint compiles the program to C and runs it, or runs it in an interpreter for debugging. For every program in these courses, both print the same bytes. | [201-00](201/00-start-here.md), [201-06](201/06-workbench.md) | ## why the fixed widths Python's integers never run out of room, so a sum or product of them is never cut short. A fixed width matches the data that sensors, files, images and network packets carry. In NumPy the price of a fixed width is a wrong answer when a value outgrows it, with a warning for a single value and none for an array. In cint the price is a fault at the exact operation, with the numbers that caused it. When a program needs more room, a wider type such as `I128` or `I1024` holds it. It needs an `as` wherever it meets a narrower value, as [301-04](301/04-big-exact-numbers.md) shows with 100 factorial. ## the same output on every compiler A cint program prints the same bytes on every compiler cint supports, and a fault prints the same record on each of them. [201-05](201/05-tests-and-goldens.md) builds a way of testing on this: save a program's output once and compare every run after it against the saved copy. ## where to start Start with [201-00](201/00-start-here.md). It sets up cint and shows its four commands.
resources.cint://cheat-sheet:
# cint 0.2.0 Cheat Sheet (SPEC-04P.2, SPEC-06P.1, SPEC-09P.1)

## 1. File & Program Structure
- File extension is `.ci` (never `.cint`, C1001). File stem must be a valid identifier `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` (no leading digits or hyphens, C3030).
- Put entry code inside `void main() { ... }` (or `MyError!void main()`). Top-level statements make a file a script whose variables are invisible to functions and tests (C3004) and where top-level arrays/structs are refused (C9102).
- Inside any block, place array declarations (`I64[4] buf;`) before scalar declarations (`I64 x = 0;`) and statements.

## 2. Types (Zero Floating Point, Zero Implicit Promotion)
- Signed integers: `I8`, `I16`, `I32`, `I64`, `I128`, `I256`, `I512`, `I1024`.
- Unsigned integers: `U8`, `U16`, `U32`, `U64` (`U128`, `U256`, `U512` are refused in 0.2.0 with C9102; `U1024` does not exist).
- Boolean: `Bool` (`true`, `false`). Conditions in `if (cond)` and `while (cond)` must be `Bool` (C2002) and must have parentheses (C1043).
- Every scalar variable requires an initializer (`I64 x = 0;`, C2050). Arrays zero-initialize (`I64[16] buf;`).
- Constants require a type: `const I64 SCALE = 1_000_000;`.

## 3. Operators & Conversions
- Checked (default): `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `<<`, `>>`, `as T`. Faults on overflow (`E_OVERFLOW`), div-by-zero (`E_DIV_ZERO`), invalid shift count (`E_SHIFT`), or out-of-range cast (`E_NARROW`).
- Wrapping: `+%`, `-%`, `*%`, `<<%`, `as% T`. Never faults on overflow.
- Saturating: `+|`, `-|`, `*|`, `as| T`. Clamps to `[T.min, T.max]`.
- Signed `/` and `%` use floor division (`-7 / 2 == -4`, `-7 % 2 == 1`). Use `div_trunc(a, b)` and `rem_trunc(a, b)` for C truncation toward zero.
- Logical operators: `&&`, `||`, `!` (no `and`/`or`). Chained comparisons `0 <= i < n` are C2102; write `0 <= i && i < n`.
- `++` and `--` are statements (`i += 1;` or `i++;`), never expressions (C1042).

## 4. Built-in Exact Arithmetic
- `muldiv(R, a, b, c, mode)`: Exact `(a * b) / c` in a double-width intermediate, rounded once by `mode` (`half_even`, `floor`, `ceil`, `zero`, `away`, `half_up`, `half_down`, `pass`). In `cint 0.2.0`, `a`, `b`, `c`, and `R` must have the same type (widen operands first with `as R`).
- `mul_full(a, b)`: Exact product in double width (`I64 * I64 -> I128`, up to `I512 * I512 -> I1024`).
- `div_round(a, b, mode)`, `isqrt(x)`, `isqrt_round(x, mode)`, `abs(x)`, `uabs(x)`, `min(a, b)`, `max(a, b)`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `rotl(x, k)`, `rotr(x, k)`.
- Reductions: `sum(R, xs)`, `dot(R, a, b)`, `count(bs)`.

## 5. Arrays, Structs, Functions, and Error Unions
- Generic array views: `I64 total[n](in I64[n] xs)` (read-only) or `void scale_in_place[n](inout I64[n] xs, I64 k)`.
- 2D indexing uses a comma: `grid[y, x]`, slicing `grid[y, 0..w]`.
- Structs: `struct Pair { I64 a; I64 b; }` constructed positionally `Pair(1, 2)`.
- Error unions: `error MathErr { bad_input }` -> `MathErr!I64 compute(I64 x)` -> `return .bad_input;` -> caller uses `try compute(x)` or `compute(x) catch 0`.
- Printing: Bare string statement `"value={x} dollars={cents:/100} hex={u:#x}\n";` (no `print()` function).
resources.cint://refusals: ## 12 Refusals of the cint tools in 0.2.0 This clause is informative. It lists the constructs that the reference runs and that a tool of cint 0.2.0 refuses, by construct, with the tool and the diagnostic, and the limits of the tools that are below the minimums of SPEC-04P.2. A refused program is not run with another meaning (8.2), and on an implementation that runs it, its outcome is the one SPEC-04P.2 specifies. The interpreter runs the SIR text that `cint` writes, so a construct that `cint` refuses does not reach it. 1. The `cint` command (`cint run`, `cint build`, `cint test` and `cint emit-c`) refuses these constructs with the diagnostic C9102, or the one that the row names, at the position shown: | Construct | Example | Position | | --- | --- | --- | | Fixed-point types `Q.` and fraction literals | `Q16.16 a = 1.5;`, `Q8.8 x = 0.25;` | the type | | `as?` from a wide type | `I64 r = v as? I64 catch -1;` with `I128 v` | the operand | | A result form on a wide type | `I128 r = add_result(a, b) catch 0;` | the call | | `switch` on a wide value | `switch (v)` with `I256 v` | the scrutinee | | `rotl` and `rotr` by a count of a wide type | `rotl(a, n)` with `U64 a`, `I128 n` | the call | | `muldiv` of narrow operands into a wide result type | `muldiv(I128, a, b, c, floor)` with `I64` operands | the call | | An exported function with a parameter or a result of a wide integer type or a fixed-point type | `export I64 low(I128 x)` | the parameter's name, or the result type | | An array declared at the top level of a script | `I64[3] a = [1, 2, 3];` | the array literal, or the declaration when it has none | | A struct type declared in a script | `struct P { I64 x; I64 y; }` before top-level statements | the struct's name | | An array literal of structs | `P[2] ps = [P(1, 2), P(3, 4)];` | the `[` of the literal | | A view variable over an array of structs | `in P[_] v = ps;` | the variable's name | | Named arguments in a call of a user function | `diff(b = 1, a = 10)` | the first name | | A step `by` in a range `for` loop | `for i in 0..10 by 3 { ... }` | the step | | A selected import | `import geo.vec.{V2, dot2};` | the `import` | | `catch` on a call of a function of an imported module | `parse.digit(c) catch -1` with `import lib.parse;` | the function's name | | A `catch` expression as the operand of another operator | `(f(1) catch 0) + 1` | the `catch` | | The wrapping negation `-%` | `I8 n = -%m;` | the operator | | `len` of a string literal | `len("abc")` | the string literal | | The format conversions `!bits` and `!lanes(T)` in a print statement | `"{x!bits}\n";`, `"{w!lanes(U8)}\n";` | the print statement | | The format kind `c` | `"{c:c}\n";` | the value of the hole | | An array, or a slice of one, as the value of a hole | `"{a}\n";`, `"{a[1..]}\n";` with `I32[3] a` | the value of the hole, or the `[` of the slice | | An empty struct type | `struct Empty { }` | the struct's name | | An array literal as an argument of a struct constructor | `Vec3([1, 2, 3])` | the `[` of the literal | | An array literal as the right operand of an assignment, to an array or a slice | `a = [3, 4];`, `a[0..2] = [3, 4];` | the `[` of the literal | | A module-level array whose extent is the name of a constant or a constant expression | `I64[N] table;`, `I64[N * 2] table;` | the name, or the operator of the expression | | An array of handles | `Handle(I64)[3] hs;` | the type | | An exported arena | `export Arena(I64, 4) store;` | the type | | An array element as the scalar `out` argument of a kernel | `total(a, r[0]);` | the `[` of the element | | A local `Arena(T)` or `Pool(T)` initialized from a module-level name | `Arena(I64) s = scratch;` | the local's name | | Arena storage, or a view variable over it, passed to a view parameter | `total(scratch[h])` | the call | | A slice of arena storage, or of a view variable over it | `scratch[h][2..4]`, `v[2..5]` | the `[` of the slice | | A dispatch of a kernel of an imported module, called after the module's name or alias | `dbl.twice(a, b);` with `import kmod.dbl;` | the kernel's name, with the diagnostic C3005 | 2. A program whose entry is a function `main`, rather than top-level statements, may declare struct types: the row of a struct declared in a script applies to scripts only. The `cint` command also reports C9102 for `==` between two arrays, which the reference rejects with the diagnostic C2013 at the same position, so both reject such a program. It reports C9102 for a fraction literal given to an integer type, as in `I64 x = 1.5;`, which the reference rejects with the diagnostic C2004 at the same position. In the same way it reports C9102, at the print statement, for the conversion `!ratio` of an integer, as in `"{x!ratio}\n";` with `I64 x`. SPEC-04P.2 7.5.4 makes that conversion C1037, and the reference reports C1037 at the value of the hole. The C3005 of a kernel called after a module's name is not a refusal in the sense of SPEC-04P.2 4, paragraph 4, whose codes begin with `C9`: the `cint` command rejects that conforming program as it rejects an undefined name. 3. In one case the direction is reversed, and the reference refuses a run that the `cint` command carries out. For `clamp(x, lo, hi)` with `lo` greater than `hi` at run time, `cint run` faults `E_DOMAIN` with the operation `clamp.checked.`, such as `clamp.checked.i64`, and the operands `x`, `lo` and `hi`, with no exact result and no limit, as SPEC-04P.2 7.2.1 states. The reference reports the outcome `refused` for that run. 4. A `gpu-cuda` build refuses a kernel whose body needs a capability that the `gpu-cuda` table lists as unsupported, with `E_UNSUPPORTED`, naming the kernel, the capability, the SIR node and the position (5.5). The `cpu-c17` build of the same program runs it. | Capability | Construct in a kernel body | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | `sat` | the saturating operators `+\|`, `-\|` and `*\|` | `b[i] = a[i] +\| a[i];` | | `div` | `/` and `%` | `b[i] = a[i] / 2;` | | `shift` | `<<` and `>>`, wrapping or checked | `b[i] = a[i] << 1;` | | `bits` | `&`, `\|`, `^`, `~` and `!` | `b[i] = a[i] & 3;` | | `neg` | unary `-` | `b[i] = -a[i];` | | `as.wrap` | the wrapping conversion `as%` | `(a[i] as% I32) as I64` | | `builtin` | every built-in function except `div_round` | `b[i] = min(a[i], 2);` | | `switch` | `switch` | `switch (a[i]) { ... }` | | `store.narrow` | a store into a view of 8-bit, 16-bit or `Bool` elements | `out U8[n] b` | | `array` | a local array | `I64[2] t;` | | `wide` | any value of `I128` to `I1024` | `in I128[n] a` | 5. Three limits of the tools of cint 0.2.0 are below the minimums that SPEC-04P.2 5.3 states. A program beyond any of them is stopped, and the reference runs it: | Quantity | Minimum in SPEC-04P.2 5.3 | Limit of the tools | Beyond the limit | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Size of one source file | 16,777,216 bytes | 4,194,304 bytes, in `cint run`, `cint build`, `cint test` and `cint emit-c` | For the file it is given, the command stops with a tool error and exit status 5; an imported module of that size is the diagnostic C3009. The reference runs a file of 5,242,880 bytes. | | Call-depth limit accepted as a semantic input | 4,096 active calls | 1,024 active calls, the constant `CINT_RT_MAX_DEPTH` of the runtime (7.10) | An entry whose depth limit is larger faults `E_UNSUPPORTED` at `call.enter` before it runs, with the limit 1,024. The reference runs a recursion 4,000 calls deep under a depth limit of 4,096. | | Size of an imported module, against the size of the root module | 16,777,216 bytes, as for every source file | A bound that grows with the size of the root module, in `cint run`, `cint build`, `cint test` and `cint emit-c`: 745,090 bytes for a root module of 34 bytes | The command stops with the diagnostic C9001 at line 0 of the root module, position `0:0`, though the imported module is under 4,194,304 bytes; SPEC-04P.2 5.3 places a C9001 that concerns a whole file at line 1. Under a root module of 34 bytes, an imported module of 745,091 bytes is C9001. Under a root module of 341 bytes, an imported module of 4,000,000 bytes runs, and so does a root module of 4,000,000 bytes that holds the same function. The reference runs the program. |

recipes.title: Exact Fixed-Point Sine and Cosine (Horner Series + Error Sweep Test)
recipes.summary: Computes sin and cos in microradians (scale 1_000_000) using range reduction and a degree-7/degree-6 Horner polynomial with muldiv, plus a test sweeping the domain to verify worst-case error.

recipes.title: Exact Fixed-Point Square Root and Natural Logarithm
recipes.summary: Computes scaled square root via isqrt_round and natural logarithm via 2*artanh((x-1)/(x+1)) after power-of-two reduction, with measured accuracy verified in a test block.

recipes.title: Wide I1024 Arithmetic and High-Precision Fixed-Point Scaling
recipes.summary: Demonstrates explicit widening to I1024 before muldiv (avoiding C9102 narrow-to-wide refusal), exact 2048-bit intermediate products, and exact decimal scaling.

recipes.title: Deterministic SVG Trajectory Generator in Pure cint
recipes.summary: Integrates a 2D harmonic oscillator with symplectic velocity-Verlet steps in integer micrometer coordinates and prints complete, self-contained SVG markup to stdout.

recipes.title: 64-Bit FNV-1a Rolling State Digest (Byte-Wise Wrapping Arithmetic)
recipes.summary: Computes a canonical 64-bit FNV-1a hash over signed I64 words one byte per round using wrapping *% and as% U64 so native, SIR interpreter, and browser BigInt mirrors agree bit-for-bit.

recipes.title: Exact Cents Ledger with Error Unions, Banker's Rounding, and Fault Tests
recipes.summary: Models deposits, withdrawals, error unions (LedgerError!I64), banker's rounding interest (muldiv half_even), exact {/100} decimal formatting, and expect_fault E_OVERFLOW testing.

recipes.title: All-or-Nothing Kernel Dispatch, Reduction, and Double Buffering
recipes.summary: Demonstrates a 1D kernel with `over [i: n]`, exact `reduce total = sum(v)` epilogue, and double-buffered arrays to avoid C5010/E_ALIAS overlap faults.

chunks.title: SPEC-00P.2
chunks.content:
# SPEC-00P.2: Overview

SPEC-00P.2, edition 2 of the overview of the cint specifications, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

This edition replaces SPEC-00P.1.

chunks.title: Foreword
chunks.content:
## Foreword

This document is the overview of the specifications published with cint 0.2.0: what cint is, how the documents fit together, where to start reading, and which claims cint makes, with their limits. It is informative. It states no rule of its own, and where it summarizes a rule, the document that states the rule governs.

chunks.title: 1 What cint is
chunks.content:
## 1 What cint is

cint is a programming language for computations whose results must be exact and the same on every machine. It is a C-family language: declarations name the type first, and functions, blocks, statements and most operators are written as in C. Source files end in `.ci`. It rests on six mechanisms:

chunks.title: 1 What cint is (part 2)
chunks.content:
- **Integers only.** Every value is an integer of a declared type, a `Bool`, or an array or struct of them. The integer types are `I8` to `I64`, `U8` to `U64` and the wide types `I128` to `I1024` and `U128` to `U512`; fixed-point types such as `Q16.16`, with 16 integer bits, counting the sign bit, and 16 fraction bits, hold multiples of 2^-16 as integers. There is no floating-point type (SPEC-04P.2 6.3).
- **Every plain operator is checked.** `a + b` gives the exact sum when it fits the type and faults when it does not. Wrapping and saturating arithmetic have their own operators, `a +% b` and `a +| b` and `add_result(a, b)` returns an error value instead of faulting. The spelling alone decides; no option changes it (SPEC-04P.2 6.7).
- **No implicit conversions.** A value changes type only through a written conversion: `as` is checked, `as%` wraps and `as?` returns an error value. A literal has no type of its own and takes the one its context requires (SPEC-04P.2 6.5, 6.6).
- **A fault stops the program with a full record.** A *fault* stops a run at an operation that cannot give a correct result. Its *fault record* names the operation, each operand with its type, the exact result, the bound crossed, the source position and the calls that led there. Program code cannot catch a fault. An expected failure is an *error* instead: a value that a function returns and its caller handles with `try` or `catch` (SPEC-04P.2 5.2.3, 6.11).
- **Three executors and a reference.** `cpu-c17` compiles a program to C17 and builds it with the host's C compiler. `cpu-sir-interp`, the interpreter, runs the compiler's intermediate form directly. `gpu-cuda` runs *kernels* on NVIDIA GPUs. A kernel is a function applied once to each point of an index space, and its run for one point is a *work-item*. *The reference*, `cint_ref`, is a separate implementation in Python whose results are the expect

chunks.title: 1 What cint is (part 3)
2 A first program
2 A first program (part 2)
chunks.content:
- `fault[E_OVERFLOW]`: the fault code and its fixed message.
- `-->` and the excerpt: the position `factorial21.ci:5:15`, the 15th character of line 5, which is the `*` of `f = f * k`.
- `operation`: `mul.checked.i64`, the checked product of two `I64` values.
- `operand`: both operands, exact and typed: the factorial of 20, and 21.
- `exact` and `limit`: the true product, and `I64.max`, the bound it crossed.
- `called from`: the call in line 12 that led there.
- `fuel-consumed` and `state` follow the record and are not part of it.

The program does not continue with a wrapped value. SPEC-04P.2 8.1 explains every line of a report.

chunks.title: 3 The documents
chunks.content:
## 3 The documents

The specifications of cint 0.2.0 are these editions:

| Edition | Title | What it covers | Kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPEC-00P.2 | Overview | This document | Informative |
| SPEC-01P.2 | Canonical encodings and identity | The bytes of values, fault records, program state, checkpoints and recordings; the identities of a program and of a run | Normative |
| SPEC-02P.1 | Kernels and executors | What an executor does to carry out a kernel dispatch, and what each executor of 0.2.0 runs and refuses | Normative |
| SPEC-03P.1 | The host interface: C and Python | How C and Python programs call cint code, lend it memory, and checkpoint and record it | Normative |
| SPEC-04P.2 | The cint language | The language and its built-in operations, faults and fuel, and how to find out why a program did what it did | Normative; Annexes B to F informative |
| SPEC-06P.1 | The cint tools | The commands, outputs and exit statuses of `cint`, the interpreter and the debug tools | Normative |
| SPEC-09P.1 | Toolchain and conformance | The compiler's intermediate form, the C it emits, what implementations agree on, the conformance suite, the bootstrap, receipts and the constructs that the tools of 0.2.0 refuse | Normative; clause 12 informative |
| GLOSSARY-P.2 | Glossary | Every defined term, with the edition and section that define it | Informative |
| REFERENCES-P.2 | References | The published works that the editions cite | Informative |

SPEC-04P.2 depends on no other document, so a reader learning the language needs only it. Each of the others serves one kind of reader, as section 4 shows.

**Editions.** An edition is named by the document's number, `P` for public, and the edition's number: SPEC-04P.2 is the second edition of SPEC-04, and SPEC-02P.1 the first of SPEC-02. Each document counts its own editions.

chunks.title: 3 The documents (part 2)
chunks.content:
- Each minor release, such as 0.2.0, publishes an edition of every document. A patch release, such as 0.2.1, publishes the next edition only of a document whose rules or listed refusals it changes.
- A released edition's text does not change. A correction that changes no meaning is published as an erratum; a change of meaning is a new edition.
- Each rule ends with its *clause identifier*, such as IM-106 or LS-17. The identifier stays with the rule when the rule moves to another section or document, and it is not reused: IM-106, the fields of a fault record, was in SPEC-01P.1 and is in SPEC-04P.2 8.1. Section numbers belong to one edition.
- Every rule has an anchor named by its clause identifier, and every section an anchor named by its title, so a link keeps working in each edition that keeps the rule or the section.
- A citation gives the edition, the section and the identifier: SPEC-04P.2 8.1, IM-106.

chunks.title: 4 Reading orders
chunks.content:
## 4 Reading orders

Each list is an order to read in, not everything worth reading.

A learner reads in this order:

1. Sections 1, 2 and 6 of this overview.
2. SPEC-04P.2, Introduction; 5.1.2, scripts and programs; 6.3.1, integer types; 6.5, literals; 6.7.6, the additive operators; 6.6, conversions.
3. SPEC-04P.2 6.10, statements; 7.5, formatting; 8.1, reading a fault report; 8.5, a first session with the debug tools.
4. SPEC-04P.2 6.9, declarations; 6.11, errors and faults; 6.12, arrays and views; 6.15.3, tests.

A C programmer reads in this order:

1. SPEC-04P.2 Annex D, cint for C and Python programmers and Annex C, what cint does where C leaves behavior undefined, and what it leaves out.
2. SPEC-04P.2 6.6, conversions, none of them implicit; 6.7.1, precedence, where the bitwise operators bind tighter than in C; 6.7.7, division, which rounds toward negative infinity.
3. SPEC-04P.2 6.12, arrays and views; 6.14, arenas, pools and handles; 6.11, errors.
4. SPEC-09P.1 7, the C that the compiler emits and SPEC-03P.1 7, calling cint code from C.

A Python user reads in this order:

1. SPEC-04P.2 Annex D, then the learner's order.
2. SPEC-03P.1 8, the Python module, in particular 8.2, borrowing arrays without a copy, and 8.6, a complete example with NumPy.
3. SPEC-04P.2 6.13, kernels and SPEC-03P.1 6.4, outputs and publication.
4. SPEC-04P.2 8.4 and SPEC-03P.1 9, checkpoints, recordings and replay.

An implementer reads in this order:

1. SPEC-04P.2 clauses 3 to 7 in order, with Annex A, the grammar and Annex B, the codes.
2. SPEC-04P.2 8.1 and 8.2, the fault record and what implementations agree on.
3. SPEC-02P.1, the executors and SPEC-01P.2, the encodings and identities.
4. SPEC-09P.1 8, agreement; 9, the conformance suite; 12, the refusals of the tools of 0.2.0; 10, the bootstrap.
5. SPEC-06P.1 7, the forms of reports and SPEC-03P.1 7, the C interface.

chunks.title: 5 What 0.2.0 includes and what it does not
5 What 0.2.0 includes and what it does not (part 2)
chunks.content: Some features are in no implementation of cint 0.2.0, the reference included. Among them are string variables and formatting into a string, enumerations, tuples, type aliases, attributes, bit fields, the `do` loop, `for` over the elements of an array, default arguments, functions that return views, reading input from files or the terminal, schedules for kernels, dispatches that write their outputs in place, the type `U1024` and executors other than the three of section 1. Each document's Future directions clause describes those of its area: SPEC-04P.2 6.16, SPEC-01P.2 10, SPEC-02P.1 12, SPEC-03P.1 11, SPEC-06P.1 13 and SPEC-09P.1 13.

chunks.title: 6 Finding out why
6.1 The fault record
chunks.content:
### 6.1 The fault record

The report of section 2 prints one fault record. Besides the fields read there, the record holds the revision of the program text, and it holds no time, no memory address and no name of a machine or an executor, so one fault gives one record everywhere. A fault in a kernel dispatch also has an address: the dispatch number, the work-item index and the step. When several work-items fault, the record describes the least of them in a fixed order, whatever order they ran in, so a GPU reports the same fault as the C executor (SPEC-04P.2 8.1, SPEC-02P.1 5.5).

chunks.title: 6.2 Agreement
chunks.content:
### 6.2 Agreement

The reference, `cint_ref`, runs the same files. It runs as `python3 -m cint_ref` with the `ref` directory of the cint source tree on `PYTHONPATH`, and `--format 5` selects the newest form of its outcome text (SPEC-09P.1 9.3):

```console
$ python3 -m cint_ref run --format 5 --stdout ref.out factorial.ci
case factorial
format 5
source reference
outcome value
stdout-bytes 40
stdout-sha256 30b3b4dbc6ca79e5fd6c441e533d6027db1fda245cabfcd3c986ea96020d5606
fuel-consumed 33
$ cint run factorial.ci | cmp - ref.out && echo same
same
```

The reference prints the outcome, not the output: the run ended normally after writing 40 bytes, whose SHA-256 digest is shown, and consumed 33 units of fuel, 1 for the script, 1 for each of the two calls and 1 for each of the 30 iterations. `--stdout` saved the output bytes, and `cmp` finds them equal to those of `cint run`.

It runs `factorial21.ci` to the same end:

```console
$ python3 -m cint_ref run --format 5 factorial21.ci
case factorial21
format 5
source reference
outcome fault
stdout-bytes 40
stdout-sha256 30b3b4dbc6ca79e5fd6c441e533d6027db1fda245cabfcd3c986ea96020d5606
fuel-consumed 55
fault.code E_OVERFLOW
fault.operation mul.checked.i64
fault.operand I64 2432902008176640000
fault.operand I64 21
fault.exact 51090942171709440000
fault.limit I64 9223372036854775807
fault.position factorial21.ci:5:15
fault.revision self
fault.source-map self
fault.address none
fault.stack-depth 1
fault.stack factorial21.ci:12:9
```

chunks.title: 6.2 Agreement (part 2)
chunks.content: The output is the 40 bytes of `factorial.ci`, since the third print wrote nothing. The fuel is the 55 of the report: 1 for the script, 1 for each of the three calls and 51 for the iterations. The fault matches the report field for field, except that the reference writes `self` for the revision and the source map, since it does not compute them. The reference shares no code with the compiler, so each checks the other, and any difference between them is a defect in one of them (SPEC-04P.2 8.2, SPEC-09P.1 8.1).

chunks.title: 6.3 Golden outputs and tests
chunks.content:
### 6.3 Golden outputs and tests

A *golden*, or golden output, is an output checked once, saved, and compared byte for byte with the output of each run after it: `cint run factorial.ci > factorial.golden` saves one, and `diff` compares. Every implementation gives the same outcome, so a golden made with one checks a run on any other. A test keeps its expectation inside the module, and `cint test` runs each test from a fresh state:

```console
$ cint test fact.ci
test fact.ci:10 "20! fits in I64" ... ok
test fact.ci:14 "21! does not" ... ok
2 of 2 tests passed
```

The second test passes because `factorial(21)` faults `E_OVERFLOW`, the fault it names; it would fail if the call returned a value (SPEC-04P.2 8.3, 6.15.3).

chunks.title: 6.4 Checkpoints and replay
chunks.content:
### 6.4 Checkpoints and replay

An *entry* is one run of a program from one of its entry points, such as a call of an exported function by a host program, and the end of an entry is a *boundary*. In a `cint workbench` session each line typed is an entry, and every entry is recorded. A *checkpoint* saves the program's state at a boundary, and *replay* runs recorded entries again and compares each outcome with the recording:

```console
$ cint workbench fact.ci
...
ci[1]> :load fact.ci
loaded fact (fact.ci)
ci[2]> fact.factorial(20)
= 2432902008176640000 : I64
ci[3]> I64 p = fact.factorial(19);
p = 121645100408832000 : I64
ci[4]> :checkpoint p19
checkpoint p19   #1   bindings 1   revisions: session@r1, fact@r1
ci[4]> p = p * 20;
ci[5]> p = p * 21;
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> entry 5:1:7
...
   = state: no store completed in this entry; context reset
...
ci[6]> p
= 2432902008176640000 : I64
ci[7]> :replay p19
replaying 3 entries from p19 to the current state (entry 4 to entry 6), comparing prints and outcomes with the recording
entry 5: E_OVERFLOW reproduced, its fault record equal to the recorded one
replay matches the recording at 3 boundaries
ci[7]> :restore p19
saved current state as auto-1
restored p19   #1
ci[7]> p
= 121645100408832000 : I64
ci[8]> :quit --yes
```

chunks.title: 6.4 Checkpoints and replay (part 2)
chunks.content:
- Loading the module is entry 1, and its function is named `fact.factorial`. An expression entry prints its value and its type.
- `I64 p` is a variable of the session, kept from entry to entry. `:checkpoint p19` saves the state while `p` holds the factorial of 19.
- Entry 5 faults. No store of it completed, so `p` still holds the factorial of 20, and the session clears the fault before the next entry.
- `:replay p19` restores the checkpoint, runs entries 4 to 6 again and finds every outcome equal to the recorded one, the fault record included. `:restore p19` makes the checkpoint's state current again.

The tools go back in time by replay from a checkpoint; they do not run a program backward (SPEC-04P.2 8.4).

chunks.title: 6.5 The debug tools
chunks.content:
### 6.5 The debug tools

`cint explain` shows what the compiler knows about a function without running it. Each *fault site*, an operation that can fault, has an identifier:

```console
$ cint explain fact.ci:factorial
module fact.ci   revision f0d0bba7a6264e17cd2556c3618e861ca5750392885362dcf3ad62407252ed69

function factorial   fact.sites:3   pure
  signature  (in n: I64) -> I64
  fault sites (3): 3 possible, 0 statically excluded
    factorial#1  fact.ci:2:12  fuel.charge      E_FUEL possible
    factorial#2  fact.ci:4:5   fuel.charge      E_FUEL possible
    factorial#3  fact.ci:5:15  mul.checked.i64  E_OVERFLOW possible
...
```

`factorial#1` is the fuel charge of each call, `factorial#2` that of each iteration and `factorial#3` the `*` that faulted in section 2. `pure` says only that the function prints nothing and calls nothing that prints.

`cint debug locate` runs an exported function as an entry, under a recording, and finds the first fault. It prints the report and the last counted operations before the fault, and `--save-case` keeps the run as a *case*, a recording that runs on another machine with the tools alone. `cint debug diff` runs a case on `cpu-c17` and on `cpu-sir-interp` and compares them at every boundary:

chunks.title: 6.5 The debug tools (part 2)
chunks.content:
```console
$ cint debug locate fact.ci --entry factorial --args I64 21 --save-case f21.case
program    fact.ci   evaluator cpu-sir-interp, recorded as the case f21.case
target     boundary 1 of 1, factorial(I64 21): the first fault, reproduced by replay
bracket    the initial state; then boundary 1
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> fact.ci:5:15
...
   = site: factorial#3
...
  ord  position           operation              operands                 value
...
   37                     add.wrap.i64           19, 1                    20
   38  fact.ci:5:15       mul.checked.i64        121645100408832000, 20   2432902008176640000
   39                     add.wrap.i64           20, 1                    21
   40  fact.ci:5:15       mul.checked.i64        2432902008176640000, 21  E_OVERFLOW
$ cint debug diff f21.case
case       f21.case   1 boundary   density entry
reference  cpu-c17
candidate  cpu-sir-interp
boundaries 1 of 1 compared
outcome    agree
```

The `site` line names `factorial#3`. Each row of the trace is one counted operation with its exact operands and value: the last two products before the fault and, between them, the step of the loop index `k`, which has no position of its own. `agree` says that both executors reached the same state and the same fault record; here `reference` names the executor that the other is compared with, not the reference implementation. SPEC-04P.2 8.5 continues with a first session and the commands a learner uses first, and SPEC-06P.1 defines every command.

chunks.title: 7 Claims and evidence
chunks.content:
## 7 Claims and evidence

Each claim is stated briefly, with the rules that carry it and its limits. Where a sentence here and a rule differ, the rule holds. Figures that support a claim come from the receipts published with cint 0.2.0, and SPEC-09P.1 11.3 shows how to run one again and compare the result.

chunks.title: 7 Claims and evidence (part 2)
chunks.clauses: CONF-03 CONF-04 CONF-14 EMIT-01 EMIT-19 EMIT-20 EMIT-21 H-16 H-20 IM-106 IM-111 IM-112
chunks.content:
1. **Exact or a fault.** Every plain arithmetic operator, and the checked conversion `as`, gives the exact result or faults, and no option changes what a spelling does.
   - Rules: SPEC-04P.2 6.7, IM-28 and IM-31; 6.7.6, IM-30; 6.6, IM-50.
   - Limits: the wrapping and saturating forms do not fault on overflow, but they do fault on a shift count out of range and on a divisor of 0.
2. **No implicit conversion.** A value changes type only through a conversion written in the program.
   - Rules: SPEC-04P.2 6.6, IM-9 and IM-50; 6.5, LS-56.
   - Limits: a literal takes its type from its context, which types the literal and converts no value.
3. **No undefined behavior.** Within the scope of SPEC-04P.2, no behavior is undefined, unspecified or implementation-defined.
   - Rules: SPEC-04P.2 4, LS-273; Annex C, IM-128.
   - Limits: the scope excludes code reached through the host interface and the memory it changes; defects in an implementation, in the C it emits or in the C compiler; hardware faults; and exhaustion of host resources that an implementation cannot detect (SPEC-04P.2 4, LS-274).
4. **A fault ends the entry with a complete record.** A fault ends the entry at once and gives one record of its operation, operands, exact result, bound and position, with no time, address or executor in it, and program code cannot catch it.
   - Rules: SPEC-04P.2 5.2.3, IM-118; 8.1, IM-106 and IM-111.
   - Limits: stores that completed before the fault remain, because sequential code is not rolled back (SPEC-04P.2 5.2.3, IM-121 and IM-122).
5. **Determinism.** Runs with the same semantic inputs write the same output bytes, end with the same fault record or none, and consume the same fuel, on every conforming implementation, executor and machine.
   - Rules: SPEC-04P.2 4, LS-272; 8.2, IM-159 and IM-160.
   - Limits: a run ended by a failure of host resources, such as memory running out

chunks.title: 7 Claims and evidence (part 3)
chunks.content:
These are not claimed:

- **Compliance with a safety or coding standard,** such as MISRA C or the SEI CERT C Coding Standard. Such a claim would need a documented assessment against named editions and rules (SPEC-04P.2 4, LS-275; SPEC-09P.1 11.4, DISC-02).
- **Anything about memory that code outside cint changes** while cint code uses it, or about what host code computes (SPEC-04P.2 4, LS-274; SPEC-03P.1 4 and 8.4).
- **Executables reproducible byte for byte.** The emitted C is reproducible; the executables built from it differ between toolchains and may differ between two builds with one toolchain (SPEC-09P.1 10.4, FIX-05).
- **That the fixpoint ties an executable to its source.** The fixpoint compares emitted C. It is not diverse double-compiling, and it does not show that an executable corresponds to the compiler's source (SPEC-09P.1 10.5, FIX-04).
- **Numerical adequacy.** An exact and repeatable result can still be a poor model of the problem it computes, for example where integers replace a floating-point computation (SPEC-04P.2 8.2, IM-160).
- **Outcomes outside the run matrix,** on other C compilers or machines (SPEC-09P.1 8.4, CONF-03).
- **Speed.** These documents make no claim about speed. A speed figure published with a release names its workload, machine, toolchain, flags and method of measurement (SPEC-09P.1 11.4, DISC-04).
- **Correctness from agreement.** Two implementations can agree and both be wrong. Agreement shows that outcomes are equal; the specifications decide which outcome is correct (SPEC-04P.2 8.2).

chunks.title: 8 The name
chunks.content:
## 8 The name

The language is spelled cint, in lowercase, also at the start of a sentence. It is not related to `CINT`, the C and C++ interpreter of the ROOT data analysis framework from CERN.

chunks.title: 9 Prior work
chunks.content:
## 9 Prior work

cint takes most of its syntax from C, as ISO/IEC 9899:2018 defines it. Its arithmetic follows languages that put the behavior on overflow in the program text. Zig writes wrapping and saturating addition as `+%` and `+|`, the spellings cint uses and cint's error sets and error unions, with `try`, `catch`, `defer` and `errdefer`, are adapted from Zig as well. Rust gives its integer types checked, wrapping and saturating arithmetic as named methods, such as `checked_add`.

A kernel is written for one work-item, as in the single-program, multiple-data model of ISPC and the rule that each work-item writes only its own part of the outputs draws on Futhark's in-place updates. Finding a fault by recording a run and replaying it has precedent in record-and-replay debuggers such as rr. Top-level statements that run in order, with no `main` function needed, come from Terry A. Davis's HolyC. REFERENCES-P.2 lists each of these works.

chunks.title: SPEC-01P.2
chunks.content:
# SPEC-01P.2: Canonical encodings and identity

SPEC-01P.2, edition 2 of the canonical encodings specification, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

This edition replaces SPEC-01P.1, "Integer machine". The rules of that edition that define types, operators, faults and fuel are stated in SPEC-04P.2, "The cint language"; this document states the byte encodings and the identities computed from them. Annex C lists every clause identifier of SPEC-01P.1 and where its rule is stated in cint 0.2.0.

chunks.title: Foreword
chunks.content:
## Foreword

This document specifies the bytes that cint 0.2.0 writes and reads: the canonical encodings of values, fault records, program state, checkpoints and recordings and the digests that identify a program and a run.

Each rule ends with one or more clause identifiers in brackets, such as [IM-149] or [IM-157]. An identifier names one rule: a rule keeps its identifier when its text moves to another section or another document, and no identifier is reused. Most identifiers of this document begin with `IM-` and come from SPEC-01P.1. A rule that another edition states, and whose bytes this document lays out, is cited in brackets with that edition's name, such as [SPEC-03P.1 H-14]: the rule is stated there, and this document gives only its encoding. Section numbers belong to this edition only.

chunks.title: Introduction
Introduction (part 2)
chunks.content:
Tools compare these bytes, not the text of reports. Two implementations agree on a fault when their records are equal, and a recording of a run holds the record and the state hash of every step, so that a replay can compare them again. Every encoding in this document follows the same conventions (5.1): integers are little-endian, every string and list carries its length in front, every optional field has a presence byte, and every binary encoding begins with a domain string that names it. A decoder can therefore read each byte without the program that wrote it, and bytes of two kinds cannot be taken for each other.

Identities are digests of canonical bytes. The *revision* of a program is a SHA-256 digest of its compiled form with every source position removed (9.1), so adding a comment leaves it unchanged. The *state hash* is a SHA-256 digest of the bytes of a program's state (7.6), and a recording chains the state hashes of the steps of a run into one digest (8.5).

chunks.title: How this document is organized
chunks.content:
### How this document is organized

Clauses 1 to 4 state what the document covers, the documents it relies on, its terms and what conformance means. Clause 5 encodes values: the conventions every encoding shares, integers of every width, fixed-point values, mathematical integers and tagged values, among them arrays, structs and handles. Clause 6 encodes the fault record, in its versions 2 and 3, and two small records that a compiled program writes beside it. Clause 7 encodes the state of a program, the checkpoint that holds it and the state hash. Clause 8 encodes recordings and cases. Clause 9 defines the identities computed from these bytes and what never enters them. Clause 10 lists future directions. Annex A works through complete encodings, Annex B specifies the operation fixture format CIF-1, and Annex C indexes the clause identifiers of SPEC-01P.1.

Each subclause of clauses 5 to 9 opens with a short summary and then has some of these parts:

- **Syntax**: the layout of the bytes, field by field, in the notation of 5.1.
- **Constraints**: the conditions that valid bytes meet. A writer produces only valid bytes, and a decoder rejects bytes that break a constraint.
- **Semantics**: what the fields mean.
- **Examples** and **Notes**: informative. They illustrate the rules and never add to them.

Byte values are written in hexadecimal, two digits a byte, such as `0f` or `ff`. Every example is the output of cint 0.2.0, of the reference, or of the program shown with it (A.4). A table of bytes lists them in the order they occur, with offsets in decimal. In such a table, `(32 bytes)` stands for a SHA-256 digest, which the text names, and `(n bytes)` for bytes that another table shows. A line `...` in shown output stands for lines left out.

chunks.title: 1 Scope
2 Normative references
chunks.content:
## 2 Normative references

The following documents are referred to in the text in such a way that some or all of their content constitutes requirements of this document. For dated references, only the edition cited applies.

- National Institute of Standards and Technology. *Secure Hash Standard (SHS)*. FIPS PUB 180-4, August 2015. Defines SHA-256.
- F. Yergeau. *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*. RFC 3629 (STD 63), November 2003.
- T. Bray, editor. *The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format*. RFC 8259 (STD 90), December 2017. Used by CIF-1 (Annex B).
- *JSON Lines*. https://jsonlines.org/. Maintained by Ian Ward. A published convention, with no RFC or ISO standard, for a file of one JSON value per line. Used by CIF-1 (Annex B).

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols
chunks.content: ## 3 Terms, definitions and symbols The terms of SPEC-04P.2 clause 3 apply, among them Z, value, type, exact result, fault, fault code, fault record, operation identifier, error, entry, fuel, call depth, frame arena, semantic input, module, array, kernel, dispatch, work-item, arena, pool, handle, revision, the reference and executor. The following terms are added. **3.1 canonical**: designated, by a named and versioned rule, as the one representation of a content or the one selection among several. Canonical says which bytes are compared, not that they are correct: two implementations can write equal canonical bytes and both be wrong. **3.2 encoding**: a rule that maps a content, such as a value or a fault record, to bytes. An encoding has a name and a version. **3.3 domain string**: the string, of the form `//v`, that begins each binary encoding of this document and the input of every digest, and names its encoding and version, such as `cint-core-1/fault/v2`. **3.4 tag**: the bytes, beginning with one byte, that name the type of a value where values of several types can occur. Also called a type descriptor. **3.5 payload**: the bytes of a value without its tag. **3.6 tagged value**: a tag followed by a payload. **3.7 presence byte**: a byte `00`, which marks an optional field as absent, or `01`, which marks it present and is followed by the field. **3.8 writer, decoder**: a *writer* is the part of an implementation that produces the bytes of an encoding; a *decoder* is the part of an implementation that reads the bytes of an encoding.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 2)
chunks.content: **3.9 context**: one instance of a program's state, held by a host program, in which entries run one at a time: its module variables, arenas and pools, its buffer registry, its counters and its fault record (SPEC-03P.1 3.4). **3.10 state**: the canonical content of a context between entries: the values of its module-level variables, its arenas and pools, its registry of buffers, its identifier counters, the fault record it holds if any, and the count of effects it has completed. **3.11 checkpoint**: the canonical bytes of a state, in an envelope that names the runtime contract, from which a context can be restored. A checkpoint is taken between entries, not inside one. A host program receives it as bytes (SPEC-03P.1 9.2), and the tools keep it in a file or, in a workbench session, under a name (SPEC-06P.1 11.1). **3.12 state hash**: the SHA-256 digest of the canonical bytes of a state. **3.13 effect**: a request that an entry makes of its host. In cint 0.2.0 the one effect is the output of a print statement, whose request is the bytes printed. **3.14 recording**: a file that holds the identity and code of a program, a checkpoint of a context when recording began, and the events that followed, in order: each entry with its arguments, its effects and its outcome, and the checkpoints, restores, cleared faults and changes of revision between entries. The state hash at each boundary is recorded and chained into one digest (3.17). From a recording the run can be replayed: its entries run again on a context restored from that checkpoint, with the recorded inputs, and each outcome and boundary is compared with the recording.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 3)
chunks.content: **3.15 case**: a recording that also holds the source text of every module of its program, so that the run can be shown, replayed and compared on another machine with no other file. **3.16 boundary**: a point of a run at which the state of its context is defined and its state hash is taken: the end of an entry that ran, or, at dispatch density, the publication of a kernel dispatch. A recording records the state hash at each boundary, and replay compares it. **3.17 digest chain**: the digest that a recording carries in its last event, computed from the state hash of its first checkpoint and of each boundary in turn, so that equal chains mean equal states, and equal fault records, at every boundary. **3.18 runtime contract version**: the name of the interface between compiled code and the runtime library, `cint-rt-3` in cint 0.2.0. **3.19 SIR text**: the canonical text form of one module's intermediate representation, specified by SPEC-09P.1. Its second line, the *sites line*, lists each *site* of the module, an operation that can fault, with its ordinal, line, column and operation identifier; each node that is a site ends with its ordinal `#n` and its source position. **3.20 source map**: the sites of every module of a program, each with its ordinal, line, column and operation identifier. The *source-map digest* is its SHA-256 digest (9.2). **3.21 record kind**: whether a fault record is a *run-time* record, produced by an entry, or a *compile-time* record, produced when a constant expression faults during translation. The kind is not in the bytes; the reader of a record knows it from the place the record came from.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 4)
chunks.content: **3.22 execution identity**: the canonical form of the semantic inputs of one entry (9.3).

chunks.title: 4 Conformance
chunks.content:
## 4 Conformance

1. In this document, "shall" states a requirement on an implementation, and "shall not" a prohibition. "May" states a permission.
2. A conforming implementation shall write every encoding that it produces exactly as this document specifies, so that for the same content every conforming implementation writes the same bytes. A structure in memory that holds the same content, such as a C structure of a fault record, is a view of it and is not compared.
3. A conforming decoder shall treat its input as untrusted. It shall reject input that breaks a constraint of this document, it shall check every length and count against the bytes that remain before it allocates memory for what follows, and when it rejects input it shall leave unchanged every state that the input would have changed [IM-148] [SPEC-03P.1 H-19a].
4. Each encoding of clauses 5 to 9 is named by its domain string; the fixture format of Annex B is named CIF-1 and is versioned as B.1 states. An encoding whose layout changes while it carries the same content takes a new version, with its own domain string, and bytes of the earlier version stay readable as that version. A change of the content that an encoding carries for a program, such as a different fault record for the same fault, is a change of the language profile.
5. The bytes of every encoding are the same on every host and every executor. No encoding depends on the host's byte order, word size or alignment or on its clock, locale, file system or environment (9.4).

chunks.title: 5.1 Conventions
chunks.content:
### 5.1 Conventions

Every encoding in this document is built from a few kinds of field, and the same rules of byte order, length and presence apply to all of them.

**Syntax**

| Notation | Bytes |
|---|---|
| `U8`, `U16`, `U32`, `U64` | An unsigned integer of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. |
| `I32`, `I64` | A signed integer of 4 or 8 bytes, in two's complement. |
| `str` | A `U32` length `n`, then `n` bytes. |
| `blob` | A `U64` length `n`, then `n` bytes. |
| `list(x)` | A `U32` count `n`, then `n` fields of the form `x`. |
| `list64(x)` | A `U64` count `n`, then `n` fields of the form `x`. |
| `opt(x)` | A presence byte: `00` alone, or `01` followed by a field of the form `x`. |
| `digest` | 32 bytes, a SHA-256 digest. |
| `"text"` | A `str` whose bytes are the ASCII characters of `text`. |

A layout lists its fields in order, one a line, each with its name, its form and what it holds.

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 5.1 Conventions (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. Every integer of more than one byte, in every encoding, is little-endian: its least significant byte comes first. A signed integer is in two's complement at its width [IM-144] [SPEC-03P.1 M-4]. 2. Every length and every count is written before the bytes or fields it counts. No encoding uses a terminator, a sentinel value or padding [IM-153]. 3. A field that may be absent is preceded by a presence byte. Absence is the byte `00` alone, never a field of zeros or another reserved value. A presence byte other than `00` or `01` is invalid. 4. Each encoding in the table of paragraph 7 begins with its *domain string*: a `str` of lowercase ASCII of the form `//v`, such as `cint-core-1/state/v1`. The last three are the inputs of digests, so the input of every digest of this document begins with one too. The domain string names the encoding and its version, so bytes of two kinds or two versions cannot decode as each other [IM-152]. 5. A quantity that a program sees as an `I64`, the canonical word of SPEC-04P.2 6.3.1, is written as an `I64`, whatever representation an implementation uses for it while a program runs: an array's extent, the capacity of an arena or a pool, a handle's length, a dispatch number, a work-item index, a step ordinal, a fuel quantity and a call-depth limit [SPEC-04P.2 IM-7, IM-8]. The lengths and counts that frame the bytes, those of `str`, `blob`, `list` and `list64`, are unsigned, as the table above gives them. 6. A decoder rejects input that ends before a field is complete, and input with bytes left over after the end of what it decodes [IM-148]. **Semantics** 7. The domain strings of cint 0.2.0 are:

chunks.title: 5.1 Conventions (part 3)
chunks.content:
| Domain string | Encoding | Section |
|---|---|---|
| `cint-core-1/fault/v2` | Fault record, version 2 | 6.1 |
| `cint-core-1/fault/v3` | Fault record, version 3 | 6.3 |
| `cint-core-1/fuel-consumed/v1` | Fuel consumed by a program's entry | 6.5 |
| `cint-core-1/error-result/v1` | Error result of a program's entry | 6.5 |
| `cint-core-1/state/v1` | State | 7.2 |
| `cint-core-1/arena/v2` | Arena block of a state | 7.3 |
| `cint-core-1/pool/v2` | Pool block of a state | 7.3 |
| `cint-core-1/registry/v1` | Registry block of a state | 7.3 |
| `cint-core-1/checkpoint/v1` | Checkpoint, `CINT-CKPT-1` | 7.5 |
| `cint-core-1/recording/v1` | Recording, `CINT-REC-1` | 8.1 |
| `cint-core-1/case/v1` | Case, `CINT-CASE-1` | 8.6 |
| `cint-core-1/recording-chain/v1` | Input of the digest chain | 8.5 |
| `cint-core-1/revision/v1` | Input of the revision identity | 9.1 |
| `cint-core-1/source-map/v1` | Input of the source-map digest | 9.2 |

8. Each encoding of this table is specified at the version that its domain string names, so the checkpoint, the recording and the case of cint 0.2.0 are specified at version 1. A change of an encoding's layout takes a new version, and bytes of the version specified here stay readable as that version (clause 4, paragraph 4).

**Examples**

9. The `I64` value 1000 is the eight bytes `e8 03 00 00 00 00 00 00`, and the `str` holding the text `fuel-v1` is `07 00 00 00 66 75 65 6c 2d 76 31`.

**Notes**

10. Because every count precedes what it counts, a decoder knows the size of each field before it reads it, and can refuse an impossible length before it allocates memory.

chunks.title: 5.2 Integer, Bool and fixed-point payloads
chunks.content: ### 5.2 Integer, Bool and fixed-point payloads The payload of a value is its bytes without a type. Every type that an encoding holds has a payload of fixed size, except the mathematical integers of 5.3. **Syntax** | Type | Payload | |---|---| | `I8`, `I16`, `I32`, `I64` | `w / 8` bytes | | `I128`, `I256`, `I512`, `I1024` | `w / 8` bytes, in limbs of 8 bytes, limb 0 first | | `U8`, `U16`, `U32`, `U64` | `w / 8` bytes | | `U128`, `U256`, `U512` | `w / 8` bytes, in limbs of 8 bytes, limb 0 first | | `Bool` | 1 byte | | `Q.` | the payload of its storage integer, of width `i + f` | **Constraints** 1. A `Bool` payload is `00` for `false` or `01` for `true`; any other byte is invalid [IM-145]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 5.2 Integer, Bool and fixed-point payloads (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. The payload of an integer of width `w` is its `w / 8` bytes, least significant first. A value of a signed type is in two's complement at width `w`, and a value of an unsigned type is its binary representation [IM-145]. 3. A value of a wide type, `I128` to `I1024` or `U128` to `U512`, is made of `w / 64` limbs. Limb 0 holds bits 0 to 63, limb 1 bits 64 to 127 and the last limb the most significant bits, including the sign bit of a signed type. The payload is the limbs in that order, each limb's 8 bytes least significant first, which makes the whole payload little-endian. There is no sign word, no length and no unused limb: every bit pattern is a value, and every value has one payload [IM-12, IM-13]. 4. The payload is the same on every host. At the C interface a wide value is an array of 64-bit limbs in the host's own byte order (SPEC-03P.1); a host whose byte order is big-endian converts each limb when it reads or writes canonical bytes. A type of the C compiler, such as `__int128` or `_BitInt(N)`, never appears in an encoding [IM-14]. 5. The payload of a value of the fixed-point type `Q.` is the payload of its raw value, the integer `v * 2^f`, in its storage type `I8`, `I16`, `I32` or `I64` of width `i + f`. The payload does not say what `f` is; the tag of 5.4 does [IM-145]. **Examples** 6. Payloads of three `I128` values: | Value | Payload | |---|---| | -1 | `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff` | | 1 | `01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | | 2^64 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | 7. The `Q16.16` value 1.5 has the raw value 98304, `0x18000`, so its payload is the `I32` payload `00 80 01 00`.

chunks.title: 5.3 Mathematical integers
chunks.content:
### 5.3 Mathematical integers

A value in Z, such as the exact result of an operation that overflowed, has no fixed width, so its payload begins with its length.

**Syntax**

```text
z:
  length   U32    n, the number of bytes that follow
  bytes    n bytes, the value in two's complement, least significant first
```

**Constraints**

1. The bytes are the shortest two's complement representation of the value: `n` is the least count of bytes whose two's complement range holds it. The value 0 has `n = 0` and no bytes. A payload is therefore invalid when its one byte is `00`, when its last byte is `00` and the byte before it is below `80`, or when its last byte is `ff` and the byte before it is `80` or above [IM-145, IM-148].
2. The bound on `n` depends on the field and the record that hold the value (6.3).

**Examples**

3. Payloads of values in Z:

| Value | Payload |
|---|---|
| 0 | `00 00 00 00` |
| -1 | `01 00 00 00 ff` |
| 127 | `01 00 00 00 7f` |
| 128 | `02 00 00 00 80 00` |
| -128 | `01 00 00 00 80` |
| 9223372036854775808 | `09 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 80 00` |

4. The value 128 needs a second byte: one byte `80` alone would be -128.
5. Adding 1 to the largest `I128` has the exact result 2^127, which needs 128 bits and a sign bit:

```cint w128.ci
I128 a = I128.max;
"{a}\n";
I128 b = a + 1;
```

```text
170141183460469231731687303715884105727
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> w128.ci:3:12
   |
 3 | I128 b = a + 1;
   |            ^ add.checked.i128
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i128
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I128 170141183460469231731687303715884105727
   = operand: I128 1
   = exact:   170141183460469231731687303715884105728
   = limit:   I128 170141183460469231731687303715884105727
   ...
```

chunks.title: 5.3 Mathematical integers (part 2)
chunks.content:
6. In the record of this fault, the operands and the exact result are these bytes, from the operand count on; the tags `15` (`I128`) and `0f` (Z) are those of 5.4:

| Offset | Bytes | Field |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `02 00 00 00` | operand count, 2 |
| 4 | `15 ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff 7f` | first operand, the largest `I128` |
| 21 | `15 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | second operand, 1 |
| 38 | `01` | exact: present |
| 39 | `0f 11 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 80 00` | exact: a Z of 17 bytes, 2^127 |

chunks.title: 5.4 Tagged values
chunks.content:
### 5.4 Tagged values

Where a field can hold values of several types, each value is written with a tag that names its type, followed by its payload.

**Syntax**

| Tag | Type | Bytes after the tag byte | Payload |
|---|---|---|---|
| `01` | `Bool` | none | 5.2 |
| `0f` | Z | none | 5.3 |
| `11` `12` `13` `14` | `I8` `I16` `I32` `I64` | none | 5.2 |
| `15` `16` `17` `18` | `I128` `I256` `I512` `I1024` | none | 5.2 |
| `21` `22` `23` `24` | `U8` `U16` `U32` `U64` | none | 5.2 |
| `25` `26` `27` | `U128` `U256` `U512` | none | 5.2 |
| `31` | `Q<i>.<f>` | the storage tag `U8`, `11` to `14`; then `f` as `U16` | 5.2 |
| `51` | array | the element tag `U8`; the rank `U8`; each extent `I64` | the elements |
| `71` | struct | the definitions and the type, below | the fields |
| `75` | `Handle` | none | 29 bytes, below |

A struct value, which only a global of a state holds (7.2), has this tag:

```text
struct-tag:
  tag          U8              71
  definitions  list(definition)
  type         U8, U32         71 and the index of the last definition
definition:
  tag          U8              71
  name         str             the struct's qualified name, module.Name, UTF-8
  layout       U8              00
  fields       list(field)
field:
  name         str             the field's name, UTF-8
  bit width    U8              00
  type         field-type
field-type:
  scalar       U8              01, 11 to 18, or 21 to 27
  struct       U8, U32         71 and the index of an earlier definition
  array        U8              52, then field-type, the rank U8 (1 to 4),
                               and for each dimension: 01 as U8, ffffffff as U32, the extent I64
```

In an array field-type, `01` is the shape form of a fixed extent and `ffffffff` stands for no size symbol, as in the type signatures of SPEC-03P.1 7.5.

chunks.title: 5.4 Tagged values (part 2)
chunks.content: A handle value, which only a global of a state holds, has this payload: ```text handle: slot U64 length I64 generation U64 container U32 the arena's or pool's identifier kind U8 00 null, 01 arena, 02 pool ``` **Constraints** 1. A tagged value is its tag followed by its payload [IM-147]. 2. In the tag `31` of a fixed-point type, the storage tag is `11`, `12`, `13` or `14` and gives the storage width `w`, and `f` is at most `w - 1`, so that the type has at least one integer bit [IM-146]. 3. In the tag `51` of an array, the element tag is `01`, `11` to `18` or `21` to `27`, the rank is 1 to 8, and each extent is at least 0. The payload is the elements' payloads in row-major order, the last index varying fastest. Its size, the product of the extents and the element size, is at most `I64.max` and equals the bytes that remain for it [IM-146, IM-148]. 4. In a struct tag, each definition lists its fields in declaration order. A field's type that is a struct refers to an earlier definition, so a definition never refers to itself or to one after it. The definitions are in the order in which a depth-first walk of the struct's type completes them, each struct once, and the struct of the value is the last, which the type names. Every name is UTF-8 and not empty [IM-146] [SPEC-03P.1 A-21]. 5. The payload of a struct value is its fields' payloads in declaration order, with no padding: a nested struct's fields in place, and an array field's elements in row-major order. Its size, computed from the definitions, equals the bytes that remain for it [IM-146, IM-148]. 6. In a handle payload the kind is `00`, `01` or `02` and every byte of a handle of kind `00`, the null handle, is `00` [IM-146, IM-148]. 7. Each field that holds a tagged value allows only some tags:

chunks.title: 5.4 Tagged values (part 3)
chunks.content:
| Field | Tags allowed |
|---|---|
| Operand of a fault record (6.1) | `01`, `0f`, `11` to `18`, `21` to `27`, `31` |
| `exact` of a fault record | `0f` |
| `limit` of a fault record | `01`, `0f`, `11` to `18`, `21` to `27`, `31` |
| Value of a global in a state (7.2) | `01`, `11` to `18`, `21` to `27`, `51`, `71`, `75` |
| Argument or result of an entry in a recording (8.4) | `01`, `11` to `14`, `21` to `24` |

   A decoder rejects any other tag in each field [IM-146, IM-148].

**Examples**

8. Tagged values (Annex A.1 has more):

| Value | Tagged bytes |
|---|---|
| `I64` -2 | `14 fe ff ff ff ff ff ff ff` |
| `U8` 255 | `21 ff` |
| `Q16.16` 1.5 | `31 13 10 00 00 80 01 00` |
| Z -1 | `0f 01 00 00 00 ff` |
| `I8[3]` {120, 120, -120} | `51 11 01 03 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 78 78 88` |

9. A module-level struct variable is one global of the state:

```cint sg.ci
struct P { I8 x; Bool b; }
P p = P(x = 5, b = true);

void main() {
    p.x = p.x + 1;
    "{p.x}\n";
}
```

```text
6
```

10. Before `main` runs, the value of the global `sg.p` in the state is these bytes:

| Offset | Bytes | Field |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `71` | tag: struct |
| 1 | `01 00 00 00` | 1 definition |
| 5 | `71` | definition 0 |
| 6 | `04 00 00 00` | name, length 4 |
| 10 | `"sg.P"` | name |
| 14 | `00` | layout |
| 15 | `02 00 00 00` | 2 fields |
| 19 | `01 00 00 00` | field name, length 1 |
| 23 | `"x"` | field name |
| 24 | `00` | bit width |
| 25 | `11` | field type `I8` |
| 26 | `01 00 00 00` | field name, length 1 |
| 30 | `"b"` | field name |
| 31 | `00` | bit width |
| 32 | `01` | field type `Bool` |
| 33 | `71 00 00 00 00` | the type: definition 0 |
| 38 | `05 01` | payload: `x` is 5, `b` is `true` |

**Notes**

11. A struct value carries its own type, with the names of its fields, so a decoder reads it without the program. A struct with nested structs and array fields is in Annex A.2.

chunks.title: 5.5 Decoding values
6.1 Layout
chunks.content:
### 6.1 Layout

The fault record is the canonical form of a fault. SPEC-04P.2 8.1 says what each field means and how a report shows it; this subclause gives its bytes.

**Syntax**

```text
fault-record:
  domain      str              "cint-core-1/fault/v2", or "cint-core-1/fault/v3" (6.3)
  code        U16              the fault code, 1 to 13
  operation   str              the operation identifier, ASCII
  operands    list(tagged)     the operands, in source order
  exact       opt(tagged)      the exact result, a Z
  limit       opt(tagged)      the bound that was crossed
  position    position         the position of the fault
  revision    opt(digest)      the revision of the program (9.1)
  source-map  opt(digest)      the source-map digest (9.2)
  address     opt(address)     the place in a kernel dispatch
  stack       list(position)   the call sites of the active calls, outermost first
position:
  path        str              the module-relative path, UTF-8
  line        U32              from 1
  column      U32              from 1
address:
  kernel      str              the kernel's qualified name, UTF-8
  dispatch    I64              the dispatch number
  phase       U8               0 entry, 1 work-item, 2 epilogue
  work-item   opt(item)        present in phase 1 only
item:
  index       I64              the work-item index
  step        I64              the step ordinal
```

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 6.1 Layout (part 2)
6.1 Layout (part 3)
chunks.content:
```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> kern.ci:2:16
   |
 2 |     next = old + 1;
   |                ^ add.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 9223372036854775807
   = operand: I64 1
   = exact:   9223372036854775808
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   ...
```

11. The record of this fault ends with these bytes, from the address on:

| Offset | Bytes | Field |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `01` | address: present |
| 1 | `09 00 00 00` | kernel, length 9 |
| 5 | `"kern.bump"` | kernel |
| 14 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | dispatch number 0 |
| 22 | `01` | phase 1, work-item |
| 23 | `01` | work item: present |
| 24 | `02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | work-item index 2 |
| 32 | `02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | step ordinal 2 |
| 40 | `01 00 00 00` | stack: 1 position |
| 44 | `07 00 00 00` | path, length 7 |
| 48 | `"kern.ci"` | path |
| 55 | `08 00 00 00` | line number 8 |
| 59 | `05 00 00 00` | column number 5 |

**Notes**

12. No field of a fault record holds a native address, a register, a time, a thread identifier, a backend name or an absolute path, so a fault has the same record on every executor and every host.

chunks.title: 6.2 A worked record
chunks.content:
### 6.2 A worked record

The record of the fault in the Introduction, byte by byte.

**Examples**
