chunks.title: 6.3 Size bounds and version 3
chunks.content: ### 6.3 Size bounds and version 3 Every field of a fault record has a bound, so a decoder can refuse an oversized record before it reads it. The bound on a Z depends on the record's version and kind. **Constraints** 1. In a run-time record of version 2, every Z, whether an operand, `exact` or `limit`, has at most 257 bytes. The largest such value is the 2048-bit product inside a checked `*` or a `muldiv` of `I1024` operands [IM-108]. 2. A compile-time record is of version 2. Its operands may be a Z of up to 513 bytes, which holds the largest integer literal with its sign, and its `exact` a Z of up to 520 bytes, which holds the largest literal scaled to the fixed-point type `Q1.63`. Its `limit` has at most 257 bytes [IM-108, IM-148]. 3. A run-time record whose operation identifier begins with `dot.checked.i1024.` is written in version 3, with the domain string `cint-core-1/fault/v3`. Every other record is written in version 2. Version 3 has the layout of version 2; it differs in its bound alone: every Z of a version 3 record has at most 264 bytes, which holds the exact sum of up to `I64.max` products of two `I1024` values [IM-108, IM-149]. 4. No compile-time record is of version 3 [IM-108, IM-149]. **Notes** 5. Each record thus has exactly one encoding: no record that version 2 can hold is written in version 3.

chunks.title: 6.4 Record kinds and decoding
6.5 Records of fuel consumed and of an error result
chunks.content:
### 6.5 Records of fuel consumed and of an error result

A compiled program run by the `cint` command reports, beside its fault record, the fuel its entry consumed and an error result when `main` returns an error. Each is a small record with its own domain string.

**Syntax**

```text
fuel-record:
  domain      str     "cint-core-1/fuel-consumed/v1"
  consumed    I64     the fuel consumed by the entry, at least 0
error-record:
  domain      str     "cint-core-1/error-result/v1"
  set         str     the error set's qualified name, module.Set
  value       str     the error value's name
  tag type    U32     the tag of the set's tag type, 21 to 24
  tag         U64     the value's tag, from 1
```

**Constraints**

1. A fuel record has exactly 40 bytes. In an error record the tag is at least 1 and fits the tag type, and nothing follows the tag.

**Semantics**

2. A program writes the fuel record when its entry ran, whether it ended normally, with an error result or with a fault. It writes the error record in place of a fault record when `main` returns an error; `cint run` then exits with status 6 (SPEC-06P.1).

**Examples**

3. A `main` that returns an error:

```console
$ cat err.ci
error LedgerError { overdrawn }

LedgerError!void main() {
    "checking\n";
    return LedgerError.overdrawn;
}
$ cint run --cache out-err err.ci
checking
error: err.LedgerError.overdrawn (tag 1)
$ od -An -tx1 -v out-err/*/run-0/fault.bin
 1b 00 00 00 63 69 6e 74 2d 63 6f 72 65 2d 31 2f
 65 72 72 6f 72 2d 72 65 73 75 6c 74 2f 76 31 0f
 00 00 00 65 72 72 2e 4c 65 64 67 65 72 45 72 72
 6f 72 09 00 00 00 6f 76 65 72 64 72 61 77 6e 22
 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
$ od -An -tx1 -v out-err/*/run-0/fuel.bin
 1c 00 00 00 63 69 6e 74 2d 63 6f 72 65 2d 31 2f
 66 75 65 6c 2d 63 6f 6e 73 75 6d 65 64 2f 76 31
 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
```

chunks.title: 6.5 Records of fuel consumed and of an error result (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. The error record names the set `err.LedgerError` and the value `overdrawn`, with the tag type `22`, the tag of `U16` and the tag 1. The fuel record holds the fuel consumed, 1.

chunks.title: 7.1 What state holds
chunks.content: ### 7.1 What state holds The state of a context is everything that one entry leaves for the next. It holds logical values only, so that two executors that agree on a program's meaning write the same state. **Semantics** 1. SPEC-03P.1 5.1 states what the state of a context holds: its program's revision, profile and fuel model, its module-level variables, its arenas, pools and registered buffers, its identifier counters and count of entries begun, the fault record it holds and its count of effects completed. 7.2 to 7.4 give their bytes [SPEC-03P.1 M-3]. 2. State contains logical values only: typed values, declared lengths and logical identifiers. It never contains a native pointer, a device allocation, padding or any other byte that depends on where or how the program runs [IM-151]. 3. A quantity of one entry is not state: the fuel allowance, the fuel consumed, the dispatch counter and the call-depth limit are inputs or results of the entry (8.4), and the local variables of active calls are gone between entries [IM-155]. 4. 7.2 gives the framing of state, its domain strings and its order. The blocks of arenas, pools and the registry (7.3) have their own domain strings, inside that framing [IM-150].

chunks.title: 7.2 State layout
chunks.content:
### 7.2 State layout

**Syntax**

```text
state:
  domain      str              "cint-core-1/state/v1"
  revision    digest           the revision of the program (9.1)
  profile     str              "cint-core-1"
  globals     list64(global)   sorted by the bytes of their names
  arenas      blob             the arena block (7.3), or empty
  pools       blob             the pool block (7.3), or empty
  registry    blob             the registry block (7.3), or empty
  next-buffer U64              the next buffer identifier
  next-arena  U64              the next arena identifier
  next-pool   U64              the next pool identifier
  entries     U64              the entry sequence number
  fuel-model  str              "fuel-v1"
  fault       opt(fault-record)  the fault record held (6.1)
  effects     I64              the effect-log position
global:
  name        str              the qualified name, module.name, UTF-8
  value       tagged           its value (5.4)
```

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 7.2 State layout (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The globals are sorted by the bytes of their names, each name strictly after the one before it; a name is not empty and is UTF-8 [IM-156]. 2. A module-level variable of an integer or `Bool` type is a global whose value has that type's tag. A module-level array is one global whose value is an array (tag `51`) with its elements in row-major order. A module-level struct variable is one global whose value has the struct tag `71`, with its type and its payload. A module-level `Handle` is one global whose value has the handle tag `75` [IM-156]. 3. Each of the arena, pool and registry blocks is a `blob`. Its length is 0 when the state has no arena, pool or registered buffer; an arena or pool block stays empty until the first operation on an arena or a pool [IM-156]. 4. The fault record is a run-time record, bounded as such (6.3) [IM-156]. 5. Each identifier counter is greater than every identifier of its kind in the state. The next buffer identifier is at least 1, and the next arena and pool identifiers are at most 2^32 [IM-156] [SPEC-03P.1 H-19a]. 6. The effect-log position is at least 0, and nothing follows it [IM-156] [SPEC-03P.1 H-19a]. **Semantics** 7. The entry sequence number counts the entries begun in the context. The effect-log position counts the effects completed; clearing a held fault changes neither [IM-156]. 8. The fault record held in state carries its own domain string, so the version of its encoding is visible inside the state bytes [IM-156]. **Examples** 9. The case that `cint debug locate` saves for `ledger.ci` (8.6) begins with a checkpoint of the state before `main` runs. Its state, from the domain string on, is these 182 bytes:

chunks.content:
| Offset | Bytes | Field |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `14 00 00 00` | domain string, length 20 |
| 4 | `"cint-core-1/state/v1"` | domain string |
| 24 | (32 bytes) | revision |
| 56 | `0b 00 00 00` | profile, length 11 |
| 60 | `"cint-core-1"` | profile |
| 71 | `01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | 1 global |
| 79 | `0e 00 00 00` | name, length 14 |
| 83 | `"ledger.balance"` | name |
| 97 | `14 64 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | value: `I64` 100 |
| 106 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | arena block: empty |
| 114 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | pool block: empty |
| 122 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | registry block: empty |
| 130 | `01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | next buffer identifier 1 |
| 138 | `01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | next arena identifier 1 |
| 146 | `01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | next pool identifier 1 |
| 154 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | entry sequence number 0 |
| 162 | `07 00 00 00` | fuel model, length 7 |
| 166 | `"fuel-v1"` | fuel model |

| 174 | `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | effect-log position 0 |

chunks.title: 7.3 Arena, pool and registry blocks
chunks.content:
### 7.3 Arena, pool and registry blocks

Each block holds one kind of storage of the context and begins with its own domain string.

**Syntax**

chunks.title: 7.3 Arena, pool and registry blocks (part 2)
chunks.content:
```text
arena-block:
  domain      str              "cint-core-1/arena/v2"
  rows        list64(arena)    by identifier, at least 1
  contents    for each module-level arena, in order of its row:
                element type (7.4), then its used elements
arena:
  id          U32              from 1
  parent      U32              the parent's identifier, 0 for a module-level arena
  retired     U8               0 or 1
  offset      I64              the offset in the parent, in elements
  capacity    I64              in elements
  used        I64              the used extent, in elements
  generation  U64
pool-block:
  domain      str              "cint-core-1/pool/v2"
  pools       list64(pool)     at least 1
pool:
  id          U32              its position in the list, from 1
  type        element type (7.4)
  capacity    I64              in slots
  used        U64              the number of slots ever taken
  top         U64              the first slot of the free list, plus 1; 0 when the list is empty
  slots       used times slot
  elements    the payload of each occupied slot's element, in slot order
slot:
  generation  U64
  mark        U8               0 vacant, 1 occupied, 2 retired
  below       U64              the next slot of the free list, plus 1; 0 at its end
registry-block:
  domain      str              "cint-core-1/registry/v1"
  entries     list64(entry)    by identifier, at least 1
entry:
  id          U64
  generation  U64
  origin      U8               1 borrowed, 2 bridge
  element     U16              the element type's tag, or 0
  storage     U8               0
  frac        U16              0
  record      U32              the struct's number, for a struct element; 0 otherwise
  extent      I64
  ceiling     U8               0 read, 1 write: the widest access a view of it may have
  publish     U8               0 none, 1 copy: whether a kernel

chunks.title: 7.3 Arena, pool and registry blocks (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Constraints**

1. An arena row has 41 bytes. Its identifier is at least 1, its retired byte is 0 or 1, its capacity and used extent are at least 0 with the used extent at most the capacity, and its generation is at most 2^64 - 2 [SPEC-03P.1 H-19a].
2. The rows are in increasing order of identifier. The module-level arenas come first, with identifiers 1 to `n`, not retired and at offset 0. A child arena's parent is an earlier row; the child lies within its parent's capacity, and, unless retired, within its parent's used extent; a child of a retired arena is retired [SPEC-03P.1 H-19a].
3. The element type of each module-level arena is followed by exactly its used elements, and the block ends after the last of them [SPEC-03P.1 M-3, H-19a].
4. Each pool's identifier is its position in the list, from 1, and there are fewer than 2^32 pools. A pool's used slots are at most its capacity. A slot has 17 bytes: a retired slot has the generation 2^64 - 2, a vacant slot a generation of at least 1, every generation is at most 2^64 - 2, and a slot that is not vacant has `below` 0. Starting at `top`, the free list visits every vacant slot exactly once and no other slot. The elements of the occupied slots follow the slots, and the block ends after the last pool [SPEC-03P.1 M-3, H-19a].
5. A registry entry has 37 bytes. The identifiers are at least 1 and increase; a generation is 1 to 2^64 - 2; the origin is 1 or 2; the storage, `frac` and state bytes are 0; `record` is 0 unless the element is a struct; the extent is at least 0; and the element, ceiling and publish fields hold values that SPEC-03P.1 6.1 defines for a registration: the element is 0 only for a borrowed buffer, the ceiling is 0 or 1, and the publish byte is 0 or 1, and 1 only when the ceiling is 1. An entry holds no contents [SPEC-03P.1 M-3, H-19a].

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.3 Arena, pool and registry blocks (part 4)
chunks.content: 6. The registry block lists the buffers that a host program has lent to the context (SPEC-03P.1). A context that only runs its program has none.

chunks.title: 7.4 Element types
chunks.content:
### 7.4 Element types

An arena or a pool holds elements of one type, which the block writes once, with the size of one element, so that a decoder can step through the elements without the program.

**Syntax**

```text
element-type:
  width        U32              the bytes of one element's payload
  definitions  list(definition) as in a struct tag (5.4)
  type         field-type       a scalar tag, 75, or 71 and the last definition's index
```

**Constraints**

1. With no definitions, the type is a scalar tag or `75`, and the width is the size of that type's payload. With definitions, the type is `71` and the index of the last definition, and the definitions follow the constraints of a struct tag, except that an array field has rank 1 [SPEC-03P.1 M-3, A-21, H-19a].

**Examples**

2. The element type of an arena of `I32` is `04 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 13`: width 4, no definitions, the tag of `I32`. Annex A.3 shows a whole arena block and pool block.

chunks.title: 7.5 Checkpoints
chunks.content:
### 7.5 Checkpoints

A checkpoint is a state in an envelope. The envelope is not hashed: it names the runtime contract under which the state was taken.

**Syntax**

```text
checkpoint:
  domain       str            "cint-core-1/checkpoint/v1"
  contract     str            the runtime contract version, "cint-rt-3"
  payload      opt(digest)    absent
  build-record opt(digest)    absent
  build        opt(digest)    absent
  state        blob           the state (7.2)
```

**Constraints**

1. The runtime contract version has 1 to 64 bytes, each a printable ASCII character from `21` to `7e`. The length of the state equals the bytes that remain, and the state's bytes are exactly one state [SPEC-03P.1 H-19, H-19a].
2. cint 0.2.0 writes the payload digest, the build record digest and the build identity as absent [SPEC-03P.1 H-15, H-19].

**Semantics**

3. The format is `CINT-CKPT-1`. A checkpoint is the bytes that a host program receives when it checkpoints a context (SPEC-03P.1), and that a workbench session saves for each of its checkpoints (SPEC-06P.1) [SPEC-03P.1 H-19].

**Examples**

4. The checkpoint at the start of the case of `ledger.ci` has 235 bytes: this envelope, then the 182 bytes of state of 7.2.

| Offset | Bytes | Field |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `19 00 00 00` | domain string, length 25 |
| 4 | `"cint-core-1/checkpoint/v1"` | domain string |
| 29 | `09 00 00 00` | runtime contract, length 9 |
| 33 | `"cint-rt-3"` | runtime contract |
| 42 | `00` | payload digest: absent |
| 43 | `00` | build record digest: absent |
| 44 | `00` | build identity: absent |
| 45 | `b6 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | state, length 182 |
| 53 | (182 bytes) | state (7.2) |

chunks.title: 7.6 State hash
chunks.content: ### 7.6 State hash **Semantics** 1. The state hash of a context is `SHA-256` of its state bytes, from the length of the state's domain string through the effect-log position, as 7.2 lays them out. The envelope of a checkpoint is not part of it [IM-154] [SPEC-03P.1 M-5]. 2. An implementation computes SHA-256 itself, and the conformance suite checks it against the digests of fixed inputs; the SHA-256 of the empty input, for example, is `e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855` [IM-154]. 3. State hashes are compared only between states of one runtime contract version. The revision is part of the state, and the revision changes with the runtime contract version (9.1), so rebuilding an unchanged program against another version changes its state hash [IM-156] [SPEC-03P.1 H-15]. **Notes** 4. The fault record held in state is part of the hashed bytes, and its position is part of the record. Moving a faulting line therefore changes the state hash of the faulted state, though the revision stays the same (9.4).

chunks.title: 7.7 Restoring a checkpoint
chunks.content:
### 7.7 Restoring a checkpoint

A restore replaces the state of a context with the state of a checkpoint. Checkpoint bytes are untrusted input, so a restore checks everything before it changes anything.

**Constraints**

1. A restore refuses a checkpoint whose runtime contract version or revision is not exactly the context's; SPEC-03P.1 9.2 states the rule [SPEC-03P.1 H-19].
2. Before it changes any state, a restore checks every constraint of clauses 5 and 7 that the bytes alone can break, and then, against the program, the following; a checkpoint that fails a check is refused, and the context is left exactly as it was [SPEC-03P.1 H-19a]:
   - the globals are exactly the program's module-level variables, each with the same qualified name and the same type;
   - the module-level arenas and pools are exactly those that the program declares, each with the same element type;
   - every struct number of the registry names a struct of the program;
   - a held fault record has a position that names a site of the program.

**Semantics**

3. A restore sets each identifier counter as SPEC-03P.1 6.1 states, so that no identifier is issued twice in a context's lifetime; a recording records the counters it chose (8.4) [SPEC-03P.1 M-11].

chunks.title: 8.1 The recording file
chunks.content:
### 8.1 The recording file

A recording holds the program's identity and code, a checkpoint of the context when recording began, and the events that followed. With them, the entries run in a context can be replayed and each step compared with what happened.

**Syntax**

```text
recording:
  header       header (8.2)     the domain string "cint-core-1/recording/v1", or "cint-core-1/case/v1"
  code         code (8.3)
  initial      blob             a checkpoint (7.5) of the context when recording began
  events       event (8.4)      one or more, the end event last
```

**Constraints**

1. The initial checkpoint is a valid checkpoint whose revision is the revision of the header. The last event is the end event, and no byte follows it [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].

**Semantics**

2. The format is `CINT-REC-1`. A host program makes a recording through a recorder (SPEC-03P.1); `cint workbench` records every session; `cint debug locate` saves a case (8.6) [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].

chunks.title: 8.2 Header
chunks.content: ### 8.2 Header **Syntax** ```text header: domain str "cint-core-1/recording/v1", or "cint-core-1/case/v1" profile str "cint-core-1" fuel-model str "fuel-v1" contract str the runtime contract version revision digest the revision of the code (9.1) source-map opt(digest) the source-map digest of the code (9.2) mode U8 0 full, 1 digest interval U64 1 density U8 0 entry, 1 dispatch ``` **Constraints** 1. The runtime contract version has 1 to 64 bytes from `21` to `7e`. The mode is 0 or 1, the interval is 1, and the density is 0 or 1 [H-14a] [SPEC-03P.1 H-14]. 2. The source-map digest is present exactly when the code gives one (9.2), and it equals the digest of the code [SPEC-03P.1 H-14]. **Semantics** 3. The interval 1 means that the state hash of every entry is recorded. At entry density the boundaries are the ends of entries; at dispatch density each dispatch of a kernel is a boundary too [H-14a] [SPEC-03P.1 H-14]. 4. In cint 0.2.0 a recording in digest mode differs from one in full mode only in its mode byte. **Examples** 5. The header of the case of `ledger.ci`, through the module count of its code:

chunks.title: 8.2 Header (part 2)
chunks.content:
| Offset | Bytes | Field |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `13 00 00 00` | domain string, length 19 |
| 4 | `"cint-core-1/case/v1"` | domain string |
| 23 | `0b 00 00 00` | profile, length 11 |
| 27 | `"cint-core-1"` | profile |
| 38 | `07 00 00 00` | fuel model, length 7 |
| 42 | `"fuel-v1"` | fuel model |
| 49 | `09 00 00 00` | runtime contract, length 9 |
| 53 | `"cint-rt-3"` | runtime contract |
| 62 | (32 bytes) | revision |
| 94 | `01` | source-map digest: present |
| 95 | (32 bytes) | source-map digest |
| 127 | `00` | mode: full |
| 128 | `01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | interval 1 |
| 136 | `00` | density: entry |
| 137 | `01 00 00 00` | code: 1 module |

chunks.title: 8.3 Code
chunks.content:
### 8.3 Code

A recording carries the code it ran, so a replay needs no other file and reproduces every fault record byte for byte.

**Syntax**

```text
code:
  modules      list(module)
module:
  path         str              the module-relative path, ending in ".ci"
  sir          blob             the module's SIR text, with its sites line
  source       opt(blob)        the module's source text
```

**Constraints**

1. Each path has 4 to 1024 bytes of UTF-8 and ends in `.ci` [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].

**Semantics**

2. The code holds every module of the program: the root module and every module it imports. Each module's SIR text is the one from which the revision (9.1) and the source-map digest (9.2) are computed. A module's source text is present when the host supplied it, and in every module of a case [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].

chunks.title: 8.4 Events
chunks.content:
### 8.4 Events

Each event is one byte that gives its kind, followed by its fields.

**Syntax**

chunks.title: 8.4 Events (part 2)
chunks.content:
```text
event 1, entry:
  sequence     U64              the entry sequence number, from 1
  form         U8               0 an exported function, 1 the program entry
  module       str              the path of the function's module; empty for the program entry
  function     str              the function's name; empty for the program entry
  arguments    list(tagged)     at most 16; none for the program entry
  fuel         I64              the fuel budget, or -1 for no budget
  depth        I64              the call-depth limit, at least 1
  frame-arena  I64              the frame-arena capacity, at least 0
  inputs       U32              0
event 2, effect:
  ordinal      I64              the effect-log position of the effect, from 0
  site         U32, U32         the module's number in the program and the site's ordinal
  name         str              "print"
  status       I32              the status that the host returned
  request      blob             the bytes printed
event 3, outcome:
  status       I32              0 to 5
  fault        opt(str)         the fault record, as a length and its bytes
  consumed     I64              the fuel consumed, 0 when the entry did not run
  result       opt(tagged)      the value returned
  error        opt(error)       the error returned
  outputs      U32              0
  state-hash   opt(digest)      the state hash after the entry
  allowance    I64              the fuel allowance at the end, or -1 for none
error:
  set          str              the error set's qualified name
  tag          U64              the error value's tag, from 1
event 4, clear:
  record       digest           SHA-256 of the fault record cleared
event 5, checkpoint:
  state-hash   digest           the state hash of the checkpoint taken
event 6, restore:
  state-hash   digest           the state hash of the checkpoint restored
  next-buffer  U64

chunks.title: 8.4 Events (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Constraints**

1. Events come in this order: an entry, then its effects and dispatch events in the order they happened, then its outcome. Effect, dispatch and outcome events occur only inside an entry, and the other events only outside one. A dispatch event occurs only at dispatch density [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].
2. In an entry event, the program entry has an empty module, an empty function and no arguments. Arguments are values of `Bool`, `I8` to `I64` or `U8` to `U64` [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].
3. The statuses of an outcome are 0 `CINT_OK` and 1 `CINT_FAULT`, for an entry that ran, and 2 `CINT_REFUSED`, 3 `CINT_BUSY`, 4 `CINT_FAULTED` and 5 `CINT_RESOURCE`, for one that did not. An outcome fits its entry [SPEC-03P.1 H-14]:
   - for an entry that ran, the state hash is present; the fault record is present exactly when the status is 1; a result and an error are never both present, and neither is present with status 1; the allowance is the entry's fuel budget, or a lower budget of at least 0 that an interrupt set; and the fuel consumed is at most the allowance when the allowance is not -1;
   - for an entry that did not run, the state hash, the result and the error are absent, the fuel consumed is 0, the allowance is the entry's fuel budget, and a fault record is present only with status 5.
4. After an outcome with status 5 the next event is the end, with reason 1, and an end with reason 1 occurs only there [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].
5. A restore event's state hash is the state hash of its checkpoint, and each counter it records is at least the checkpoint's [SPEC-03P.1 H-14, M-11].
6. The count of the end event equals the number of events before it [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 8.4 Events (part 4)
chunks.content:
7. An effect's request is the bytes that its print statement wrote. The concatenation of the requests of an entry's effects is what the entry printed, including the bytes printed before a fault [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].
8. A revision event records a change of the context's program to another revision between entries, with that revision's code, so that a replay applies it [SPEC-03P.1 H-14, H-19b].

**Examples**

9. The events of the case of `ledger.ci`: the program entry, its one print and its outcome, a fault; then the end. The 151 bytes of the fault record are those of 6.2.

chunks.title: 8.5 Digest chain
chunks.content:
### 8.5 Digest chain

The digest chain folds the state hash of every boundary into one digest, so that two recordings with equal chains passed through equal states with equal fault records.

**Syntax**

```text
D_0 = SHA-256( "cint-core-1/recording-chain/v1", the state hash of the initial checkpoint )
D_k = SHA-256( "cint-core-1/recording-chain/v1", D_(k-1), boundary_k )
boundary:
  entry        U64              the index of the boundary's entry event, counting events from 0
  kind         U8               0 the end of an entry, 1 a dispatch
  dispatch     opt(I64)         the dispatch number
  state-hash   digest           the state hash at the boundary
  fault        opt(str)         the fault record, as a length and its bytes
```

The domain string enters each digest as a `str`, its length then its bytes.

**Constraints**

1. Each entry that ran, with status 0 or 1, adds one boundary of kind 0 at its outcome, with the outcome's state hash and fault record. An entry that did not run adds none.
2. A dispatch event adds a boundary of kind 1 with its number and state hash and no fault record, unless the outcome of its entry follows it directly with the same state hash. That outcome's boundary of kind 0 then carries the dispatch number, and the dispatch adds no boundary of its own.
3. The head of the chain is the last `D_k`, and the end event holds it.

**Notes**

4. The chain detects a difference at a boundary. A difference that appears and disappears between two boundaries leaves the chain unchanged. Annex A.4 recomputes the chain of the case of `ledger.ci`.

chunks.title: 8.6 Cases
chunks.content:
### 8.6 Cases

A case is a recording that carries its program's source text, so that the debug tools can show the source of every position in it.

**Constraints**

1. A case has the domain string `cint-core-1/case/v1` and is in full mode, and every module of its code, and of the code of each revision event, has its source text. A decoder refuses a case without one, or in digest mode [SPEC-03P.1 H-14b].

**Semantics**

2. The format is `CINT-CASE-1`. Apart from its domain string, a case is laid out as a recording [SPEC-03P.1 H-14b].

**Examples**

3. `cint debug locate` runs a program on the interpreter and saves the run as a case. `cint debug replay` decodes the case, replays it, compares each boundary with the recording and prints the case's revision, its source-map digest, the head of its digest chain and the final state hash:

```console
$ cint debug locate ledger.ci --save-case ledger.case --out dbg
program    ledger.ci   evaluator cpu-sir-interp, recorded as the case ledger.case
target     boundary 1 of 1, the program entry: the first fault, reproduced by replay
...
$ cint debug replay ledger.case
case       ledger.case   1 boundary   3 events   mode full   density entry
revision   359672553c501187e1e53e4878d6ede8f1994b52ce0c64c8f3ec4fbdf3f9b3db
source-map 8c97a22e8332385f6b94e1782030208003280b8e6859b1775f2a93caa402e87e
boundary  event  entry                          outcome                  fuel
       1      2  the program entry              faulted E_NARROW         3
replay     ok, 1 of 1 boundary compared with the recording
chain      e54344d0fb4bcc2af778845380e8b60127eb639189fad8b9df78e45b60c34795
state      6699607c6fabf35dc4931ef60208e1fdf6cde9838caf325470be34ce0807a279
```

chunks.title: 8.6 Cases (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. The revision is the one in the report of 6.2, recomputed by the interpreter from the SIR text in the case. The chain line is the head of the digest chain, and the state line the state hash after the entry, both as the end and outcome events of 8.4 hold them.

chunks.title: 8.7 Decoding a recording
9.1 Revision identity
chunks.content: ### 9.1 Revision identity The revision identity of a program names its meaning under one runtime contract. It is computed from the program's SIR text with every source position removed, so it changes when the program's operations change and not when only their positions do. **Syntax** ```text revision = SHA-256( "cint-core-1/revision/v1" str "cint-core-1" str, the profile contract str, the runtime contract version modules U32, the number of modules for each module, in the byte order of its path: path str, the module-relative path, UTF-8 text blob, the module's position-free SIR text ) ``` **Semantics** 1. The *position-free SIR text* of a module is its SIR text with its `sites` line and every position annotation removed, and its site ordinals kept; SPEC-09P.1 6.5 states the rule [SPEC-09P.1 SIR-17]. 2. The revision of a program is the digest above, over the root module and every module it imports. It is computed over the program's meaning, not over its source formatting, and not over an executable or a kernel binary [IM-157] [SPEC-09P.1 SIR-17]. 3. This one value is the revision of fault records (6.1), of state (7.2), of checkpoints and of recordings and cases (8.2). There is no second digest of a program's code [IM-157] [SPEC-03P.1 H-15]. 4. The runtime contract version is an input: rebuilding an unchanged program against another runtime contract version changes its revision, and so the state hash of each of its states [IM-157] [SPEC-03P.1 H-15]. 5. The fuel model is not an input of the revision; it is a separate input of execution identity (9.3) [SPEC-09P.1 SIR-17]. **Notes**

chunks.title: 9.1 Revision identity (part 2)
chunks.content: 6. Adding a comment, a blank line or a space or moving a function, changes positions and leaves the revision unchanged. Reordering two statements, or adding an operation that can fault, changes the site ordinals and therefore the revision.

chunks.title: 9.2 Source-map digest
chunks.content:
### 9.2 Source-map digest

The source-map digest records the positions that the revision leaves out: with it, a site ordinal in a recording can be traced to a line and column.

**Semantics**

1. The source-map digest of a program is a SHA-256 digest over the `sites` line of each module's SIR text, which lists every site's ordinal, line, column and operation; SPEC-09P.1 6.5 states the rule and its bytes [SPEC-09P.1 SIR-17].
2. Every executor computes the source-map digest from the same SIR text, so every executor gets the same value. A recording holds it in its header and in each revision event (8.2) [SPEC-09P.1 SIR-17].

chunks.title: 9.3 Execution identity
chunks.content:
### 9.3 Execution identity

The execution identity of an entry is the canonical form of everything that decides its outcome.

**Semantics**

1. The execution identity of an entry is the tuple of its semantic inputs, from the profile and the fuel model to its frame-arena capacity; SPEC-04P.2 8.2 states the rule [SPEC-04P.2 IM-159].
2. A recording holds each of these in canonical form: the header holds the profile, the fuel model, the revision and the source-map digest; the entry event holds the entry, its arguments as tagged values and its three limits; the state hash before the entry is the state hash of the boundary or checkpoint before it; and each effect event holds the status that the host supplied for the effect [SPEC-04P.2 IM-159] [SPEC-03P.1 H-14].
3. SPEC-04P.2 8.2 states what two entries with equal execution identity agree on: their output, their fault record, their fuel consumed and the state they leave.

chunks.title: 10 Future directions
chunks.content:
## 10 Future directions

This clause is informative. It lists encodings that the design of cint names and that cint 0.2.0 does not write; none of them is a rule of this edition.

1. **Arguments and supplied effects as digests.** An entry's arguments, with the full contents of any array a host lends, encoded under `cint-core-1/args/v1` and hashed, and a digest of what the host supplied to the entry, so that an execution identity is a short tuple of digests.
2. **View identities in fault records.** A tag for the identity of a view, with its buffer, generation, shape, strides and permission and none of its contents, so that the record of a reduction can name the view it read.
3. **Fixed-point globals.** A module-level variable of a fixed-point type as a global of state, with the tag `31`.
4. **Build digests.** The payload digest, the build record digest and the build identity of a checkpoint's envelope and of a recording, written and checked.
5. **Fuller recordings.** Digest mode that records digests of the contents of lent buffers instead of the contents; input and output records; registration and release events; a state-hash interval above 1.
6. **A tree state hash.** A state hash built from digests of fixed-size chunks of each buffer, so that a device can hash its own memory and transfer only digests.
7. **Migrations.** A checkpoint restored into another revision of its program through a migration that the program declares, recorded as an event.
8. **`U1024`.** An unsigned 1024-bit type, with its own tag.

chunks.title: A.4 Recomputing the digest chain
chunks.content:
### A.4 Recomputing the digest chain

1. This Python program reads a case or a recording at entry density whose entries all ran, recomputes its digest chain from the rules of 8.5, and prints the head:

```python chain.py
import hashlib, struct, sys

def u(d, at, n): return int.from_bytes(d[at:at + n], "little"), at + n
def s(d, at): n, at = u(d, at, 4); return d[at:at + n], at + n
def b(d, at): n, at = u(d, at, 8); return d[at:at + n], at + n
def frame(t): return struct.pack("<I", len(t)) + t
DOMAIN = frame(b"cint-core-1/recording-chain/v1")

chunks.title: A.4 Recomputing the digest chain (part 2)
chunks.content:
d = open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read()
at = 0
for _ in range(4): _, at = s(d, at)        # domain, profile, fuel model, contract
at += 32                                    # revision
at += 1 + 32 * d[at]                        # source-map digest
at += 1 + 8 + 1                             # mode, interval, density
mods, at = u(d, at, 4)
for _ in range(mods):
    _, at = s(d, at)
    _, at = b(d, at)
    at += 1 + (8 + u(d, at + 1, 8)[0] if d[at] else 0)
ckpt, at = b(d, at)
c = 4 + len(b"cint-core-1/checkpoint/v1")
_, c = s(ckpt, c)
c += 3                                      # three absent digests
state, c = b(ckpt, c)
chain = hashlib.sha256(DOMAIN + hashlib.sha256(state).digest()).digest()
index = entry = 0
while True:
    kind = d[at]; at += 1
    if kind == 1:
        entry = index
        at += 8 + 1
        _, at = s(d, at); _, at = s(d, at)
        n, at = u(d, at, 4)
        assert n == 0
        at += 24 + 4
    elif kind == 2:
        at += 8 + 8
        _, at = s(d, at)
        at += 4
        _, at = b(d, at)
    elif kind == 3:
        at += 4
        fault = None
        if d[at]:
            fault, at = s(d, at + 1)
        else:
            at += 1
        at += 8 + 1 + 1 + 4
        assert d[at] == 1
        h = d[at + 1:at + 33]; at += 33 + 8
        rec = struct.pack("<Q", entry) + b"\x00\x00" + h
        rec += b"\x00" if fault is None else b"\x01" + frame(fault)
        chain = hashlib.sha256(DOMAIN + chain + rec).digest()
    elif kind == 8:
        assert d[at + 1:at + 33] == chain
        break
    index += 1
print(chain.hex())
```

2. On the case of 8.6 it prints the chain that `cint debug replay` prints:

```console
$ python3 chain.py ledger.case
e54344d0fb4bcc2af778845380e8b60127eb639189fad8b9df78e45b60c34795
```

chunks.title: Annex B (normative) Operation fixtures, CIF-1
chunks.content: ## Annex B (normative) Operation fixtures, CIF-1

chunks.title: B.1 Format
chunks.content: ### B.1 Format An operation fixture tests one operation on given operands, with no program around it. A file of fixtures in the format CIF-1 lists them, one a line. **Syntax** | Key | Content | |---|---| | `id` | The fixture's identifier, unique in its file, such as `div.checked.i64.007`. | | `status` | `"S"`. | | `op` | The operation identifier, with its rounding mode when the operation rounds. | | `args` | An array of typed values, the operands in order. | | `expect` | Exactly one of `{"value": typed value}`, `{"fault": fault}`, `{"compile_error": code}` and `{"reject": true}`. | | `derivation` | Optional: a string that says how the expected result was derived. | A typed value is `{"t": type, "v": integer}`, such as `{"t": "I64", "v": "-7"}`; a fixed-point value is `{"t": type, "raw": integer}`, its raw value, such as `{"t": "Q16.16", "raw": "98304"}`; an array is `{"t": "I8[3]", "v": ["120", "120", "-120"]}`. A fault is an object with the key `code` and, when the fixture asserts them, `exact`, `limit`, `index` and `operands`. **Constraints** 1. A CIF-1 file is JSON Lines: UTF-8, one JSON object a line, each line ended by a line feed, with the keys in the order of the table [IM-168]. 2. Every integer is a JSON string of decimal digits with an optional leading `-`, so that no JSON reader loses precision; RFC 8259 notes that JSON numbers are interchangeable exactly only between -(2^53 - 1) and 2^53 - 1 [IM-168]. 3. A fault object has `code` and, when the record has them, `exact`, `limit`, `index` (for `fold_checked`) and `operands` (an array of typed values) [IM-169]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: B.1 Format (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. Each fixture maps to a program: one that declares the operands with their types, applies the operation once, and whose expected outcome has the same operation identifier, fault code, operands, `exact` and `limit` [IM-167]. 5. A fixture is frozen once published. A change of meaning takes a new group of fixtures under a new profile, never an edit; a change of encoding with the same content takes a new version of the format, and fixtures of the old version stay valid in it [IM-170]. 6. Every implementation, the reference included, produces the expected result of every fixture. The reference computes in Python with exact integers and fractions and shares no code with the C implementation [IM-170]. **Examples** 7. Four fixtures, the third of fixed point and the fourth of `fold_checked`, which faults at index 1 when the running sum 120 + 120 leaves `I8`: ```console $ cat sample.cif1.jsonl {"id":"add.checked.i64.001","status":"S","op":"add.checked.i64","args":[{"t":"I64","v":"9223372036854775807"},{"t":"I64","v":"1"}],"expect":{"fault":{"code":"E_OVERFLOW","exact":"9223372036854775808","limit":"9223372036854775807"}}} {"id":"rem.checked.i64.003","status":"S","op":"rem.checked.i64","args":[{"t":"I64","v":"7"},{"t":"I64","v":"-2"}],"expect":{"value":{"t":"I64","v":"-1"}}} {"id":"mul.checked.q16_16.002","status":"S","op":"mul.checked.q16_16.half_even","args":[{"t":"Q16.16","raw":"1"},{"t":"Q16.16","raw":"98304"}],"expect":{"value":{"t":"Q16.16","raw":"2"}}} {"id":"fold_checked.add.i8.001","status":"S","op":"fold_checked.add.i8","args":[{"t":"I8","v":"0"},{"t":"I8[3]","v":["120","120","-120"]}],"expect":{"fault":{"code":"E_OVERFLOW","exact":"240","limit":"127","index":"1"}}} $ python3 -m cint_ref cif1 sample.cif1.jsonl cif1: 4 records, 4 agree, 0 disagree, 0 unsupported, 0 invalid ```

chunks.title: B.1 Format (part 3)
chunks.content: 8. The remainder of 7 by -2 is -1, because `%` takes the quotient rounded toward negative infinity (SPEC-04P.2 6.7.7). The `Q16.16` values 2^-16 (raw 1) and 1.5 (raw 98304) have the product 1.5 times 2^-16, the raw value 1.5, which rounds half to even to the raw value 2.

chunks.title: Annex C (informative) Clause index

chunks.title: SPEC-02P.1
chunks.content:
# SPEC-02P.1: Kernels and executors

SPEC-02P.1, edition 1 of the kernels and executors specification, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

chunks.title: Foreword
chunks.content:
## Foreword

This document specifies what an executor of cint 0.2.0 does to carry out a kernel dispatch, and how each of the three executors of that release does it. It is the companion of SPEC-04P.2, whose clause 6.13 states what a kernel and a dispatch mean to a program.

Each rule ends with one or more clause identifiers in brackets. An identifier, such as F-5 or B-16a, names one rule across editions and documents: a rule keeps its identifier when its text moves to another section or another document, and an identifier is never reused. Code comments, test files and other documents cite rules by these identifiers. Identifiers that begin with `A`, `P` or `X` name rules of kernels, here and in SPEC-04P.2; in SPEC-03P.1 the same letters name rules of the host interface, which are other rules. A rule that another edition states is cited in brackets with that edition's name, such as [SPEC-04P.2 X-1]: the rule is stated there, and this document says what an executor does to keep it. Section numbers belong to this edition only.

chunks.title: Introduction
Introduction (part 2)
chunks.content: In the second dispatch, work-items 1 and 3 both overflow. The fault reported is the one at the lower work-item, 1, whichever an executor meets first. Its address names the kernel `scale` of module `scale`, the second dispatch of the entry (numbered from 0), the work-item phase, work-item 1 and step 2: the place `b[i]` is step 0, the read `a[i]` step 1 and the product step 2. Nothing of the faulted dispatch is published, so `b` still holds `3 -6 9 12`. Every executor of cint 0.2.0 is required to report this same record (clause 4).

chunks.title: How this document is organized
chunks.content:
### How this document is organized

Clauses 1 to 4 give the scope, the references, the terms and what conformance means. Clause 5 describes a dispatch: its phases, its number, the checks it makes before any work-item runs, the step ordinal, and the choice and content of the fault it reports. Clause 6 gives the test that decides whether the arguments of a dispatch may overlap. Clause 7 states how outputs are held back until a dispatch succeeds. Clause 8 states how a work-item is evaluated and charged fuel, and clause 9 how reductions are computed so that their results do not depend on the order of evaluation. Clause 10 states the obligations of every executor and describes `cpu-c17`, `cpu-sir-interp` and `gpu-cuda`. Clause 11 works one kernel through the rules on all three. Clause 12 lists directions that cint 0.2.0 does not implement.

Subclauses follow the shape of SPEC-04P.2: a summary, then **Semantics**, **Faults**, **Examples** and **Notes** as a subclause needs them. Examples and notes are informative. Every example is a complete program, and its output is shown exactly as cint 0.2.0 prints it on `cpu-c17`; the reference gives the same outcome. Where a tool of that release refuses an example (4, paragraph 4), the output shown is the reference's. A line `...` in shown output stands for lines left out. Sessions of the tools are shown in console blocks, with each command after `$ ` and each entry of a session after its prompt.

chunks.title: 1 Scope
2 Normative references
chunks.content:
## 2 Normative references

The following documents are referred to in the text in such a way that some or all of their content constitutes requirements of this document. For dated references, only the edition cited applies.

- ISO/IEC 9899:2018, *Information technology: Programming languages: C* (C17). Used for the C that `cpu-c17` emits and the C17 component `cpu-sir-interp`.
- NVIDIA. *Parallel Thread Execution ISA*, version 9.4. Used for the device code of `gpu-cuda`: sections 9.7.1.3 (`mul`), 9.7.2.1 and 9.7.2.2 (`add.cc`, `addc`) and 9.7.15.5 (`atom`).
- NVIDIA. *CUDA Driver API Reference Manual*, version 13.4. Used for section 6.27, Module Management, through which `gpu-cuda` loads its device code.

The other cint documents of the same release, SPEC-04P.2, SPEC-01P.2, SPEC-03P.1 and SPEC-09P.1, are named in the text where they hold detail.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols
chunks.content: ## 3 Terms, definitions and symbols The terms of SPEC-04P.2 clause 3 apply, among them *value*, *fault*, *fault record*, *operation identifier*, *refusal*, *the reference*, *executor*, *entry*, *fuel*, *view*, *kernel*, *dispatch*, *work-item* and *revision*. In addition: **3.1 iteration space**: the set of index tuples given by a kernel's `over` clause. Each tuple is one work-item. **3.2 work-item index**: the position of a work-item's index tuple in the row-major order of the iteration space, counted from 0. For `over [y: h, x: w]`, the work-item `(y, x)` has index `y * w + x`. **3.3 owned block**: the elements of an `out` or `inout` array argument that one work-item may write: those whose leading indices are the work-item's index tuple. **3.4 uniform, varying**: a value in a kernel body is *uniform* when it is the same for every work-item of a dispatch, and *varying* otherwise. **3.5 contribution**: the value a work-item adds to a reduction when it executes a `reduce` statement. **3.6 phase**: one of the three parts of a dispatch: *entry* (numbered 0), in which the arguments are checked; *work-item* (1), in which the work-items run; and *epilogue* (2), in which the reductions are completed. **3.7 entry check**: a check a dispatch makes in its entry phase, before any work-item runs. **3.8 dispatch number**: the position of a dispatch among the dispatches of its entry, counted from 0. **3.9 step ordinal**: the position of an operation among the counted operations a work-item has evaluated, counted from 0 (5.4).

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 2)
chunks.content: **3.10 address**: the part of a fault record that locates a fault in a dispatch: the kernel's qualified name, the dispatch number, the phase, and, in the work-item phase, the work-item index and the step ordinal. **3.11 canonical fault**: the fault a dispatch reports: the least of the faults it could raise, in the order of 5.5. **3.12 staging**: storage that holds the outputs of a dispatch until they are published. A program cannot observe it. **3.13 publish**: to make every output of a dispatch visible at once. **3.14 storage**: the elements a view reaches into: an array, an arena, or a region registered through the host interface. Views made from one array share its storage. **3.15 addressed storage**: the set of element offsets that a view reaches (6.2). **3.16 bounding interval**: the smallest interval of element offsets that contains a view's addressed storage (6.2). **3.17 host, device**: the *host* is the processor that runs a program's sequential code; a *device* is a GPU on which an executor runs work-items. **3.18 placement**: the memory, host or device, that holds a view's storage. **3.19 capability profile**: the record of what an executor admits and what it refuses (10.2). **3.20 launch**: one start of device code over a range of work-item indices. **3.21 fault word**: the 64-bit location in device memory that holds the least index of a work-item that faulted on the device (10.6).

chunks.title: 3.22 Symbols
chunks.content:
### 3.22 Symbols

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `N` | The number of work-items of a dispatch: the product of the extents of its iteration space. |
| `k` | The index of the work-item of the canonical fault. |
| `abs(s)` | The absolute value of the integer `s`. |
| `gcd(a, b, ...)` | The greatest common divisor of the integers listed, not all 0. |
| `C(i)` | The total fuel that work-item `i` charges when it runs to its end or to its first fault. |

chunks.title: 4 Conformance
chunks.content: ## 4 Conformance 1. In this document, "shall" states a requirement on an executor or on a program, and "shall not" a prohibition. "May" states a permission. 2. An executor conforms to this document when, for every dispatch it admits, it produces the outcome of the procedure of 5.1: the same output bytes, the same reduction results, the same fuel consumed, the same dispatch numbers and the same fault record as the reference. For a dispatch it does not admit, it refuses with `E_UNSUPPORTED`, during translation or in the entry phase, before any output is written and before any fuel is charged; it does not run the dispatch in a narrower or approximate form (10.1) [Q-2]. 3. `cpu-c17` is the executor against which the others are compared, and every executor is compared with the reference on the conformance suite, as SPEC-09P.1 5.3 states; where an executor or the reference differs from this document, this document governs, and the difference is a defect [SPEC-09P.1 BACK-03]. 4. As SPEC-04P.2 clause 4 states, an implementation may also refuse a construct that it does not implement, with a diagnostic whose code begins with `C9`. The program stays conforming, and on an implementation that runs it, its outcome is the one this document specifies. SPEC-09P.1 lists the constructs that the cint tools of each release refuse.

chunks.title: 5.1 The phases of a dispatch
chunks.content: ### 5.1 The phases of a dispatch A dispatch has three phases. In the entry phase it checks its arguments and charges its fuel. In the work-item phase it runs the body once for every point of the iteration space. In the epilogue it completes the reductions. Its outputs are published only after all three succeed. This subclause states the procedure whose outcome every executor gives. **Semantics** 1. An executor shall give every dispatch the outcome of the procedure of SPEC-04P.2 6.13.6, whatever order of execution it uses, sequential or parallel. That procedure makes the entry checks of 5.3, the last of which charges the dispatch's fuel. It then runs each work-item in ascending index, as an independent sequential program charged as 8.4 states, and then completes the reductions (9.3) and publishes the outputs (clause 7). It stops at the first fault [SPEC-04P.2 X-1]. 2. A dispatch is synchronous: the statement after it starts only when the dispatch has published its outputs. The dispatches of an entry are carried out in program order. An executor may prepare a dispatch before the one ahead of it completes, but if the one ahead faults, the prepared one is discarded: it publishes nothing and takes no dispatch number. An executor shall not begin a dispatch that reads the outputs of an earlier dispatch until the earlier one has published them [F-12]. 3. A fault in any phase ends the entry, as every fault does (SPEC-04P.2 5.2.3). **Notes** 4. The procedure defines an outcome, not a method. `cpu-c17` and the interpreter follow it as written. `gpu-cuda` runs the work-item phase on a device, with many work-items at once, and recovers the outcome of the procedure by the protocol of 10.6.

chunks.title: 5.2 Dispatch numbers
5.3 Entry checks
chunks.content: ### 5.3 Entry checks Before any work-item runs, a dispatch checks that its arguments are usable and that it can pay for its work-items. The checks run in a fixed order, so that a dispatch with several faulty arguments reports the same fault on every executor. **Semantics** 1. A dispatch makes the checks of Table 1 in the order of the table. Within a check, the arguments are taken in the order in which their parameters are declared, and the dimensions of each in order. The first check that fails gives the fault of the dispatch, in the entry phase; no further check runs and no work-item runs [F-5]. Table 1. Entry checks, in order.

chunks.title: 5.3 Entry checks (part 2)
chunks.content:
| Check | What is checked | Fault | Operation | Operands | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The storage of each array argument has not been released or reset since the view was made | `E_STALE_HANDLE` | `bind.stale` | parameter; the view's generation (`U64`) | the storage's current generation (`U64`) |
| 2 | Each argument of an `out` or `inout` parameter is a view that may be written | `E_ALIAS` | `bind.permission` | parameter | none |
| 3 | Each array argument has the parameter's element type | `E_UNSUPPORTED` | `bind.type` | parameter | none |
| 3 | Each array argument has the parameter's rank | `E_SHAPE` | `bind.type` | parameter; the view's rank | the declared rank |
| 4 | Every array argument is held in memory that the executor runs the dispatch on | `E_UNSUPPORTED` | `bind.placement` | the first parameter that differs | none |
| 5 | The size symbols bind, and every extent agrees (SPEC-04P.2 6.13.2) | `E_SHAPE` | `bind.shape` | parameter; dimension; the argument's extent | the extent computed from the declaration |

| 9 | The fuel left in the entry covers `N` units (8.4) | `E_FU

chunks.title: 5.3 Entry checks (part 3)
chunks.content: A *generation* is a count that each storage keeps and that its release or reset advances; a view records the generation of its storage when the view is made, and check 1 compares the two. A parameter is given by its position in the declaration, counted from 0, and a dimension likewise. Every operand of a `bind` operation is an `I64` unless the table says otherwise, and no entry check has an exact result. 2. Checks 1 to 3 and 5 to 7 depend only on the program and its arguments, and decide the same way on every executor. Check 4 depends also on the memory an executor runs on, and decides the same way when the arguments are placed where each executor runs. Check 8 is a refusal by one executor: its fault is not compared between executors [F-5]. 3. Check 9 comes after check 8, so a dispatch that an executor does not admit is never charged. No entry check changes state or charges fuel except check 9, whose charge is made only when every other check has passed [F-5]. 4. All array arguments of one dispatch shall have the same placement, and that placement shall be one the executor runs on. No executor moves program data between host and device memory to meet this rule; a program moves data explicitly, through the host interface (SPEC-03P.1). The one exception is the read-back of 10.6, which serves only to describe a fault [V-12]. 5. Placement is not part of any outcome. Output bytes, reduction results and fault records do not depend on it, and the descriptor of a view in a fault record (6.3) leaves it out [V-13]. 6. Checks 2 and 3 fail only for a dispatch issued through the host interface: for a dispatch written in cint source, translation rejects the same mismatches with a diagnostic (SPEC-04P.2 6.13.2). **Faults**

chunks.title: 5.3 Entry checks (part 4)
5.4 Step ordinal
5.4 Step ordinal (part 2)
chunks.content:
```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> step5.ci:2:17
   |
 2 |     r[i] = a[i] + b[i] * c[i];
   |                 ^ add.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2

   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807

```

**Notes**

6. A step ordinal says which operation of a work-item faulted, and the position and the operation identifier of the record say the same in source terms. An executor that cannot count steps on its own hardware may obtain the ordinal by running the faulting work-item again (10.6).

chunks.title: 5.5 Canonical fault selection
chunks.content: ### 5.5 Canonical fault selection Several work-items of one dispatch can fault, and a work-item can fault while a reduction would also fault in the epilogue. One of these faults is reported, chosen by a rule that does not depend on the order in which an executor met them. **Semantics** 1. The faults of a dispatch are ordered by the key (phase, work-item index, step ordinal). Faults of the entry phase are ordered by the order of the checks of 5.3, and faults of the epilogue by the declaration order of the reduction targets (9.3). The canonical fault of a dispatch is the least fault under this key, and it is the one reported [F-3] [SPEC-04P.2 IM-112]. 2. Across dispatches, the dispatch number orders faults. Because a fault ends the entry, the first dispatch that faults is the last dispatch of its entry [F-3]. 3. The order is logical. It makes no claim about which hardware thread faulted first in time, and an executor that meets faults in another order shall still report the least [F-4]. **Examples** 4. The work-item `(y, x)` of a 3 by 4 iteration space has index `4 * y + x`. Work-items `(2, 1)` and `(2, 3)`, indices 9 and 11, both divide by 0; work-item 9 is reported: ```cint index2d.ci kernel recip[h, w](in I64[h, w] a, out I64[h, w] b) over [y: h, x: w] { b[y, x] = 1000 / a[y, x]; } void run() { I64[3, 4] a = [[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 8], [9, 0, 10, 0]]; I64[3, 4] b; recip(a, b); } run(); ``` ```text fault[E_DIV_ZERO]: division by zero --> index2d.ci:2:20 | 2 | b[y, x] = 1000 / a[y, x]; | ^ div.checked.i64 | = operation: div.checked.i64 = operand-count: 2 = operand: I64 1000 = operand: I64 0 = exact: none = limit: none ... = address: index2d.recip, dispatch 0, phase 1, work-item 9, step 2 ... ```

chunks.title: 5.5 Canonical fault selection (part 2)
5.6 The fault record of a dispatch
chunks.content: ### 5.6 The fault record of a dispatch A fault in a dispatch has the record of every fault (SPEC-04P.2 8.1), with an address added. This subclause states what the address and the other fields hold in each phase. **Semantics** 1. The record of a fault in a dispatch holds, beyond the fields of every fault record, the address of the fault: the kernel's name qualified by its module, the dispatch number and the phase. A fault in the work-item phase also holds the work-item index and the step ordinal; a fault in the entry or the epilogue phase holds neither [F-8]. 2. The operation, operands, exact result and limit are, in the entry phase, those of Table 1; in the work-item phase, those of the operation that faulted, as SPEC-04P.2 states for it; in the epilogue, those of the reduction (9.3) [F-8]. 3. The position is: in the entry phase, the dispatch, at the kernel's name in the dispatch statement; in the work-item phase, the operator or subscript that faulted; in the epilogue, the operation named in the `reduce` statement. The stack of a work-item or epilogue fault has the dispatch as its innermost entry. The stack of an entry-phase fault is that of the code that issued the dispatch, as for a fault at the entry of a call. A dispatch is not a call: it is charged only the fuel of 8.4 [F-8]. 4. Details of an executor, a device or the native code are not part of the record. A tool may show them beside it, marked as not part of the record [F-8]. 5. A fault of check 7 also carries a descriptor of each of the two views (6.3). **Notes**

chunks.title: 5.6 The fault record of a dispatch (part 2)
chunks.content: 6. `cint run` prints the address as one line, `= address: module.kernel, dispatch D, phase P, work-item W, step S`, with `none` for a field the phase does not have. Examples 4 to 6 of 5.5 show it for the work-item phase and the epilogue, and examples 8 and 9 of 5.3 for the entry phase. SPEC-06P.1 describes the report, and SPEC-01P.2 the encoding of the record.

chunks.title: 6 Aliasing: the overlap test
chunks.content: ## 6 Aliasing: the overlap test

chunks.title: 6.1 What the test establishes
chunks.content:
### 6.1 What the test establishes

Every output of a dispatch must share no element with any other array argument (SPEC-04P.2 6.13.2). This clause gives the test with which an executor establishes that, and states its limits.

**Semantics**

1. An executor establishes that an `out` or `inout` argument shares no element with another array argument by the test of 6.3, at entry check 7. As SPEC-04P.2 6.13.2 states, the test is sufficient but not exact: a pair it shows disjoint shares no element, and every other pair faults `E_ALIAS`, whether the two views overlap or not [SPEC-04P.2 A-3].
2. The same test serves every way of issuing a dispatch, and no assertion by a program that two arguments are independent is taken as evidence [SPEC-04P.2 A-3].

chunks.title: 6.2 Addressed storage and bounding interval
chunks.content:
### 6.2 Addressed storage and bounding interval

A view reaches a set of elements of its storage. The test of 6.3 reasons about that set through its offsets and through the interval that contains it.

**Semantics**

1. A view of rank `r` has an origin, the offset in its storage of the element with all indices 0, and an extent and a stride for each dimension, and its element at an index tuple has the offset that SPEC-04P.2 6.12.4 gives, computed exactly [SPEC-04P.2 V-4].
2. The addressed storage of a view is the set of the offsets of all its index tuples. It is empty when any extent is 0. When every extent is positive, the bounding interval of the view is the closed interval `[lo, hi]`, where `lo` is the origin plus `stride * (extent - 1)` summed over the dimensions with a negative stride, and `hi` is the origin plus the same sum over the dimensions with a positive stride. It is the smallest interval that contains the addressed storage, and `lo` and `hi` are both addressed. A view is formed only when its bounding interval lies within its storage (SPEC-04P.2 6.12.4) [SPEC-04P.2 V-5].

**Examples**

3. This example lists views of `I32[8, 16] m` and of `I32[8] a`, with their origins, strides and bounding intervals:

| View | Origin | Extents | Strides | Bounding interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `m[.., 0..8]` | 0 | (8, 8) | (16, 1) | [0, 119] |
| `m[.., 8..16]` | 8 | (8, 8) | (16, 1) | [8, 127] |
| `m[.., 0..16 by 2]` | 0 | (8, 8) | (16, 2) | [0, 126] |
| `m[.., 1..16 by 2]` | 1 | (8, 8) | (16, 2) | [1, 127] |
| `a` | 0 | (8) | (1) | [0, 7] |
| `reverse(a, 0)` | 7 | (8) | (-1) | [0, 7] |

chunks.title: 6.3 The pairwise test
chunks.content: ### 6.3 The pairwise test The pairwise test applies three tests in order, each of which can show two views disjoint. A pair that none of them shows disjoint is refused. **Semantics** 1. For each `out` or `inout` parameter `p`, in declaration order, and each other array parameter `q`, in declaration order, the arguments of `p` and `q` are tested; a pair of two `out` or `inout` parameters is tested once, from the earlier of the two. The tests are applied in order, and the first that shows the pair disjoint accepts it [A-5]: 1. *Empty test*: the view of `p` or the view of `q` has no elements. 2. *Interval test*: the bounding intervals of the two views, taken as ranges of bytes in one memory, do not intersect. Views of two arrays that share no memory never intersect. 3. *Gcd test*: the two views have the same storage and the same element size; `g` is the greatest common divisor of `abs(stride)` over every dimension of either view whose extent is above 1; and `g >= 2` and `origin(p) mod g` differs from `origin(q) mod g`. 2. A pair that no test of paragraph 1 shows disjoint faults `E_ALIAS` [A-5]. 3. The gcd test is sound. A dimension of extent 1 adds nothing to any offset, and every other dimension adds a multiple of its stride, which is a multiple of `g`. Every offset of either view is therefore congruent to its origin modulo `g`, and two views whose origins differ modulo `g` have no offset in common [A-5]. 4. No more general test is made. Whether two strided views share an element is in general an integer feasibility problem, which NumPy's documentation of `numpy.shares_memory` calls NP-complete; the interval test corresponds to `numpy.may_share_memory`. A disjoint layout that these tests do not show disjoint is refused, and the remedy is a layout that they do show, or an explicit copy [A-6]. **Faults**

chunks.title: 6.3 The pairwise test (part 2)
6.3 The pairwise test (part 3)
6.4 The write-view test
chunks.content: ### 6.4 The write-view test An `out` or `inout` argument must reach a distinct element for each index tuple, or two work-items could write one element. Views made in cint source always do; a view that arrives through the host interface is checked at entry check 6. **Semantics** 1. A view with no elements passes. Otherwise, discard the dimensions of extent 1 and sort the others by `abs(stride)`, ascending, ties by ascending dimension number, as `d1, d2, ...`. The view passes when `abs(stride(d1)) >= 1` and, for every `j > 1`, `abs(stride(dj))` is at least 1 plus the sum, over every `i < j`, of `abs(stride(di)) * (extent(di) - 1)` [A-7]. 2. A view that passes reaches a distinct offset for each index tuple: each dimension in the sorted order steps past every offset that the dimensions before it can reach. The test is sufficient but not exact [A-7]. **Faults** 3. `E_ALIAS` is raised at entry check 6 by the first `out` or `inout` argument that does not pass. The record holds the operation identifier `bind.injective` and one `I64` operand, the parameter's position, with no exact result and no limit. Its position is the dispatch [A-7] [SPEC-04P.2 A-4]. **Examples** 4. Row-major and column-major views pass, and so do their reversals, transposes and regular slices. The view of extents (2, 2) and strides (1, 1) fails, and it does reach offset 1 twice. The view of extents (3, 2) and strides (2, 3) reaches the distinct offsets 0, 3, 2, 5, 4 and 7, but fails, because 3 is less than `1 + 2 * 2`. **Notes** 5. In cint source, the views a program can form all pass: slices take a step that is a positive literal, and `reverse` and `transpose` keep distinct offsets distinct.

chunks.title: 6.5 When the checks run
7.1 Publish on success
chunks.content: ### 7.1 Publish on success A dispatch writes its outputs to staging and publishes them only when it has succeeded. A program, or a host, therefore sees either every output of a dispatch or none. **Semantics** 1. An executor writes every output of a dispatch to staging, and publishes the outputs, or nothing, as SPEC-04P.2 6.13.4 states [SPEC-04P.2 P-1]. 2. Neither a statement of the program nor a call of the host interface made after a dispatch can observe some of its outputs published and others not (SPEC-04P.2 6.13.4); code outside the program that reads borrowed host memory while a dispatch runs is outside this rule (SPEC-03P.1) [SPEC-04P.2 P-2]. 3. After a dispatch faults, the host observes: every `in`, `out` and `inout` argument unchanged; every variable bound to a scalar `out` unchanged; the fault record of 5.6; the fuel consumed of 8.4; the dispatch count advanced by one; and the context faulted until the host clears or restores it [P-11]. 4. No way of staging is observable. Publication does not change the identity of the storage or invalidate a view of it, and every view of the storage, made before or after the dispatch, reads the published elements afterward [P-5]. **Examples** 5. A `cint-workbench` session runs entries one at a time and keeps their variables, so it can show what a faulted dispatch leaves. The first dispatch publishes `total = 5`; the second faults at work-item 1, and `total` keeps 5:

chunks.title: 7.1 Publish on success (part 2)
chunks.content:
```console
$ cint-workbench
...
ci[1]> kernel total_checked[n](in I64[n] x, out I64 s) over [i: n] { reduce s = fold_checked(add, 0, x[i]); }

total = 3 : I64

ci[6]> data[0] = 9223372036854775807;

chunks.title: 7.2 A staged `inout`
7.3 Copy-out
chunks.content: ### 7.3 Copy-out **Semantics** 1. Every executor of cint 0.2.0 publishes every output by *copy-out*: it gives the output storage of its own for staging, of the same kind of memory as the output, and on success copies the staged elements into the output. For an `inout`, the staging starts as a copy of the elements before the dispatch. An output in device memory is staged in device memory, never through host memory [P-5, B-16d]. 2. On a fault, the staging is discarded and the outputs are not touched [SPEC-09P.1 BACK-10]. 3. A kernel that a host program calls directly lists each copy of publication in the copy report of its entry (SPEC-03P.1). A dispatch issued from cint source copies the same way and does not list its copies [P-5a]. 4. Storage that an executor uses for its own purposes during a dispatch, such as the fault word and the scratch of 10.5 and 10.6, is not program data and is not listed as a copy [B-16d].

chunks.title: 7.4 Steps made of several dispatches
chunks.content: ### 7.4 Steps made of several dispatches **Semantics** 1. A sequence of dispatches is not published as a unit. A step of a program that needs several dispatches gets all-or-nothing behavior by double buffering: every dispatch of the step writes into a second set of arrays, and the program uses that set as its current state only after the last dispatch of the step succeeds. If a dispatch faults, the entry ends before the exchange and the first set still holds the last complete step [P-13]. **Notes** 2. The worked example of clause 11 alternates two arrays in this way: each dispatch reads one and writes the other.

chunks.title: 8 Execution of a work-item
chunks.content: ## 8 Execution of a work-item

chunks.title: 8.1 Independence of work-items
chunks.content: ### 8.1 Independence of work-items **Semantics** 1. A work-item cannot observe another work-item, so every order of running the work-items, concurrent orders included, gives the same staged outputs and the same canonical fault, as SPEC-04P.2 6.13.6 states; contributions to reductions and charges of fuel are combined only by the rules of clause 9 and 8.4 [SPEC-04P.2 X-2]. 2. A kernel body has no memory shared between work-items, no barrier, no atomic operation and no other way for work-items to communicate [W-1]. 3. Because of paragraphs 1 and 2, the canonical fault can be addressed by work-item and step, and a single work-item can be run again, alone, to describe a fault (10.6) [W-2].

chunks.title: 8.2 Uniform and varying values
chunks.content: ### 8.2 Uniform and varying values **Semantics** 1. Every expression in a kernel body is uniform or varying. Size symbols and scalar `in` parameters are uniform. The over variables are varying. An expression is varying when an operand is varying, when it reads an array element at a varying index, or when it is a local variable assigned under varying control flow; local variables are classified by inference [X-3]. 2. The distinction never changes meaning: a varying `if`, `while` or `break` means exactly what it means in the sequential procedure of 5.1, and an executor carries it out by masking, by divergent threads, or in any other way that gives that meaning [X-5]. 3. The body is written for one work-item. It has no lane indices, vector types or masks. For `over [y: h, x: w]`, work-item `i` runs with `y = i / w` and `x = i % w`; for more dimensions the tuple is the row-major decomposition of `i` in the same way [X-6]. **Notes** 4. The distinction serves executors in lowering a body and tools in describing it. The single-work-item body and the distinction between uniform and varying values follow the SPMD model of ISPC (Bibliography).

chunks.title: 8.3 Evaluation inside a work-item
chunks.content:
### 8.3 Evaluation inside a work-item

**Semantics**

1. Within a work-item, statements and expressions are evaluated and checked as SPEC-04P.2 6.13.3 states, and an executor may reorder, combine or vectorize the work only when the result, including which fault occurs first and its operands, is unchanged [SPEC-04P.2 X-7].

chunks.title: 8.4 Fuel
chunks.content:
### 8.4 Fuel

A dispatch is charged fuel in two parts: one unit for each work-item, at entry, and the charges its work-items make as they run, as sequential code would.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 8.4 Fuel (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. Fuel is charged against the budget of the current entry, as SPEC-04P.2 6.13.6 states; there is no budget per work-item [SPEC-04P.2 X-8].
2. The dispatch charge of `N` units, one for each work-item, is made once, at entry check 9; if it would take the entry's consumed fuel above its budget, the dispatch faults `E_FUEL` in the entry phase and no work-item runs [SPEC-04P.2 X-8].
3. Inside a work-item, loop iterations and calls charge one unit each, as in sequential code, and the charges are ordered by ascending work-item index, then by evaluation order within a work-item [SPEC-04P.2 X-8].
4. The canonical `E_FUEL` fault inside a dispatch is the first charge, in the order of paragraph 3, at which the entry's consumed fuel (everything consumed before the dispatch, plus `N`, plus the charges of every lower work-item, plus the charges this work-item made before) would exceed the budget. Its step ordinal is the number of counted operations the work-item evaluated before the charge [SPEC-04P.2 X-8].
5. The fuel consumed by a dispatch is that of SPEC-04P.2 6.13.6 and SPEC-09P.1 8.5: on success, `N` plus every charge of every work-item; after a fault at work-item `k`, `N` plus the charges of work-items 0 to `k - 1` plus the charges of `k` made before its fault; after an entry-phase fault, nothing. A charge that faults `E_FUEL` is not counted, and neither is any charge made by a work-item above `k` on an executor that ran it [SPEC-04P.2 X-8] [SPEC-09P.1 BACK-09].
6. An executor that runs work-items in parallel computes the same consumption and the same canonical fault from the exact prefix sums of the total charges `C(i)` of the work-items, as SPEC-09P.1 8.5 states [SPEC-09P.1 BACK-09].
7. Running a work-item or a group of work-items again, to describe a fault, charges no fuel (SPEC-09P.1 8.5) [SPEC-09P.1 BACK-12].

**Faults**

chunks.title: 8.4 Fuel (part 3)
8.4 Fuel (part 4)
chunks.content:

    I64[1000] a;
    I64[1000] r;
    a[900] = 9223372036854775807;
    count_up(a, r);
    return r[999];

$ cint-workbench budget.ci
...

ci[3]> :run go() --check cpu-c17
...

  --> budget.ci:4:19

...

...

ci[4]> :fuel 6002
fuel: 6002 units per entry
ci[4]> :run go() --check cpu-c17
fault[E_FUEL]: fuel allowance exhausted
  --> budget.ci:3:5
   |

   |     ^ fuel.charge
   |
   = operation: fuel.charge
   = operand-count: 0
   = exact:   none
   = limit:   I64 6002
...
   = address: budget.count_up, dispatch 0, phase 1, work-item 500, step 1
