
chunks.title: 8.6 A complete example with NumPy (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. The first call borrows `pos` and `vel` and writes `nxt`; the copy report lists the one copy, of `nxt` from staging storage. `np.asarray(nxt)` is a read-only export, and passing it to `total` borrows it again for the call.
2. The second call passes the arrays bare, so each is borrowed for that call. Work-item 5 faults at `vel[i] * dt`, 2^62 times 16; the fault names the operation, both operands, the exact result and the bound. `nxt` keeps what the first call published.
3. The context is then Faulted, and `total` raises `cint.Faulted` without running. The held fault happened while work-items ran, so `nothing_ran` is false and the host decides what state to rebuild. After `clear_fault`, `total(pos)` gives 0 + 1 + ... + 7 = 28.

chunks.title: 9 Host effects, checkpoints and replay
chunks.content: ## 9 Host effects, checkpoints and replay

chunks.title: 9.1 Output effects and ambient access
chunks.content: ### 9.1 Output effects and ambient access cint code reaches the world outside its context only through what the host supplies. The one effect every library has is output: a print statement. **Semantics** 1. cint source has no clock, environment, file, network, thread or random-source operation. Each of these reaches cint code only through what a host program supplies, so an entry's outcome depends only on its semantic inputs and on what crossed the boundary (SPEC-04P.2 5.2.7) [H-8]. 2. A print statement is an output effect: an effect with no result. Its bytes reach the host through the output callback (7.3), or are discarded. While a context records, each print statement is written to the recording as an effect with the bytes and the status the host returned; on replay the bytes are compared with the recording and not printed, and a difference stops replay with `CINT_DIVERGED` [H-7]. **Examples** 3. Each entry of the library `counter.ci` of 9.3, example 9, runs a print statement. While `record.py` records, each print is written to the recording as an effect, and the replays of that example compare its bytes with the recording.

chunks.title: 9.2 Checkpoints
chunks.content:
### 9.2 Checkpoints

A checkpoint is a context's state as bytes. Restoring it into a context of the same program gives back that state exactly, on either CPU executor and on any machine.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 9.2 Checkpoints (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A checkpoint is an envelope, which holds the format name, the runtime contract and the digests of the build, and the canonical state of 5.1, which holds the revision identity. The envelope is not hashed. A checkpoint is taken between entries, of a Ready or a Faulted context. Restoring a checkpoint whose revision identity differs from the program's is refused with `CINT_REFUSED`, and so is one whose runtime contract version is not exactly that of the context's runtime. A checkpoint taken on another executor or machine, with the same revision identity, is accepted [H-19]. 2. Checkpoint bytes are untrusted input. A restore checks every structural rule before it replaces any state: minimal encodings, known tags and lengths, arena extents within capacity, child arenas within their parents, registry extents consistent with stored contents, pool slots within capacity, distinct and vacant free-list entries, generations within range, identifier counters above every identifier present and no trailing bytes. Malformed input is refused with `CINT_REFUSED`, and the context is unchanged [H-19a]. 3. The revision identity of a program is a SHA-256 digest over the profile, the runtime contract and the canonical intermediate form of the program with every module it imports, as SPEC-01P.2 specifies. It is the same for every executor and every machine, and it changes when the program or the runtime contract changes. A fault record, a checkpoint and a recording each carry it [H-15]. 4. In Python, `Context.checkpoint()` returns the bytes, `Context.restore(data)` restores them, `Context.state_hash()` gives the 32-byte state hash and `cint.read_checkpoint(data)` decodes a checkpoint into a read-only view of its globals, arenas, pools, registry, counters and fault record. 5. Between entries, a context can move to another

chunks.title: 9.3 Recordings and replay
chunks.content:
### 9.3 Recordings and replay

A recording holds the context's initial state, every call the host made on the context and every outcome, so that a run can be checked again without its environment. Replay makes the same calls on a new context and compares each outcome.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 9.3 Recordings and replay (part 2)
9.3 Recordings and replay (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Examples**

9. The library below has module state:

```cint
// counter.ci: a library with module state, for checkpoints and recordings.
I64 tally = 0;

export I64 bump(I64 amount) {
    tally += amount;
    "tally is {tally}\n";
    return tally;
}
```

The program records a session with a checkpoint, a restore and a fault, replays it on both CPU executors, stops a replay after two entries, and reads the checkpoint it took:

```python
# record.py: checkpoints, a recording, and its replay on both CPU executors.
import cint

mod = cint.load("counter.ci")
with cint.Recorder("run.cintrec") as rec:
    ctx = mod.context(record=rec)
    print(ctx.bump(2), ctx.bump(40))
    saved = ctx.checkpoint()
    print(ctx.bump(1))
    ctx.restore(saved)
    print(ctx.bump(10))
    try:
        ctx.bump(2**62)
        ctx.bump(2**62)
    except cint.OverflowFault as f:
        print(f.operation, f.operands)
    ctx.clear_fault()
    final = ctx.state_hash()

for backend in ("ref", "cpu"):
    result = cint.replay(mod, "run.cintrec", backend=backend)
    print(backend, result.status, result.boundaries, result.final_state_hash == final)

part = cint.replay(mod, "run.cintrec", stop=2)
print(part.status, part.stopped, part.boundaries)
fresh = mod.context()
fresh.restore(part.checkpoint)
print(fresh.bump(0))

view = cint.read_checkpoint(saved)
print(view.globals)
```

```console
$ python3 record.py
2 42
43
52
add.checked.i64 (4611686018427387956, 4611686018427387904)
ref ok 6 True
cpu ok 6 True
ok True 2
42
(Global(name='counter.tally', type='I64', value=42),)
```

chunks.title: 9.3 Recordings and replay (part 4)
chunks.content: 10. The restore takes `tally` back to 42, so the next `bump(10)` gives 52. The second `bump(2**62)` overflows; the fault and the cleared fault are recorded. Each replay makes the six entries again, compares every outcome and ends with the same state hash. The replay stopped after two entries leaves `tally` at 42, which a new context restores from the replay's checkpoint.

chunks.title: 10.2 Dispatches within one entry
chunks.content:
### 10.2 Dispatches within one entry

An entry can issue several dispatches, and each publishes its outputs when it completes. This program calls `twice` of `grid.ci` (8.2), a function that issues two dispatches of the kernel `double_it`, the first writing `b` from `a` and the second writing `a` from `b`. It then calls `double_it` directly with two work-items that overflow.

```python
# dispatches.py: two dispatches in one entry, and the fault of the lowest work-item.
import numpy as np
import cint

mod = cint.load("grid.ci")
ctx = mod.context()

a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int64)
b = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int64)
ctx.twice(a=cint.borrow(a, writable=True), b=cint.borrow(b, writable=True))
print(a.tolist(), b.tolist())

a = np.array([1, 2**61, 3], dtype=np.int64)
b = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int64)
try:
    ctx.twice(a=cint.borrow(a, writable=True), b=cint.borrow(b, writable=True))
except cint.OverflowFault as f:
    print(f.operation, "dispatch", f.dispatch, "work item", f.work_item)
print(a.tolist(), b.tolist())
ctx.clear_fault()

x = np.zeros(1000, dtype=np.int64)
x[900] = 2**62
x[7] = 2**62
try:
    ctx.double_it(x, y=cint.empty((1000,), "I64"))
except cint.OverflowFault as f:
    print(f.operation, "dispatch", f.dispatch, "work item", f.work_item)
```

```console
$ python3 dispatches.py
[4, 8, 12] [2, 4, 6]
add.checked.i64 dispatch 1 work item 1
[1, 2305843009213693952, 3] [2, 4611686018427387904, 6]
add.checked.i64 dispatch 0 work item 7
```

chunks.title: 10.2 Dispatches within one entry (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. The first call leaves `b` equal to twice the old `a`, and then `a` equal to twice `b`.
2. In the second call, dispatch 0 completes and publishes `b`, whose second element is 2^62. Dispatch 1 faults at work-item 1, where 2^62 + 2^62 is 2^63. Nothing of dispatch 1 is published: `a` holds what it held before the call, and `b` keeps what dispatch 0 published (6.4 paragraph 1).
3. Dispatch numbers count from 0 in each entry. The direct call of `double_it` is a new entry, so its one dispatch is number 0. Work-items 7 and 900 both overflow, and the fault reported is that of work-item 7, the lowest index, on every executor (9.3 paragraph 7).

## 11 Future directions

This clause describes interfaces that cint 0.2.0 does not provide. It states no requirement.

chunks.title: 11 Future directions (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. **Host functions with declared effects.** A host program supplies functions that cint code declares with `extern` and calls, each with one effect class: `pure`, whose result depends only on its arguments; `observe`, whose results a recording holds and replay returns without calling the host; or `unrestricted`, at which replay stops. A function's class is the greatest of its own and its callees', as the effect field of the reflection table (7.4) is for an export that prints.
2. **Fortran.** `cint build` writes, for each module, a Fortran module of `bind(C)` interfaces and a C shim that implements them, so that a Fortran program calls exports with its own arrays and never handles a view.
3. **The migration assistant.** A set of commands reads a floating-point routine, measures the ranges its variables take on stated inputs, proposes a fixed-point format for each, writes a cint skeleton, and compares the port with the original in a report.
4. **Input hazard checks.** With `check_inputs`, the Python package hashes each borrowed input at entry and again before each publication of a dispatch that reads it, and faults the entry when the two differ; while recording, it snapshots borrowed inputs instead. The check detects a change by a foreign writer that persists to the second hash and no other, so the limit of 8.4 paragraph 3 remains.
5. **A generated module header.** `cint build --lib` writes, beside the library, a C header that declares each wrapper with its export's signature and effect class in a comment, the module descriptor and `cint_library_desc`, so that a host program includes it in place of the declarations it writes in 7.3 and 10.1.

chunks.content:
# SPEC-04P.2: The cint language

SPEC-04P.2, edition 2 of the cint language specification, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

chunks.title: Foreword
chunks.content:
## Foreword

This document specifies the cint programming language. cint 0.2.0 implements this edition, except for the constructs that its tools refuse (4, paragraph 4).

Each rule ends with one or more clause identifiers in brackets, such as [LS-17] or [IM-30]. An identifier names one rule across editions: a rule keeps its identifier when its text moves to another section or another document, and an identifier is never reused. Section numbers belong to this edition only.

This edition replaces SPEC-04P.1, "Language surface". It also takes over the rules of SPEC-01P.1 that define types, operators, faults and fuel; SPEC-01P.2 keeps the byte encodings. Annex F lists every rule that moved and where it is now.

```text
after 4: 30

fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
```

The seventh addition would give 140, so the program stops there. The six lines it wrote before the fault stay written, and the report names the operation, both operands, the exact result and the bound it crossed. The program never continues with a wrapped value.

chunks.title: How this document is organized
chunks.content:
### How this document is organized

Clauses 1 to 4 state what the document covers, the documents it relies on, its terms and what conformance means. Clause 5 describes the environment a program is translated and run in: modules and scripts, diagnostics, faults, fuel, call depth and the limits of an implementation. Clause 6 defines the language, from the concepts it rests on through types, lexical elements, expressions, declarations and statements, to arrays, views, kernels and memory. Clause 7 defines the built-in operations. Clause 8 explains how to find out why a program did what it did: the fault record, the agreement of every implementation on every outcome, golden outputs and tests, checkpoints and replay and the debug tools. Annex A gives the complete grammar. The other annexes are informative, except B.3, which states the form of operation identifiers: the diagnostic and fault codes, how cint treats each kind of behavior that C leaves undefined, a guide for C and Python programmers, the open questions and an index of clause identifiers.

Each subclause of clauses 6, 7 and 8 opens with a short summary and then has some of these parts:

- The **summary**: informative. It introduces the subclause and states no rule; where it and a rule differ, the rule governs.
- **Syntax**: the grammar of the construct, in the notation of 6.1.
- **Constraints**: rules checked when the program is translated. A program that breaks a constraint is rejected with a diagnostic and does not run.
- **Semantics**: what the construct means when the program runs.
- **Faults**: the faults the construct can raise, and what each fault record holds.
- **Examples** and **Notes**: informative. A note or example may cite the identifiers of the rules it illustrates and adds no rule of its own.

chunks.title: How this document is organized (part 2)
chunks.content: Every example in this document is a complete program or a complete part of one, and its output is shown as cint 0.2.0 prints it, except where a value is replaced by a placeholder in angle brackets, which the text explains. Where a tool of that release refuses an example (4, paragraph 4), the output shown is the reference's. A line `...` in shown output stands for lines left out.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols
chunks.content: ## 3 Terms, definitions and symbols For the purposes of this document, the following terms and definitions apply. Other terms are defined where they first appear, in italic type. Terms explicitly defined in this document are not to be presumed to refer implicitly to similar terms defined elsewhere. **3.1 Z**: the set of mathematical integers, of unbounded size. **3.2 value**: what an object (3.33) holds or an expression produces, together with its type. A value of an integer type is an element of Z in the type's range, and a value of a fixed-point type is a multiple of 2^-f in its range. The other values are those of `Bool`, of error sets and of handle types, and the arrays and structs built from them (6.3). **3.3 type**: the set of values an object (3.33) may hold and the operations defined on them. An integer type has a *range* from its minimum `MIN(T)` to its maximum `MAX(T)`. **3.4 exact result**: the result of an arithmetic operation computed in Z, before any check against the range of the result type. For an operation that rounds, the exact result is the value after its one rounding, before the range check (6.7.15). **3.5 checked operator**: an operator that gives the exact result when it is in the range of the result type and otherwise raises a fault. Every plain operator is checked: an arithmetic operator spelled without a `%` or `|` suffix, such as `+`, `/`, `%` or `<<`. **3.6 wrapping operator**: an operator spelled with a `%` suffix after an arithmetic operator (`+%`, `-%`, `*%`, `<<%` and unary `-%`), whose result is the exact result reduced modulo 2 to the power of the type's width into the type's range. A wrapping operator does not fault on overflow.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 2)
chunks.content: **3.7 saturating operator**: an operator spelled with a `|` suffix after an arithmetic operator (`+|`, `-|`, `*|`), whose result is `sat(T, v)` (3.45) for the exact result `v`. A saturating operator does not fault on overflow. **3.8 result form**: a built-in operation, such as `add_result`, that returns an error union (3.13) instead of raising the fault its checked operator would raise. **3.9 fault**: the stop of a run at an operation that cannot give a correct result, such as an overflow, a division by zero or an index outside an array (5.2.3). **3.10 fault code**: the name of the kind of a fault, such as `E_OVERFLOW`. **3.11 fault record**: the description of a fault that an implementation produces: its fault code, the operation, the operands, the exact result, the bound that was crossed, the source position, and the identity of the program. **3.12 operation identifier**: the name of an operation in a fault record, such as `add.checked.i64`. **3.13 error, error set, error union**: an *error set* is a type declared with `error`, whose values are named errors (6.3.7). An *error* is a value of an error set, returned by a function to report an expected failure; unlike a fault, an error is handled by the program, with `try` or `catch`. An *error union* `E!T` is a function result that holds a `T` or a value of the error set `E` (6.3.7). **3.14 translation**: everything an implementation does with a program before it runs: reading the source text, checking the constraints, and compiling or preparing the program.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 3)
chunks.content: **3.15 diagnostic**: a message an implementation reports during translation when a program breaks a constraint. A diagnostic has a code, the letter `C` followed by four digits, and a source position. **3.16 refusal**: the report by an implementation that it will not run a valid program, or a kernel dispatch, because it cannot execute it exactly. A refused program is not rejected: it stays conforming. A refusal is reported during translation when the need is known then, and otherwise when an entry or a kernel dispatch begins, before any of its work runs. A refused program is never run with a different meaning. **3.17 implementation**: a set of programs that translates and runs cint programs. **3.18 the reference**: the implementation `cint_ref`, written to follow this document directly, whose results are the expected results of the conformance suite. **3.19 executor**: the part of an implementation that runs a translated program (8.2, Note 13). **3.20 entry**: one run of a program from its entry point: the top-level statements of a script, the function `main`, a `test` block or an exported function called from a host program. **3.21 fuel**: a count of steps (calls, loop iterations, reductions and kernel dispatches) that an entry is charged as it runs. An entry with a fuel allowance of `B` faults at the charge that would take its consumed fuel above `B`. **3.22 call depth**: the number of user-function calls active at one time in an entry. **3.23 frame arena**: the storage that holds the local arrays of active function calls, counted in elements.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 4)
chunks.content: **3.24 semantic input**: a value that decides the outcome of an entry: the program, its input values, the effects the host supplied to it (8.2, paragraph 2), the fuel allowance, the call-depth limit and the frame-arena capacity. **3.25 module**: one source file. Scripts and importable modules are defined in 5.1.2. **3.26 array**: a fixed number of elements of one type, stored in order. **3.27 view**: a typed, shaped window onto array storage, given by its element type, its rank, an extent and a stride for each dimension, and whether it may be written (6.3.5, 6.12.4). **3.28 kernel**: a function that runs once for each point of an iteration space, writing its results to output views that only that point may write. **3.29 dispatch**: one call of a kernel over an iteration space. Each point of the space is a *work-item*. **3.30 arena, pool, handle**: an *arena* is a region of storage with a fixed capacity from which objects are taken and released together; a *pool* is a fixed set of slots that are taken and released one at a time; a *handle* is a checked reference to an object in an arena or a pool. **3.31 revision**: the identity of a program, a digest computed as SPEC-01P.2 specifies. Source positions are not part of it (8.1), and it depends on the runtime contract version (3.43, 8.4). A fault record names the revision its source positions refer to. **3.32 golden**: an output, or the text of a whole outcome (8.3), saved from a run whose output was checked once, kept with the program, and compared byte for byte with the output of each later run of the program on the same inputs (8.3).

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 5)
chunks.content: **3.33 object**: storage that holds a value: a variable, an element of an array, or a field of a struct (6.2.2). **3.34 size parameter**: a name, bound at each call or dispatch, for an extent of an array or view argument; inside the body it is a read-only `I64` (6.9.5, 6.13.2). **3.35 sequential code**: the code of a program outside kernel bodies (6.13). **3.36 raw value, storage integer**: the integer `r` of the storage type of a fixed-point type that stands for the value `r / 2^f` (6.3.2). **3.37 boundary**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.16. A boundary is a point of a run at which the state of its context (3.44) is defined and its state hash is taken, such as the end of an entry (3.20) that ran. **3.38 case**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.15. A case is a recording (3.40) that also holds the source text of every module of its program, so that the run can be replayed on another machine with no other file. **3.39 checkpoint**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.11. A checkpoint is the canonical bytes of the state of a context (3.44), taken between entries, from which the context can be restored. **3.40 recording**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.14. A recording is a file that holds the identity and code of a program, a checkpoint (3.39) taken when recording began, and the entries and other events that followed, in order. **3.41 SIR text**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.19. SIR text is the canonical text form of the intermediate representation of one module.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 6)
chunks.content: **3.42 source map**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.20. A source map lists each operation that can fault in every module of a program, with its ordinal, line, column and operation identifier (3.12). **3.43 runtime contract version**: as defined in SPEC-01P.2, 3.18. The runtime contract version names the interface between compiled code and the runtime library: `cint-rt-3` in cint 0.2.0. **3.44 context**: as defined in SPEC-03P.1, 3.4. A context is one instance of a program's state, held by a host program, in which entries (3.20) run one at a time.

chunks.title: 3.45 Symbols
chunks.content:
### 3.45 Symbols

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MIN(T)`, `MAX(T)` | The least and greatest values of the integer type `T`. |
| `w` | The width of an integer type in bits. |
| `in(T, v)` | True when `MIN(T) <= v <= MAX(T)`. |
| `wrap(T, v)` | The value of `T` congruent to `v` modulo 2^`w`. |
| `sat(T, v)` | `MIN(T)` if `v < MIN(T)`, `MAX(T)` if `v > MAX(T)` and `v` otherwise. |
| `floor(x)` | The greatest integer not greater than the rational `x`. |
| `ceil(x)` | The least integer not less than the rational `x`. |
| `log2(x)` | The base-2 logarithm of the positive rational `x`. |
| `min(a, b)`, `max(a, b)` | The lesser and the greater of `a` and `b`. |
| `clamp(v, l, h)` | For `l <= h`, `min(max(v, l), h)`. |
| `2^k` | 2 raised to the power `k`. |
| `\|a\|` | The absolute value of `a`. |

chunks.title: 4 Conformance
chunks.content: ## 4 Conformance

chunks.title: 4 Conformance (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. In this document, "shall" states a requirement on a program or on an implementation, and "shall not" a prohibition. "May" states a permission. A rule on programs is a constraint, checked during translation, unless it says that a run that breaks it faults. 2. A *conforming program* is one that satisfies every constraint of this document. A conforming program has exactly one outcome for each set of semantic inputs: it ends normally after writing specified output bytes, or it stops with one fault, described by one fault record, after writing a specified prefix of its output [LS-272]. 3. A *conforming implementation* shall: - reject every program that breaks a constraint, with a diagnostic as described in 5.1.3, and produce no executable code for it; - for every conforming program that it runs, produce the outcome this document specifies: the same output bytes, the same fuel consumed and a fault record equal in every field except `revision` and `source-map` to that of every other conforming implementation (8.2, paragraph 3); - refuse a conforming program, or a kernel dispatch, that it cannot execute exactly: during translation when the need is known then, and otherwise with the fault `E_UNSUPPORTED` when the entry or the dispatch begins, before any of its work runs (5.2.5) [IM-129]. 4. An implementation may refuse a construct that it does not implement, with a diagnostic whose code begins with `C9`. Such a refusal is not a rejection: the program stays conforming, and on an implementation that runs it, its outcome is the one this document specifies [SPEC-09P.1 CONF-14]. The code C9102 has two uses: it diagnoses a constraint that names no code of its own, and, since it begins with `C9`, it can also report a refusal. The reference tells the two uses apart. A program that the reference rejects breaks a constraint and is not co

chunks.title: 5 Environment
chunks.content:
## 5 Environment

This clause describes the setting in which a program is translated and run. Translation (5.1) turns source files into a program or rejects them with diagnostics. Execution (5.2) runs the program as entries into a context, writes its output, stops it at a fault, and bounds it by fuel, call depth and frame storage. Implementation limits (5.3) say how large a program every implementation accepts.

chunks.title: 5.1.1 Source files and modules
chunks.content: #### 5.1.1 Source files and modules A cint program is written in source files. The contents of a module decide whether it is a script, which runs, or an importable module, which other modules use. **Syntax** ```ebnf module = [ profile_decl ] { import_decl } { top_item } ; profile_decl = "profile" STRING ";" ; ``` `import_decl` and `top_item` are defined in 6.15.1. **Constraints** 1. A source file has a name that ends in `.ci`, and its contents are source text as 6.4.1 describes. A file whose name ends in `.cint` is not a source file of this language and is rejected with C1001, reported at line 1, at the first character. This edition gives no diagnostic for other names, which are not source files by the first sentence [LS-3]. 2. A profile declaration, when present, shall be the first item of the file; anywhere else it is a syntax error (C1050). It shall name `cint-core-1`, the profile this document defines; a file whose declaration names any other profile is refused (3.16) [LS-8]. **Semantics** 3. Each source file is one module [LS-3]. A file without a profile declaration is written in `cint-core-1` [LS-8]. **Examples** 4. A profile declaration that names the profile changes nothing: ```cint profiled.ci profile "cint-core-1"; "profile checked\n"; ``` ```text profile checked ```

chunks.title: 5.1.2 Scripts and programs
chunks.content: #### 5.1.2 Scripts and programs A program starts from one module, its root. The root is either a script, whose top-level statements run in source order, or a module that defines a function `main`. A module with only declarations is an importable module: it has no entry of its own and is used through `import`. **Constraints** 1. A script, a module with at least one top-level statement (paragraph 5), cannot be imported (C3010) [LS-220]. 2. A program that is not a script may define its entry as `void main()` or as `E!void main()` for an error set `E`. A module that has both top-level statements and `main` is rejected with C3011, at the name `main` [LS-221]. 3. A variable declared at the top level of a script is a local of the script's entry. It is visible from its declaration to the end of the script, and never inside a function, kernel or test: naming it there is C3004 [LS-219]. 4. The diagnostics whose cause depends on whether a module is a script (C3004, C3010, C3011, and C6004 for a module-level initializer that is not constant, 6.9.3) carry a note. The note names the first top-level statement, in source order, that makes the module a script, or says that the module has none. The note changes neither the code nor the position of the diagnostic [LS-312]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 5.1.2 Scripts and programs (part 2)
chunks.content: 5. A *script* is a module that contains at least one top-level statement [LS-218]. A `test` block is not a statement and does not make a module a script [LS-312]. 6. An *importable module* contains only imports, declarations, tests and `static_assert` [LS-220]. 7. When a script runs, its top-level statements run in source order, as one entry (5.2.1) [LS-218]. 8. In a script, the declarations of structs, error sets, arenas, pools, functions, kernels and constants are visible throughout the module, whatever their order. An arena or pool is created with the context, before the first statement runs [LS-219]. 9. A program with `main` runs `main` as its entry. When `main` has the result type `E!void` and returns an error, the entry ends with that error as its result (5.2.1) [LS-221]. 10. There is one meaning for every way a program runs. A script run by `cint run`, a program with `main`, and the same statements entered in a `cint workbench` session have the same types, the same arithmetic and the same faults, whichever executor (3.19) runs them, except that a variable declared at a session prompt is a module-level variable (paragraph 12), where in a script it is a local of the entry (paragraph 3) [LS-222]. 11. What is entered in a `cint workbench` session, other than a command, is `cint-core-1` source. The session's own commands, such as `:checkpoint` and `:inspect`, form a separate command language that SPEC-06P.1 defines [LS-223]. 12. In a `cint workbench` session, an entry that is a single expression prints its value and its type. A variable declared at the prompt is a module-level variable of the session's own module, so a function declared later can read it [LS-224]. **Examples** 13. A script may call a function declared after the call:

chunks.title: 5.1.2 Scripts and programs (part 3)
5.1.2 Scripts and programs (part 4)
chunks.content:
```console
$ cint workbench
cint workbench   profile cint-core-1   backend cpu-sir-interp   new session
ci[1]> 7 / 2
= 3 : I64
ci[2]> I64 x = 5;
x = 5 : I64
ci[3]> I64 triple() { return x * 3; }
triple : () -> I64   revision session@r2
ci[4]> triple()
= 15 : I64
ci[5]> I8 small = 100;
small = 100 : I8
ci[6]> small + small
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> entry 6:1:7
   |
 1 | small + small
   |       ^ add.checked.i8
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i8
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I8 100
   = operand: I8 100
   = exact:   200
   = limit:   I8 127
...
```

**Notes**

19. `cint run` needs a program: a root module with neither top-level statements nor `main` has no entry, and `cint run` stops with a usage error. `cint test` runs the tests of such a module (6.15.3).
20. SPEC-06P.1 describes the session in full, including how a redefinition in a live session makes a new revision of the session's module. A session names the revisions of its module `session@r1`, `session@r2` and so on and the `backend` field of its first line names the executor (3.19).
21. A function that needs the value of a script variable takes it as a parameter (example 15).

chunks.title: 5.1.3 Diagnostics
chunks.content: #### 5.1.3 Diagnostics When a program breaks a constraint, the implementation rejects it with a diagnostic: a code, a position and a message. The code and the position belong to the language, so implementations that report a code for a program report the same first one (4, paragraph 4 and B.1 state where cint and the reference differ). A run-time fault (5.2.3) is reported in the same layout. **Semantics** 1. A diagnostic has a *code*, the letter `C` followed by four digits, and a *position*, the file, line and column (6.4.2) of the offending construct. The first digit of the code gives its category [LS-283]: | Codes | Category | |---|---| | C1xxx | Files, source text, tokens and syntax | | C2xxx | Types, conversions, constants and views | | C3xxx | Names, modules and tests | | C4xxx | Statements, control flow and names used as keywords | | C5xxx | Parameter modes and kernels | | C6xxx | Evaluation during translation | | C9xxx | Implementation limits and refusals (5.3; 4, paragraph 4) | The subclause that defines each code states its position; Annex B lists every code with that subclause.

chunks.title: 5.1.3 Diagnostics (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. The position of a diagnostic is the first character of the offending construct. Where a construct can be read two ways, the subclause that defines the code names the token: for example, C2003 is reported at the literal, inside any parentheses and at the `-` of a negative literal; C3001 at the declared name; C6001 at the operator that faulted. A diagnostic that concerns a whole file is reported at line 1, at the first character [LS-278]. 3. Translation finds errors in phases: first forming tokens from the source text, then parsing, then checking names, types and constant expressions. The first diagnostic reported is the least, in the order of line, then column, then code, among the errors of the earliest phase that finds any. An implementation may report further diagnostics after the first, in the same order, at most 100 for a module, followed by a count of the rest. The output is deterministic [LS-282]. 4. Only the code and the position are compared between implementations; the message and the notes are text for the reader [LS-312]. 5. The text form has two severities: `error`, for a diagnostic, after which the program is rejected and nothing runs, and `fault`, for a run-time fault (5.2.3). `cint-core-1` defines no warnings: every construct is either valid or rejected [LS-277]. 6. The text form of a diagnostic or a fault has this layout [LS-276]: ```text []: --> :: | NN | | | =

chunks.title: 5.1.3 Diagnostics (part 3)
chunks.content: The caret marks the position. A diagnostic may add `= note:` lines and one `= help:` line, and a tool may add ` in ` to the position line. For a fault, the `

chunks.title: 5.1.3 Diagnostics (part 4)
chunks.content:
**Examples**

10. This example shows a literal that does not fit its type. The caret marks the literal:

```cint fit_level.ci
I8 level = 200;
"{level}\n";
```

```text
error[C2003]: literal does not fit its type
  --> fit_level.ci:1:12
   |
 1 | I8 level = 200;
   |            ^
```

11. A lexical error is reported before a type error on an earlier line, because forming tokens is the earlier phase. `007` is a decimal literal with a leading zero (6.4.5):

```cint phases.ci
I8 a = 300;
I64 b = 007;
"{a} {b}\n";
```

```text
error[C1022]: invalid integer literal
  --> phases.ci:2:9
   |
 2 | I64 b = 007;
   |         ^
```

12. This example shows the machine form of a diagnostic and of a fault. The program `fit.ci` is `fit_level.ci` above; `add_one.ci` prints `start` and then faults inside the function `add_one`:

```console
$ cint --json run fit.ci
{"code":"C2003","column":12,"file":"fit.ci","line":1,"message":"literal does not fit its type","schema":"CINT-DIAG-1","severity":"error"}
$ cint --json run add_one.ci
start
{"address":null,"code":"E_OVERFLOW","column":14,"exact":{"t":"Z","v":"9223372036854775808"},"file":"add_one.ci","limit":{"t":"I64","v":"9223372036854775807"},"line":2,"noncanonical":{"fuel_consumed":"2"},"operands":[{"t":"I64","v":"9223372036854775807"},{"t":"I64","v":"1"}],"operation":"add.checked.i64","revision":"<hash>","schema":"CINT-FAULT-1","severity":"fault","source_map":null,"stack":[{"column":12,"file":"add_one.ci","line":6}]}
```

   `<hash>` stands for the `revision` value, 64 hexadecimal digits that identify the program (3.31). `stack` holds the position of the call `add_one(big)`.

**Notes**

13. `cint run` writes diagnostics and fault reports to its standard error, and the program's output to its standard output. It prints neither the `help` line nor the function name of paragraph 6.

chunks.title: 5.2.1 Program start and termination
chunks.content: #### 5.2.1 Program start and termination A program runs inside a context, one entry at a time. The context holds what lasts between entries; an entry is one run from an entry point to its end. **Semantics** 1. A *context* is the state of one loaded program: its module-level variables, its arenas and pools and its fault record. It lasts across entries until the host program that created it destroys it (SPEC-03P.1) [IM-117]. 2. Each entry (3.20) has its own fuel allowance (5.2.4), call-depth limit (5.2.5) and frame arena (5.2.6), and counts its own fuel and its own kernel dispatches [IM-117]. 3. `cint run` creates a context and runs one entry in it: the top-level statements of a script, or `main` (5.1.2). Each `test` block runs as an entry in a fresh context of its own (6.15.3). 4. An entry ends in one of three ways [LS-221]: - it *completes*: the last top-level statement of the script finishes, or the entry function returns; - it *ends with an error*: `main`, of result type `E!void`, returns an error value of `E`; - it *faults* (5.2.3). 5. An entry that ends with an error is not faulted: the error value is its result, the context is not faulted and its output stands. `cint run` reports the error on its standard error, as 6.11.7 states, and exits with the status of Note 7 [LS-221]. **Examples** 6. This example shows a program whose `main` returns an error: ```cint config_check.ci error Config { missing, invalid } Config!void main() { "checking\n"; return .invalid; } ``` The output written before the `return` stands, and `cint run` reports the error and exits with status 6: ```console $ cint run config_check.ci checking error: config_check.Config.invalid (tag 2) ``` **Notes**

chunks.title: 5.2.1 Program start and termination (part 2)
chunks.content: 7. The exit status of `cint run` is 0 when the entry completes, 1 when it faults, 2 when the program is rejected with a diagnostic, and 6 when `main` returns an error. SPEC-06P.1 lists every status.

chunks.title: 5.2.2 Output
chunks.content:
#### 5.2.2 Output

Output is the bytes a program prints.

**Semantics**

1. A program's output is the sequence of bytes that its print statements write, in the order they run (6.10.10, with the formatting of 7.5). The bytes depend only on the program and its semantic inputs (5.2.7), never on the host's locale or platform, so the same entry writes the same bytes on every implementation (8.2). `cint run` writes them to its standard output.

**Examples**

2. Output written before a fault stands. The fault report follows it:

```cint partial.ci
for i in 1..=3 {
    "line {i}\n";
}
U8 level = 255;
level += 1;
"not reached\n";
```

```text
line 1
line 2
line 3
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> partial.ci:5:7
   |
 5 | level += 1;
   |       ^ add.checked.u8
   ...
```

chunks.title: 5.2.3 Faults
chunks.content: #### 5.2.3 Faults A fault stops a run at an operation that cannot give a correct result. It is reported with everything needed to see why: the operation, its operands, the exact result and the bound it crossed, and where it happened. **Semantics** 1. Every fault has one of these *fault codes*. The number is the code's value in the encoded fault record (SPEC-01P.2) [IM-104]:

chunks.title: 5.2.3 Faults (part 2)
chunks.content:
| Code | Number | Raised by | Rules |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `E_OVERFLOW` | 1 | A checked operator, conversion or named operation whose exact or rounded result is outside the range of its type | 6.7, 6.6, 7.2, 7.3 |
| `E_DIV_ZERO` | 2 | A division or remainder whose divisor is 0, `muldiv` included | 6.7.7, 7.2 |
| `E_BOUNDS` | 3 | An index outside an extent, a slice whose bounds are not valid, a full arena or pool or an exhausted frame arena | 6.12, 6.14, 5.2.6 |
| `E_SHAPE` | 4 | Views whose shapes disagree, a negative extent, `min` or `max` of an empty input, or a dispatch whose work-item count exceeds `MAX(I64)` | 6.12, 7.3, 7.4, 6.13 |
| `E_SHIFT` | 5 | A shift or rotation count outside `0` to `w - 1` | 6.7.8 |
| `E_NARROW` | 6 | A checked conversion whose value is outside the target's range, or a `c` hole whose value is not a Unicode scalar value | 6.6, 7.5.3 |
| `E_ALIAS` | 7 | A writable argument that overlaps another argument, or operands of `copy` that overlap | 6.9.5, 6.12.5, 6.13, 7.4 |
| `E_STALE_HANDLE` | 8 | A handle that is not valid for one of the reasons of 6.14.4, among them the null handle and a handle whose generation has ended, or an allocation from or a reset of a retired arena | 6.14 |
| `E_FUEL` | 9 | A charge point that would exceed the entry's fuel allowance | 5.2.4 |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | 10 | An entry, a dispatch or a call depth whose type, operation or layout the implementation cannot carry out exactly, found when the entry or the dispatch begins (3.16) | 4, 5.2.5 |
| `E_DOMAIN` | 11 | `isqrt`, `isqrt_round` or a fixed-point square root of a negative value, or `clamp` with its bounds in the wrong order | 7.2 |
| `E_DEPTH` | 12 | A call that would exceed the entry's call-depth limit | 5.2.5 |
| `E_ASSERT` | 13 | A failed `assert` outside a test | 6.10.9 |

chunks.title: 5.2.3 Faults (part 3)
chunks.content: 2. A fault ends the current entry at once. No later operation of the entry runs, its deferred statements do not run (6.10.7), and the entry has no result [IM-118]. 3. Program code cannot catch, inspect or resume a fault. No construct of the language observes a fault raised in its own context: the context is the only fault boundary, and a fault is handled by the program that supervises the context, through the host interface. A failure that a program is meant to handle is an error, returned as a value (6.11) [IM-118]. 4. A fault sets the fault record of the context. The record stays: every further entry into the context fails at once with the same record, which the host receives, until the host resets the context. Resetting clears the fault record and changes no other state. A host that wants an earlier state restores a checkpoint (8.4) [IM-118]. 5. After a fault, the state of the context is [IM-121]: | Part of the state | What it holds | |---|---| | Module-level variables and arrays written by sequential code | Every store of every statement that completed before the fault, including statements of functions that the faulting statement called; not the store of the faulting statement itself (6.2.4) | | Outputs of the kernel dispatch that faulted | Not published: their previous contents remain (6.13.6) | | Fault record | The record of the fault (8.1) | | Fuel consumed by the entry | The sum of the charges that succeeded; a charge that faults `E_FUEL` is not counted (5.2.4) | | Local variables of active calls | Not part of the state; the debug tools can show them (8.5) |

chunks.title: 5.2.3 Faults (part 4)
chunks.content: 6. Sequential code (3.35) does not roll back stores [IM-122]. 7. A fault report names the fault code, the operation, every operand, the source position and the call path. The *operation identifier* is lower case and has the form `name.form.t` (B.3), with a second type for a conversion and a rounding mode where one applies: `add.checked.i64`, `shl.wrap.u32`, `as.checked.i64.i8`, `div.checked.i128` [LS-284]. 8.1 describes every field of the record and how to read a report. 8. Every value in a report is printed exactly, in decimal, with its type. When a fault concerns a range, the report prints the bound that was crossed as `limit`. A value is never abbreviated, rounded or written in scientific notation. A fixed-point operand is shown as its type, the word `raw` and its raw value (3.36), from which its exact decimal value follows (8.1) [LS-280]. 9. Each fault code records these fields beyond the operation and the position [LS-285]: | Code | Fields | |---|---| | `E_OVERFLOW` | the operands, the exact result and the bound crossed | | `E_DIV_ZERO` | the dividend and the divisor | | `E_BOUNDS` | the index or the bounds of a slice, the dimension and the extent | | `E_SHAPE` | the extents that disagree | | `E_SHIFT` | the value and the count; the limit is the largest valid count, `w - 1` | | `E_NARROW` | the value, and the bound of the target type it crossed | | `E_ALIAS` | the two arguments that overlap | | `E_STALE_HANDLE` | the handle and the generations that disagree | | `E_FUEL` | the allowance, as the limit | | `E_DEPTH` | the depth limit | | `E_UNSUPPORTED` | the operation that cannot be carried out | | `E_DOMAIN` | the operand | | `E_ASSERT` | the two operands of a comparison condition, or none |

chunks.title: 5.2.3 Faults (part 5)
chunks.content: 10. A fault record is never shortened to fit a fixed-size structure. Its operands can exceed 1,024 bits: the exact product of two `I1024` values needs up to 2,047 bits [LS-286]. 11. A host resource that runs out or fails, such as memory for a host allocation, a file or device error or a failing host callback, is not a fault. It is an outcome of the host interface (SPEC-03P.1): it has no fault record, and the entry it ends has no execution identity (8.2) [IM-105]. 12. A fault during the evaluation of a constant expression at translation is not a run-time fault; it is the diagnostic C6001, which carries the same fault code and operands (6.8). **Examples** 13. This example shows a fault inside a function. The report adds one `called from` line for each active call, outermost first: ```cint called.ci I64 add_one(I64 v) { return v + 1; } "start\n"; I64 big = I64.max; I64 next = add_one(big); "{next}\n"; ``` ```text start fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range --> called.ci:2:14 | 2 | return v + 1; | ^ add.checked.i64 | = operation: add.checked.i64 = operand-count: 2 = operand: I64 9223372036854775807 = operand: I64 1 = exact: 9223372036854775808 = limit: I64 9223372036854775807 ... = stack-depth: 1 = called from: called.ci:6:12 ... ``` 14. A division by zero has no exact result and no limit: ```cint by_zero.ci I64 total = 10; I64 items = 0; I64 mean = total / items; "{mean}\n"; ``` ```text fault[E_DIV_ZERO]: division by zero --> by_zero.ci:3:18 | 3 | I64 mean = total / items; | ^ div.checked.i64 | = operation: div.checked.i64 = operand-count: 2 = operand: I64 10 = operand: I64 0 = exact: none = limit: none ... ```

chunks.title: 5.2.3 Faults (part 6)
chunks.content:
15. A failed `assert` outside a test faults `E_ASSERT` at the first character of its condition, and records both operands of the comparison. The message is not evaluated:

```cint asserted.ci
I64 have = 3;
I64 want = 4;
assert(have == want, "counts differ");
"after\n";
```

```text
fault[E_ASSERT]: assertion failed
  --> asserted.ci:3:8
   |
 3 | assert(have == want, "counts differ");
   |        ^ assert.checked.bool
   |
   = operation: assert.checked.bool
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 3
   = operand: I64 4
   ...
```

**Notes**

16. In C, signed overflow, division by zero and an index outside an array are undefined behavior: the program may continue with any value. In cint each is a fault, reported at the operation. Annex C lists the others.
17. A program that needs a change of state to happen entirely or not at all keeps two copies and switches between them, or writes the new state with a kernel, whose outputs are published only when every work-item succeeds (6.13.6).

chunks.title: 5.2.4 Fuel
chunks.content: #### 5.2.4 Fuel Fuel counts the steps an entry takes: calls, loop iterations, reductions and kernel dispatches. An entry may be given a fuel allowance, and it faults when a step would take it past the allowance. **Semantics** 1. Fuel is counted in units of the fuel model `fuel-v1`, at the charge points of paragraph 3. It is not elapsed time and not a count of machine instructions: the fuel an entry consumes is the same on every conforming implementation, every executor and every optimization level [IM-137]. 2. Each entry has a *fuel allowance* `B`, an `I64` with `B >= 0` and its consumed fuel starts at 0. A host that passes a value that is not such an `I64` (for example `2^63` as an unsigned 64-bit value) is not accepted when the entry starts (SPEC-03P.1). An entry may have no allowance: it still counts fuel, and only a charge that would carry its count past `MAX(I64)` faults `E_FUEL`, with the limit `I64 9223372036854775807` [IM-137]. 3. The charge points of `fuel-v1` are these, and nothing else charges fuel [IM-139]:

chunks.title: 5.2.4 Fuel (part 2)
chunks.content:
| Charge point | Units |
|---|---:|
| A call of a user function, including the entry function and the implicit entry of a script, after the depth check and before the parameters are bound | 1 |
| Each iteration of a `for` or `while` loop, including the first, after the condition is `true` and before the body runs | 1 |
| A reduction over `n` elements (`sum`, `fold_checked`, `sum_wrap`, `sum_sat`, `min`, `max`, `count` and `dot` over an array), once, before any element is read | `ceil(n / 64)`, and 0 for `n = 0` |
| A kernel dispatch of `N` work-items, once, after the entry checks of the dispatch pass (6.13.6, paragraph 7) and before any work-item runs; the calls and loop iterations inside each work-item then charge as above, in work-item order | `N` |
| Operators, conversions and named scalar operations at any width, even when written as calls (`abs`, `muldiv`, `isqrt`, `add_result` and the others); array assignment and initializers; `copy`, `fill` and other operations that iterate over elements | 0 |

chunks.title: 5.2.4 Fuel (part 3)
chunks.content: 4. When a charge would make the entry's consumed fuel exceed `B`, the charge point faults `E_FUEL` with the operation identifier `fuel.charge` and the limit `B`. The step does not happen: the call is not entered, the iteration does not begin, the reduction reads no element, the dispatch does not start. The fault's position is the loop keyword for an iteration, the callee name for a call or a reduction, the function's name in its declaration for an entry function, the `test` keyword for a test block, and the first top-level statement for the implicit entry of a script [IM-141]. 5. At a call, the arguments are evaluated first, then the checks on entry to the callee run in their stated order (shapes, then overlap of writable arguments, 6.9.5), then the depth check (5.2.5), then the fuel charge, then the body. A call that fails a check is not charged [LS-141]. 6. An implementation may charge in batches, such as a loop's whole trip count at once, only when the result is the same on every input: the same position of an `E_FUEL` fault, the same consumed count and the same state at the fault [IM-142]. 7. With an allowance, every entry ends: each iteration, call, reduction and dispatch is charged, the work between two charge points is bounded by the program's text and the extents of the arrays it reads and writes, and the iterations and calls inside each work-item of a kernel are charged as they occur [IM-143, IM-140]. 8. Fuel is counted per entry. It does not accumulate across entries and is not part of the context's state. The fuel an entry consumed is part of its outcome (8.2) [IM-137]. **Examples**

```console
target     boundary 1 of 1, the program entry: the first fault, reproduced by replay
bracket    the initial state; then boundary 1
fault[E_FUEL]: fuel allowance exhausted
  --> countdown.ci:2:1

...

...
```

**Notes**

12. Operators and named scalar operations charge nothing because the cost of each is bounded by the width of its operands, and the number of them between two charge points is bounded by the program's text [IM-140].
13. 5.2.7 gives the allowance of `cint run`, and SPEC-06P.1 lists the allowance each tool gives.

chunks.title: 5.2.6 The frame arena
chunks.content: #### 5.2.6 The frame arena The local arrays of sequential code (3.35) live in a region of fixed capacity, the frame arena and not on a native stack. Its capacity is counted in elements, so a program runs out of it at the same declaration on every implementation, and running out is a fault, not a crash. **Constraints** 1. A local array whose extent is a size parameter (3.34), such as `I64[n] tmp;`, is permitted only in sequential code. In a kernel body it is diagnosed C9102 at that extent, since the private arrays of a kernel have constant extents (6.13.3) [LS-110]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 5.2.6 The frame arena (part 2)
chunks.content:
2. Each local array of sequential code is storage of the entry's frame arena (3.23). The arena's capacity, and the use of it, are counted in elements: each element counts once, whatever its type [LS-110].
3. The capacity is a semantic input of the entry (5.2.7). Its default, and the least capacity an implementation shall accept, is 2,097,152 elements [LS-110].
4. Each entry starts with an empty frame arena. A local array is charged its number of elements when its declaration runs, after its shape is checked (6.12.1) and before its initializer, and is released when its block exits, however the block exits. The charges therefore follow the nesting of blocks and the depth of recursion, and an array declared in a loop body is charged once in each iteration and released before the next [LS-110].
5. Scalars, structs, view variables and the private arrays of a kernel are not charged. The top-level arrays of a script are locals of its entry and are charged [LS-110].
6. A declaration whose charge would exceed the capacity faults `E_BOUNDS` with the operation identifier `arena.alloc`, at the declared name. The operands are three `I64` values: the elements requested, the elements in use and the capacity. The record has no exact result and no limit [LS-110].
7. An implementation need not charge the local arrays of an entry when it proves that, over every call path, the entry never uses more than 2,097,152 elements: no run within the semantic inputs can then exhaust the arena [LS-110].

**Examples**

8. Each call of `nest` holds 100,000 elements. Twenty nested calls fit; the twenty-first does not. `E_BOUNDS` covers an exhausted frame arena (5.2.3), so the message reads `index out of bounds`:

chunks.title: 5.2.6 The frame arena (part 3)
5.2.7 Semantic inputs
chunks.content:
#### 5.2.7 Semantic inputs

The outcome of an entry is decided by its semantic inputs (3.24) and by nothing else. Three of them are numbers that bound the entry, given by the host program or the tool that starts it.

**Semantics**

1. The fuel allowance (5.2.4), the call-depth limit (5.2.5) and the frame-arena capacity (5.2.6) are given for each entry by the host program, by the configuration of the tool (SPEC-06P.1), or by the tool that starts the entry. A value given explicitly replaces the default [LS-144, IM-137, LS-110].
2. `cint run` starts its entry with these values [LS-144, LS-110]:

| Semantic input | Range | `cint run` |
|---|---|---|
| Fuel allowance | an `I64` from 0, or none | none |
| Call-depth limit `D` | an `I64` from 1 | 256 |
| Frame-arena capacity | at least 2,097,152 elements | 2,097,152 elements |

3. 8.2 states what agreement on an outcome means, and what never enters it: the time, the machine, the locale, the scheduling of threads and the addresses of native storage.

chunks.title: 5.3 Implementation limits
chunks.content: ### 5.3 Implementation limits Every implementation accepts programs at least as large as the limits below. **Semantics** 1. A conforming implementation shall accept every program within these limits [LS-311]: | Quantity | Limit | |---|---| | Size of a source file | at least 16,777,216 bytes | | Nesting of blocks and of expressions, not counting `else if` chains | at least 256 | | `else if` arms in one chain | no limit other than the file's size | | Cases in one `switch` | at least 65,536 | | Parameters of one function | at least 64 | | Fields of one struct | at least 4,096 | | Length of an identifier | exactly 255 bytes: a longer identifier is C1012 on every implementation (6.4.4) | | Magnitude of a literal | exactly `2^4096 - 1`: a larger literal is C1023 on every implementation (6.4.5) | | Rank of an array or view | exactly 4 (6.12) | | Call-depth limit `D` accepted as a semantic input | at least 4,096 active calls (5.2.5) | | Frame-arena capacity accepted as a semantic input | at least 2,097,152 elements (5.2.6) | 2. The rows that say "exactly" bind every implementation; the others are minimums. An implementation may accept more [LS-311]. 3. A program beyond one of an implementation's own limits is rejected with a diagnostic whose code begins with `C9`: C9001 for a capacity or output size, reported at line 1 when it concerns a whole file, and C9004 for nesting beyond the implementation's limit, at the construct that exceeds it. The implementation shall not miscompile or truncate the program [LS-311].

chunks.title: 6 Language
chunks.content:
## 6 Language

This clause defines the language: the notation of its grammar, the concepts it rests on, its types, lexical elements, literals, conversions, expressions, declarations, statements, errors, arrays and views, kernels, memory and modules.

chunks.title: 6.1 Notation
chunks.content: ### 6.1 Notation This subclause gives the notation of the Syntax parts and the symbols used in rules. Clause 3 defines the terms. 1. Syntax is written in a form of EBNF: `=` defines a rule, `;` ends it, `|` separates alternatives, `[ x ]` is optional, `{ x }` is repeated zero or more times, `( )` groups, quoted text is a terminal, and `(* *)` encloses a comment [LS-295]. 2. The names of lexical rules, which form tokens, are written in capitals, such as `IDENT` and `DEC_INT`. Tokens are formed by maximal munch (6.4.2), and white space and comments between tokens are skipped. The other rules are written in lower case and are built from tokens [LS-295]. 3. A Syntax part states the structure of a construct only. The rules on types, on mixing operators, on exhaustive `switch` and the like are its Constraints. Annex A collects every Syntax part [LS-295]. 4. Rules use the symbols of 3.45, with these values. For an integer type `T` of width `w`: when `T` is signed, `MIN(T)` is `-2^(w-1)` and `MAX(T)` is `2^(w-1) - 1`; when `T` is unsigned, `MIN(T)` is 0 and `MAX(T)` is `2^w - 1`. `wrap(T, v)` is the one value `r` with `in(T, r)` and `r` congruent to `v` modulo `2^w`. `clamp(v, l, h)`, for `l <= h`, is `min(max(v, l), h)`. `2^k` is 2 raised to the power `k`. These symbols have the same values as the built-in operations of the same names (7.2.1), without their faults [IM-1]. 5. Numbers in rules and tables are decimal unless written with the prefix `0x` [IM-1].

chunks.title: 6.2.1 Values
chunks.content: #### 6.2.1 Values Every value a program computes has a type: an integer in its type's range, a fixed-point value, a `Bool`, an error value, a handle, or an array or struct of these. How a machine stores an integer is not part of its meaning. **Semantics** 1. A value of an integer type is a member of Z within the type's range. Its meaning does not depend on how it is represented [IM-5]. 2. Only the operations defined on bits see a representation: the bitwise operators, the rotations, the wrapping conversion `as%`, the wrapping shift `<<%`, the conversions `!bits` and `!lanes` of a hole (7.5.4), and the encodings of SPEC-01P.2. For these, a signed value has the two's complement bit pattern of its type's width. Everywhere else, only the mathematical value can be observed [IM-5]. 3. `Bool` has the values `false` and `true` and is not an integer type (6.3.3). Arrays and structs hold values of the types of 6.3. **Examples** 4. The value -1 of type `I8` has the bit pattern `11111111`, which `as%` reads as the `U8` value 255. The plain operators see only the value: ```cint values.ci I8 a = -1; U8 bits = a as% U8; I8 b = a * a; "{bits} {b} {a & 15}\n"; ``` ```text 255 1 15 ```

chunks.title: 6.2.2 Objects and storage durations
chunks.content:
#### 6.2.2 Objects and storage durations

An *object* is storage that holds a value: a variable, an element of an array or a field of a struct. Each object exists for a stated span, its *storage duration* and holds a value of its type for the whole span.

**Semantics**

1. A local variable, including a parameter, exists from the moment its declaration runs, or its function is entered, until its block exits, however the block exits. A local array is storage of the frame arena (5.2.6) [LS-112].
2. The variables declared at the top level of a script are locals of the script's entry (5.1.2): they exist until the entry ends.
3. A module-level variable of an importable module, or of a program with `main`, exists as long as the context and keeps its value from one entry to the next (6.9.3).
4. The bytes of a string literal exist for the whole run and cannot be written (6.4.8).
5. Objects in arenas and pools exist until their arena is reset or their slot is released (6.14).
6. Every object holds a value of its type from the moment it exists: a variable of an integer, fixed-point, `Bool` or error-set type has a required initializer, and an array or struct without one is filled with zeros (6.9.1). No object is read before it holds a value.
7. A view refers to the storage of another object. A view cannot be stored, so it never outlives that object (6.12).

6.2.3 Scopes and visibility (part 2)

```text
  --> too_early.ci:1:3

```

chunks.title: 6.2.4 Evaluation order
chunks.content: #### 6.2.4 Evaluation order Every expression is evaluated in one order, left to right, and every operand is evaluated exactly once. So when an expression could fault in more than one place, the first fault in that order is the fault, on every implementation. **Constraints** 1. A call always has parentheses. Naming a function without calling it is rejected: as a statement, such as `f;`, with C4012, and where a value is expected, such as `I64 y = twice;`, with C4010 [LS-142]. 2. A call statement whose function returns a value other than `void` shall use the value or discard it with `_ =` (6.11); otherwise it is C4011 [LS-143]. 3. Assignment, compound assignment, `++` and `--` are statements, not expressions. They have no value and cannot appear inside an expression (6.7.14) [IM-97]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.2.4 Evaluation order (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. The operands of an operator are evaluated left to right, each completely, including any fault it raises, before the next begins. The operator is applied after its operands are evaluated [IM-92, LS-137]. 5. A call evaluates the callee, then each argument from left to right, then performs the call. Named arguments are evaluated in the order written. The elements of an array literal and the arguments of a struct constructor are evaluated from left to right [IM-93, LS-137]. 6. `&&`, `||`, `? :` and `catch` evaluate only the operands that the result requires [IM-94, LS-138]. 7. No operand is evaluated twice, and none is skipped because an implementation can predict its value, if its evaluation could fault [IM-95]. 8. Consequently, the first fault in evaluation order is the fault of the expression [IM-96]. 9. An assignment `place = expr` evaluates the subexpressions of the place, such as an array and its indices, from left to right and checks them first, then evaluates `expr`, then stores. `place op= expr` reads the place once, when the place is checked [IM-98, LS-139]. 10. The store of the statement that faults does not happen. Every store, and every output, of a statement that completed before the fault remains, including those of statements in functions that the faulting statement called [IM-99]. 11. In sequential code, stores become observable in program order. An implementation may reorder or remove a store only when no run, including one that faults later, can observe the difference in the state of the context [IM-100]. 12. Every intermediate result has the type of its operation. There is no integer promotion, no evaluation in a wider type and no i

chunks.title: 6.2.4 Evaluation order (part 3)
6.2.4 Evaluation order (part 4)
6.3 Types
chunks.content:
### 6.3 Types

Every object and every expression of a cint program has a type, and the type is known when the program is translated. The type decides which values an object can hold, which operators apply to it, and what happens when a result does not fit. This section describes each kind of type: its values, how its name is written, and when two types are the same. The conversions between types are in 6.6, the operators in 6.7 and the declarations that create objects in 6.9.

cint has no floating-point type and no pointer type, and no value changes type without a conversion written in the program (6.6), except that a value of an error set converts to a larger set (6.3.7).

**Semantics**

1. The types are:

| Kind | Types | Values | Section |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integer | `I8` `I16` `I32` `I64` `I128` `I256` `I512` `I1024`, `U8` `U16` `U32` `U64` `U128` `U256` `U512` | the integers in the type's range | 6.3.1 |
| Fixed point | `Q<i>.<f>`, such as `Q16.16` | the multiples of 2^-f in the type's range | 6.3.2 |
| Boolean | `Bool` | `false` and `true` | 6.3.3 |
| Array | an element type and a shape, such as `I64[8]` or `I32[2, 3]` | a fixed number of elements of the element type | 6.3.4 |
| View | `in` or `inout` before an array type, such as `in I64[_]` | a window onto the elements of an array | 6.3.5 |
| Struct | a name declared with `struct` | one value for each field | 6.3.6 |
| Error set and error union | a name declared with `error`; `E!T` | the values of the set; a `T` or an error | 6.3.7 |
| Arena, pool and handle | `Arena(T)`, `Pool(T)`, `Handle(T[])`, `Handle(T)` | an arena, a pool or a checked reference into one | 6.3.8 |

   [LS-50]

2. The integer types and the fixed-point types are the *numeric types*. The numeric types and `Bool` are the *scalar types*.

chunks.title: 6.3 Types (part 2)
chunks.content: 3. Two integer types, or two fixed-point types, are the same type only when their names are the same. Two struct types, or two error sets, are the same type only when they come from the same declaration, so two structs with the same fields are different types. An operator, an assignment or an argument that needs one type and is given another is diagnosed C2001 (6.6) [IM-56].

chunks.title: 6.3.1 Integer types
chunks.content: #### 6.3.1 Integer types An integer type holds every integer from its minimum to its maximum, and no other value. Its name is `I` for a signed type or `U` for an unsigned type, followed by its width in bits. The types of 8 to 64 bits are the usual machine integers. The *wide types*, `I128` to `I1024` and `U128` to `U512`, are integer types like the others, with larger ranges. **Syntax** ```ebnf INT_TYPE = "I8" | "I16" | "I32" | "I64" | "I128" | "I256" | "I512" | "I1024" | "U8" | "U16" | "U32" | "U64" | "U128" | "U256" | "U512" ; (* spelled as IDENT *) ``` **Constraints** 1. The bounds of a `for` range shall have type `I64`, as an array index does (6.12.2). A bound of another integer type is diagnosed C2001, even when its value fits; `as I64` (6.6) converts it [IM-7, IM-9]. **Semantics** 2. An integer type `T` of width `w` has the range `MIN(T)` to `MAX(T)`. For a signed type these are -2^(w-1) and 2^(w-1) - 1; for an unsigned type, 0 and 2^w - 1 [IM-4, IM-6]: | Type | `w` | `MIN(T)` | `MAX(T)` | |---|---:|---:|---:| | `I8` | 8 | -128 | 127 | | `I16` | 16 | -32768 | 32767 | | `I32` | 32 | -2147483648 | 2147483647 | | `I64` | 64 | -9223372036854775808 | 9223372036854775807 | | `I128` | 128 | -2^127 | 2^127 - 1 | | `I256` | 256 | -2^255 | 2^255 - 1 | | `I512` | 512 | -2^511 | 2^511 - 1 | | `I1024` | 1024 | -2^1023 | 2^1023 - 1 | | `U8` | 8 | 0 | 255 | | `U16` | 16 | 0 | 65535 | | `U32` | 32 | 0 | 4294967295 | | `U64` | 64 | 0 | 18446744073709551615 | | `U128` | 128 | 0 | 2^128 - 1 | | `U256` | 256 | 0 | 2^256 - 1 | | `U512` | 512 | 0 | 2^512 - 1 | 3. A value of an integer type is an integer in Z, within the type's range. How a value is stored does not change its meaning (6.2.1).

chunks.title: 6.3.1 Integer types (part 4)
chunks.content:
13. In C, the width of `int` and `long` depends on the platform, and an operand narrower than `int` is promoted before arithmetic. In cint each width is fixed by the type's name, and an `I8` operand stays an `I8`: there is no promotion.

14. The byte layout of integer values in storage and in fault records is given by SPEC-01P.2, and their layout at the C interface by SPEC-03P.1.

chunks.title: 6.3.2 Fixed-point types
chunks.content: #### 6.3.2 Fixed-point types A fixed-point type holds numbers with a fixed number of binary fraction digits. `Q16.16` has 16 integer bits, counting the sign bit, and 16 fraction bits: every value is a whole multiple of 2^-16, from -32768 up to 32768 - 2^-16. A value is stored as a signed integer, its raw value, equal to the number times 2^16. The number 1.5 is stored as 98304, and the step between two neighboring values is 2^-16, which is 0.0000152587890625. Fixed point serves where a C program would use floating point for numbers of a known resolution and range, such as positions, rates and gains. Each value is an exact multiple of the resolution, and an operation that rounds does so once, by a named rounding mode: `half_even` unless the program names another. **Syntax** ```ebnf FIXED_TYPE = "Q" nonzero { digit } "." ( "0" | nonzero { digit } ) ; ``` 1. A fixed-point type name is one token with no space inside: `Q16.16`, `Q1.15`, `Q8.0`. The number before the point is `i` and the number after it is `f` [LS-36]. **Constraints** 2. `i + f` shall be 8, 16, 32 or 64; otherwise the name is diagnosed C2005. The grammar makes `i` at least 1 and `f` at least 0 [IM-55, LS-36]. **Semantics** 3. `Q.` is a signed type. `i` counts the integer bits, the sign bit included and `f` counts the fraction bits. Its *storage type* is the signed integer type of width `w = i + f`: `I8`, `I16`, `I32` or `I64` [IM-54, IM-55]. 4. A value of `Q.` is the rational number `r / 2^f`, where the integer `r`, the value's *raw value*, is a value of the storage type. The raw value is also called the *storage integer* (3.36). The type therefore has exactly 2^w values, one for each raw value; its *resolution*, the difference between neighboring values, is 2^-f; and its range is -2^(i-1) to 2^(i-1) - 2^-f [IM-54]:

chunks.title: 6.3.2 Fixed-point types (part 2)
chunks.content:
| Type | Storage type | Resolution | Least value | Greatest value |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| `Q1.15` | `I16` | 2^-15 | -1 | 1 - 2^-15 |
| `Q8.8` | `I16` | 2^-8 | -128 | 128 - 2^-8 |
| `Q8.0` | `I8` | 1 | -128 | 127 |
| `Q16.16` | `I32` | 2^-16 | -32768 | 32768 - 2^-16 |
| `Q32.32` | `I64` | 2^-32 | -2^31 | 2^31 - 2^-32 |
| `Q4.60` | `I64` | 2^-60 | -8 | 8 - 2^-60 |

5. `Q.min` and `Q.max` are the least and the greatest value of `Q`, and `Q.epsilon` is its resolution, the value whose raw value is 1. All three are constant expressions (6.8) [LS-51].

6. Two fixed-point types are the same type only when both `i` and `f` are equal, as 6.3 states. `Q16.16` and `Q8.24` are different types, and `Q16.16` is a different type from its storage type `I32`. A value moves from one of these types to another only by a conversion (6.6), and the raw value of a fixed-point value is read and written with `.raw` (6.6).

7. Every operation on a fixed-point value is defined on its raw value. Addition, subtraction, negation and comparison act on the raw values exactly as on the storage type, and do not round. Multiplication, division and square root compute their result in an intermediate of 2w bits and round it once to the type's resolution, by `half_even` unless the program names another mode; the rounding modes are defined in 6.7.15. As on integers, the plain operators fault when a result does not fit, the wrapping operators wrap the raw value and the saturating operators clamp it. The rules are in 6.7 and 7.2 [IM-54].

**Examples**

8. This example shows the number, its raw value, the resolution and the range of `Q16.16`:

```cint fixed_basics.ci
Q16.16 a = 1.5;
Q16.16 b = -0.25;
"{a} is stored as {a.raw}\n";
"{b} is stored as {b.raw}\n";
"resolution {Q16.16.epsilon}\n";
"range {Q16.16.min} to {Q16.16.max}\n";
```

chunks.title: 6.3.2 Fixed-point types (part 3)
chunks.content:
```text
1.5 is stored as 98304
-0.25 is stored as -16384
resolution 0.0000152587890625
range -32768.0 to 32767.9999847412109375
```

9. Formats trade range for resolution. `Q8.0` holds the integers of `I8`:

```cint fixed_formats.ci
"Q1.15:  {Q1.15.min} to {Q1.15.max}, step {Q1.15.epsilon}\n";
"Q8.8:   {Q8.8.min} to {Q8.8.max}, step {Q8.8.epsilon}\n";
"Q8.0:   {Q8.0.min} to {Q8.0.max}, step {Q8.0.epsilon}\n";
"Q32.32: step {Q32.32.epsilon}\n";
```

```text
Q1.15:  -1.0 to 0.999969482421875, step 0.000030517578125
Q8.8:   -128.0 to 127.99609375, step 0.00390625
Q8.0:   -128.0 to 127.0, step 1.0
Q32.32: step 0.00000000023283064365386962890625
```

10. A number that is not a multiple of the resolution has no exact value in the type. The decimal 0.1 is one: written with a `round` clause (6.4.6), it takes the nearest value, which is closer in `Q16.16` than in `Q8.8`:

```cint fixed_grid.ci
Q16.16 tenth = 0.1 round half_even;
Q8.8 coarse = 0.1 round half_even;
"{tenth} (raw {tenth.raw})\n";
"{coarse} (raw {coarse.raw})\n";
```

```text
0.100006103515625 (raw 6554)
0.1015625 (raw 26)
```

11. `Q17.16` would need 33 bits of storage:

```cint fixed_name.ci
Q17.16 x = 1.0;
"{x}\n";
```

```text
error[C2005]: fraction, fixed-point, enum literal, or rounding rule
  --> fixed_name.ci:1:1
   |
 1 | Q17.16 x = 1.0;
   | ^
```

**Notes**

12. Some documentation names a fixed-point format by its fraction bits alone, and calls `Q1.15` "Q15". A cint type name always gives both numbers, and `i` includes the sign bit.

13. `cint-core-1` has no unsigned fixed-point type and no fixed-point type wider than 64 bits.

14. ISO C has no fixed-point type, and a C program that needs one scales an integer by hand. A `Q` type is that scaled integer with the scale in its type, so the compiler keeps track of the scale and of every rounding.

chunks.title: 6.3.3 Bool
chunks.content: #### 6.3.3 Bool `Bool` is the type of conditions and of the results of comparisons. It has two values, `false` and `true`. It is not an integer type: an integer does not become a `Bool`, and a `Bool` takes part in no arithmetic. **Syntax** ```ebnf bool_literal = "false" | "true" ; ``` The type is written `Bool`, one of the alternatives of `base_type` (A.5). **Constraints** 1. The condition of `if`, `while` and `for`, the first operand of `?:` and the operands of `&&`, `||` and `!` shall have type `Bool`. An integer in one of these places is diagnosed C2002; a comparison such as `n != 0` gives a `Bool` [IM-10, LS-135]. 2. `Bool` is not a numeric type. An arithmetic or bitwise operator with a `Bool` operand is diagnosed C2103. Of the comparisons, only `==` and `!=` apply to `Bool` (6.7.10) [LS-50]. **Semantics** 3. `Bool` has the two values `false` and `true`, written as the literals `false` and `true`. In storage, a `Bool` occupies one byte, which holds 0 for `false` and 1 for `true` [IM-10, LS-50]. 4. A `Bool` converts to an integer type with `as`, and no conversion goes from an integer to `Bool`, as 6.6 states. **Examples** 5. A comparison gives a `Bool`, and `as` turns a `Bool` into 0 or 1: ```cint bool.ci I64 n = 3; Bool odd = n % 2 != 0; if (odd && n > 2) { "odd and above 2\n"; } "{odd} {odd as I64} {(!odd) as U8}\n"; ``` ```text odd and above 2 true 1 0 ``` 6. An integer is not a condition: ```cint bool_condition.ci I64 n = 3; if (n) { "nonzero\n"; } ``` ```text error[C2002]: condition is not `Bool` --> bool_condition.ci:2:5 | 2 | if (n) { | ^ ``` **Notes** 7. In C, any scalar value is a condition and a comparison gives an `int`. In cint, `if (n)` is diagnosed and a comparison gives a `Bool`.
