chunks.title: 6.3.7 Error sets and error unions
chunks.content: #### 6.3.7 Error sets and error unions An error set is a type whose values name the expected ways an operation can fail, such as `ParseError.bad_digit`. An error union `E!T` is the result type of a function that returns either a value of type `T` or a value of the error set `E`. Errors are ordinary values that the program handles; they are not faults (5.2.3). Returning, propagating and handling errors with `return`, `try` and `catch` is specified in 6.11. **Syntax** ```ebnf error_decl = "error" IDENT [ ":" INT_TYPE ] ( "{" IDENT { "," IDENT } [ "," ] "}" | "=" qualified { "|" qualified } ";" ) ; union_type = qualified "!" ( "void" | base_type ) ; qualified = IDENT [ "." IDENT ] ; ``` A `union_type` appears only as the result type of a function (6.9.4). **Constraints** 1. The constraints on the underlying type of an error set and on the operands of a combined set (paragraph 9) are stated in 6.9.7. 2. A call of a function whose result is an error union shall be consumed where it is made, as 6.11.2 states (C2040). 3. The short form `.name`, used where the set is known, and the form `C.name`, for a combined set `C`, name a value only when exactly one member set declares `name`. When several do, both forms are diagnosed C2044, and the value is written with the set that declares it, such as `QueueError.full` [LS-97]. 4. A value of an error set converts to an error set that holds all of its values: at `try`, at `return`, in an assignment or an initializer, as an argument, and as an operand of `==` or `!=` whose other operand has the larger set. It does not convert the other way: that is diagnosed C2042 at `try` and at `return`, and C2001 elsewhere [LS-97].

chunks.title: 6.3.7 Error sets and error unions (part 2)
chunks.content: 5. Error-set values are compared only with `==` and `!=`; an ordering comparison is diagnosed C2103. No error value is 0, so an array or struct variable that holds error-set values, directly or inside a field or an element, needs an initializer: a declaration without one is diagnosed C2054. A variable of an error-set type, like every scalar variable, needs one too (C2050, 6.9.1) [LS-91, LS-314]. **Semantics** 6. `error Name { a, b, c }` declares an error set whose values are `Name.a`, `Name.b` and `Name.c`. Where the set is known from the context, a value may be written `.a` [LS-92]. 7. The values of a set are numbered from 1 in the order of declaration; the number of a value is its *tag*, and 0 means success. The numbers are stored in the set's underlying type, `U16` unless the declaration names another. Adding a value at the end of a set keeps the numbers of the earlier values. An error value is its number alone and carries no other data [LS-93]. 8. What a value of an error union `E!T` holds is stated in 6.11.2.

chunks.title: 6.3.7 Error sets and error unions (part 3)
6.3.7 Error sets and error unions (part 4)
6.3.7 Error sets and error unions (part 5)
chunks.content: 16. A caller that needs more detail than an error value carries passes an argument for it, such as an `inout` struct. An error-set type for array elements and fields lets a program record why each of many inputs failed.

chunks.title: 6.3.8 Arena, pool and handle types
6.4 Lexical elements
chunks.content:
### 6.4 Lexical elements

The source text of a module is read as a sequence of tokens: identifiers, keywords, literals and punctuators, separated by white space and comments. Each lexical subclause below gives its part of the lexical grammar; Annex A collects them [LS-296].

chunks.title: 6.4.1 Source text
chunks.content: #### 6.4.1 Source text Source text is UTF-8. Outside literals and comments it is ASCII. A small set of characters that can make text display differently from how it is read is rejected everywhere. **Constraints** 1. Source text shall be valid UTF-8 without a byte-order mark. A byte-order mark at the start of the file, an invalid UTF-8 sequence, or a byte 0x00 anywhere in the file is C1002 [LS-4]. 2. Outside string literals, character literals and comments, only ASCII characters may appear. Any other character is C1013 [LS-5]. 3. The following characters shall not appear unescaped anywhere, comments and string literals included. Each is C1003, reported at the character [LS-4, LS-6]: - the bidirectional formatting characters U+202A to U+202E and U+2066 to U+2069; - the separators U+2028 and U+2029, which some editors display as line breaks; - every code point with the Unicode property `Default_Ignorable_Code_Point`, such as U+200B, U+200D, U+2060 and U+FEFF after the start of the file. 4. A control character other than horizontal tab (U+0009), line feed (U+000A), and a carriage return immediately followed by a line feed shall not appear unescaped (C1004) [LS-7]. **Semantics** 5. A character excluded by paragraph 3 may be written in a string literal as an escape, such as `\u{200D}` (6.4.8) [LS-6]. **Examples** 6. The zero-width space U+200B, written as an escape, is three bytes of UTF-8 in the string: ```cint zero_width.ci I64 size_of[n](in U8[n] s) { return n; } I64 k = size_of("a\u{200B}b"); "{k}\n"; ``` ```text 5 ``` **Notes**

chunks.title: 6.4.1 Source text (part 2)
chunks.content: 7. Rejecting the bidirectional and invisible characters rules out the forms of the attack known as Trojan Source (CVE-2021-42574) that rely on those characters, in which code displays differently from how a compiler reads it. Characters that look alike but differ, inside string literals and comments, are not rejected.

chunks.title: 6.4.2 Lines, columns and white space
chunks.content: #### 6.4.2 Lines, columns and white space A line ends at a line feed, or at a carriage return followed by one. Positions in diagnostics and fault reports count lines and columns from 1. **Constraints** 1. A line ends at a line feed (LF) or at a carriage return followed by a line feed (CR LF). A carriage return not followed by a line feed is C1004 [LS-9]. **Semantics** 2. Lines are numbered from 1. Columns are numbered from 1 and count Unicode scalar values from the start of the line; a tab counts as one column [LS-10]. 3. White space, which is spaces, tabs and line ends, separates tokens and has no other meaning. Indentation has no meaning [LS-11]. 4. Tokens are formed by *maximal munch*: at each point, the longest sequence of characters that forms a valid token is taken. `a+%b` is `a`, `+%`, `b`, and `x<<%2` is `x`, `<<%`, `2` [LS-12]. **Examples** 5. In the second line, a tab comes before `U8` and another after `=`. The `+` is at the eleventh column, counting each tab as one, and the caret line repeats the tabs so that the caret stands under the `+` (5.1.3): ```cint tabs.ci U8 a = 200; U8 b = a + a; "{b}\n"; ``` ```text fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range --> tabs.ci:2:11 | 2 | U8 b = a + a; | ^ add.checked.u8 ... ``` 6. Maximal munch reads `a--b` as `a`, `--`, `b`, and `--` cannot appear in an expression. With a space, `a - -b` subtracts a negated `b`: ```cint munch.ci I64 a = 5; I64 b = 2; I64 c = a - -b; I64 d = a--b; "{c} {d}\n"; ``` ```text error[C1042]: `++` or `--` used as an expression --> munch.ci:4:10 | 4 | I64 d = a--b; | ^ ```

chunks.title: 6.4.3 Comments
6.4.4 Identifiers and keywords
chunks.content: #### 6.4.4 Identifiers and keywords An identifier names something the program declares. Keywords are reserved and cannot be names. The names of the built-in types and functions are not keywords, but they are declared already and cannot be declared again. **Syntax** ```ebnf letter = "A" .. "Z" | "a" .. "z" | "_" ; digit = "0" .. "9" ; IDENT = letter { letter | digit } ; (* not a KEYWORD; at most 255 bytes *) ``` **Constraints** 1. An identifier is a letter or `_` followed by letters, digits and `_`. Identifiers are case-sensitive and at most 255 bytes long; a longer identifier is C1012 on every implementation [LS-15]. 2. A name that is a capital `I`, `U`, `Q` or `T` followed only by digits is reserved for type names, whether or not a type of that name exists, and is C1010 when declared: `Q32` is not a valid variable name [LS-17]. 3. These words are keywords and shall not be used as identifiers. Where a name is expected, a keyword is C4012 [LS-18, LS-19]: ```text as assert break by case catch const continue default defer distinct do else enum errdefer error expect_fault export fallthrough false for if import in in_place inout kernel out over profile reduce return schedule secret static_assert struct switch test true try type var void where while ``` No construct of this edition uses eight of these keywords; they are reserved, and A.2, paragraph 7 names them.

chunks.title: 6.4.4 Identifiers and keywords (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. The names of the built-in functions, such as `len`, `min`, `sum` and `count`, are not keywords, but they are visible in every module without an import, as if declared before its first line, and shall not be declared again (C3001). 7.1 lists them [LS-22]. 5. A fault name, such as `E_OVERFLOW` in a test header (6.15.3), is an identifier checked against the fault codes of 5.2.3. A name that begins `E_` and is not one of them is C1011 [LS-23, LS-297]. **Semantics** 6. `round` and `at` are identifiers that the grammar matches by spelling in the positions where it names them: `round` right after the target type of a conversion (`x as I32 round floor`) and right after a fraction literal (`0.1 round half_even`), and `at` in a test header (6.15.3). Elsewhere each is an ordinary identifier [LS-20, LS-297]. 7. The built-in type names are `I8`, `I16`, `I32`, `I64`, `U8`, `U16`, `U32`, `U64`, `I128`, `I256`, `I512`, `I1024`, `U128`, `U256`, `U512`, every fixed-point name `Q.`, `Bool`, `Arena`, `Pool` and `Handle`, which 6.3 defines. The built-in error set is `ArithError` (6.3.7). The name `Str` is reserved and names no type in this edition [LS-21]. 8. Every built-in type name starts with a capital letter [LS-21]. **Examples** 9. Identifiers are case-sensitive, and `round` is an ordinary name outside a rounding clause: ```cint names.ci I64 count2 = 2; I64 Count2 = 3; I64 _tmp = 4; I64 round = 5; "{count2} {Count2} {_tmp} {round}\n"; ``` ```text 2 3 4 5 ``` 10. This example shows a name of the reserved form: ```cint reserved_q.ci I64 Q32 = 1; "{Q32}\n"; ``` ```text error[C1010]: invalid name --> reserved_q.ci:1:5 | 1 | I64 Q32 = 1; | ^ ``` 11. This example shows a keyword where a name is expected: ```cint keyword_name.ci I64 kernel = 1; "{kernel}\n"; ```

chunks.title: 6.4.4 Identifiers and keywords (part 3)
chunks.content:
```text
error[C4012]: statement form not permitted
  --> keyword_name.ci:1:1
   |
 1 | I64 kernel = 1;
   | ^
```

12. A built-in function name cannot be declared again:

```cint builtin_name.ci
I64 count = 3;
"{count}\n";
```

```text
error[C3001]: duplicate name
  --> builtin_name.ci:1:5
   |
 1 | I64 count = 3;
   |     ^
```

13. This example shows a misspelled fault name:

```cint fault_name.ci
test "bad name" expect_fault E_OVERFLW {
    I8 a = 127;
    a += 1;
}
"x\n";
```

```text
error[C1011]: invalid name
  --> fault_name.ci:1:30
   |
 1 | test "bad name" expect_fault E_OVERFLW {
   |                              ^
```

**Notes**

14. Identifiers are ASCII only. C and C++ admit other characters in identifiers; cint does not, which keeps out the names that look alike because of characters outside ASCII.
15. The examples of this document name declared types with a capital letter too, such as a struct `Body` or an error set `IoError`; the grammar does not require it.

**Notes**

15. In C, `0755` is octal and means 493. cint rejects it, and the octal value is written `0o755`.
16. In C, `-2147483648` is the negation of `2147483648`, which does not fit `int`, so the least `int` cannot be written as a literal. In cint, `-2147483648` is one literal, of value `MIN(I32)` in context `I32`.

chunks.title: 6.4.6 Fraction literals
chunks.content: #### 6.4.6 Fraction literals A fraction literal writes an exact rational number with digits on both sides of a point, such as `1.5`. It is used for the fixed-point types of 6.3.2, never for an integer type. **Syntax** ```ebnf FRAC_LIT = DEC_FRAC | HEX_FRAC ; DEC_FRAC = DEC_INT "." digit { [ sep ] digit } ; HEX_FRAC = HEX_INT "." hexdigit { [ sep ] hexdigit } ; ``` **Constraints** 1. A fraction literal has at least one digit on each side of the point: `1.` and `.5` are not literals. Digit separators follow 6.4.5 on each side [LS-33]. 2. A fraction literal may take only a fixed-point type. In any other context it is C2004: `I64 x = 1.5;` is rejected [LS-35]. **Semantics** 3. A decimal fraction literal denotes the exact rational its digits write: `0.1` is 1/10. A hexadecimal fraction literal is read in radix 16 on both sides: `0x1.8` is 3/2 [LS-33, LS-35]. 4. Because a fraction needs a digit after the point, `1..5` is the three tokens `1`, `..` and `5`, and `0x1..5` is `0x1`, `..` and `5` [LS-34]. 5. How a fraction literal takes a fixed-point type, and when it must be followed by a `round` clause, is stated in 6.5. **Examples** 6. This example shows fraction literals in fixed-point contexts. The second line prints each storage integer (6.3.2): ```cint fractions.ci Q16.16 half = 0.5; Q16.16 h2 = 0x1.8; Q8.0 whole = 100.0; Q16.16 grouped = 1_000.000_5 round half_even; "{half} {h2} {whole} {grouped}\n"; "{half.raw} {h2.raw} {whole.raw} {grouped.raw}\n"; ``` ```text 0.5 1.5 100.0 1000.0005035400390625 32768 98304 100 65536033 ``` 7. A fraction literal cannot initialize an integer: ```cint fraction_int.ci I64 x = 1.5; "{x}\n"; ``` ```text error[C2004]: a fraction literal cannot have the integer type I64 ... ``` 8. A range of integers is not a fraction:

chunks.title: 6.4.6 Fraction literals (part 2)
6.4.7 Character literals
6.4.8 String literals
chunks.content: #### 6.4.8 String literals A string literal writes a sequence of bytes, the UTF-8 encoding of its text with each escape replaced. It is what a print statement writes, the message of an `assert`, the name of a test and the text passed to a function that reads bytes. **Syntax** ```ebnf STRING = '"' { str_char | escape | "{{" | "}}" | hole } '"' ; str_char = (* any Unicode scalar value except '"', "\", "{", "}" and a line end *) ; escape = "\" ( "\" | '"' | "'" | "n" | "r" | "t" | "0" | "x" octdigit hexdigit | "u{" hexdigit [ hexdigit [ hexdigit [ hexdigit [ hexdigit [ hexdigit ] ] ] ] ] "}" ) ; ``` `hole` is defined in 7.5. A hole `{expr}` prints the value of `expr`. **Constraints** 1. The escapes are these, and any other backslash sequence is C1032, reported at the backslash [LS-42, LS-43]: | Escape | Bytes | |---|---| | `\\`, `\"`, `\'` | the character after the backslash | | `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\0` | 0x0A, 0x0D, 0x09, 0x00 | | `\xHH` | the one byte `HH`, from 00 to 7F | | `\u{H...}`, with 1 to 6 hexadecimal digits | the UTF-8 encoding of the Unicode scalar value; a surrogate, U+D800 to U+DFFF, or a value above U+10FFFF is C1031 | 2. A literal `{` or `}` is written `{{` or `}}` in every string literal. A single `{` begins a hole, an expression whose value is written in its place; a single `}` without its `{` is C1039 [LS-44]. 3. Holes are permitted only in print statements and in the message of an `assert`. A hole anywhere else, such as in the name of a test or in a literal passed as an argument, is C1033 [LS-44]. 4. A string literal shall not contain an unescaped line end (C1034) [LS-46]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.4.8 String literals (part 2)
6.4.8 String literals (part 3)
chunks.content:
14. This example shows an unknown escape:

```cint bad_escape.ci
"bad \q escape\n";
```

```text
error[C1032]: invalid character or string literal
  --> bad_escape.ci:1:6
   |
 1 | "bad \q escape\n";
   |      ^
```

**Notes**

15. A string literal in C ends with a hidden zero byte, and a zero byte inside it ends it early for most library functions. A cint string literal has no terminator, and a zero byte is an ordinary byte.

chunks.title: 6.4.9 Punctuators
chunks.content: #### 6.4.9 Punctuators Punctuators are the operators and separators of the language. Several operators come in three spellings that differ in what happens when the exact result is out of range: the plain spelling faults, the spelling with `%` wraps and the spelling with `|` saturates. **Semantics** 1. The punctuators are [LS-48]: ```text + - * / % << >> checked arithmetic and shifts +% -% *% <<% wrapping forms +| -| *| saturating forms & | ^ ~ bitwise == != < <= > >= comparison && || ! logical ? : conditional expression = += -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= |= ^= +%= -%= *%= <<%= +|= -|= *|= assignment ++ -- increment and decrement statements as% as? conversions .. ..= ranges ( ) [ ] { } , ; . @ ! also in error-union types ``` 2. `as%` and `as?` are single tokens with no space inside: `a as % U8` is a syntax error (C1050) [LS-49]. The word `as` itself is a keyword (6.4.4). No production of this edition uses the punctuator `@`. 3. chunks.title: 6.5 Literals and context typing
chunks.content: ### 6.5 Literals and context typing A literal has no type of its own. It takes the type its context gives it, such as the type of the variable it initializes or of the other operand of an operator, and it must fit that type exactly. There is no implicit conversion between types afterward, except from an error set to a larger one (6.3.7, 6.6), so a literal's context decides how the arithmetic around it is done. **Constraints** 1. An integer, character or fraction literal shall be exactly representable in the type its context gives it. An integer or character literal that does not fit is C2003, reported at the literal, inside any parentheses or at the `-` of a negative literal [LS-53, IM-20]. Representability is a property of the literal alone: with `I8 x`, `x + 300` is C2003, while `x + 100` is valid and its addition is checked when it runs [LS-58]. 2. An operator expression whose operands are all literals is evaluated during translation with its run-time meaning; a fault there is C6001 (6.8) [LS-54]. 3. A context-typed error value, such as `.overdrawn`, needs a context that gives its error set; with none it is C2007 [LS-60]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.6 Conversions
chunks.content: ### 6.6 Conversions A value changes type only through a conversion that the program writes. `x as T` converts `x` to the type `T` and faults when the value does not fit; `x as% T` wraps the value into `T`; `x as? T` returns an error instead of faulting. There are no implicit conversions: not in arithmetic, not in assignment, and not from a narrower integer type to a wider one. The one exception is a value of an error set, which converts to a larger set (6.3.7). A conversion that changes a fixed-point value's resolution or makes it an integer rounds once, by the mode its `round` clause names, or by `half_even` when it has none. **Syntax** ```ebnf conv_expr = unary_expr { conv_op type [ round_clause ] } ; conv_op = "as" | "as%" | "as?" ; round_clause = "round" IDENT ; ``` 1. `as%` and `as?` are single tokens (6.4.9). The `IDENT` after `round` is the name of a rounding mode (6.7.15). **Constraints** 2. A value of one numeric type shall not be used where another type is required. An operand, an initializer, an argument or a returned value of the wrong type is diagnosed C2001, even when every value of its type fits the required type: with `I32 a` and `I64 b`, `b + a` is diagnosed, and `b + (a as I64)` is valid [IM-9, IM-50, LS-134]. 3. A conversion from `Bool` shall be written with `as`, and its target shall be an integer type: `as%` and `as?` from a `Bool`, and a conversion in either direction between `Bool` and a fixed-point type, are diagnosed C2008. A conversion whose source is a struct is diagnosed C2008 as well [LS-135]. 4. There is no conversion from an integer to `Bool`: `n as Bool` is diagnosed C2056, and a comparison such as `n != 0` gives a `Bool` [IM-10, LS-135].

chunks.title: 6.6 Conversions (part 2)
chunks.content: 5. A `round` clause is permitted only on a conversion that rounds: from a fixed-point type to an integer type, or to a fixed-point type with fewer fraction bits (paragraphs 11 and 12). On any other conversion it is diagnosed C2009. The name after `round` shall be a rounding mode (C3007) [IM-69, LS-133]. 6. A conversion binds tighter than every binary operator, and conversions group from left to right: `a as I64 + b` is `(a as I64) + b`, and `x as I32 as% I16` converts twice. A unary operator directly before a conversion needs parentheses (6.7.2) [LS-136]. **Semantics** 7. Each conversion has three forms. For a source value `x`, a target type `T` and the value `v` that paragraphs 9 to 13 define [IM-50, LS-133]: - `x as T`, the *checked conversion*, gives `v` when `in(T, v)` and otherwise faults; - `x as% T`, the *wrapping conversion*, gives `wrap(T, v)` for an integer `T`, and for a fixed-point `T` the value whose raw value is `wrap(S, v)`, where `S` is the storage type of `T` and `v` the raw value the conversion computes; - `x as? T`, the *result-returning conversion*, gives a value of type `ArithError!T`: `v` where `x as T` would give it, and `ArithError.narrow` where `x as T` would fault. It is consumed with `try`, `catch` or `_ =` (6.11). 8. A conversion to a type whose range holds every value of the source type, such as `I32` to `I64` or `U8` to `I16`, gives the source value and never faults. Between two integer types of the same width, `as%` keeps the bit pattern: `-1` as `I8` becomes 255 as `U8` [IM-50]. 9. From an integer type to an integer type, `v` is the value of `x` [IM-50]. 10. From an integer type to `Q.`, the conversion is exact: `v` is the raw value `x * 2^f`, and the checked conversion faults when it is outside the storage type [IM-68].

chunks.title: 6.6 Conversions (part 3)
chunks.content: 11. From `Q.` to `Q.`: when `g >= f`, `v` is the raw value of `x` times 2^(g - f), exact; when `g < f`, `v` is the raw value of `x` divided by 2^(f - g), rounded once by the mode of the `round` clause, `half_even` when there is none. The range check or the wrap applies to `v` after the rounding [IM-68, IM-69]. 12. From `Q.` to an integer type, `v` is the value of `x` rounded once to an integer by the mode of the `round` clause, `half_even` when there is none. The range check or the wrap applies to `v` after the rounding [IM-68, IM-69]. 13. From `Bool` to an integer type, `v` is 0 for `false` and 1 for `true` [IM-10, LS-135]. 14. When the source of a conversion is a literal operand (6.5) of an integer or character literal, the conversion applies to the literal's value in Z, which has no type: `(18446744073709551615) as U64` is valid, and `-1 as% U64` is 18446744073709551615. Any other source whose operands are all literals is typed `I64` first (6.5): `(200 + 100) as% U8` converts the `I64` value 300 [IM-26]. 15. `x.raw`, for `x` of `Q.`, is the raw value of `x` as a value of the storage type. `Q.raw(n)` is the value of the fixed-point type `Q` whose raw value is `n`; `n` shall have exactly the storage type of `Q` (C2001). Both are exact and never fault: `Q16.16.raw(n)` with the `I32` 98304 is 1.5, and its `.raw` is 98304 again [IM-57, LS-38]. **Faults**

6.7 Expressions
chunks.content:
### 6.7 Expressions

An expression computes a value from operands. This subclause defines the operators of cint from those that bind tightest to those that bind loosest, then the result forms, which report an arithmetic failure as an error value, then assignment, and last the rounding modes that every rounding operation names. Literals and their typing are in 6.4 and 6.5, conversions in 6.6, the order in which operands are evaluated in 6.2.4, and the operations called by name in clause 7.

The operators apply to every integer type of 6.3.1, from `I8` to `I1024` and from `U8` to `U512`, with the same meaning at every width: a wide type is an ordinary integer type. The arithmetic operators, the comparisons and negation also apply to fixed-point types (6.3.2), as each subclause states.

**Semantics**

1. An arithmetic operator has up to three spellings, one for each form: the plain spelling is a checked operator, the spelling with `%` a wrapping operator, and the spelling with `|` a saturating operator (3.5 to 3.7). The spelling alone chooses the form; no mode, option or build setting changes it [IM-28].

| Operation | Checked | Wrapping | Saturating | Result form (6.7.12) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Add | `a + b` | `a +% b` | `a +\| b` | `add_result(a, b)` |
| Subtract | `a - b` | `a -% b` | `a -\| b` | `sub_result(a, b)` |
| Multiply | `a * b` | `a *% b` | `a *\| b` | `mul_result(a, b)` |
| Divide | `a / b` | none | none | `div_result(a, b)` |
| Remainder | `a % b` | none | none | `rem_result(a, b)` |
| Shift left | `a << k` | `a <<% k` | none | `shl_result(a, k)` |
| Shift right | `a >> k` | none | none | none |
| Negate | `-a` | `-%a` | `0 -\| a` | `sub_result(0, a)` |

Conversions have forms of their own (6.6).

chunks.title: 6.7 Expressions (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. A wrapping or saturating operator never faults on overflow. Two conditions still fault in every form: a shift count outside its range (6.7.8) and a divisor of 0 (6.7.7) [IM-31]. 3. As 6.2.4 states, every intermediate result has the type of the operation that produced it: no operand is promoted, and nothing is computed in a wider type except inside the built-in operations that say so (clause 7). **Notes** 4. A fault record names the faulting operation by an operation identifier (3.12) of the form `name.form.t` (B.3). `form` is `checked`, `wrap` or `sat`, and `t` is the token of the operand type: the type's name in lower case (`i8`, `u64`, `i128`), or `q_` for the fixed-point type `Q.` (`q16_16`). An operation that rounds adds the rounding mode it used: `mul.checked.q16_16.half_even`. Annex B lists every operation identifier, and 8.1 describes the whole record.

chunks.content: | Level | Operators | Grouping | Defined in | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | call `f(...)`, index `a[...]`, member `x.f` | left to right | 6.7.4 | | 2 | unary `-` `-%` `~` `!` `try` | right to left | 6.7.5, 6.11 | | 3 | `as` `as%` `as?`, each with an optional `round` clause | left to right | 6.6 | | 4 | `*` `/` `%` `*%` `*\|` | left to right | 6.7.7 | | 5 | `+` `-` `+%` `-%` `+\|` `-\|` | left to right | 6.7.6 | | 6 | `<<` `>>` `<<%` | left to right | 6.7.8 | | 7 | `&` | left to right | 6.7.9 | | 8 | `^` | left to right | 6.7.9 | | 9 | `\|` | left to right | 6.7.9 | | 10 | `==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=` | none | 6.7.10 | | 11 | `&&` | left to right | 6.7.11 | | 12 | `\|\|` | left to right | 6.7.11 | | 13 | `? :` | right to left | 6.7.13 | | 14 | `catch` | none | 6.11 | 2. An operator of a tighter level takes its operands before an operator of a looser level: `a + b * c` is `a + (b * c)`, and `b + a as I64` is `b + (a as I64)`. Operators of one level group as the table says: `a - b - c` is `(a - b) - c`, and `p ? x : q ? y : z` is `p ? x : (q ? y : z)` [LS-149]. 3. The two levels without grouping do not chain. A comparison whose operand is an unparenthesized comparison is rejected (6.7.2), and a second `catch` after a fallback, as in `f() catch 0 catch 1`, is a syntax error (C1050) [LS-149]. 4. Parentheses override the levels: a parenthesized expression is one operand, whatever operators it contains [LS-149]. 5. The bitwise operators bind tighter than the comparisons, so `flags & MASK == 0` is `(flags & MASK) == 0` [LS-150]. 6. A few combinations that the levels would accept are rejected unless they are parenthesized (6.7.2). **Examples** 7. This example shows levels and grouping: ```cint prec_basic.ci I64 a = 2 + 3 * 4; I64 b = 10 - 4 - 3; I64 c = 100 / 10 / 5; I64 d = -2 * 3; I32 n = 7; I64 e = a + n as I64; "{a} {b} {c} {d} {e}\n"; ```

6.7.3 Primary expressions
chunks.content:
#### 6.7.3 Primary expressions

A primary expression is an operand that no operator builds: a literal, a name, a parenthesized expression, an array literal, an error value typed by its context, or a property of a type. Each is defined where its type is; this subclause collects them.

**Syntax**

```ebnf
primary      = literal
             | STRING { STRING }
             | IDENT
             | ( INT_TYPE | "Bool" | FIXED_TYPE ) [ "." IDENT ]
             | FIXED_TYPE "." "raw" "(" [ args ] ")"
             | "(" expr ")"
             | array_literal
             | "." IDENT ;
literal      = INT_LIT | CHAR_LIT | FRAC_LIT [ round_clause ] | bool_literal ;
```

`bool_literal` is defined in 6.3.3 and `array_literal` in 6.12.1. A `STRING` operand is a string literal passed as an argument (6.4.8).

**Semantics**

1. A literal denotes a value in Z, or a rational number for a fraction literal. It has no type of its own and takes the type of its context (6.4.5 to 6.4.8, 6.5). A fraction literal appears only where the context is a fixed-point type, and one that is not on that type's grid needs a `round` clause (6.4.6, 6.7.15).
2. A name denotes a variable, constant, parameter, function, type or imported module in scope (6.2.3). As an operand, a variable or a parameter gives its current value.
3. A parenthesized expression has the type and the value of the expression it encloses. Parentheses group (6.7.1) and do not convert, and a literal in parentheses is still a literal operand (6.5).
4. An array literal `[a, b, c]` lists the elements of an array in order; nested array literals give arrays of rank 2 and above (6.12.1).
5. `.name` is a value of an error set, typed by its context (6.3.7, 6.11).
6. `T.min` and `T.max` give the bounds of the integer or fixed-point type `T` (6.3.1, 6.3.2), and `Q<i>.<f>.raw(n)` gives the fixed-point value whose raw value is `n` (6.3.2).

The operand of `-` shall have an integer or a fixed-point type. The operand of `-%` and of `~` shall have an integer type. Any other operand type is diagnosed C2103 [IM-47, IM-60]. 2. The operand of `!` shall have type `Bool` (6.3.3); any other type is diagnosed C2002. 3. The argument of `abs` shall have an integer or a fixed-point type. The argument of `uabs` shall have a signed integer type from `I8` to `I512`; any other type, `I1024` included, is diagnosed C2103 [IM-34]. 4. A `-` directly before a numeric or character literal forms a negative literal (6.4.5), which is one operand and not a negation. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.7.6 Additive operators
chunks.content: #### 6.7.6 Additive operators `+` adds and `-` subtracts. Each has three spellings that differ only in what happens when the exact result is outside the range of the type: the plain operator faults, the wrapping operator reduces the result modulo 2^`w`, and the saturating operator clamps it to the nearer bound. On fixed-point operands the six operators act on the raw values and do not round. **Syntax** ```ebnf add_expr = mul_expr { ( "+" | "-" | "+%" | "-%" | "+|" | "-|" ) mul_expr } ; ``` **Constraints** 1. Both operands shall have the same integer type, or the same fixed-point type, after a literal operand takes its type from the other operand (6.5). There is no implicit conversion: mixing `I32` with `I64`, `I64` with `U64` or `Q16.16` with `I32` or with another fixed-point type, is diagnosed C2001 [IM-29, LS-156]. 2. The six operators have the same precedence and group from left to right, so plain, wrapping and saturating forms may be mixed: `a +% b + c` is `(a +% b) + c` [LS-152]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.7.6 Additive operators (part 2)
chunks.content: 3. The result has the type `T` of the operands. Let `v` be `a + b` or `a - b`, computed in Z [IM-32]. 4. For `+` and `-`, the result is `v` when `in(T, v)`. Otherwise the operation faults [IM-30]. 5. For `+%` and `-%`, the result is `wrap(T, v)` [IM-30]. 6. For `+|` and `-|`, the result is `sat(T, v)` [IM-30]. 7. For an unsigned type, `a - b` with `a < b` has a negative exact result and therefore faults; `a -% b` wraps and `a -| b` gives 0 [IM-32]. 8. When `T` is a fixed-point type, the operators act on the raw values `A` and `B` of the operands (6.3.2): `v` is `A + B` or `A - B`, paragraphs 4 to 6 apply to `v` with the range of the raw values, and the result is the value of `T` whose raw value that gives. Nothing rounds. A literal operand denotes its exact value in `T`, so with `a` of type `Q16.16`, `a + 1` adds 1.0 [IM-60]. 9. For an integer type, the result forms `add_result(a, b)` and `sub_result(a, b)` give `v` when it is in range and the error `ArithError.overflow` otherwise (6.7.12). **Faults** 10. The fault record holds the operation identifier `add.checked.t` or `sub.checked.t`, where `t` is the token of `T` (`i64`, `u8`, `i128`, `q16_16`); both operands; the exact result `v`; and, as the limit, the bound that `v` crossed. chunks.title: 6.7.7 Multiplicative operators
chunks.content: #### 6.7.7 Multiplicative operators `*` multiplies, `/` divides and `%` gives the remainder. Integer `/` rounds the quotient toward negative infinity, called floor division, and `%` gives the remainder that goes with it, which has the sign of the divisor. On fixed-point operands, `*` and `/` form the exact product or quotient and round it once, half to even unless another mode is named. **Syntax** ```ebnf mul_expr = conv_expr { ( "*" | "/" | "%" | "*%" | "*|" ) conv_expr } ; ``` **Constraints** 1. Both operands shall have the same integer type, or for `*`, `*%`, `*|` and `/` the same fixed-point type, after a literal operand takes its type from the other operand (6.5). Mixing two types is diagnosed C2001, including two fixed-point types of different formats and a fixed-point type with an integer type. The built-in operations `qmul` and `mul_int` multiply such pairs (7.2.4) [IM-29, LS-156]. 2. `%` is not defined on fixed point; a fixed-point operand of `%` is diagnosed C2103 [LS-160, IM-66]. 3. The five operators have the same precedence and group from left to right, as 6.7.1 states: `a / b * c` is `(a / b) * c`. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.7.7 Multiplicative operators (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. On integers, let `v` be `a * b` computed in Z. `*` gives `v` when `in(T, v)` and otherwise faults; `*%` gives `wrap(T, v)`; `*|` gives `sat(T, v)` [IM-32, IM-30]. 5. For `b` other than 0, `a / b` is `floor(a / b)`: the rational quotient rounded toward negative infinity [IM-35, LS-158]. 6. For `b` other than 0, `a % b` is `a - b * (a / b)`. So `a == (a / b) * b + a % b` holds, `|a % b| < |b|`, and a remainder other than 0 has the sign of the divisor: `-7 / 2` is -4 and `-7 % 2` is 1 [IM-35, LS-158]. 7. When `b` is 0, `/` and `%` fault, `0 / 0` included [IM-39]. 8. When `T` is signed, `a` is `MIN(T)` and `b` is -1, the quotient `-MIN(T)` is out of range, so `/` faults. The remainder is 0, which is in range, so `MIN(T) % -1` is 0 and does not fault, on every implementation, including one whose processor traps on that division [IM-39, IM-40]. 9. There is no wrapping or saturating form of `/` or `%` [IM-41]. Truncating and Euclidean division are built-in operations (7.2). 10. Integer division under another rounding mode is the built-in operation `div_round(a, b, mode)`: the rational quotient `a / b`, rounded once by `mode` (6.7.15) and then checked against `T`. `div_round(a, b, floor)` equals `a / b`, and `div_round(a, b, trunc)` equals `div_trunc(a, b)` [LS-159, IM-44]. 11. On a fixed-point type `Q.`, let `A` and `B` be the raw values of `a` and `b`. `a * b` forms the exact product `A * B`, then the raw result `R = round(A * B / 2^f, half_even)`; `*` checks `R` against the range of the raw values, `*%` wraps it and `*|` saturates it [IM-61, IM-62, LS-160]. 12. On a fixed-point type, `a / b` forms the exact `A * 2^f` and gives the raw result `R = round(A * 2^f / B, half_even)`, checked

chunks.title: 6.7.8 Shifts and rotations
chunks.content: #### 6.7.8 Shifts and rotations `<<` shifts left and `>>` shifts right. A left shift is a multiplication by a power of 2, checked like `*`; `<<%` keeps the low `w` bits instead. A right shift is a floor division by a power of 2, which never overflows. A shift count outside 0 to `w - 1` faults in every form; it is never reduced modulo `w`. The built-in operations `rotl` and `rotr` rotate the bits of an unsigned integer. **Syntax** ```ebnf shift_expr = add_expr { ( "<<" | ">>" | "<<%" ) add_expr } ; ``` `rotl(a, k)` and `rotr(a, k)` are calls (6.7.4). **Constraints** 1. The left operand shall have an integer type; a shift of a `Bool` or of a fixed-point value is diagnosed C2103 [IM-60]. 2. The count, the right operand, may have any integer type, independent of the type of the left operand. A literal count has type `I64`, and a literal left operand takes its type from the context of the whole shift, not from the count (6.5) [IM-45, LS-156]. 3. The first argument of `rotl` and `rotr` shall have an unsigned integer type; a signed argument is diagnosed C2103. Their count may have any integer type [IM-45]. 4. A shift with an arithmetic operand needs parentheses (6.7.2). **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.7.8 Shifts and rotations (part 2)
chunks.content: 5. The result has the type `T` of the left operand, of width `w`. The type of the count never affects it [IM-45]. 6. The count `k` is compared as a value in Z. Every shift form, `<<%` and `>>` included and `rotl` and `rotr`, require `0 <= k <= w - 1` and fault otherwise. A count is never reduced modulo `w`: `x << 64` on `I64` faults; it does not give `x` and does not give 0 [IM-45, LS-157]. 7. `a << k` is `v = a * 2^k` computed in Z: the result is `v` when `in(T, v)`, and otherwise the operation faults [IM-45, LS-156]. 8. `a <<% k` is `wrap(T, a * 2^k)`: the low `w` bits of the two's complement pattern shifted left [IM-45]. 9. `a >> k` is `floor(a / 2^k)`. For a signed type it is an arithmetic shift and for an unsigned type a logical one. It never overflows [IM-45]. 10. There is no logical right shift of a signed type. `I1024` has no unsigned type of its width [IM-46]. 11. `rotl(a, k)` and `rotr(a, k)` rotate the `w`-bit pattern of `a` left or right by `k` bits [IM-45]. **Faults** 12. The fault `E_SHIFT` is raised by a shift or a rotation whose count `k` is outside 0 to `w - 1`. The record holds `shl.checked.t` for `<<`, `shl.wrap.t` for `<<%`, `shr.checked.t` for `>>` or `rotl.checked.t` or `rotr.checked.t`, where `t` names the type of the left operand only; as operands, the left operand and then the count, the count with its own type; no exact result; and as the limit `w - 1` as an `I64`, for every count out of range, negative counts included. Its position is the operator token, or the callee name of a rotation [IM-45, IM-185]. 13. The fault `E_OVERFLOW` is raised by `<<` when `a * 2^k` is out of range. The record holds `shl.checked.t`, both operands, the exact result `a * 2^k`, and the bound it crossed as the limit. Its position is the operator token [IM-45]. **Examples**

chunks.title: 6.7.11 Logical operators
chunks.content:
#### 6.7.11 Logical operators

`&&` and `||` combine two conditions. Each evaluates its right operand only when the left operand does not already decide the result, so the right operand can rely on what the left one tested. `!` is in 6.7.5.

**Syntax**

```ebnf
or_expr  = and_expr { "||" and_expr } ;
and_expr = cmp_expr { "&&" cmp_expr } ;
```

**Constraints**

1. Each operand shall have type `Bool` (6.3.3); an operand of another type is diagnosed C2002. An integer `x` is tested as `x != 0`.
2. `&&` and `||` in one expression need parentheses (6.7.2).

**Semantics**

3. `a && b` is `true` when both operands are `true`. `b` is evaluated only when `a` is `true` (6.2.4).
4. `a || b` is `true` when either operand is `true`. `b` is evaluated only when `a` is `false` (6.2.4).

**Examples**

5. The right operands divide by `b` only when `b` is not 0:

```cint logical.ci
I64 a = 5;
I64 b = 0;
Bool ok = b != 0 && a / b > 1;
Bool ok2 = b == 0 || a / b > 1;
"{ok} {ok2}\n";
```

```text
false true
```

6. An integer is not a condition:

```cint logical_int.ci
I64 a = 5;
Bool ok = a && true;
"{ok}\n";
```

```text
error[C2002]: condition is not `Bool`
  --> logical_int.ci:2:11
   |
 2 | Bool ok = a && true;
   |           ^
```

chunks.title: 6.7.12 Result forms
chunks.content: #### 6.7.12 Result forms A result form computes what a checked operator computes, but where the operator would fault it returns an error instead. A program uses one where an overflow, a divisor of 0 or a bad shift count is an expected outcome that it handles: the result is an error union (6.3.7), and the program consumes it with `try` or `catch` (6.11). **Syntax** The result forms are calls of built-in operations (6.7.4): `add_result(a, b)`, `sub_result(a, b)`, `mul_result(a, b)`, `div_result(a, b)`, `rem_result(a, b)` and `shl_result(a, k)`. The conversion `x as? T` is the result form of `as` (6.6). **Constraints** 1. The operands shall have the types the checked operator requires: two integers of one type, a literal operand taking its type from the other operand and two literal operands having type `I64`; for `shl_result`, a left operand of an integer type and a count of any integer type. Two types are diagnosed C2001, and a `Bool` operand C2103 [IM-29, IM-28]. 2. A result form has the type `ArithError!T`, where `T` is the operand type. Like every error union it shall be consumed by `try`, by `catch` or by `_ =` (6.11); a result form used in any other way is diagnosed C2040 [IM-30]. **Semantics** 3. `ArithError` is a built-in error set (6.3.7) with four values, in this order: `overflow`, `div_zero`, `shift` and `narrow`. Its values are numbered 1 to 4 in that order, with an underlying type `U16`. Each value mirrors one fault code: `overflow` mirrors `E_OVERFLOW`, `div_zero` `E_DIV_ZERO`, `shift` `E_SHIFT`, and `narrow` `E_NARROW` [IM-188]. 4. A result form holds the value that its checked operation gives when that operation does not fault, and otherwise the `ArithError` value that mirrors the fault the operation would raise. It never faults [IM-30, IM-188]:

6.7.14 Assignment, compound assignment, `++` and `--`
chunks.content: #### 6.7.14 Assignment, compound assignment, `++` and `--` An assignment stores a value in a place. A compound assignment such as `x += y` combines the place's value with another value and stores the result, and `x++` and `x--` add or subtract 1. All of them are statements: none has a value, and none can appear inside an expression. **Syntax** ```ebnf simple_stmt = place assign_op expr | place ( "++" | "--" ) | [ "try" ] call ; place = IDENT { "." IDENT | "[" index_list "]" } ; assign_op = "=" | "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/=" | "%=" | "<<=" | ">>=" | "&=" | "|=" | "^=" | "+%=" | "-%=" | "*%=" | "<<%=" | "+|=" | "-|=" | "*|=" ; ``` **Constraints** 1. Assignment, compound assignment, `++` and `--` are statements, not expressions. An assignment written as the condition of an `if` or a `while` is diagnosed C1041, `++` or `--` inside an expression C1042, and an assignment inside any other expression is a syntax error (C1050) [LS-164, LS-166]. 2. The left side shall be a *place*: a variable, an element of an array or view, or a field of a struct, that the program may write. Assigning to a `const` is diagnosed C2058; the parameters that a function may not write are in 6.9.5. 3. In `p = e`, the value of `e` shall have the type of `p`, a literal taking that type (6.5); another type is diagnosed C2001. 4. A compound form exists for every binary arithmetic and bitwise operator: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `+%=`, `-%=`, `*%=`, `<<%=`, `+|=`, `-|=` and `*|=`. `p op= e` has the constraints of `p op e` (6.7.6 to 6.7.9) [LS-165]. 5. The name after `round`, and the name in the mode argument of a built-in operation, shall be one of the nine mode names of the table below. Any other name is diagnosed C3007 [IM-42]. 2. A `round` clause may follow the target type of a conversion that rounds (6.6) and a fraction literal (6.4.6). After a conversion that does not round it is diagnosed C2009 (6.6). **Semantics** 3. 6.8 Constant expressions and compile-time evaluation
chunks.content: ### 6.8 Constant expressions and compile-time evaluation Some values are computed while the program is translated: the initializer of a `const` declaration, the extent of a module-level array, a `case` item, the condition of `static_assert` and every maximal constant expression (paragraph 4). This *compile-time evaluation* uses the operators and the types of a run. A constant expression is typed first and then evaluated with checked, wrapping or saturating arithmetic exactly as it would be at run time, so a computation gives the same value whether it is done at translation or at run time. A fault at translation is reported as the diagnostic C6001, with the fault's operands. **Constraints** 1. The following shall be constant expressions: the initializer of a `const` declaration (6.9.2); the initializer of a module-level variable of an importable module (6.9.3); an extent of a module-level array (6.12.1, 6.12.6) and of an array in a kernel body (6.13.3); a `case` item (6.10.5); the condition of `static_assert` (6.10.9); and the capacity of an arena or a pool (6.14.1). Anything else in these places is diagnosed C6004, except in an extent of an array in a kernel body, where it is diagnosed C9102 (6.13.3) [LS-264]. **Semantics** 2. A *constant expression* is an expression built only from literals, names declared with `const`, the type properties `T.min`, `T.max` and `Q.epsilon`, the operators of 6.7, the conversions `as` and `as%`, the constructor `Q.raw(n)` and the named operations of 7.2, each with constant operands. A variable, a function call, the member `.raw`, `as?` and `catch` are not constant expressions [IM-23].

chunks.title: 6.8 Constant expressions and compile-time evaluation (part 2)
chunks.content: 3. A constant expression is typed by the rules of 6.5, exactly as if it were evaluated at run time, and is then evaluated with the meaning of 6.6, 6.7 and 7.2: the checked, wrapping and saturating forms, the rules for shift counts and the rounding of fixed point apply unchanged. No expression is evaluated in Z as a whole: every intermediate result has the type of its operation, as at run time [IM-23, IM-103, LS-265]. 4. The unit of compile-time evaluation is the *maximal constant expression*: a constant expression that is not an operand of a larger constant expression. Every maximal constant expression is evaluated at translation, wherever it appears, including inside an expression that is evaluated at run time [IM-23, LS-264]. 5. Inside a maximal constant expression, `&&`, `||` and `?:` evaluate only the operands that their result requires, as at run time (6.2.4). An operand they skip is type-checked and its literals are checked against their types, but it is not evaluated: `false && (1 / 0 == 0)` is `false`, and `true ? 1 : 1 / 0` is 1 [IM-23]. 6. A constant operand that `&&`, `||` or `?:` of a non-constant expression may skip is not evaluated at translation. It is evaluated at run time when the run reaches it, and faults then if its evaluation faults. With `I64 x`, `x == 2 && (1 / 0 == 0)` is translated, and faults `E_DIV_ZERO` when it is evaluated with `x` equal to 2 [IM-23, LS-264]. 7. A constant expression that its statement always evaluates is evaluated at translation, even when the statement is in a branch that a run does not reach [IM-23, LS-264]. 8. A checked conversion whose source is a literal operand (6.6) is decided at translation wherever it appears, in an operand that `&&`, `||` or `?:` skips as well [IM-23].

chunks.content: 23. A C compiler may fold `2000000000 * 2 / 4` to any value, because signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, and C requires a diagnostic only where a constant expression is required. In cint the folding is done in the declared type and reports the overflow with its operands, as a run would.

chunks.title: 6.9 Declarations
chunks.content:
### 6.9 Declarations

A declaration introduces a name and says what it stands for: a variable, a constant, a function, a struct type or an error set. This subclause gives the form of each declaration, the rules checked when it is translated, and what it does when it runs. The types that declarations name are defined in 6.3, where a name is visible in 6.2.3, and the order in which expressions are evaluated in 6.2.4.

chunks.title: 6.9.1 Variables
chunks.content: #### 6.9.1 Variables A variable declaration names an object, gives its type and gives its first value. A variable of an integer, fixed-point, `Bool` or error-set type always has an initializer, so no object is read before it holds a value (6.2.2). An array or struct variable without an initializer starts with every element and field equal to 0. A *view variable* names a window onto array storage that already exists. **Syntax** ```ebnf var_decl = type IDENT [ "=" expr ] ";" ; view_decl = ( "in" | "inout" ) type IDENT "=" expr ";" ; ``` **Constraints** 1. A variable of an integer type, of a fixed-point type, of `Bool` or of an error-set type shall have an initializer. A declaration without one is diagnosed C2050 at the declared name [LS-104]. 2. An array or struct variable that holds error-set values needs an initializer (C2054, 6.3.7). 3. A view variable is declared with `in`, which gives read-only access, or `inout`, which gives read and write access, and shall have an initializer: an array or a view of the same element type and rank. Its type writes `_` for each extent, which the initializer supplies. An `inout` view variable shall be initialized from storage that may be written; a read-only source is diagnosed C2067 [LS-106]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.9.1 Variables (part 2)
6.9.1 Variables (part 3)
6.9.2 Constants
6.9.2 Constants (part 2)
chunks.content: 7. A constant takes the place of both C's `#define` of a value and C's `const` object: it has a type, it is checked like any other expression, and no program can write it.

chunks.title: 6.9.3 Module-level variables
chunks.content: #### 6.9.3 Module-level variables A variable declared at the top level of an importable module, or of a program that defines `main`, is a *module-level variable*: it exists as long as the context, keeps its value from one entry to the next (5.2.1), and every function of its module can use it. Its initial value is fixed during translation, so the order in which modules start cannot be observed. The top-level variables of a script are different: they are locals of the script's entry (5.1.2). **Syntax** ```ebnf top_item = [ "export" ] declaration | test_decl | static_assert | statement ; declaration = const_decl | var_decl | func_decl | kernel_decl | struct_decl | error_decl | memory_decl ; ``` `var_decl` is in 6.9.1, `memory_decl` in 6.14.1 and `export` in 6.15.2. **Constraints** 1. The initializer of a module-level variable shall be a constant expression (6.8). An array literal or a struct constructor whose items are all constant expressions, nested literals and constructors included, is a constant initializer of a variable of its type. Any other initializer is diagnosed C6004 at its first character [LS-113]. 2. The constant initializer is checked as the same initializer of a local variable would be, and a fault during its evaluation is diagnosed C6001 [LS-113]. 3. An arena or a pool (6.14) is declared at the top level of the module, in a script as well as in an importable module, with a constant capacity; another capacity is diagnosed C6004 [LS-113]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.9.3 Module-level variables (part 2)
6.9.4 Functions
6.9.4 Functions (part 2)
6.9.4 Functions (part 3)
chunks.content:
11. A call evaluates its arguments, runs the entry checks of 6.9.5, checks the call depth and charges fuel (5.2.5, 5.2.4), and then runs the body. A function may call itself, as deep as the call-depth limit of the entry allows (5.2.5).
12. A function returns a scalar, a struct, a handle, an error-set value or an error union. To produce an array, it fills an `inout` array parameter (6.9.5, example 15).

chunks.title: 6.9.5 Parameters and arguments
6.9.5 Parameters and arguments (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A parameter without a mode has mode `in`. `inout` applies to arrays, views and structs; an `inout` parameter of an integer, `Bool` or error-set type is diagnosed C2064 [LS-119]. 2. `out` is a parameter mode of kernels (6.13.2). A function writes an array through an `inout` parameter, and an `out` parameter of a function is diagnosed C5001 at the mode [LS-119]. 3. A parameter is assigned, or written through, only when its mode is `inout`: C2060 otherwise [LS-120]. 4. An `inout` argument shall be storage the caller may write: a variable, a field or element of one or a writable view. A read-only argument for an `inout` parameter is diagnosed C2067 [LS-119]. 5. A call supplies exactly one argument for each parameter. Positional arguments come first, then *named arguments*, written `name = value`. Too few or too many arguments are diagnosed C2022; a parameter that receives two arguments is C2062; a name that is not a parameter is C2063; a positional argument after a named one is C2069 [LS-126]. 6. An `inout` argument shall not overlap any other argument of the same call, read-only or writable. An overlap known during translation is diagnosed C5010; other overlaps are checked when the call is made (paragraph 13). Read-only arguments may overlap each other [LS-121]. 7. An argument that is a module-level variable, or a view of one, shall not be passed in any mode to a function that writes that variable, directly or through any function it calls. A function writes a module-level variable when it assigns it, or calls a function that does, directly or through any chain of calls in the program. A call that breaks this rule is diagnosed C5012 at the argument [LS-122]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.9.5 Parameters and arguments (part 3)
chunks.content: 8. An `in` argument is read-only for the duration of the call. A scalar is passed by value. For an array or struct, whether the function receives a copy or a reference cannot be observed, because constraints 6 and 7 rule out every write that could show the difference [LS-119, LS-122]. 9. An `inout` argument is passed by reference: every write the function makes is visible to the caller when the call returns [LS-119]. 10. Named arguments are matched to the parameters of the same name and evaluated in the order they are written, like all arguments (6.2.4) [LS-126]. 11. When a call is made, after its arguments are evaluated and before fuel is charged, its *entry checks* run in this order, and the first that fails is the fault: the permission of each view, the element type and rank, the binding and agreement of shapes and the overlap of `inout` arguments. A handle argument is not among them: passing a handle does not check it, and a handle that is not valid faults with `E_STALE_HANDLE` at its first dereference in the callee (6.14.4) [LS-123]. **Faults**

chunks.title: 6.9.5 Parameters and arguments (part 4)
6.9.5 Parameters and arguments (part 5)
6.9.5 Parameters and arguments (part 6)
6.9.6 Structs
chunks.content: #### 6.9.6 Structs A struct groups named fields of fixed types into one value. A struct declaration names the type and its fields; a struct value is made by calling the type's name like a function, with one argument for each field. A field is read and written with `.` (6.7.4): `p.x`, `o.left.v`, `b.cells[1]`. The struct type itself, its values and its copying are described in 6.3.6. **Syntax** ```ebnf struct_decl = "struct" IDENT "{" { field } "}" ; field = type IDENT ";" ; call = IDENT [ "." IDENT ] "(" [ args ] ")" ; ``` A constructor is a `call` (6.7.4) whose callee names a struct type. **Constraints** 1. The fields of a struct shall have distinct names: C3001 at the second name [LS-112]. 2. The types a field may have, and the rule that a struct does not contain itself, are stated in 6.3.6. 3. A constructor supplies every field exactly once, by position in declaration order or by name, under the rules of 6.9.5, constraint 5. A missing field is diagnosed C2020 at the constructor; extra arguments are C2022 [LS-77]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.9.6 Structs (part 2)
6.9.6 Structs (part 3)
6.9.7 Error sets
6.9.7 Error sets (part 2)
6.10 Statements
chunks.content:
### 6.10 Statements

A statement is one step of a program. The statements of a block run one after another, in the order written. Every statement either ends with `;` or is a braced construct such as `if` or `while`, and the bodies of all compound statements are blocks in braces. A statement has no value: assignment, `++` and `--` are statements (6.7.14), so an assignment cannot appear inside a condition.

chunks.title: 6.10.1 Blocks and simple statements
chunks.content: #### 6.10.1 Blocks and simple statements A *block* is a sequence of statements in braces. It may stand anywhere a statement may, and it starts a new scope: a name declared in it is visible from its declaration to the closing brace (6.2.3). A *simple statement* is a call, an assignment or an increment, followed by `;`. **Syntax** ```ebnf block = "{" { statement } "}" ; statement = block | const_decl | var_decl | view_decl | simple_stmt ";" | discard | print_stmt | if_stmt | [ IDENT ":" ] loop_stmt | switch_stmt | jump_stmt | defer_stmt | assert_stmt | static_assert | reduce_stmt ; simple_stmt = place assign_op expr | place ( "++" | "--" ) | [ "try" ] call ; ``` **Constraints** 1. There is no empty statement. A `;` where a statement is expected, as in `if (c);` or after the closing brace of a compound statement, is diagnosed C1040 [LS-163]. 2. Only these stand as statements: a declaration, a call (with `try` where its result is an error union, 6.11), an assignment or compound assignment, `++` or `--`, a discard `_ = expr`, a print statement, the compound statements of this clause, and, in a kernel, a `reduce` statement (6.13.5). Any other expression followed by `;`, such as `x + 1;`, is diagnosed C4012 at its first character. A type followed by a keyword where a name is expected, as in `I64 do = 1;`, is also C4012, at the type [LS-167]. **Semantics** 3. The statements of a block run in order. A block ends when its last statement completes, or earlier through `return`, `break`, `continue`, `try` or a fault; the deferred statements of 6.10.7 run when it ends other than by a fault [LS-163]. **Examples**

chunks.title: 6.10.1 Blocks and simple statements (part 2)
6.10.2 The if statement
6.10.3 The while statement
chunks.content: #### 6.10.3 The while statement `while` runs a block for as long as a condition stays true. The condition is tested before each iteration, so the block may not run at all. **Syntax** ```ebnf while_stmt = "while" "(" expr ")" block ; ``` **Constraints** 1. The condition shall be in parentheses and the body shall be a block: C1043. The condition has type `Bool` (C2002) [LS-169]. **Semantics** 2. The condition is evaluated. When it is `true` the body runs and the statement repeats; when it is `false` the statement ends. Each iteration is charged fuel (5.2.4), so a loop that does not end stops at the entry's fuel allowance when it has one (5.2.4) [LS-169]. **Examples** 3. This example shows a loop that counts: ```cint while_count.ci I64 n = 1; while (n < 100) { n *= 3; } "{n}\n"; ``` ```text 243 ```

chunks.title: 6.10.4 The for statement
chunks.content: #### 6.10.4 The for statement `for` has two forms. The *range form*, `for i in 0..n`, runs a block once for each integer of a range, which is the common case. The *C form*, `for (init; condition; update)`, is C's loop, for iteration that the range form does not express. **Syntax** ```ebnf for_stmt = "for" IDENT "in" range block | "for" "(" for_init ";" expr ";" simple_stmt ")" block ; range = expr ( ".." | "..=" ) expr [ "by" expr ] ; for_init = type IDENT "=" expr | simple_stmt ; ``` **Constraints** 1. In both forms the body shall be a block, and in the C form the header shall be in parentheses: C1043 [LS-170]. 2. In the range form, the bounds have type `I64`; a literal bound takes that type. A bound of another type is diagnosed C2001; a conversion, as in `for i in 0..(n as I64)`, gives it the type `I64` [LS-172]. 3. The loop variable of the range form is read-only in the body: an assignment to it is diagnosed C2052 [LS-173]. 4. The step after `by` shall be a constant expression other than 0: C2053 [LS-175]. 5. In the C form, `for_init` declares a variable or is a simple statement, the condition has type `Bool`, and the update is a simple statement [LS-170]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.10.4 The for statement (part 2)
6.10.4 The for statement (part 3)
6.10.5 The switch statement
chunks.content: #### 6.10.5 The switch statement `switch` selects one of several blocks of statements by the value of an integer, `Bool` or error value. A case lists single values and inclusive ranges. Control does not pass from one case to the next unless the case ends with `fallthrough;`, and every value of the type is handled, by a case or by `default`. **Syntax** ```ebnf switch_stmt = "switch" "(" expr ")" "{" { case_clause } [ default_clause ] "}" ; case_clause = "case" case_item { "," case_item } ":" statement { statement } ; case_item = or_expr [ "..=" or_expr ] ; default_clause = "default" ":" statement { statement } ; ``` **Constraints** 1. The value tested, the *scrutinee*, has an integer type, `Bool` or an error-set type. Another type is diagnosed C4026 [LS-177]. 2. A case item is a constant expression (6.8) or an inclusive range `lo..=hi` of constant expressions, of the scrutinee's type. An item that is not constant is diagnosed C6004. A half-open range `lo..hi` is diagnosed C4022, and a range with `lo > hi` is C4024 [LS-177]. 3. No value shall appear in two items of one `switch`: C4021 at the second of the two items [LS-181]. 4. A case clause shall have at least one statement: C4023 at its `case`. Values that share a body are listed in one clause, `case 1, 3:` [LS-179]. 5. A `switch` shall have a `default` clause or cover every value of the scrutinee's type: every value of an error set, both values of `Bool` or the full range of an integer type. Otherwise it is diagnosed C4020 at `switch` [LS-182]. 6. `default` shall be the last clause and appear at most once: C4025 [LS-183]. 7. `fallthrough;` shall be the last statement of a clause that another clause follows: C4014 otherwise [LS-178]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.10.5 The switch statement (part 2)
6.10.6 break, continue and labels
6.10.7 defer and errdefer
chunks.content: #### 6.10.7 defer and errdefer `defer` schedules a statement to run when the enclosing block ends, so that cleanup is written next to the setup it undoes. `errdefer` schedules a statement that runs only when the function returns an error. Neither runs after a fault: a fault stops the program where it happens (5.2.3). **Syntax** ```ebnf defer_stmt = ( "defer" | "errdefer" ) ( block | simple_stmt ";" | discard ) ; ``` **Constraints** 1. A deferred statement shall not contain a `return`, `try`, `break` or `continue` that would leave it: C4030. A `break` or `continue` of a loop inside the deferred statement is permitted [LS-187]. 2. A deferred statement may consume an error union with `catch` or `_ =` (6.11); `try` is excluded by constraint 1 [LS-320]. 3. `errdefer` appears only where an error can leave its block: in a function whose result is an error union, and in a test (6.15.3). Elsewhere it could not run and is diagnosed C4031: in a function or kernel whose result is not an error union, at the top level of a script, and inside a deferred statement [LS-322]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.10.7 defer and errdefer (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. `defer` schedules its statement to run when the enclosing block ends by reaching its closing brace, by `return`, `break` or `continue` or by `try` passing an error on. The statements deferred in one block run in the reverse of the order in which they were scheduled [LS-185]. 5. A deferred statement reads its variables when it runs, not when it is scheduled [LS-186]. 6. `return expr;` evaluates `expr`, then runs the pending deferred statements, then returns the value of `expr`. A deferred statement cannot change the value returned [LS-316]. 7. A `defer` in a loop body is scheduled in each iteration and runs when that iteration's block ends, including by `continue` or `break` [LS-318]. 8. A deferred statement scheduled inside a `catch (e) { ... }` block runs when that block ends [LS-319]. 9. At the top level of a script, a deferred statement runs when the script's entry ends normally, by reaching the end of the script or by `return;` [LS-321]. 10. `errdefer` runs only when the function ends by returning an error, through `return .name;` or through `try` or when an error leaves a test (6.15.3). Such statements run together with the deferred statements of the same blocks, in reverse order of scheduling. No form of `errdefer` gives access to the error [LS-189]. 11. Running a deferred statement charges no fuel of its own; the calls and loop iterations inside it are charged as anywhere else (5.2.4). A fault inside a deferred statement is an ordinary fault, at its own position, with the call stack of the function that scheduled it [LS-317]. 12. Deferred statements do not run after a fault. A fault ends the entry at once, and its fault record describes the state at the fault (5.2.3) [LS-188]. **Examples**

chunks.title: 6.10.7 defer and errdefer (part 3)
6.10.7 defer and errdefer (part 4)
6.10.8 The return statement
chunks.content: #### 6.10.8 The return statement `return` ends the current function and gives its result. At the top level of a script it ends the script, and in a test it ends the test. **Syntax** ```ebnf return_stmt = "return" [ expr ] ";" ; ``` **Constraints** 1. `return;` appears in a function whose result is `void` or `E!void`, in a test, and at the top level of a script. `return expr;` appears in a function with any other result. Any other combination is diagnosed C2066 [LS-190]. 2. In a function whose result is `E!T`, `expr` is either a value of type `T` or a value of the error set `E` (6.11.2) [LS-190]. **Semantics** 3. `return` runs the pending deferred statements (6.10.7) and ends the function, giving the value of `expr` to the caller [LS-190]. 4. At the top level of a script, `return;` ends the script's entry normally. In a test, `return;` ends the test as if its body had completed (6.15.3) [LS-190]. **Examples** 5. `return;` ends a script early: ```cint return_script.ci defer { "script ends\n"; } "before\n"; return; "not reached\n"; ``` ```text before script ends ```

chunks.title: 6.10.9 assert and static_assert
chunks.content: #### 6.10.9 assert and static_assert `assert` checks a condition when the program runs and stops it with a fault when the condition is false. `static_assert` checks a condition during translation. When the condition of `assert` is a comparison, the fault record holds both compared values, so the report shows what the values were, not only that the check failed. **Syntax** ```ebnf assert_stmt = "assert" "(" expr [ "," STRING { STRING } ] ")" ";" ; static_assert = "static_assert" "(" expr [ "," STRING ] ")" ";" ; ``` **Constraints** 1. The condition has type `Bool`: C2002 [LS-191]. 2. The condition of `static_assert` is a constant expression (6.8). When it is `false`, the program is diagnosed C6010 [LS-192]. **Semantics** 3. `assert` evaluates its condition. When it is `true`, the statement completes. When it is `false`, the program faults `E_ASSERT`. The message, including any hole in it, is not evaluated and is not part of the fault record [LS-191]. 4. `assert` is checked in every build and every program; no option removes it [LS-191]. **Faults** 5. The fault `E_ASSERT` is raised by `assert` when its condition is `false`. The record holds the operation identifier `assert.checked.bool`. When the condition is a comparison, its operands are the two compared values, with their types; otherwise it has no operands. It has no exact result and no limit. Its position is the first character of the condition [LS-191]. **Examples** 6. A failed comparison shows both sides: ```cint assert_fail.ci I64 total = 7 * 6; assert(total == 42); "ok\n"; assert(total < 40, "total is too large"); "not reached\n"; ```

chunks.title: 6.10.9 assert and static_assert (part 2)
chunks.content:
```text
ok
fault[E_ASSERT]: assertion failed
  --> assert_fail.ci:4:8
   |
 4 | assert(total < 40, "total is too large");
   |        ^ assert.checked.bool
   |
   = operation: assert.checked.bool
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 42
   = operand: I64 40
   = exact:   none
   = limit:   none
   ...
```

7. A static assertion that fails stops translation:

```cint assert_static.ci
const I64 SLOTS = 4;
static_assert(SLOTS * 2 == 9, "eight slots expected");
"x\n";
```

```text
error[C6010]: compile-time evaluation rule
  --> assert_static.ci:2:1
   |
 2 | static_assert(SLOTS * 2 == 9, "eight slots expected");
   | ^
```

**Notes**

8. C's `assert` is removed when `NDEBUG` is defined, and a failure prints only the text of the condition. A cint `assert` stays in every program, and its record holds the values compared.

chunks.title: 6.10.10 Print statements
chunks.content: #### 6.10.10 Print statements A string literal standing as a statement prints itself. Each hole `{...}` in it is replaced by the text of the value inside, as 7.5 describes. Printing is the only output a program has, and its bytes are part of the program's outcome: the same on every implementation, operating system and locale. **Syntax** ```ebnf print_stmt = STRING { STRING } ";" ; ``` **Constraints** 1. A kernel body shall not contain a print statement: C5020 (6.13.3) [LS-196]. **Semantics** 2. A print statement writes the formatted bytes of its string literals, in order, to the program's output. Adjacent literals form one statement [LS-193]. 3. No newline is added. The bytes written are exactly the UTF-8 bytes of the formatted text, and a line feed is written as one byte, 10, on every operating system [LS-194]. 4. The text of each hole is the same on every locale, operating system and executor, as 7.5.1 states. 5. Printing is an effect of the entry: a recording of a run holds the bytes printed, and replay reproduces them (8.4) [LS-196]. 6. 7.5.1 gives the order in which the holes of a statement are evaluated, and what is written when one of them faults. **Examples** 7. Adjacent literals form one statement, and no newline is added between statements: ```cint print_adjacent.ci I64 n = 7; "line one, " "n = {n}\n"; "no newline here, "; "{{braces}}\n"; ``` ```text line one, n = 7 no newline here, {braces} ``` 8. A fault in a hole stops the statement before it writes anything: ```cint print_fault.ci I8 x = 100; "start\n"; "x = {x}, doubled = {x + x}\n"; ```

chunks.title: 6.10.10 Print statements (part 2)
chunks.content:
```text
start
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> print_fault.ci:3:24
   |
 3 | "x = {x}, doubled = {x + x}\n";
   |                        ^ add.checked.i8
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i8
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I8 100
   = operand: I8 100
   = exact:   200
   = limit:   I8 127
```

chunks.title: 6.11 Errors and faults
chunks.content:
### 6.11 Errors and faults

A program meets two kinds of failure. An *error* is an expected outcome that the program handles: bad input, a full buffer, an account that would be overdrawn. A function reports one by returning a value of an error set, and its caller must deal with it. A *fault* is the stop of a run at an operation that cannot give a correct result (3.9), such as an overflow or an index outside an array: the operation stops the program, and no program code can catch it (5.2.3). This clause defines how errors are returned and handled, and how an error differs from a fault.

An error is a value of an error set (6.9.7), returned by a function whose result type is an error union (6.11.2). Returning it is an ordinary return: the caller receives it, and no other code runs on the way except the deferred statements of the returning function (6.10.7) [LS-128]. 2. A fault is raised by an operation; no statement raises one by name. Program code cannot construct, catch, inspect or resume a fault; a fault ends the entry with its fault record (5.2.3), and an `expect_fault` test only observes it (6.15.3) [LS-128]. 3. Arithmetic that may legitimately fail, such as a division by a value that may be 0, is written with a *result form*, which returns an error where the plain operator would fault: `div_result(a, b)`, `add_result(a, b)` and the other forms of 6.7.12, and the conversion `x as? T` of 6.6. Their errors are values of the built-in error set `ArithError` and are handled as any other error [IM-120].

6.12 Arrays and views
chunks.content:
### 6.12 Arrays and views

An array holds a fixed number of elements of one type, and a view is a typed, shaped window onto the elements of an array. Arrays are how a program holds data in bulk; views are how it hands that data to functions and kernels without copying it. This section covers declaring arrays (6.12.1), reaching one element (6.12.2), taking part of an array as a view (6.12.3), passing views to functions (6.12.4), the rules for copying between arrays and views (6.12.5), and arrays declared at module level (6.12.6). The built-in operations on arrays and views, such as `len`, `extent`, `copy`, `transpose`, `reverse` and `reshape`, are in 7.4.

The examples of this section declare their arrays inside functions, most often inside `void main()` (5.1.2).

chunks.title: 6.12.1 Array objects and initializers
6.12.1 Array objects and initializers (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The element type of an array is an integer type, a fixed-point type (6.3.2), `Bool`, an error set (6.3.7), a struct type or a handle type (6.14). The rank of an array or view type is 1 to 4: an array or view type with more than four extents is diagnosed C9102 at its `[` [V-1, V-2, M-24]. 2. Each extent of a declared array is an `I64` expression whose value is known when the declaration runs: in a function body, an `I64` constant expression, a size parameter of the function (6.9.5), or an expression of constants and size parameters; in a module-level declaration and in a kernel body, a constant expression. Any other extent is diagnosed C6004, and in a kernel body C9102 (6.13.3). A constant extent below 0 is diagnosed C2015 [LS-62]. 3. The extent `_` accepts any extent. It is written only in the type of a parameter or of a view variable (6.12.4); in the type of a declared array, such as `I64[_] a;`, it is diagnosed C9102. `I64[]` is shorthand for `I64[_]` [LS-66]. 4. An array literal that initializes an array shall have exactly as many items as the extent it fills, at every level of nesting (C2011). A trailing comma is permitted. A brace list such as `{1, 2}` is not an array literal and is a syntax error (C1050) [LS-67]. 5. `==`, `!=` and the ordering comparisons are not defined on arrays: comparing two arrays is diagnosed C2013 [LS-71]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.12.2 Indexing
chunks.content: #### 6.12.2 Indexing An index expression names one element: `a[i]` in an array of rank 1, `m[i, j]` in an array of rank 2, and so on. Indices count from 0. Every index is checked against its extent, and an index outside the array stops the program with a fault instead of reaching other storage. **Syntax** ```ebnf postfix_expr = ( call | primary ) { "[" index_list "]" | "." IDENT } ; index_list = index { "," index } ; ``` `call` is in 6.7.4 and `primary` in 6.7.3. An `index` is an `expr`, or a range, which makes a slice (6.12.3). **Constraints** 1. Every index has type `I64`. A literal index is typed `I64`. An index of another integer type is diagnosed C2001; `as I64` (6.6) converts it [LS-64]. 2. An index expression gives at most as many indices as the rank of the array or view it indexes. More indices, as in `a[0, 1]` for an array `a` of rank 1, are diagnosed C9102 at the `[` [LS-65]. 3. Indexing the result of a partial index directly, `m[i][j]`, is diagnosed C2010. The element is written `m[i, j]` [LS-65]. 4. An element of a view without write permission is not assignable. Assigning to an element of an `in` parameter is diagnosed C2060, and assigning to an element of an `in` view variable is diagnosed C9102 [M-27]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.12.2 Indexing (part 2)
6.12.2 Indexing (part 3)
6.12.3 Slicing and index bases
chunks.content: #### 6.12.3 Slicing and index bases A range in an index position takes a *slice*: a view of part of an array, sharing the array's storage. `a[2..5]` is the three elements `a[2]`, `a[3]` and `a[4]`; writing through a slice writes the array. A step, `by k`, takes every `k`-th element and a negative step runs backward. **Syntax** ```ebnf index_list = index { "," index } ; index = expr | [ expr ] ".." [ expr ] [ "by" expr ] | [ expr ] "..=" expr [ "by" expr ] ; ``` An index expression with at least one range in it is a slice. **Constraints** 1. The bounds of a range have type `I64`, as an index does (C2001) [LS-64]. 2. The step after `by` is an integer constant expression other than 0. A step that is not a constant, or is 0, is diagnosed C2053 [LS-161]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.12.3 Slicing and index bases (part 2)
chunks.content: 3. A slice is a view of the storage of the expression it is taken from. Taking a slice copies no element. The slice has the permission of that expression: a slice of an `in` view is read-only [LS-161, LS-162]. 4. In each dimension, an index removes the dimension and a range keeps it. `m[.., j]` is column `j` of a rank-2 array, a rank-1 view whose consecutive elements are a row's length apart; `m[i, 1..3]` is part of row `i` [LS-161]. 5. With a positive step `k` (1 when `by` is absent), `a[lo..hi]` holds the elements at `lo`, `lo + k`, `lo + 2k` and so on, below `hi`. `a[lo..=hi]` is `a[lo..hi + 1]`, with the addition exact. An omitted first bound is 0 and an omitted second bound is the extent, so `a[..]` is the whole dimension [LS-161, IM-186]. 6. With a negative step `k`, the range runs downward from its first bound: `a[f..g by k]` holds the elements at `f`, `f + k` and so on, above `g` and `a[f..=g by k]` includes `g`. An omitted first bound is the last index, `n - 1` for extent `n` and an omitted second bound runs through index 0. `a[.. by -1]` is the whole dimension reversed [LS-161]. 7. For a dimension of extent `n`, a range with a positive step is valid when `0 <= lo <= hi <= n` after omitted bounds are filled in. A range with a negative step is valid when `-1 <= g <= f <= n - 1` for `f..g`, and when `0 <= g <= f + 1 <= n` for `f..=g`. A valid range may be empty: `a[3..3]`, `a[3..=2]`, `a[n..]`, and a reversed range whose bounds meet, are empty slices, not faults [LS-161, LS-162]. 8. Every array and view is indexed from 0 in every dimension. The first element of a slice has index 0, whatever its position in the array it was taken from: in `in I64[_] v = a[2..5];`, `v[0]` is `a[2]` [LS-64, V-7]. **Faults**
