chunks.title: 6.12.4 Views as parameters
chunks.content:
#### 6.12.4 Views as parameters

An array passed to a function arrives as a view: the function reads, and with `inout` writes, the caller's elements in place, and nothing is copied. A view can also be a local variable, declared with `in` or `inout` (6.9.1). Every view carries its extents, so a function written for `in I64[_]` works on a whole array, a slice, a row or a column, and checks every index against the extent of what it received.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.12.4 Views as parameters (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A view consists of: the storage it refers to; its element type; its rank `r`, from 1 to 4 (6.12.1); for each dimension `k`, an extent `n[k]` and a *stride* `s[k]`, the signed distance in elements between consecutive indices of that dimension; its *origin* `o`, the position in the storage of the element whose indices are all 0; and its *permission*, read or write, where write also permits reading. Strides and the origin are counted in elements, whatever the element type [V-1, V-3, M-24]. 2. The element of a view at indices `(i[0], ..., i[r-1])` is the element at position `o + i[0] * s[0] + ... + i[r-1] * s[r-1]` of its storage, computed exactly [V-4, M-24a]. 3. A declared array is a view of its own storage with origin 0 and row-major strides: for `I32[3, 4] m`, the strides are 4 and 1. A slice, a partial index, `transpose`, `reverse` and `reshape` (7.4) each give a new view of the same storage, with other extents, strides and origin and copy no element. A stride may be negative, as in a reversed view [V-10, V-16]. 4. `reshape` gives a view only when the new shape addresses the same elements in the same row-major order as the view it is applied to; otherwise an implementation refuses the program (3.16, 7.4) [V-11]. 5. A view is formed only if every element it can address lies within its storage, and every access through a formed view checks each index against its extent (6.12.2, 6.12.3). No view reaches storage outside the array it was taken from [V-5, V-6, M-25]. 6. Two views of the same storage see the same elements: a write through one is read through every other at once [V-10]. 7. A view has at most the permission of the expression it is taken from. An `in` parameter or view variable has read permission and an `inou

6.12.5 Aliasing and copies
chunks.content: #### 6.12.5 Aliasing and copies Elements move between arrays only by an explicit copy: an array declared with an initializer, an array assignment or `copy`. A copy requires equal shapes, and its source and destination must not overlap unless they are the same view. When they might overlap, the program copies through storage it declares; no implementation inserts a hidden temporary. **Constraints** 1. The source and destination of an array assignment, an array initializer and `copy(dst, src)` shall have the same shape. A difference known at translation is diagnosed C2012 [LS-70]. 2. When the source and destination of an array assignment or a `copy` provably overlap at translation, and are not the same view, the program is diagnosed C5010 [LS-70]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.12.5 Aliasing and copies (part 2)
chunks.content: 3. A declaration with a type and no permission keyword declares a new array. If its initializer is an array or a view, the elements are copied into the new array, and a write to the new array after the declaration does not reach the source: `I32[8, 8] left = m[.., 0..8];` is a copy. A declaration with `in` or `inout` declares a view, which shares the storage of its initializer: `inout I32[_, _] left = m[.., 0..8];` writes `m` [LS-69]. 4. Array assignment `b = a`, where `b` is an array, a view with write permission or a slice of one, and `copy(dst, src)` copy every element of the source to the destination in row-major order [LS-70]. 5. The run-time checks of a copy follow the evaluation of the destination place and the source in their order (6.2.4). The shape check comes first, then the overlap check, and only then is any element written. A copy that faults writes no element [IM-187, LS-70]. 6. The source and destination of a copy shall be shown disjoint, or be exactly the same view. They are shown disjoint when either has no elements, when the lowest and highest positions each addresses do not overlap, or when both are views of one storage whose strides share a common factor `g` of at least 2 and whose origins differ modulo `g`. SPEC-02P.1 gives the procedure in full. A copy of a view onto exactly the same view has no effect. Any other pair faults `E_ALIAS` [LS-70]. 7. To move data within one array between places that may overlap, a program copies through an array it declares. No implementation stages a copy through hidden storage [LS-70]. 8. Arguments bound to `inout` parameters of a function call follow the overlap rule of 6.9.5. **Faults**

chunks.title: 6.13 Kernels
chunks.content:
### 6.13 Kernels

A kernel is a function written for one point of an iteration space. A *dispatch* runs it once for every point, each run a *work-item*, over arrays passed as arguments. Every work-item reads the values its arguments held before the dispatch and writes only its own part of the outputs, so no work-item can see another, and the outputs are the same whatever order the work-items run in. If every work-item succeeds, all outputs appear at once; if any faults, none does.

This section states the meaning of a kernel and of a dispatch: declarations (6.13.1), parameters (6.13.2), the body (6.13.3), the dispatch statement (6.13.4), reductions (6.13.5) and the reference meaning that every executor reproduces (6.13.6). The executors of cint 0.2.0 that run kernels, and what each of them shall do to give that meaning, are in SPEC-02P.1.

chunks.title: 6.13.1 Kernel declarations
6.13.1 Kernel declarations (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. Every parameter has a mode, `in`, `out` or `inout`; a parameter without one is a syntax error (C1050). A kernel has no result type: a type before the kernel's name is diagnosed C1010 [LS-244]. 2. Each size parameter appears alone as an extent of at least one array parameter. A size parameter that appears in no such extent is diagnosed C2065 [K-5]. 3. A kernel has at least one parameter of mode `out` or `inout`. A kernel without one is diagnosed C9102 at its name [K-3]. 4. An array parameter has an integer or fixed-point element type, and a scalar parameter an integer or fixed-point type. A parameter of any other type, such as `Bool` or a struct, is diagnosed C5028 [LS-246]. 5. A scalar parameter has mode `in` or `out`. A scalar `inout` parameter is diagnosed C2064 [K-2]. 6. With an over clause of `d` variables, every array parameter of mode `out` or `inout` has rank `d` or more, and its first `d` extents are the over clause's extents, written the same way and in the same order. A parameter of lower rank or with other leading extents is diagnosed C9102 at its name [K-8]. 7. Each extent of an array parameter, each over extent and each side of a `where` constraint is a shape expression: a size parameter, a decimal literal or a size parameter plus or minus a decimal literal. A `where` constraint compares two of them with `==`, `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=`. Any other extent or comparison, such as `I64[n * 2]` or `where n != 0`, is diagnosed C9102 [K-1]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.13.1 Kernel declarations (part 3)
6.13.1 Kernel declarations (part 4)
6.13.2 Parameter modes and shapes
chunks.content:
#### 6.13.2 Parameter modes and shapes

The mode of a kernel parameter says what the body may do with it. An `in` array is read, an `out` array is written, and an `inout` array is both read and written; a scalar `in` is a value shared by every work-item, and a scalar `out` receives the result of a reduction (6.13.5). When a dispatch begins, the size parameters are bound from the arguments, every extent is checked, and the arguments are checked for overlap, before any work-item runs.

| Mode | Kind | The body may | The body may not | Argument |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `in` | array | read any element | write | a view, with read or write permission |
| `in` | scalar | read the value, which is the same for every work-item | assign it | a value of exactly the parameter's type |
| `out` | array | write the elements of its owned block | read | a view with write permission |
| `out` | scalar | be the target of one `reduce` statement | read or assign it | a variable of exactly the parameter's type |
| `inout` | array | read any element; write the elements of its owned block | write other elements | a view with write permission |

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 6.13.2 Parameter modes and shapes (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. An `in` parameter is not assigned: a write to an element of an `in` array or to a scalar `in` is diagnosed C2060 [K-2]. 2. The body does not read an array `out` parameter, and it does not read or assign a scalar `out` parameter except through its `reduce` statement. Such a read or assignment is diagnosed C9102 [K-2]. 3. An array argument has the element type and the rank of its parameter (C2001). An argument for an `out` or `inout` array has write permission (C2067). When the extents of every argument are known at translation, the checks of paragraph 6 run then, and a mismatch is diagnosed C2012 [K-2, K-4, K-7]. 4. An argument for a scalar `in` parameter has exactly the parameter's type (C2001); a literal argument takes the parameter's type. An argument for a scalar `out` parameter is a variable of exactly the parameter's type: another type is diagnosed C2001, and an argument that is not a variable, such as a literal, is diagnosed C2067 [K-2, K-4]. 5. An argument for an `out` or `inout` parameter that provably overlaps another array argument at translation, such as the same array passed twice, is diagnosed C5010 [LS-245]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.13.2 Parameter modes and shapes (part 3)
chunks.content: 6. Size parameters are bound in two passes over the array parameters, in declaration order and, within each, dimension by dimension. The first pass binds each size parameter at its first occurrence alone as an extent, to the argument's extent there. The second pass evaluates every extent with checked `I64` arithmetic and compares it with the argument's extent; the first difference faults. For `kernel k[n](in I64[n + 1] a, out I64[n] b)` with `a` of extent 5 and `b` of extent 3, the first pass binds `n` to 3 from `b`, and the second reports `a`, whose extent should be 4 [K-6]. 7. After binding, the constraints of the `where` clause are evaluated in written order, and the first that is false faults [K-1]. 8. `in` arguments may overlap each other, and one view may be passed to several `in` parameters [A-1]. 9. The elements of every `out` or `inout` argument shall be disjoint from the elements of every other array argument of the same dispatch, whatever its mode [A-2]. 10. Overlap is decided by the tests of 6.12.5, paragraph 6, given in full in SPEC-02P.1. A pair those tests show disjoint is accepted; every other pair, whether it overlaps or the tests cannot decide, faults `E_ALIAS`. Some pairs that share no element therefore fault. The same tests apply to every dispatch, whether cint code or a host program issues it, and nothing a program states about its arguments counts as evidence that they are disjoint [A-3]. 11. Every view bound to an `out` or `inout` parameter shall address a distinct element for each index tuple. A view that fails the test of SPEC-02P.1 for this property faults `E_ALIAS` [A-4, M-26]. 12. These checks run when the dispatch begins, before any work-item. A fault here is in the *entry phase* of the dispatch: its address has a dispatch numbe

chunks.title: 6.13.2 Parameter modes and shapes (part 4)
chunks.content:
**Faults**

13. The fault `E_SHAPE` is raised by an argument extent that differs from the extent the second pass computes. The fault record holds the operation identifier `bind.shape`; three operands, the parameter's position counted from 0, the dimension counted from 0 and the argument's extent, all `I64`; no exact result; and the computed extent as the limit, an `I64`. Its position is the kernel name of the dispatch [K-6].
14. The fault `E_OVERFLOW` is raised when an extent expression `n + c` or `n - c` leaves the range of `I64`, with the operation identifier `add.checked.i64` or `sub.checked.i64`. A computed extent below 0 faults `E_SHAPE` [K-6].
15. The fault `E_SHAPE` is raised by a false `where` constraint. The fault record holds the operation identifier `bind.where`; three operands, the constraint's position in the clause counted from 0 and the values of its left and right sides, all `I64`; no exact result and no limit [K-1].
16. The fault `E_ALIAS` is raised by a pair of arguments not shown disjoint. The fault record holds the operation identifier `bind.alias` and two `I64` operands: the position of the `out` or `inout` parameter and the position of the other parameter. It has no exact result and no limit [A-3].

6.13.3 The body
chunks.content:
#### 6.13.3 The body

A kernel body is ordinary sequential code with three kinds of limit: it writes outputs only at its own work-item's indices, it writes every element it owns, and it does nothing whose effect another work-item or the rest of the program could see while the dispatch runs.

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 6.13.3 The body (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. An over variable is not assigned (C2052) [LS-247]. 2. Every write to an array parameter of mode `out` or `inout` has the over variables, in order, as its first indices. Any further indices address the owned block and may be any `I64` expressions. A write of another form is diagnosed C5031 [LS-248, K-10]. 3. Every element of the owned block of every array `out` parameter is written on every path through the body that completes. A kernel satisfies this rule when its writes fit one of two patterns; a kernel whose writes fit neither is diagnosed C5031 [LS-248, K-10a]: - a write whose indices are exactly the over variables, executed unconditionally, in both branches of an `if` with an `else`, or in every case of a `switch` with a `default`; - a nest of `for` loops, one for each dimension of the owned block, each over that dimension's full range `0..E` with a bound that is the same for every work-item, whose innermost body writes the element with the loop variables in dimension order, unconditionally and before any `break` or `continue`; the nest itself runs under the conditions of the first pattern. 4. A kernel body does not contain a print statement (C5020), a `defer` statement (C5021), `try` or a value of an error union type (C5022), a dispatch (C5023) or a use of a module-level variable (C5025). Named constants and the built-in operations of clause 7 may be used [LS-250, K-11]. 5. A local array in a kernel body, a *private array*, has constant extents and its number of elements times the width of its element type, counting a `Bool` element as 8 bits, is at most 32,768 bits: at most 512 `I64` elements, or 4,096 `U8` elements. A private array with an extent that is not constant is diagnosed C9102 at that extent, and a private array above this size is diagnos

chunks.title: 6.13.3 The body (part 3)
6.13.3 The body (part 4)
6.13.3 The body (part 5)
6.13.4 Dispatch
chunks.content: #### 6.13.4 Dispatch A dispatch is written like a call statement: the kernel's name and its arguments. It runs every work-item, then publishes the outputs, before the next statement runs. **Syntax** ```ebnf call = IDENT [ "." IDENT ] "(" [ args ] ")" ; ``` A dispatch is a `call` whose callee names a kernel, standing as a statement (6.10.1). `args` is as for any call (6.7.4). **Constraints** 1. A dispatch is a statement and has no value. A dispatch used as an expression is diagnosed C2001, and `try` before a dispatch is diagnosed C2043 [LS-251]. 2. A dispatch is written in sequential code. A dispatch inside a kernel body is diagnosed C5023 (6.13.3). **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.13.4 Dispatch (part 2)
chunks.content: 3. A dispatch runs its kernel's work-items as 6.13.6 defines. It is synchronous: when it completes, the statement after it runs and observes the published outputs [K-14, LS-251]. 4. Every dispatch is *staged*. The work-items write into storage of their own, which the program cannot observe. If the dispatch completes without a fault, every `out` and `inout` array argument and every scalar `out` variable is *published*: given its new elements at once. If the dispatch faults, nothing is published, and every argument and every variable bound to a scalar `out` holds exactly what it held before the dispatch [P-1, LS-251]. 5. No statement after a dispatch can observe some of its outputs updated and others not [P-2]. 6. In a dispatch, an `inout` parameter has copy-in, copy-out meaning. Every read of it, at any index and at any time during the dispatch, gives the element's value from before the dispatch, including a work-item's read of an element it has already written. Elements that no work-item writes keep their values [P-4, LS-251]. 7. A fault in a dispatch ends the entry, as any fault does (5.2.3): no statement of the entry after it runs [K-14]. 8. Every dispatch takes the next *dispatch number* of the entry, from 0 in program order, whether it completes or faults [P-3, LS-288]. 9. A dispatch issued through the host interface makes the same checks in the same order and has the same outcome as the same dispatch written in cint source. SPEC-03P.1 describes that interface [K-15]. **Examples** 10. This example shows copy-in and copy-out. Each work-item but the last copies its right neighbor, and every read sees the value from before the dispatch:

6.13.5 Reductions in kernels
chunks.content:
#### 6.13.5 Reductions in kernels

A reduction combines one value from each work-item into one scalar result: a sum, a count, a minimum or a maximum. It is written as a `reduce` statement whose target is a scalar `out` parameter. Contributions are combined in ascending work-item index, so a reduction whose result depends on order, such as a checked fold, has one result whatever order the work-items ran in.

**Syntax**

```ebnf
reduce_stmt = "reduce" IDENT "=" reduction ";" ;
reduction   = ( "sum" | "sum_wrap" | "sum_sat" | "min" | "max" | "count" ) "(" expr ")"
            | "fold_checked" "(" "add" "," expr "," expr ")" ;
```

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 6.13.5 Reductions in kernels (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A `reduce` statement appears only in a kernel body, and its target is a scalar `out` parameter. A `reduce` statement outside a kernel body, or with another target, such as a local variable, is diagnosed C9102 [R-1]. 2. Each scalar `out` parameter is the target of exactly one `reduce` statement. A `reduce` statement is not inside a loop; it may be inside an `if`. A scalar `out` parameter that is the target of no `reduce` statement, a second `reduce` statement to one target, and a `reduce` statement inside a loop are diagnosed C9102 [R-1, LS-249]. 3. The contribution of `sum(e)` has an integer type, and the target has an integer type. In `fold_checked(add, init, e)`, `e` and `init` have exactly the target's type, and `init` is the same for every work-item. The contribution of `sum_wrap`, `sum_sat`, `min` and `max` has exactly the target's type. The contribution of `count(c)` is a `Bool`, and the target is an `I64`. Another type is diagnosed C2001; a conversion of the contribution, as in `fold_checked(add, 0, x[i] as I64)`, gives it the target's type [LS-249]. 4. For fixed-point contributions, the target of `sum` has the type of the contributions, as 7.3 states for `sum(R, xs)`. A target of another type is diagnosed C9102. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.13.6 Meaning of a dispatch
chunks.content:
#### 6.13.6 Meaning of a dispatch

The meaning of a dispatch is defined by a sequential procedure: check the arguments, run the work-items one at a time in ascending index, combine the reductions, publish. Every executor gives the outcome of this procedure, including on a GPU, where many work-items run at once and several may fault: the fault reported is always the one the procedure reaches first.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.13.6 Meaning of a dispatch (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A dispatch of `N` work-items means the following procedure [X-1]: 1. Run the entry checks of 6.13.2, then charge the dispatch's fuel (paragraph 7). If one fails, that fault is the dispatch's fault; stop. 2. For each work-item index `i` from 0 to `N - 1`, run the body as an independent sequential program, with the over variables set to the index tuple of `i`, fresh local variables, fuel charged to the entry, every read of an `in` or `inout` argument giving its value from before the dispatch, every write to an `out` or `inout` argument going to work-item `i`'s owned block in staging, and each `reduce` statement contributing to its reduction. If a work-item faults, that fault is the dispatch's fault; stop. 3. Complete the reductions and check their results (6.13.5). If one faults, that fault is the dispatch's fault; stop. 4. Publish the outputs (6.13.4). 2. A work-item reads only values from before the dispatch and its own local state, and writes only its own owned blocks in staging. Contributions to reductions and charges of fuel are combined only by the rules of 6.13.5 and paragraph 7. Every order of running the work-items, including running them at the same time, therefore gives the same outputs and the same fault [X-2]. 3. A dispatch has three *phases*: entry (0), work-items (1) and epilogue (2). When more than one fault could occur, the fault of the dispatch is the least by phase, then by work-item index, then by step ordinal. It is the fault the procedure of paragraph 1 reaches first, whichever fault an executor's hardware met first in time [LS-287]. 4. If the fault of a dispatch is at work-item `k`, every work-item with a lower index completed without a fault [R-8]. 5. The record of a fault in a dispatch holds, beyond the fields of every fault record (8.1), the *address* of the fault

chunks.content:
**Examples**

8. Two work-items overflow, at indices 2 and 4. The fault reported is at work-item 2, whichever an executor reached first:

```cint kernel_lowest.ci
kernel square[n](in I32[n] x, out I32[n] y) over [i: n] {
    y[i] = x[i] * x[i];
}

void main() {
    I32[6] x = [1, 2, 50000, 3, 46341, 4];
    I32[6] y;
    square(x, y);
    "{y[0]}\n";
}
```

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> kernel_lowest.ci:2:17
   |
 2 |     y[i] = x[i] * x[i];
   |                 ^ mul.checked.i32
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i32
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I32 50000
   = operand: I32 50000
   = exact:   2500000000
   = limit:   I32 2147483647
   ...
   = address: kernel_lowest.square, dispatch 0, phase 1, work-item 2, step 3
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: kernel_lowest.ci:8:5
   = fuel-consumed: 7 (not part of the fault record)
   ...
```

The step ordinal counts the place `y[i]` as step 0, the two reads of `x[i]` as steps 1 and 2, and the product as step 3. The fuel consumed is 1 for the call of `main` and 6 for the dispatch of six work-items; the body has no loop or call.

**Notes**

9. No output of the faulted dispatch in this example is published: `y` holds what it held before. A host program that runs the entry, or a checkpoint taken after it, observes `y` unchanged (SPEC-03P.1, 8.4).

chunks.title: 6.14 Arenas, pools and handles
chunks.content:
### 6.14 Arenas, pools and handles

An arena and a pool are storage that a program declares once, at module level, with a fixed capacity, and then reuses. An arena hands out runs of elements one after another and takes them all back at once with `reset`. A pool holds single elements in slots, taken with `insert` and given back one at a time with `remove`. The program refers to what it was given through a *handle*. Every use of a handle is checked: a handle whose storage was given back, or that belongs to another arena or pool, faults with `E_STALE_HANDLE` instead of reading other data. Storage is returned only by `remove` and `reset`, never by a free of an address, and no handle is a raw address.

The type forms are in 6.3.8. This section states the declarations (6.14.1), arenas (6.14.2), pools (6.14.3), handles and the stale-handle fault (6.14.4), views of arena storage (6.14.5) and how the frame arena that holds local arrays relates to them (6.14.6).

chunks.title: 6.14.1 Declarations
chunks.content:
#### 6.14.1 Declarations

An arena or a pool is declared at the top level of a module with its element type and its capacity. Functions reach it by its name, or through a parameter of type `Arena(T)` or `Pool(T)`. Handles are ordinary values that can be copied and stored.

**Syntax**

```ebnf
memory_decl = ( "Arena" | "Pool" ) "(" memory_elem "," expr ")" IDENT ";" ;
memory_type = ( "Arena" | "Pool" ) "(" memory_elem ")"
            | "Handle" "(" memory_elem [ "[" [ "_" ] "]" ] ")" ;
memory_elem = INT_TYPE | "Bool" | qualified ;         (* an integer, Bool or struct type *)
```

`memory_decl` is a top-level declaration (6.9.3). `memory_type` is a type (6.3.8).

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 6.14.1 Declarations (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A memory declaration appears at the top level of a module. Inside a function, a test or a block it is diagnosed C4012 at its first token [M-20]. 2. The capacity is a constant expression of type `I64` (6.9.3) whose value is at least 0. A negative capacity is diagnosed C6006 at the capacity [M-20]. 3. The element type `T` of an arena or a pool is an integer type, `Bool` or a struct type [M-19]. 4. A value of type `Arena(T)` or `Pool(T)` is a parameter, or a local variable with an initializer; such a local without an initializer is diagnosed C9102 at its name. It is not stored in a module-level variable, a struct field, an array, an arena or a pool, and it is not returned: each of these is diagnosed C2051 at its type. It is not assigned after its declaration: C2058 at the target of the assignment [M-20b]. 5. The operations that change an arena or a pool, `alloc`, `alloc_result`, `child`, `reset`, `insert`, `insert_result` and `remove`, are applied to a module-level name, a local or an `inout` parameter. Applied to an `in` parameter they are diagnosed C2067 at the receiver, and an assignment through a dereference of an `in` parameter, such as `a[h][0] = 0`, is diagnosed C2060 at its target [M-20b]. 6. A handle has the type that the operation creating it gives: `alloc` gives `Handle(T[])` and `insert` gives `Handle(T)`, where `T` is the element type. A handle of another type where one is required, such as a `Handle(I64[])` given to a pool's `remove`, is diagnosed C2001 at it [M-20a]. 7. Handles, arenas and pools are not compared: `==` and the other comparisons on them are diagnosed C2103 at the left operand [M-20a]. **Semantics**

6.14.1 Declarations (part 4)
6.14.1 Declarations (part 5)
chunks.content:
**Notes**

20. An arena holds one element type. Data of several types that is allocated together goes in a struct element, as in 6.14.2, or in several arenas.

chunks.title: 6.14.2 Arenas
chunks.content: #### 6.14.2 Arenas An arena hands out runs of consecutive elements, each run after the last, and takes them all back at once with `reset`. A run is reached through its handle, as a view of rank 1. A *child* arena is carved out of a parent for allocations that end sooner than the parent's. **Syntax** ```ebnf call = IDENT [ "." IDENT ] "(" [ args ] ")" ; ``` An arena operation is a `call` `a.alloc(n)`, `a.alloc_result(n)`, `a.child(n)` or `a.reset()`, where the name `a` denotes an arena (6.7.4). The dereference `a[h]` is an index expression (6.12.2) whose index is a handle. **Constraints** 1. The argument of `alloc`, `alloc_result` and `child` has type `I64`; another type is diagnosed C2001 [M-19]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.14.2 Arenas (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. An arena of capacity `c` has a *used extent* `u` and a *generation* `g`, both 0 when it is created. Its storage is `c` elements, numbered from 0 [M-14, M-19]. 3. `a.alloc(n)`, for `0 <= n` and `u + n <= c`, gives the run of elements `u` to `u + n - 1`, sets each of them to 0 (every field to 0 for a struct element), and increases `u` by `n`. It returns a handle with slot `u` (the used extent before the allocation), length `n`, generation `g`, the arena's number and kind 1 (6.14.4). `alloc(0)` gives a handle of length 0. An allocation does not move an earlier one [M-14, M-19]. 4. `a.alloc_result(n)` is the result form (3.8) of `alloc`, of type `AllocError!Handle(T[])`. Where `u + n` exceeds `c` for a count `n` of at least 0, it changes nothing and returns `AllocError.full`, the one value of the built-in error set `AllocError` (6.3.7), whose tag is `U16 1`. A negative count faults as for `alloc` [M-19]. 5. `a[h]`, for a handle `h` that is valid in `a` (6.14.4), is the run of `h` as a view of rank 1 whose extent is the handle's length. It has write permission, except where `a` is an `in` parameter, where it has read permission. `a[h][i]` is an element of the run: its index is checked against the run's extent (6.12.2), so no index reaches a neighboring run [M-14a, M-20a]. 6. `a.reset()` increases `g` by 1 and sets `u` to 0. Every handle given before the reset is stale from then on (6.14.4), and the next allocation starts at element 0 [M-14]. 7. `a.child(c)` charges `c` elements to `a` as `a.alloc(c)` does, and faults as it does. It returns a new arena of type `Arena(T)`: its elements are the charged elements of `a`, its element type is that of `a`, its capacity is `c`, its used extent and its generation are 0, and it takes the next arena number (6.14.1). `child` has no result form [M-20, M-13]. 8. Resetting a child does not change its

6.14.3 Pools
chunks.content:
#### 6.14.3 Pools

A pool holds up to its capacity of single elements, each in a *slot*. `insert` stores a value in a free slot and returns a handle to it; `remove` frees the slot. A freed slot is used again, and from then on the handle to its old contents is stale.

**Syntax**

```ebnf
call = IDENT [ "." IDENT ] "(" [ args ] ")" ;
```

A pool operation is a `call` `p.insert(v)`, `p.insert_result(v)` or `p.remove(h)`, where the name `p` denotes a pool (6.7.4). The dereference `p[h]` is an index expression (6.12.2) whose index is a handle.

**Constraints**

1. The argument of `insert` and `insert_result` has the element type `T` of the pool, and that of `remove` has type `Handle(T)`. Another type is diagnosed C2001 [M-20a].

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.14.3 Pools (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. A pool of capacity `c` has the slots 0 to `c - 1`. Each slot is *vacant*, *occupied* or *retired*, and has a generation, a `U64` that starts at 0. In a new pool every slot is vacant [M-15]. 3. `p.insert(v)` stores `v` in a vacant slot, marks the slot occupied and returns a handle with the slot's index, length 1, the slot's generation, the pool's number and kind 2 (6.14.4). The slot is the one most recently vacated by `remove` and not taken since; when there is none, it is the vacant slot of lowest index. The handles a program obtains are therefore fixed by its sequence of operations [M-18, M-12]. 4. `p.insert_result(v)` is the result form (3.8) of `insert`, of type `AllocError!Handle(T)`. When the pool is full it changes nothing and returns `AllocError.full` (6.14.2) [M-19]. 5. A pool is *full* when every slot is occupied or retired [M-19]. 6. `p[h]`, for a handle `h` that is valid in `p` (6.14.4), is the slot's element as a place. It can be read, assigned whole, or have a field read or assigned, as in `bodies[h].mass += 5` [M-20a]. 7. `p.remove(h)` checks `h` as `p[h]` does. It then marks the slot vacant and increases its generation by 1, so `h` and every copy of it are stale from then on [M-15, M-17a]. 8. A generation does not wrap. A `remove` that would set a slot's generation to 2^64 - 1 marks the slot retired instead, and no `insert` takes a retired slot [M-16]. **Faults**

chunks.title: 6.14.3 Pools (part 3)
6.14.3 Pools (part 4)
6.14.4 Handles and stale handles
chunks.content: #### 6.14.4 Handles and stale handles A handle records where its element or run is, and the generation under which it was given. Each use compares it with the arena or pool it is used in. A handle that no longer matches faults with `E_STALE_HANDLE`, and the record says which check failed. **Semantics** 1. A handle has five fields. Its canonical form is 32 bytes, little-endian, with the fields at these offsets [M-12]: | Offset | Field | Type | Arena handle | Pool handle | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | slot | `U64` | the first element of the run | the slot index | | 8 | length | `I64` | the number of elements of the run | 1 | | 16 | generation | `U64` | the arena's generation at the allocation | the slot's generation at the insertion | | 24 | container | `U32` | the arena's number | the pool's number | | 28 | kind | `U8` | 1 | 2 | | 29 | reserved | 3 bytes | 0 | 0 |

chunks.title: 6.14.4 Handles and stale handles (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. The *null handle* has every field 0, and it is the only handle of kind 0. A decoder of the canonical form rejects 32 bytes whose reserved bytes are not 0 or whose kind is not 0, 1 or 2 [M-12]. 3. A handle `h` is *valid* in an arena `a` when all of these hold: `a`, and every arena that `a` was carved from, is not retired; `h` has `a`'s number as its container and kind 1; `h`'s generation equals `a`'s generation; `h`'s length is at least 0; and `h`'s slot plus its length, computed without overflow, is at most `a`'s used extent [M-14]. 4. A handle `h` is valid in a pool `p` when `h` has `p`'s number as its container and kind 2, its slot is below `p`'s capacity, that slot is occupied, and the slot's generation equals `h`'s generation [M-15, M-17]. 5. Each dereference, `a[h]` or `p[h]` and each `remove`, checks its handle before anything else, and a handle that is not valid faults. Copying, storing, passing and returning a handle does not check it [M-17]. 6. When a handle is not valid for more than one reason, the first reason in this order is reported [M-17]: | Order | Reason | Code | Condition | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | `null` | 1 | the handle is the null handle | | 2 | `container` | 6 | the handle's container or kind is not that of the arena or pool it is used in | | 3 | `retired` | 2 | the arena, an arena it was carved from, or the pool slot is retired | | 4 | `generation` | 3 | the handle's generation differs from the current generation | | 5 | `extent` | 4 | in an arena, slot plus length exceeds the used extent; in a pool, the slot is at or above the capacity | | 6 | `vacant` | 5 | in a pool, the slot is not occupied | **Faults**

6.15 Modules, programs and tests
chunks.content:
### 6.15 Modules, programs and tests

A program is made of modules. This clause gives how one module uses another, what a module makes visible to the modules that import it, and how a module states tests that `cint test` runs. Scripts, programs with `main` and importable modules are defined in 5.1.2.

chunks.title: 6.15.1 Modules and imports
chunks.content:
#### 6.15.1 Modules and imports

Each source file is one module (5.1.1), and its path names it. A module uses another by importing it, and then reaches the other module's exported names through a qualifier. A module is translated from its own source and the exported declarations of the modules it imports: there are no header files, prototypes or include guards.

**Syntax**

```ebnf
import_decl = "import" module_path
              [ "as" IDENT | "." "{" IDENT { "," IDENT } [ "," ] "}" ] ";" ;
module_path = IDENT { "." IDENT } ;
top_item    = [ "export" ] declaration
            | test_decl
            | static_assert
            | statement ;
declaration = const_decl | var_decl | func_decl | kernel_decl
            | struct_decl | error_decl | memory_decl ;
```

`module` is in 5.1.1, the declarations in 6.9, 6.13.1 and 6.14.1 and `test_decl` in 6.15.3. A `statement` among the top-level items makes the module a script (5.1.2).

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 6.15.1 Modules and imports (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A module's path relative to the source root (paragraph 11) names it: each `/` becomes `.` and the final `.ci` is removed, so the file `geo/vec.ci` is the module `geo.vec`. Each segment of the path, the last without `.ci`, shall be an identifier (6.4.4) and shall not be one of the device names `con`, `prn`, `aux`, `nul`, `com1` to `com9` and `lpt1` to `lpt9`, in any mix of upper and lower case. Two module paths of one program shall not be equal when ASCII letters are compared without regard to case. A path that breaks one of these rules is diagnosed C3030 at the start of that file, position `:1:1` [LS-225]. 2. Every `import` declaration shall come before every other item of the module except a profile declaration (5.1.1). An import after another item is diagnosed C3012 at its `import` [LS-226]. 3. The file of each imported module shall be readable under the source root. An import whose module file cannot be read is diagnosed C3009 at its module path [LS-225]. 4. A module shall not import itself, directly or through other modules. The import that closes a cycle is diagnosed C3003 at its module path [LS-230]. 5. Each name in a module is declared once, whatever it names: a type, a function, a constant, a variable, an error set, a kernel, an arena, a pool or an import. A second declaration of a name is diagnosed C3001 at the second declared name. There is no overloading: two functions with the same name and different parameters are two declarations of one name [LS-228]. 6. An import declares one name in the importing module: the last segment of the module path, or the identifier after `as`. A second import that declares the same name, or another declaration of it, is diagnosed C3001, as paragraph 5 states [LS-228]. 7. A selected import, `import a.b.{X, y};`, declares each listed name in th

chunks.content: 7. `export` gives no access from a program written in another language. A host program calls the exported functions of a cint library through the host interface, which SPEC-03P.1 defines with the signatures it accepts.

chunks.title: 6.15.3 Tests
chunks.content: #### 6.15.3 Tests A test is a named block at the top level of a module that checks what the module's code does. `cint test` runs the tests of a program, each in a fresh context, and reports which passed. A test either expects its body to complete or expects one fault, which its header names. 8.3 shows how tests serve as golden outputs. **Syntax** ```ebnf test_decl = "test" STRING [ "expect_fault" IDENT [ "at" DEC_INT ] ] block ; ``` **Constraints** 1. A test appears at the top level of a module of any kind: a script, a program with `main` or an importable module. A test inside a function or a block is a syntax error, C1050 [LS-232]. 2. The name of a test is a string literal without holes. A hole in it is diagnosed C1033 [LS-233]. 3. Two tests of one module shall not have the same name. The second is diagnosed C3020 at its `test` [LS-233]. 4. `expect_fault` appears only in a test header. Anywhere else it is diagnosed C3021 at `expect_fault` [LS-237]. 5. The name after `expect_fault` is a fault code of 5.2.3. A name that begins `E_` and is not one is diagnosed C1011 (6.4.4) [LS-236]. 6. A test may name every declaration of its module, private ones included and the exported names of the modules its module imports. It shall not name a top-level variable of a script: C3004 (5.1.2) [LS-232]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.15.3 Tests (part 2)
chunks.content: 7. Every translation checks the tests of each module, so `cint run` reports a diagnostic in a test as `cint test` does. Only `cint test` runs tests. It runs no entry of the program: the top-level statements of a script and the function `main` do not run during `cint test`, unless a test calls `main` [LS-232, LS-239]. 8. Each test runs as one entry (3.20) in a fresh context: every module-level variable starts at its initial value and every arena and pool is empty. No test can observe the effects of another [LS-234]. 9. `cint test FILE` runs the tests of every module of the program whose root is `FILE`. It takes the modules in the byte order of their paths relative to the source root, and the tests of each module in source order, so the report is the same on every run [LS-234]. 10. A test without `expect_fault` passes when its body completes, by reaching its end or by `return;`. It fails when an `assert` fails, when any other fault occurs, or when an error leaves it [LS-235]. 11. In a test body, `try` admits an error of any set, and an error that leaves the test through `try` fails it, as 6.11.3 states. The report names the error as `cint run` names an error result of `main` (6.11.7). A test that expects an error binds it with `catch` and checks it with `assert` [LS-315]. 12. A test with `expect_fault E_NAME` passes when its body faults and the fault's code is `E_NAME`. It fails when the body completes, when an error leaves it, or when it faults with another code. The fault ends the test as a fault ends any entry (5.2.3): nothing after it runs, deferred statements do not run, and the test's context is discarded. A fault is not caught or resumed, so a test checks one fault, and several faults take several tests [LS-236]. 13. A failed `assert` is the fault `E_ASSERT` (6.10.9), so `expect_fault E_ASSERT` expects an a

6.16 Future directions
chunks.content:
### 6.16 Future directions

This subclause lists constructs that are not part of this edition. Annex A has no production for them, and an implementation rejects or refuses a program that uses one (A.1, paragraph 4). Listing a construct here does not commit any edition to define it, or to use the spelling shown. Each entry says what a program writes instead in this edition.

chunks.title: 6.16.1 Types and values
chunks.content:
#### 6.16.1 Types and values

1. This edition has no string type, whose values a program could store, compare and pass. A string literal is print text or a read-only argument (6.4.8).
2. This edition has no byte-string literals such as `b"..."`, no raw string literals, in which backslashes are not escapes, and no string literals of several lines. A string literal is UTF-8 text on one line, with the escapes of 6.4.8.
3. This edition has no enumerations. `const` declarations (6.9.2) name the values.
4. This edition has no tagged unions and no optional values. An error union (6.3.7) carries either a value or an error.
5. A rounding mode is not a value in this edition, so a program cannot store, pass or compare one. A mode is written as a bare name in a `round` clause or a mode argument (6.7.15).
6. This edition has no unsigned fixed point, and no fixed-point format whose integer and fraction bits total more than 64 (6.3.2).
7. This edition has no `U1024`. The widest unsigned type is `U512` (6.3.1).
8. This edition has no type properties such as `T.bits`, `T.frac_bits`, `T.bytes` and `offset`, no packed structs and no bit fields. The width of each type is fixed by its name (6.3), and the layout of a struct is not observable from a program.
9. This edition has no error sets with a signed underlying type, no error-set variables at module level and no conversion of an error value to its integer tag (6.3.7, 6.9.7).
10. A constant has a scalar type in this edition (6.9.2), so a constant array such as `const I32[4] PRIMES = [2, 3, 5, 7];` cannot be declared.
11. A program cannot declare a function or a type with a type parameter. The operations of clause 7 accept several types, and `Arena(T)`, `Pool(T)` and `Handle(T[])` (6.3.8) are the only types with a parameter.

chunks.title: 6.16.2 Declarations and statements
chunks.content:
#### 6.16.2 Declarations and statements

12. This edition has no `var` declarations, which take a local's type from its initializer. An initializer made only of literals has no type of its own (6.5), so a declaration names its type.
13. A parameter has no default value. A call names every argument, positionally or by name (6.9.5).
14. A function has no `where` clause on its size parameters. A kernel may have one (6.13.1).
15. This edition has no tuples, so a function cannot return several values to be unpacked, as in `(q, r) = divmod(7, 2);`. A function returns one value and writes others through `inout` parameters (6.9.5).
16. This edition has no `do` loops, which test the condition after the body. A `while` loop with a `break` (6.10.3, 6.10.6) does the same.
17. A loop does not run over the elements of an array or a view, as in `for i, x in a { }`. A `for` statement runs over a range of indices (6.10.4).
18. An array or a view has no declared lower bound, such as `I64[1..=m]`. Every array and view is indexed from 0 in every dimension (6.12.3).
19. A function cannot return an array or a view, and a view cannot be stored at module level. A function writes its array results into a view parameter (6.12.4).
20. A constant expression cannot call a user function, and no operation makes the contents of a file a constant array. A constant expression holds literals, constants, operators and the named operations of 7.2 (6.8).
21. This edition has no attributes, such as an annotation on an export that sets how a function is called from C, Python or Fortran. The host interface of every export is the one SPEC-03P.1 defines (6.15.2).

chunks.title: 6.16.3 Operations
chunks.content:
#### 6.16.3 Operations

22. The result forms (6.7.12) take integer operands only, so `add_result`, `sub_result`, `mul_result`, `div_result` and `sqrt_result` on fixed-point operands are not in this edition. A fixed-point operation that cannot give its result faults.
23. This edition has no saturating conversion `x as| T`. For an integer `x`, `clamp(x, lo, hi) as T`, with `lo` and `hi` the bounds of `T`, gives the value clamped to the range of `T` (7.2.1).
24. `++` and `--` do not apply to a fixed-point place. `x += 1.0;` adds one to a fixed-point `x` (6.7.14).
25. This edition has no wrapping or saturating division (`div_wrap`, `div_sat`), no wrapping or saturating square root (`sqrt_wrap`, `sqrt_sat`), and no `divmod`, which needs tuples (paragraph 15). 7.2.2 gives the division functions.
26. `clamp` does not take fixed-point operands (7.2.1).
27. An integer literal has no exponent notation, such as `1e9`. Digit separators keep long literals readable: `1_000_000_000` (6.4.5).
28. A fraction literal is not the source of a conversion, as in `2.5 as I32`. A fraction literal takes a fixed-point type from its context (6.5), and that value converts (6.6).
29. A reduction does not run along one axis of an array of rank 2 or more, `fold_checked` takes no user function and does not apply `mul` to fixed-point elements, and `dot` does not take arrays of rank 2 (7.3).
30. This edition has no `equal(a, b)` or `swap(a, b)` on arrays, no operators such as `a + b` on whole arrays, no `reshape` that copies, no `transpose` of a rank other than 2, and no `extent` or `reverse` with a dimension computed at run time (7.4).
31. A kernel body calls no user function (6.13.3).
32. A program cannot format into an array, as in `format(buf, ...)`, and structs, error values, handles and arrays of rank 2 or more have no default rendering (7.5.2).

chunks.title: 6.16.4 Memory
chunks.content:
#### 6.16.4 Memory

33. An arena or a pool cannot hold fixed-point elements, and a kernel body cannot declare one (6.14).

chunks.title: 7 Library
chunks.content:
## 7 Library

The library is the set of operations a program calls by name without declaring or importing them: integer and fixed-point arithmetic that needs a wider intermediate or a named rounding, reductions over arrays, functions that measure, fill, copy and re-view arrays and the formatting that print statements apply to values. A library operation follows the rules of the operators. A checked operation gives an exact result, or a result rounded once by a mode the program names, and checks that result against its type; when the result does not fit, it faults with a record that names the operation, its operands and the bound it crossed. The wrapping and saturating operations (`sum_wrap`, `sum_sat`, `mul_wrap`, `mul_sat`) never fault on overflow.

The result forms `add_result` to `shl_result` are in 6.7.12. The members of arenas and pools, such as `alloc` and `insert`, are in 6.14.

chunks.title: 7.1 Reserved names and arguments
chunks.content:
### 7.1 Reserved names and arguments

Library names are reserved in every module, so `sum` or `min` means the same thing in every program. A call of a library operation is written like a function call, but some of its arguments are not values: a type that names the result, a rounding mode or an operation, each written as a bare name.

**Constraints**

1. The names in this table are the built-in functions. They are visible in every module without an import. A declaration of one of them, of any kind and in any scope, is diagnosed C3001 [LS-145].

| Names | Subclause |
|---|---|
| `abs`, `uabs` | 6.7.5 |
| `div_round`; `mul`, `div`, `mul_wrap`, `mul_sat` | 6.7.7 |
| `rotl`, `rotr` | 6.7.8 |
| `min`, `max`, `clamp` | 7.2.1 |
| `div_trunc`, `rem_trunc`, `div_euclid`, `rem_euclid` | 7.2.2 |
| `mul_full`, `muldiv`, `isqrt`, `isqrt_round` | 7.2.3 |
| `sqrt`, `qmul`, `mul_int` | 7.2.4 |
| `add_result`, `sub_result`, `mul_result`, `div_result`, `rem_result`, `shl_result` | 6.7.12 |
| `sum`, `fold_checked`, `sum_wrap`, `sum_sat`, `count`, `dot`; `min` and `max` over an array | 7.3 |
| `len`, `extent`, `size`, `copy`, `fill`, `transpose`, `reverse`, `reshape` | 7.4 |

chunks.title: 7.1 Reserved names and arguments (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. The names `divmod`, `equal`, `swap`, `lower`, `wrap_bits`, `random`, `format`, `utf8`, `embed`, `to_device`, `to_host`, `rescale3`, `rescale3_rem`, `shl3`, `sign` and `tdot` are reserved for built-in operations: a declaration of one of them is diagnosed C3001, as for the names of paragraph 1, and this edition gives them no meaning [LS-145]. 3. Three kinds of argument are names, not values [LS-146, LS-307]: - A *type argument* is a type name written as the first argument of `muldiv`, `sum`, `dot` or `qmul`. It names the result type. Only these built-ins take a type argument; a type name as an argument of a user function is diagnosed C3007. - A *mode argument* is the name of a rounding mode (6.7.15), written bare as the last argument of `div_round`, `muldiv`, `isqrt_round`, `mul`, `div`, `mul_wrap`, `mul_sat`, `sqrt`, `qmul` or `dot`. A mode position is resolved by its position, not by looking the name up, so a variable named `floor` does not change `div_round(a, b, floor)`. Any other name in a mode position is diagnosed C3007. - An *operation argument* is `add` or `mul`, written bare as the first argument of `fold_checked`. Any other name there is diagnosed C3007. 4. A built-in takes no named arguments (C2063). A call with the wrong number of arguments for the built-in is diagnosed C2022 [LS-145]. 5. Where the description of a built-in gives several value arguments one type `T`, they shall have the same type, and mixing two types is diagnosed C2001. A literal argument takes the type of the typed arguments. When every such argument is a literal, `T` is the type that the context of the call requires, or `I64` when the context requires none (6.5) [LS-145]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.1 Reserved names and arguments (part 3)
chunks.content:
6. Each call of a built-in is one operation. It gives its result or raises one fault, positioned at the name of the built-in in the call, whatever the implementation computes internally [IM-51].

**Examples**

7. A mode position takes the mode's name even when a variable has the same name:

```cint mode_position.ci
I64 floor = 10;
"{div_round(7, 2, floor)} {div_round(7, 2, ceil)} {floor}\n";
```

```text
3 4 10
```

8. A library name cannot be declared:

```cint reserved_name.ci
I64 count = 0;
"{count}\n";
```

```text
error[C3001]: duplicate name
  --> reserved_name.ci:1:5
   |
 1 | I64 count = 0;
   |     ^
```

**Notes**

9. In C, a local variable may hide a library function of the same name. A cint program cannot declare these names at all, so a reader of `sum(xs)` or `min(a, b)` never needs to look for a declaration.

chunks.title: 7.2 Integer and fixed-point operations
chunks.content:
### 7.2 Integer and fixed-point operations

These functions compute what an operator cannot: the lesser or greater of two values, quotients rounded toward zero or by the Euclidean convention, products and quotients that need a wider intermediate, square roots and fixed-point products of two formats or of a fixed-point value and an integer. Each gives an exact or once-rounded result and checks it against its result type, as a checked operator does.

| Call | Arguments | Result | Faults |
|---|---|---|---|
| `min(a, b)`, `max(a, b)` | `T` integer or fixed point | `T` | none |
| `clamp(x, lo, hi)` | `T` integer | `T` | `E_DOMAIN` |
| `div_trunc(a, b)`, `div_euclid(a, b)` | `T` integer | `T` | `E_DIV_ZERO`, `E_OVERFLOW` |
| `rem_trunc(a, b)`, `rem_euclid(a, b)` | `T` integer | `T` | `E_DIV_ZERO` |
| `mul_full(a, b)` | `T` of `I8` to `I512` or `U8` to `U256` | integer type of width 2`w`, same signedness | none |
| `muldiv(R, a, b, c, mode)` | `T` integer; `R` any integer type | `R` | `E_DIV_ZERO`, `E_OVERFLOW` |
| `isqrt(x)`, `isqrt_round(x, mode)` | `T` integer | `T` | `E_DOMAIN`, `E_OVERFLOW` |
| `sqrt(a)`, `sqrt(a, mode)` | `Q<i>.<f>` | the same type | `E_DOMAIN`, `E_OVERFLOW` |
| `qmul(R, a, b)`, `qmul(R, a, b, mode)` | `a`, `b` fixed point of any formats; `R` fixed point | `R` | `E_OVERFLOW` |
| `mul_int(a, n)` | `a` fixed point; `n` any integer type | the type of `a` | `E_OVERFLOW` |

The other built-in operations on single values are stated with the operators they complete: `abs` and `uabs` in 6.7.5; `div_round`, and the fixed-point `mul`, `div`, `mul_wrap` and `mul_sat` with a rounding mode, in 6.7.7; `rotl` and `rotr` in 6.7.8; and the result forms in 6.7.12. The rounding modes are in 6.7.15.

chunks.title: 7.2.1 min, max and clamp
chunks.content: #### 7.2.1 min, max and clamp `min` and `max` choose one of two values, and `clamp` limits a value to a range. None of them computes a new value, so none can overflow. **Constraints** 1. The two arguments of `min(a, b)` and of `max(a, b)` shall have one integer or fixed-point type `T`. The three arguments of `clamp(x, lo, hi)` shall have one integer type `T` [LS-145, IM-49]. 2. When `lo` and `hi` are both constant expressions and `lo > hi`, the call of `clamp` is diagnosed C6006 [IM-49]. 3. A call of `min` or `max` whose last argument is an array or a view is the reduction of 7.3, not this function. **Semantics** 4. `min(a, b)` gives the lesser and `max(a, b)` the greater of the two values. On fixed point they compare the values, which is the order of the storage integers [IM-49]. 5. When `lo <= hi`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)` gives `lo` if `x < lo`, `hi` if `x > hi` and `x` otherwise. `min` and `max` never fault, and `clamp` faults only as paragraph 6 states [IM-49]. **Faults** 6. The fault `E_DOMAIN` is raised by `clamp` when `lo > hi` at run time, whatever `x` is. The record holds the operation identifier `clamp.checked.t` and the operands `x`, `lo` and `hi`. It has no exact result and no limit [IM-49]. **Examples** 7. This example shows `min`, `max` and `clamp`, including a value that `clamp` raises to its lower bound and one that it lowers to its upper bound: ```cint min_max.ci I64 t = -7; "{min(t, 2)} {max(t, 2)} {clamp(t, -5, 5)} {clamp(12, -5, 5)}\n"; ``` ```text -7 2 -5 5 ``` 8. Constant bounds in the wrong order are found during translation: ```cint clamp_bounds.ci I64 x = 9; "{clamp(x, 5, 1)}\n"; ``` ```text error[C6006]: compile-time evaluation rule --> clamp_bounds.ci:2:3 ... ```

chunks.title: 7.2.2 Division functions
chunks.content: #### 7.2.2 Division functions The operators `/` and `%` divide with the quotient rounded toward negative infinity (6.7.7). These functions give the two other conventions in common use. | Function | Quotient `q` | Remainder `r` | |---|---|---| | `a / b`, `a % b` (6.7.7) | `floor(a / b)` | zero or the sign of `b` | | `div_trunc(a, b)`, `rem_trunc(a, b)` | rounded toward zero | zero or the sign of `a` | | `div_euclid(a, b)`, `rem_euclid(a, b)` | the `q` for which `0 <= r < \|b\|` | never negative | **Constraints** 1. The two arguments of each function of this subclause shall have one integer type `T`. A fixed-point argument is diagnosed C2103 [IM-36]. **Semantics** 2. For `b != 0`, `div_trunc(a, b)` is the rational `a / b` rounded toward zero, and `rem_trunc(a, b)` is `a - b * div_trunc(a, b)` [IM-36]. 3. For `b != 0`, `div_euclid(a, b)` is the integer `q` for which `r = a - b * q` satisfies `0 <= r < |b|`, and `rem_euclid(a, b)` is that `r` [IM-36]. 4. In each pair, `a == q * b + r` holds exactly. The quotients of `div_trunc` and `div_euclid` are checked against `T`: when the exact quotient is outside the range of `T`, the function faults [IM-36, IM-39]. 5. For signed `T`, `MIN(T)` divided by -1 has the quotient `-MIN(T)`, which is outside the range, so `div_trunc` and `div_euclid` fault. Its remainder is 0, so `rem_trunc(MIN(T), -1)` and `rem_euclid(MIN(T), -1)` give 0 and do not fault. An implementation shall give 0 for these remainders and shall not trap [IM-39, IM-40]. **Faults**

chunks.title: 7.2.2 Division functions (part 2)
chunks.content:
6. The fault `E_DIV_ZERO` is raised by every function of this subclause when `b == 0`, before any other check. The record holds the operation identifier `<name>.checked.t`, for example `rem_euclid.checked.i64`, and the operands `a` and `b`. It has no exact result and no limit. Its position is the name of the function in the call [IM-39].
7. The fault `E_OVERFLOW` is raised by `div_trunc` and `div_euclid` when the quotient is outside the range of `T`. The record holds the same operation and operands, the exact quotient, and the bound it crossed [IM-39].

**Examples**

8. The three conventions differ when the operands have opposite signs:

```cint division_forms.ci
I64 a = -7;
I64 b = 2;
"{a / b} {a % b}\n";
"{div_trunc(a, b)} {rem_trunc(a, b)}\n";
"{div_euclid(a, b)} {rem_euclid(a, b)}\n";
"{div_euclid(7, -2)} {rem_euclid(7, -2)}\n";
```

```text
-4 1
-3 -1
-4 1
-3 1
```

9. The remainders of `MIN(T)` by -1 are 0; the quotient does not fit:

```cint trunc_overflow.ci
I64 m = I64.min;
I64 d = -1;
"{rem_trunc(m, d)} {rem_euclid(m, d)}\n";
I64 q = div_trunc(m, d);
```

```text
0 0
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> trunc_overflow.ci:4:9
   |
 4 | I64 q = div_trunc(m, d);
   |         ^ div_trunc.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: div_trunc.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 -9223372036854775808
   = operand: I64 -1
   = exact:   9223372036854775808
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   ...
```

10. This example shows division by zero:

```cint euclid_zero.ci
I64 a = 5;
I64 z = 0;
"{rem_euclid(a, z)}\n";
```

```text
fault[E_DIV_ZERO]: division by zero
  --> euclid_zero.ci:3:3
   |
 3 | "{rem_euclid(a, z)}\n";
   |   ^ rem_euclid.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: rem_euclid.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 5
   = operand: I64 0
   = exact:   none
   = limit:   none
   ...
```

**Notes**

chunks.title: 7.2.2 Division functions (part 3)
chunks.content: 11. Fortran's `MOD` truncates, like C's `%` and corresponds to `rem_trunc`; Fortran's `MODULO` corresponds to `%`. A remainder that must lie in `0` to `|b| - 1`, such as an index into a ring buffer, is `rem_euclid` whatever the sign of `b`.

chunks.title: 7.2.3 Wide intermediates
chunks.content: #### 7.2.3 Wide intermediates An operator never computes in a wider type than its operands. When a computation needs more bits in the middle than at the end, such as a product that is divided at once, the program asks for it by name. Each of these functions keeps its intermediate exact and rounds at most once. **Constraints** 1. The arguments of `mul_full(a, b)` shall have one type `T` among `I8` to `I512` and `U8` to `U256`; `I1024` and `U512` are diagnosed C2103 [IM-51]. 2. In `muldiv(R, a, b, c, mode)`, `a`, `b` and `c` shall have one integer type `T`. `R` may be `T` or any other integer type [IM-53]. 3. The argument of `isqrt(x)` and of `isqrt_round(x, mode)` shall have an integer type `T` [IM-51]. **Semantics** 4. `mul_full(a, b)` gives the exact product `a * b` as a value of the integer type of width 2`w` and the same signedness as `T`: `I16` for `I8`, `I128` for `I64`, `I1024` for `I512`, `U128` for `U64`, `U512` for `U256`. Every such product fits, so `mul_full` never faults [IM-51]. 5. `muldiv(R, a, b, c, mode)` forms the exact product `a * b`, divides it by `c` as a rational, rounds the quotient once by `mode` and checks the rounded value against `R`. The product is never narrowed, whatever the widths of `T` and `R` [IM-51, IM-53]. 6. `isqrt(x)` gives `floor(sqrt(x))`: the unique `r >= 0` with `r * r <= x < (r + 1) * (r + 1)` [IM-51]. 7. `isqrt_round(x, mode)` gives the square root of `x` rounded by `mode`. The square root of an integer is never exactly halfway between two integers, so every `half_` mode gives the nearest integer. The rounded value is checked against `T` [IM-51]. **Faults**

chunks.title: 7.2.4 Fixed-point operations
chunks.content: #### 7.2.4 Fixed-point operations A fixed-point value `Q.` is held as a storage integer `A`, its value being `A / 2^f` (6.3.2). The operators combine values of one format. These functions take a square root, multiply values of two different formats and multiply a fixed-point value by an integer. Each rounds at most once, on the exact result, and checks the rounded storage integer against the range of the result's storage type. **Constraints** 1. The argument of `sqrt(a)` and of `sqrt(a, mode)` shall have a fixed-point type. An integer argument is diagnosed C2103; `isqrt` is the integer square root [IM-67]. 2. In `qmul(R, a, b)` and `qmul(R, a, b, mode)`, `R` shall be a fixed-point type and `a` and `b` values of fixed-point types, of any formats. An integer argument is diagnosed C2103 [IM-63]. 3. In `mul_int(a, n)`, `a` shall have a fixed-point type and `n` an integer type of any width [IM-64]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.2.4 Fixed-point operations (part 2)
chunks.content:
4. For `a` of `Q<i>.<f>` with storage integer `A >= 0`, `sqrt(a, mode)` gives the value whose storage integer is `isqrt_round(A * 2^f, mode)`, computed in an intermediate of at least 2`w` bits. `sqrt(a)` uses `half_even`. The storage integer is then checked against the range of the storage type. For `i >= 2` the root is always in range; for `Q1.<f>`, the modes that round up can reach `2^(w - 1)`, which is not [IM-67].
5. For `a` of `Q<ia>.<fa>` with storage integer `A`, `b` of `Q<ib>.<fb>` with storage integer `B`, and `R` of `Q<ir>.<fr>`, `qmul(R, a, b, mode)` forms the exact product `A * B`, whose scale is `2^(fa + fb)`. When `fa + fb > fr` the storage integer of the result is `A * B / 2^(fa + fb - fr)` rounded once by `mode`, and `qmul(R, a, b)` uses `half_even`. Otherwise it is `A * B * 2^(fr - fa - fb)`, exactly and nothing rounds. The storage integer is then checked against the range of `R` [IM-63].
6. `mul_int(a, n)` gives the value of the type of `a` whose storage integer is `A * n`, exactly, checked against the range of that type. Nothing rounds [IM-64].

chunks.title: 7.3 Reductions
chunks.content:
### 7.3 Reductions

A reduction combines the elements of an array or a view into one value. Checked and saturating additions do not give the same result in every order: with `M` the maximum of `I64`, `(M + 1) + (-1)` faults while `M + (1 + (-1))` gives `M` and in `I8` saturating `120 + 120 - 120` gives 7 left to right but 120 right to left. So each reduction is a named operation whose result is defined independently of how an implementation schedules the work [IM-73].

| Call | Result | Order | Faults |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sum(xs)`, `sum(R, xs)` | the exact sum, checked once against `R` (default: the element type) | any | `E_OVERFLOW` at the final check |
| `fold_checked(add, init, xs)`, `fold_checked(mul, init, xs)` | `init` combined with each element in turn, each step checked | logical order | `E_OVERFLOW` at the first step out of range |
| `sum_wrap(xs)` | the exact sum, wrapped to the element type | any | none |
| `sum_sat(xs)` | `0` combined with each element in turn by `+\|` | logical order | none |
| `min(xs)`, `max(xs)` | the least or greatest element | any | `E_SHAPE` when `xs` is empty |
| `min(init, xs)`, `max(init, xs)` | as above, with `init` included | any | none |
| `count(mask)` | the number of `true` elements, as an `I64` | any | none |
| `dot(R, a, b)` | the exact sum of the products `a[k] * b[k]`, checked once against `R` | any | `E_SHAPE`, `E_OVERFLOW` |

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 7.3 Reductions (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The array argument of a reduction, `xs`, `mask`, `a` or `b`, shall be an array or a view; any other argument is diagnosed C2103. Every reduction but `dot` accepts any rank from 1 to 4 [IM-77]. 2. The elements shall have an integer or fixed-point type, diagnosed C2103 otherwise, except for `count`, whose elements shall be `Bool` (C2001) [IM-77]. 3. In `sum(R, xs)`, `R` shall be an integer type when the elements are integers; any integer `R` is allowed, wider or narrower than the elements. When the elements are fixed point, `R` is the element type. Any other `R` is diagnosed C9102 [IM-77, R-4]. 4. In `fold_checked(op, init, xs)` and in `min(init, xs)` and `max(init, xs)`, `init` shall have the element type (C2001). The operation `mul` is allowed on integer elements [IM-77]. 5. `dot(R, a, b)` shall have a type as its first argument (C3007). `a` and `b` shall be rank-1 arrays or views of one element type (C2001). `R` is an integer type when the elements are integers and a fixed-point type when they are fixed point, and a mode argument may follow only for fixed point [IM-87]. 6. A reduction across the work-items of a kernel is written with a `reduce` statement (6.13.5). **Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.3 Reductions (part 3)
chunks.content: 7. The *logical order* of the elements of an array or view is the row-major order of their logical indices, in which the last index varies fastest. It does not depend on the layout of the storage, on strides, or on where the view begins [IM-74]. 8. `sum(xs)` and `sum(R, xs)` compute the exact sum of the elements in Z and check it once against `R`, which is the element type when omitted. Partial sums are never checked, so every order of addition gives the same result. The final check is a range check on an exact value, so it raises `E_OVERFLOW`, not the `E_NARROW` of a conversion [IM-77, IM-78, IM-82]. 9. An implementation may compute a sum of `n` signed or unsigned `w`-bit elements in any accumulator of at least `w + ceil(log2(n))` bits, in any association order, because no partial sum can leave that range; or by any other method that gives the exact sum. For `I64` and narrower elements an `I128` accumulator is enough [IM-80]. 10. `fold_checked(add, init, xs)` sets an accumulator of the element type to `init` and then, for each element `x` in logical order, sets it to `acc + x` with a checked addition in the element type; `fold_checked(mul, init, xs)` uses a checked multiplication. The result is the final accumulator. A fault is raised at the least index `j` whose step leaves the range. For `add`, the accumulator after element `j` is `init + x_0 + ... + x_j` exactly, so an implementation may compute exact prefix sums in a wider accumulator and report the least `j` whose prefix is out of range [IM-77, IM-83]. 11. `sum_wrap(xs)` gives `wrap(E, s)`, where `E` is the element type and `s` the exact sum. Wrapped addition is associative and commutative, so every order gives this result [IM-77, IM-82]. 12. `sum_sat(xs)` sets an accumulator to 0 and, for each element `x`

chunks.title: 7.3 Reductions (part 4)
chunks.content: **Faults** 19. Every fault of a reduction is positioned at the name of the built-in in the call [IM-77]. 20. The fault `E_OVERFLOW` is raised by `sum` when the exact sum is outside the range of `R`. The record holds the operation identifier `sum.checked.e.r`, which always names both the element type and `R`, one operand, the count of elements `n` as an `I64`, the exact sum as the exact result, and the bound of `R` it crossed. It does not hold the elements [IM-81]. 21. The fault `E_OVERFLOW` is raised by `fold_checked` at the least index `j` whose step leaves the range. The record holds the operation identifier `fold_checked.add.e` or `fold_checked.mul.e`, the operands `j` as an `I64`, the accumulator before step `j` and the element `x_j`, both in the element type, the out-of-range result as the exact result, and the bound it crossed [IM-83]. 22. The fault `E_SHAPE` is raised by `min(xs)` and `max(xs)` when `xs` is empty. The record holds the operation identifier `reduce_min.checked.e` or `reduce_max.checked.e` and one operand, `I64 0`, the count. It has no exact result and no limit [IM-77]. 23. The fault `E_SHAPE` is raised by `dot` when `a` and `b` have different extents, before any fuel is charged. The record holds the operation identifier `dot.checked.e.r`, the operands `I64 0`, the dimension and the extent of `b` as an `I64`, no exact result and the extent of `a` as the limit [IM-87]. 24. The fault `E_OVERFLOW` is raised by `dot` when the result is outside the range of `R`, with the record of `sum`: the count `n`, the exact sum, rounded for fixed point, and the bound of `R`. For fixed point the operation is `dot.checked.q.r` followed by `.mode` only when the operation rounds [IM-87]. **Examples** 25. This example shows four reductions of the same three values:

chunks.content:
### 7.4 Array operations

These functions report the shape of an array or view, fill and copy elements and give new views of the same elements in another order or shape. A view function moves no element; it gives a view with other extents and strides over the same storage (6.12).

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `len(a)` | the extent of a rank-1 array or view, as an `I64` |
| `extent(a, d)` | the extent of dimension `d`, counted from 0, as an `I64` |
| `size(a)` | the number of elements, the product of the extents, as an `I64` |
| `fill(dst, v)` | sets every element of `dst` to `v` |
| `copy(dst, src)` | copies the elements of `src` into `dst` |
| `transpose(a)` | a view of a rank-2 array or view with its two dimensions exchanged |
| `reverse(a, d)` | a view in which dimension `d` runs backward |
| `reshape(a, e1, ...)` | a view of the elements of `a`, in logical order, with the extents `e1, ...` |

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 7.4 Array operations (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The first argument of each function shall be an array or a view, diagnosed C2103 otherwise [LS-145]. 2. The argument of `len` shall have rank 1; `len` of an array of higher rank is diagnosed C2014; `extent` and `size` measure such an array [LS-145]. 3. The dimension `d` of `extent(a, d)` and of `reverse(a, d)` is an `I64` constant expression whose value is a dimension of `a`, from 0 to its rank minus 1 [LS-145]. 4. The destination of `fill` and of `copy` shall be a writable array or view, a place the function may write (C2067). The value of `fill` shall have the element type. The source of `copy` shall have the element type and rank of the destination (C2001), and where both extents of a dimension are known during translation they shall be equal (C2012) [LS-145]. 5. When the storage that the two arguments of `copy` name is known during translation to overlap without being the same view, the call is diagnosed C5010 (6.12.5) [LS-145]. 6. The argument of `transpose` shall have rank 2. The extents `e1, ...` of `reshape` are `I64` values (C2001), from one to four of them [LS-145]. **Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.4 Array operations (part 3)
chunks.content:
7. `len`, `extent` and `size` read the shape and never fault [LS-145].
8. `fill(dst, v)` stores `v` in every element of `dst`. `copy(dst, src)` stores each element of `src` in the element of `dst` at the same logical index. A `copy` whose two arguments are the same view stores nothing [LS-145].
9. `transpose(a)` gives the view whose element `[i, j]` is the element `[j, i]` of `a`. `reverse(a, d)` gives the view whose index `k` in dimension `d` names the element at index `extent(a, d) - 1 - k` of `a`. `reshape(a, e1, ...)` gives the view with extents `e1, ...` whose elements, in logical order, are the elements of `a` in logical order; this edition defines it when the product of `e1, ...` equals `size(a)` and the elements of `a` are stored contiguously in row-major order. Outside that condition `reshape` has no result in this edition, and an implementation refuses the program (3.16). Each view function gives a view of the same storage, which is writable when `a` is; no element is copied [LS-145].

**Faults**

10. The fault `E_SHAPE` is raised by `copy` when the extents of `src` and `dst` differ in a dimension, before any element is stored. The fault record is that of a copy, as 6.12.5, paragraph 9, states, and its position is the name `copy`.
11. The fault `E_ALIAS` is raised by `copy` when `src` and `dst` are not shown disjoint (6.12.5) and are not the same view, after the shape check and before any element is stored. The fault record is that of a copy, as 6.12.5, paragraph 10, states.

**Examples**

chunks.content:
### 7.5 Formatting

A print statement (6.10.10) writes its string literals with each hole `{...}` replaced by the text of a value. This subclause defines that text. Every value prints exactly: an integer in full in decimal, whatever its width and a fixed-point value as the exact decimal expansion of its value. No value is ever rounded for display unless the hole asks for a precision, and none is printed in scientific notation [IM-90, IM-91, LS-210].

chunks.title: 7.5.1 Holes
chunks.content: #### 7.5.1 Holes A hole names an expression and, optionally, how to print it: the expression's own text before its value, a conversion applied first and a format specification. **Syntax** ```ebnf hole = "{" hole_expr [ "=" ] [ "!" conversion ] [ ":" spec ] "}" ; hole_expr = or_expr ; conversion = "bits" | "raw" | "lanes" "(" lane_type ")" | "ratio" ; (* "ratio" is reserved, 7.5.4 *) lane_type = "I8" | "I16" | "I32" | "I64" | "U8" | "U16" | "U32" | "U64" ; ``` `or_expr` is the expression of 6.7 without an unparenthesized conditional expression or `catch`. `spec` is in 7.5.3, and which `lane_type` applies to which value is in 7.5.4. **Constraints** 1. Holes may appear in the string literals of a print statement and in the message of an `assert` (6.10.9). A hole in any other string literal is diagnosed C1033 [LS-198]. 2. The hole expression is the longest prefix of the hole's text that is an `or_expr`. It shall not be empty and shall not contain a string literal or a brace, and a conditional expression in it shall be in parentheses: `{(ok ? a : b)}`. A hole that breaks these rules, has text left over after its expression, or names a conversion other than those of 7.5.4 and `ratio` is diagnosed C1035 [LS-198, LS-199]. 3. The value of a hole shall not be a struct, a handle, an arena or a pool; such a hole is diagnosed C1037 [LS-214]. A hole whose value is an error value, or an array or view of rank 2 or more, has no rendering in this edition (6.16), and an implementation refuses a program that has one (3.16). The other values, of an integer type, a fixed-point type or `Bool` and rank-1 arrays and views of them, are rendered as 7.5.2 states. 4. A literal brace in a string literal is written twice, `{{` or `}}`; a single `}` is diagnosed C1039 [LS-215]. **Semantics**

chunks.content: #### 7.5.2 Default rendering Each type has one default text, the one a hole without a specification prints. **Semantics** 1. An integer of any width prints as its exact value in decimal: a `-` before a negative value, no sign before any other, no leading zeros and no grouping. `I1024` and `U512` values print every digit [IM-90, LS-214]. 2. A fixed-point value prints as the shortest exact decimal expansion of its value with at least one digit after the point: `3.0`, `-0.25`. The value `A / 2^f` of a `Q.` always has a terminating decimal expansion of at most `f` fractional digits, so the default rendering is always exact [IM-90, LS-207, LS-214]. 3. A `Bool` prints as `true` or `false` [IM-90, LS-214]. 4. A rank-1 array or view prints as `[`, its elements in order separated by `, `, then `]`, every element, each rendered as the hole specifies [LS-214]. **Examples** 5. 7.5.3 Format specifications (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. *Width, fill and alignment.* `width` is the minimum length of the text in Unicode scalar values. A shorter text is padded with the fill character, a space by default: after the text for `<`, before it for `>`, and on both sides for `^`, with the extra character, when the padding is odd, on the right. A text longer than the width is never truncated. Width and alignment apply to every rendering, `Bool` included and to each element of an array, not to the array as a whole [LS-202, LS-211, LS-212]. 5. *Sign.* `-` prints a sign before negative values only, the default. `+` prints `+` before zero and positive values. A space prints a space before them [LS-202]. 6. *Zero padding.* The `0` flag with a width pads with `0` digits between the sign, or the radix prefix, and the digits, to the width [LS-202]. 7. *Kinds.* An integer prints by its mathematical value in every kind, with `-` before a negative value: `{-255:x}` is `-ff`. `d` is decimal, the default; `x` and `X` are hexadecimal with lowercase or uppercase digits; `o` is octal; `b` is binary. With `#`, the prefix `0x`, `0o` or `0b` precedes the digits, always in lowercase, so `{255:#X}` is `0xFF`. The storage bit pattern of a negative value is printed only through the `!bits` conversion of 7.5.4 [LS-202, LS-203, LS-204]. 8. *Groups.* `_` separates every three digits in decimal and every four in `x`, `X`, `o` and `b`, counted from the right; `,` separates every three digits in decimal [LS-202]. 9. *Balanced ternary.* `t` prints the shortest `0t` literal (6.4.5) of the value: the prefix `0t`, then the digits `N`, `0` and `P` for -1, 0 and 1, most significant first, with no leading `0` digit; the sign is carried by the digits. `{8:t}` is `0tP0N`, `{-8:t}` is `0tN0P` and `{0:t}` is `0t0`. The text is always a valid literal of th
