7.5.4 Conversions
chunks.content: #### 7.5.4 Conversions A conversion, after the `!` of a hole, prints a value through another reading of the same bits: the two's complement pattern of an integer, the storage integer of a fixed-point value, or an integer split into lanes. **Constraints** 1. `!bits` applies to integers and to fixed-point values, `!raw` to fixed-point values only and `!lanes(T)` to integers only, with `T` an unsigned type whose width divides the width of the value. Any other use, any conversion applied to `Bool`, `!ratio` applied to an integer and `!bits` together with the kind `t` or `c`, are diagnosed C1037 [LS-201, LS-213]. **Semantics** 2. `!bits` gives the two's complement bit pattern of the value as an unsigned integer of the same width: for `I8` -1 it is 255. On a fixed-point value it is the pattern of the storage integer. With `x`, `X`, `o` or `b`, the digits are padded with zeros to the full width of the type [LS-201]. 3. `!raw` gives the storage integer of a fixed-point value, a signed integer, as `x.raw` does (6.3.2). The format specification then applies with the rules of integers [LS-201]. 4. `!lanes(T)` splits the bit pattern of the value into lanes of the width of `T`, lane 0 the least significant and prints them as an array of `T` values, lane 0 first. The format specification applies to each lane [LS-201]. 5. The conversion name `ratio` is reserved, and this edition gives `!ratio` no meaning. Applied to an integer or to `Bool` it is diagnosed C1037 (paragraph 1); applied to a fixed-point value, an implementation refuses the program (3.16) [LS-201]. **Examples** 6. 8 Faults, agreement and debugging
chunks.content:
## 8 Faults, agreement and debugging

This clause explains how to find out why a program did what it did. 8.1 reads the record that a fault produces, field by field. 8.2 states which outcomes of a run are identical on every implementation, executor and machine and how to compare two runs. 8.3 shows how saved outputs and tests detect a change of behavior. 8.4 describes checkpoints, recordings and replay and 8.5 introduces the debug tools through a first session. What a fault is, and the state a fault leaves, are in 5.2.3; fuel and call depth are in 5.2.4 and 5.2.5.

chunks.title: 8.1 The fault record
chunks.content:
### 8.1 The fault record

A fault stops the entry that raised it (5.2.3) and produces one fault record: a fixed set of fields that say what failed, with which values, where, and in which program. The record holds no time, no memory address and no name of an executor, so every conforming implementation produces, for the same fault, a record equal in every field except `revision` and `source-map` (8.2). Every tool prints the record in one layout, the *fault report*.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 8.1 The fault record (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A fault produces exactly one fault record. Its fields are [IM-106, LS-278]: - `code`: the fault code (Annex B). - `operation`: the operation identifier of the operation that faulted, such as `add.checked.i64`, at most 64 ASCII characters (Annex B). - `operands`: every operand of that operation as a typed value, exact and never rounded or shortened, in source order; at most 8. - `exact`: the value that failed the range check. For an operation that does not round, it is the exact result (3.4). For an operation that rounds, such as `muldiv`, `div_round` or a conversion with a `round` clause, it is the value after the operation's one rounding. A record of `E_OVERFLOW` or `E_NARROW` has it; a record of another code has none unless the subclause of its operation gives one. - `limit`: the bound that was crossed: `MIN(T)` or `MAX(T)` of the result type, the largest permitted shift count, the extent of the indexed dimension, the fuel allowance or the depth limit. A record with no bound to cross, such as one of `E_DIV_ZERO`, has none. - `position`: the module-relative path of the source file, such as `month.ci`, the line and the column, both counted from 1 and the column counted in Unicode scalar values, of the operator token or of the callee's name for a call. - `revision`: the revision (3.31) of the program to which the position refers. - `source-map`: the digest of the program's *source map*, the table that gives the line and column of each fault site. The revision leaves source positions out, so an edit that only moves code, such as reformatting, keeps the revision; this field is the one that ties the record's positions to the source text they were taken from. SPEC-01P.2 defines the digest and the encoding of the whole record. - `address`: present only for a fault inside a kernel dispatch (paragraph 4). - `stack`: the call

chunks.title: 8.1 The fault record (part 3)
8.1 The fault record (part 4)
chunks.content: 5. The *step ordinal* numbers the counted operations that a work-item evaluates, from 0, in evaluation order, including those inside the functions it calls. The step ordinal of a fault is the ordinal of the operation that faulted. Each evaluation of these operations is counted: every arithmetic operator in each of its plain, wrapping and saturating forms, the shifts and unary `-` included; every conversion; every subscript and every slice, whether it reads or is the place of a store; every call of a built-in operation of clause 7; and every call of a user function, counted at the call, before the callee's own operations. Literals, reads of variables, comparisons, the bitwise operators `&`, `|`, `^` and `~`, the logical operators, the conditional operator itself, loop control and fuel charges are not counted [IM-113]. 6. An operation is counted even when the compiler has proved that it cannot fault, and however it is compiled. In the kernel body `out[i] = a[i] + b[i] * c[i];`, with the `+` overflowing, the place `out[i]` is step 0, because the place is evaluated first, `a[i]` is 1, `b[i]` 2, `c[i]` 3, `*` 4 and `+` 5, so the step ordinal is 5 [IM-114]. 7. The canonical order is a definition, not a statement about which processor lane failed first. Every executor reports the canonical fault, in whatever order it ran the work-items; SPEC-02P.1 states how an executor that runs work-items in parallel finds it [IM-115].

8.1 The fault record (part 7)
chunks.content:
| Line | What it says here |
|---|---|
| `after deposit ...` | The program's own output: three lines written before the fault, on the standard output. The report follows on the standard error. |
| `fault[E_OVERFLOW]` | The fault code, then the fixed message for that code. |
| `--> month.ci:3:18` | The position: file `month.ci`, line 3, the 18th character of the line, which is the `+` of `total + cents`. |
| excerpt | Line 3 of the source, a caret under the `+`, and the operation beside it. |
| `operation` | `add.checked.i64`, the checked `+` of two `I64` values. |
| `operand-count`, `operand` | Two operands in source order: `total`, which is 2434 after three deposits, and `cents`, the fourth amount. The record holds values, not names. |
| `exact` | The sum of the operands in Z, which `I64` cannot hold. |
| `limit` | `I64.max`, the bound that the exact result crossed. |
| `revision` | Left out above: 64 hexadecimal digits that identify the program (3.31). |
| `source-map` | The field for the digest of the source map (paragraph 1). cint 0.2.0 records none, so it reads `none`. |
| `address` | `none`: the fault is not inside a kernel dispatch. |
| `stack-depth`, `called from` | Two active calls, outermost first. The script's top-level statements are the entry and add no position; they call `month` at `month.ci:16:9`, and `month` calls `add_cents` at `month.ci:10:17`. |
| `fuel-consumed` | 10: 1 when the entry begins, 1 for the call of `month`, 4 for the iterations of the loop and 4 for the calls of `add_cents` (5.2.4). |
| `state` | What the fault left: the program stopped, and its output holds what it wrote before the fault (5.2.3). |

chunks.title: 8.1 The fault record (part 10)
chunks.content:
The address reads: kernel `scale` of module `scale`; dispatch 0, the first of the entry; phase 1, the work-items; work-item 2, whose element 3000000 times 1000 is 3000000000. Work-item 4 would fault as well, but 2 is the lower index. The step ordinal is 2: in `ys[i] = xs[i] * 1000;` the place `ys[i]` is step 0, `xs[i]` step 1 and the `*` step 2. The dispatch `scale(xs, ys)` at line 9 is a position of the stack, as a call is. The reference writes the phase by name and the address as the dispatch number, the work-item index and the step ordinal, and writes `self` for the revision and the source map, which it does not compute (8.2).

**Notes**

14. A report is read in three steps. The position and the excerpt show which operation failed. The operands and the exact result show why: which values were combined, and how far the result lies outside the type. The stack shows how the program reached that operation, from the outermost call inward.

15. After the source is edited, a saved report can point at a line that now holds other code. The revision changes with every change of the compiled program, so a report whose revision differs from the program's belongs to other code. An edit that only moves code, such as reformatting, changes positions but not the revision; that is what the `source-map` field is for (paragraph 1).

16. The `fuel-consumed` line is not part of the record, but the fuel an entry consumes is one of the outcomes on which every implementation agrees (8.2).

17. cint 0.2.0 records no source map in the `source-map` field of a fault record: every report of 0.2.0 prints `none` there. A recording and a case name the digest of the source map in their header (8.4), and `cint debug replay` prints it (8.5).

chunks.title: 8.2 Determinism and agreement
8.2 Determinism and agreement (part 2)
chunks.content: 2. The effects the host supplied are its answers to the entry's requests, in order: the status of each, its result, and the contents it wrote into the program's arrays. The requests the entry sent out are not among them. In this document "deterministic" means only this: equal execution identity gives the five equal outcomes of paragraph 1. Host time, thread scheduling, memory addresses and host effects that were not recorded are not inputs of an entry, so none of them can change an outcome. A conforming implementation agrees with the reference on every execution in the scope of both, except in the `revision` and `source-map` fields of a fault record (paragraph 3). An entry ended by a failure of host resources, such as the host running out of memory, has no execution identity, and this paragraph says nothing about it. The *build identity* of a compiled program, which names the executable or kernel binary that a build produced, is separate: an x86-64 executable and a CUDA kernel binary of the same program have different build identities and the same revision. Agreement says nothing about whether a program's integer results are numerically adequate for the problem it models, for example in place of a floating-point computation; that is a separate question with its own evidence [IM-160].

chunks.title: 8.2 Determinism and agreement (part 3)
chunks.content:
3. A program is in the scope of both the reference and a compiler when the reference runs it and the compiler builds it without a refusal (4, paragraph 4). For such a program and the same semantic inputs, the compiled program and the reference write the same output bytes, consume the same fuel and end with fault records equal in every field except `revision` and `source-map`, which the reference does not compute and writes as `self`. A disagreement is a defect of one of them or an ambiguity in this document, never a choice between them. Agreement on one program is a measurement of that program and shows nothing about another [SPEC-09P.1 REF-06].

4. Every tool runs the same compiled form of a program: `cint run`, `cint test`, `cint workbench`, `cint debug`, `cint interp`, and every executor. No tool has arithmetic, fault or post-fault rules of its own. A difference between any two of them on the same semantic inputs is a defect.

5. Observation does not change meaning. Inspecting, watching, tracing, checkpointing and recording never change the state of a run, its step ordinals, the fuel it consumes or its fault.

**Examples**

6. The reference is run as `python3 -m cint_ref` (SPEC-09P.1), and `--format 4` selects the text form of an outcome shown below. The output of `month.ci` (8.1, Example 10) has the same digest under `cint` and under the reference, and the reference ends with the same fault record:

7. The fuel allowance is a semantic input. Given an allowance of 9, the same program has another outcome, and every implementation gives it: the tenth charge, for the fourth call of `add_cents`, faults `E_FUEL`. The record's position is that call, its limit is the allowance, and it has no operands and no exact result. The output is the same 66 bytes, because the fault comes after the third print:

8. With `--json`, `cint run` writes the record as one JSON object, after the program's output:

chunks.title: 8.2 Determinism and agreement (part 5)
chunks.content:
```console
$ cint --json run month.ci
after deposit 0: 1999
after deposit 1: 2424
after deposit 2: 2434
{"address":null,"code":"E_OVERFLOW","column":18,"exact":{"t":"Z","v":"9223372036854777434"},"file":"month.ci","limit":{"t":"I64","v":"9223372036854775807"},"line":3,"noncanonical":{"fuel_consumed":"10"},"operands":[{"t":"I64","v":"2434"},{"t":"I64","v":"9223372036854775000"}],"operation":"add.checked.i64","revision":"92b1e2717518c491d86f09d90528fa1930c049c76f2c4aad6f9e0392f84da4ac","schema":"CINT-FAULT-1","severity":"fault","source_map":null,"stack":[{"column":9,"file":"month.ci","line":16},{"column":17,"file":"month.ci","line":10}]}

The key `schema` names the format, `CINT-FAULT-1`. Every value is a string of decimal digits beside its type, as in `{"t":"I64","v":"2434"}`, so a JSON reader that converts numbers to binary floating point cannot change it; the exact result has the type `Z`. The key `revision` holds the program's revision, which the report of 8.1 left out. What is not part of the record is under `noncanonical`, here the fuel consumed.

**Notes**

chunks.title: 8.2 Determinism and agreement (part 6)
chunks.content:
9. To compare a run A with a run B, for two implementations, two executors or two machines:
   - Fix the semantic inputs: the same program text, so the same revision; the same input values; the same fuel allowance, depth limit and frame-arena capacity.
   - Keep the output and the report apart: `cint run p.ci > a.out 2> a.err`.
   - Compare the output bytes with `cmp` or a digest.
   - Compare the reports from the `fault[` line through the last `called from` line, and the `fuel-consumed` line. Under `--json`, compare every key outside `noncanonical`, and `fuel_consumed` inside it.
   - A difference in any of these is a defect of A or of B, not a property of the program. Reduce the program to the smallest one that still shows it. For two executors on one recorded run, `cint debug diff` makes this comparison at every boundary (8.5).

10. Two agreeing runs can still differ in what is not an outcome: the time and memory they take, the files a build writes, the text of the `state` line, which each tool words for its own context, and the lines under `noncanonical`. The reference writes `self` where an implementation writes the revision and the source map.

11. Agreement shows that two implementations give the same outcome, not that either outcome is what the programmer intended. Two implementations can agree and both be wrong. This document decides which outcome is correct, and the conformance suite checks it on many programs.

12. In C, two compilers or one compiler at two optimization levels, can produce different output from one program whose behavior is undefined or unspecified, such as a signed overflow or an unsequenced modification. cint has no such behavior (Annex C), so a difference between two cint implementations is a defect of one of them or an ambiguity in this document (paragraph 3).

chunks.title: 8.2 Determinism and agreement (part 7)
chunks.content: 13. cint 0.2.0 has three executors (3.19): `cpu-c17`, which compiles the program to C; `cpu-sir-interp`, the interpreter `cint-interp`; and `gpu-cuda`, which runs kernels on NVIDIA GPUs.

**Notes**

7. A golden is only as good as its one check. Read the output before saving it, and check it against an independent computation where one exists: here, 8.25 percent of 2434 cents is 200.805 cents, which rounds to 201.

8. When a comparison with a golden fails, read the difference before replacing the golden. A golden replaced to make a comparison pass checks nothing.

9. A test states its expectation inside the module and runs with every `cint test`; a saved output records everything the program prints, including lines no test mentions. A program that prints a report benefits from both.

10. A golden made with any conforming implementation, on any executor or machine, is valid for every other (8.2). A golden that differs between two of them shows a defect in one of them, not a property of the program.

chunks.title: 8.4 Checkpoints, recordings and replay
chunks.content:
### 8.4 Checkpoints, recordings and replay

A host program runs a cint program as a sequence of entries (3.20), and the end of an entry is a *boundary*. At a boundary no function of the program is running, and the program's *state* is its module-level variables, its arenas and pools and its fault record, with its identifier counters, its count of entries begun and its count of effects completed (SPEC-01P.2, 3.10). A *checkpoint* saves the state at a boundary. A *recording* saves everything needed to run a sequence of entries again, and *replay* runs them again and checks each boundary against the recording. The debug tools go back in time by replay: they never run a program backward.

The examples of this subclause drive entries with `cint workbench`, which 8.5 introduces: each line of cint source typed after the prompt `ci[N]>` is one entry, and a line that starts with `:` is a command.

**Semantics**

1. Boundaries are the ends of entries, and the host program decides where entries begin and end. Program code cannot make a boundary inside an entry, and the locals of a running function are not part of the state, so no checkpoint is taken in the middle of a loop. A program that does all its work in one `main` has one boundary, at its end. In a session, each entry is one step (Note 11).

chunks.title: 8.4 Checkpoints, recordings and replay (part 2)
chunks.content:
2. A checkpoint holds the state at a boundary, which carries the program's revision, inside an *envelope*, a header that names the format, the runtime contract version (3.43) and the build of the program that wrote it (SPEC-01P.2); the envelope is not part of any identity. Restoring a checkpoint into a program of another revision fails. A checkpoint taken on another executor or by another build of the same revision is accepted. A build of the same source under another runtime contract version has another revision, so a checkpoint does not restore across that change: a restore requires the checkpoint's runtime contract to be exactly the context's [SPEC-03P.1 H-19].

3. Restoring a checkpoint makes its state current exactly, the fault record included, together with the fuel allowance and depth limit that were in force when it was taken. Before a restore, a session saves the current state as an automatic checkpoint `auto-N`, unless a checkpoint of the same state exists, so a restore loses nothing. A restore does not rewind the outside world: output printed after the checkpoint stays printed.

chunks.title: 8.4 Checkpoints, recordings and replay (part 6)
chunks.content:
Step by step:

- `cint workbench ledger.ci` loads the module as entry 1; its exports are named `ledger.deposit` and `ledger.balance`.
- Entry 2 deposits 1999. `:checkpoint paid` saves the state at the boundary after entry 2, with the revision of each loaded module: `ledger@r1` is the first revision of `ledger` in the session.
- Entries 3 and 4 deposit 425 and 10. Entry 5 faults. Its `state` line says that no store of the entry completed, so `balance` keeps 2434, and that the session cleared the fault before the next entry. Entry 6 reads 2434.
- `:effects` lists the recording: each entry with its value or fault, its fuel and the first 8 hexadecimal digits of the state digest at its boundary. The clearing of the fault, `context reset`, is an event of its own.
- `:save-case ledger.case` writes a case that starts from the checkpoint `paid` and holds entries 3 to 6. None of them printed, so the case holds no effects.
- `:watch ledger.balance` asks for each change of the balance at a boundary. `:replay paid` restores `paid` and runs entries 3 to 6 again: the watch reports the changes at entries 3 and 4, entry 5 faults again with a record equal to the recorded one, and all 4 boundaries match the recording.
- `:goto 3` saves the current state as `auto-1`, then makes the boundary after entry 3 current by restore and replay. Entry 7 reads 2424 there. Entries typed after `:goto` start a new branch, named after the boundary.
- `:restore paid` saves the current state as `auto-3` and makes `paid` current, where entry 8 reads 1999. `:diff auto-1` compares the current state with `auto-1`, binding by binding: the balance differs, and both values are shown.

chunks.content:
`chain` is the head of the chain of digests over the events replayed, and `state` the state digest at the last boundary replayed. Its first 8 digits are those that `:effects` showed for the same boundary: entry 6 for the whole case, entry 4 for `--to 2`. Boundary 2, entry 4 of the session, is the last change of the balance; the fault at boundary 3 stored nothing.

**Notes**

11. A program meant to be stepped through is written as a module whose exported function performs one step, called once for each step by its host program or by `:run` in a session. Each call then ends at a boundary that can be checkpointed, watched and replayed.

12. A checkpoint costs storage in proportion to the state; replay costs time in proportion to the distance from the nearest checkpoint. Checkpoints taken often make replay short.

chunks.title: 8.5 The debug tools
chunks.content:
### 8.5 The debug tools

Five more commands of `cint` run the debug tools and the interpreter. `cint workbench` runs a *session*: cint source entered one entry at a time, with commands to inspect, checkpoint, restore and replay; `cint repl` runs the same session loop. `cint explain` describes what the compiler knows about a function without running it. `cint debug` finds the fault of a program or a recording, replays recordings and cases and compares two executors on a case. `cint interp FILE` runs a program on `cpu-sir-interp`, as `cint run` runs it on `cpu-c17`. The `backend` and `evaluator` fields of their output name the executor (3.19). This subclause teaches a first session and the commands used most; SPEC-06P.1 defines every command, option and output format.

**Semantics**

1. A session compiles each entry with the compiler that `cint run` uses and runs it on `cpu-sir-interp`. The type rules are those of clause 6: a session has no conversions, dynamic types or relaxed overflow checks of its own. The same entry in a session and in a compiled program gives the same values, output, state after a fault and fault record except its `revision`.

chunks.title: 8.5 The debug tools (part 2)
chunks.content:
2. A session follows these rules:
   - A line that starts with `:` is a command. Any other line is cint source, a declaration, a statement or an expression, and is one entry.
   - Entries are numbered from 1, and the prompt `ci[N]>` shows the number the next entry takes. `:load` and `:run` each make one entry; the other commands make none. A position inside an entry is written `entry N:line:column`.
   - An entry that is not complete at the end of a line continues on the next, after the prompt `..>`.
   - A declaration adds to the *session module*. A variable declared at the prompt is a module-level variable of it, which keeps its value from entry to entry and is part of the state. A declaration makes a new revision of the session module.
   - An expression entry prints its value and its type.
   - Entries typed after a restore or a `:goto` start a new *branch* of the session's recording (8.4, example 9).
   - `cint workbench FILE` loads the module `FILE` as entry 1, which the session shows as the line `ci[1]> :load FILE`. Its exports are named with the module's name, as in `ledger.deposit`.
   - `:run f(args)` calls the exported function `f` of the session module as the entry itself, as `cint run` calls a program's entry, so `f` adds no position to a stack. An expression entry `f(args)` is an entry that calls `f`, and that call is a position of the stack.

3. This clause uses the following commands:

chunks.title: 8.5 The debug tools (part 3)
chunks.content:
| Command | What it does |
   |---|---|
   | `:load FILE` | Compiles and loads a module, as a new revision, and brings its exports into scope. |
   | `:run f(args)` | Calls the exported function `f` as the entry. |
   | `:inspect EXPR [/hex]` | Shows the value of `EXPR` exactly, and in hexadecimal with `/hex`. It is not an entry and changes nothing. |
   | `:trace` | Lists the counted operations of the last entry, by replaying it on `cpu-sir-interp`. |
   | `:fuel N`, `:depth N` | Sets the fuel allowance or the depth limit of each entry. By default an entry has no allowance and a depth limit of 256; `:fuel none` removes the allowance. |
   | `:checkpoint NAME` | Saves the state at the current boundary under a name. |
   | `:restore NAME` | Makes the state of a checkpoint current (8.4). |
   | `:diff NAME` | Compares the current state with a checkpoint, binding by binding. |
   | `:watch EXPR` | Evaluates `EXPR` at every boundary and reports each change. |
   | `:replay NAME` | Runs the recorded entries again from a checkpoint and compares each outcome with the recording. |
   | `:goto N`, `:goto fault` | Makes current the boundary after entry `N`, or after the entry that faulted, by restore and replay. |
   | `:effects` | Lists the recording of the current branch. |
   | `:save-case PATH` | Writes a case (8.4) for `cint debug`. |
   | `:quit [--yes]` | Ends the session; `--yes` ends it without asking about unsaved work. |

chunks.title: 8.5 The debug tools (part 4)
chunks.content:
4. `cint explain FILE:NAME` describes the function or kernel `NAME` of the module `FILE` without running it: its signature, with the mode of each parameter; its effect class, `pure` when it prints nothing and calls nothing that prints, and `observe` otherwise (`pure` here means only that; such a function may write module state); every *fault site*, an operation that can fault, with its identifier `NAME#n`, its position, its operation identifier and its fault code, and whether a fault there is possible or excluded; its fuel charges; and its compiled form. A site's identifier is fixed for a revision, and the `site` line of a fault report names the site that faulted.

5. `cint debug locate PROGRAM --entry NAME` runs the exported function `NAME` of a module as the entry, on `cpu-sir-interp` under a recording, and replays the recording to the first boundary that ends in a fault or an error result. It prints the fault report, the *bracket*, which is the last boundary before that one and the boundary itself, and the last counted operations of the faulting entry. Given a recording or a case in place of a program, it replays that. With `--changed BINDING` it looks instead for the last boundary at which the binding changed, scanning backward: it replays the last interval between checkpoints, then the one before, until it finds the change. It does not bisect, because a value can change and change back between two checkpoints. `--save-case PATH` keeps what it recorded as a case.

chunks.title: 8.5 The debug tools (part 7)
chunks.content:
Step by step:

- The first line names the language profile, `cint-core-1`, and the executor that runs each entry, `cpu-sir-interp`.
- `6 * 7` is an expression entry, and prints its value and type.
- `I8 small = 100;` declares a module-level variable of the session module.
- `small + 27` is 127, `I8.max`. `small + 28` faults at `entry 4:1:7`, the `+` in line 1 of entry 4. The stack is empty because the fault is in the entry's own code. Under `noncanonical`, `site` names the fault site `wb_entry#2` of the entry's compiled code.
- `small +| 28` is the saturating form, which gives 127 and does not fault (6.7.6).
- `:inspect` shows the value exactly and in hexadecimal; it makes no entry, so the prompt stays at 6.
- The declaration of `cube` takes three lines, continued after `..>`. It makes the second revision of the session module, `session@r2`.
- `:run cube(2097151)` makes `cube` the entry: 2097151 cubed fits in `I64`. `:run cube(2097152)` faults at the second `*`, because 2^42 times 2^21 is 2^63, one more than `I64.max`. The position `entry 6:2:18` lies in the text of entry 6, where `cube` was declared; `workbench-position` says that entry 8 ran it. The stack is empty because `:run` makes `cube` the entry.
- `:trace` replays the last entry and lists its counted operations: the first `*` gave 4398046511104 and the second faulted.

9. This example shows limits in a session. With a fuel allowance of 3, the call of `deposit` inside `deposit_all` would be the fourth charge: 1 when the entry begins, 1 for the call of `deposit_all` and 1 for the first iteration. With a depth limit of 2, the entry has depth 1 and `deposit_all` depth 2, so the call of `deposit` would exceed the limit and is not entered:

Both faults are at the callee's name of the call that failed, have no operands and no exact result, and have the allowance or the limit as their limit. The stack holds one position, the call of `deposit_all` in the entry; the call of `deposit` that failed is the record's position, not a position of the stack (8.1, paragraph 2).

10. `cint explain` lists the fault sites of `deposit`. Lines about analysis, fuel charges and how each executor compiles the function are left out:

```console
$ cint explain ledger.ci:deposit
module ledger.ci   revision fe98a3096002b4f1708db7ae5b9254a718cc55103ac59c209538413ab8ec92da

function deposit   ledger.sites:4   pure
  signature  (in cents: I64) -> I64
  fault sites (2): 2 possible, 0 statically excluded
    deposit#1  ledger.ci:4:12  fuel.charge      E_FUEL possible
    deposit#2  ledger.ci:5:23  add.checked.i64  E_OVERFLOW possible
...
  sir
export func @ledger.deposit(%cents: I64) -> I64 {
  fuel.charge 1                                  #1 @ledger.ci:4:12
  %t0 = load.global @balance
  %t1 = add.checked.i64 %t0, %cents              #2 @ledger.ci:5:23
  store.global @balance, %t1
  %t2 = load.global @balance
  return %t2
}
```

The function line gives `ledger.sites:4`, the line of `deposit` in the module's SIR text (3.41), the textual form of the compiled program, not a source position: the SIR text is a separate file with its own line numbers. `deposit` is `pure`: it prints nothing. It has two fault sites: `deposit#1`, the fuel charge when the function is called, and `deposit#2`, the `+` at line 5. The section `sir` is the function's part of that SIR text, the compiled form, which `cpu-sir-interp` runs; `#1` and `#2` mark the two sites. The module's revision is the one in the reports of the next example.

The entry is `month`, so its call of `deposit_all` at line 18 is the outermost position of the stack. The `state` line names IM-121, the state after a fault (5.2.3); `reached by replay` says that `locate` reached that state by replaying the recording. The bracket is the initial state and boundary 1, because the run has one entry. The trace shows the loop of `deposit_all` reading each amount, calling `deposit` and adding, until the fourth addition faults.

**Notes**

14. A routine for an unexpected fault has these steps:
   - Read the report (8.1): the position, the operands and the exact result say what failed, and the stack says how the program got there.
   - Run `cint explain` on the function to see its fault sites; the report's `site` line names the one that faulted.
   - Run `cint debug locate` on the program to see the operations that led to the fault, and keep the run as a case with `--save-case`.
   - Run `cint debug diff` on the case. `agree` means the two executors agree on this compiled form; a defect in the compiler that produced the form is not excluded. Any other outcome points at one of the executors.
   - Fix the program, then add a test or a golden (8.3) that would have caught the fault.

15. In a trace, `ord` numbers the operations of the whole entry from 0, in evaluation order. A row with `-` is a return, listed but not numbered. An `add.wrap.i64` row that the source does not contain, without a position in Example 11, is a loop's step of its index variable from one value to the next. The step ordinal of a kernel fault (8.1, paragraph 5) is a different count: it starts at 0 in each work-item and does not count loop steps. The operands and values of a trace are exact, and the row that faulted shows the fault code as its value.

chunks.title: Annex A (normative) Grammar
chunks.content:
## Annex A (normative) Grammar

This annex is the complete grammar of the language: every token and every syntactic form that a program of this edition may contain. Clauses 6 and 7 give each form with its meaning, in Syntax parts that use the names and definitions of this annex; a Syntax part that shows only some alternatives of a production says so. This annex collects the forms in one place and adds the rules that decide between two readings of the same text.

chunks.title: A.1 Notation
chunks.content: ### A.1 Notation 1. A production has the form `name = definition ;`. In a definition, `|` separates alternatives, `[ x ]` is optional, `{ x }` is repeated zero or more times, `( )` groups, quoted text is a terminal, `"a" .. "z"` is any character in that range, and `(* *)` encloses a comment. Lexical productions, which define tokens, have names in capitals; the others define the syntax over tokens [LS-295]. 2. A source file is read as a sequence of tokens from first character to last. At each point the token taken is the longest that the lexical productions allow. White space and comments may separate two tokens and are otherwise ignored; they are required only between two tokens that would otherwise read as one, such as a keyword and an identifier [LS-295]. 3. The grammar gives the form of a program. A text that it produces may still break a constraint of clauses 5 to 7, which a diagnostic reports, such as an operand of the wrong type, a constant out of range, or a `switch` that does not cover its values. Those rules are not repeated here [LS-295]. 4. A text that the grammar does not produce is not a program of this edition. A.8 lists the forms outside the grammar that are diagnosed with a code of their own. The forms listed in 6.16, among them `var` declarations, `enum` declarations and tuples, are reserved: this edition gives them no meaning, and an implementation rejects or refuses a program that uses one and does not run it. The reference refuses such a program (3.16). Any other text outside the grammar is a syntax error, C1050 [LS-295].

chunks.title: A.2 Lexical grammar
A.2 Lexical grammar (part 2)
A.2 Lexical grammar (part 3)
chunks.content:
6. A token that begins with a digit extends over every letter, digit and `_` that follows it and over a following `.` only when a digit follows the point (a hexadecimal digit after `0x`), so `1..5` is `1`, `..`, `5`, and `12ab` is one token that matches no production. The whole token shall match `INT_LIT` or `FRAC_LIT`. A literal's magnitude is within the limit of 5.3 (C1023) [LS-296].
7. A word that matches `IDENT` and is a `KEYWORD` is that keyword. Every keyword is reserved, including `distinct`, `do`, `enum`, `in_place`, `schedule`, `secret`, `type` and `var`, which no production of this edition uses. The words `as%` and `as?` are single tokens: `as` followed at once by `%` or `?` [LS-296].
8. The spellings of `INT_TYPE`, `Bool` and the mode and operation names are identifiers, not keywords. A declaration shall not declare a name that matches `I`, `U`, `Q` or `T` followed only by digits (C1010) [LS-296].
9. Outside comments, character literals and string literals, every character of a source file is ASCII (C1013). A `\x` escape gives a value from 00 to 7F, and a backslash sequence that `escape` does not produce, such as `\xff`, is C1032; a `\u{...}` escape gives a Unicode scalar value, not a surrogate code point and not above U+10FFFF (C1031). A character literal holds exactly one character or escape [LS-296].
10. Fault names, mode names, the operation names `add` and `mul` as the first argument of `fold_checked` (7.3), and the words `round` and `at` are identifiers, matched by their spelling in the positions where the productions name them. A fault name shall be one of the codes of 5.2.3 (C1011) [LS-297].

chunks.title: A.3 Holes and format specifications
A.4 Modules and declarations
A.4 Modules and declarations (part 2)
A.5 Types
A.6 Statements
chunks.content: ### A.6 Statements 18. The productions of statements are these [LS-301]: ```ebnf block = "{" { statement } "}" ; statement = block | const_decl | var_decl | view_decl | simple_stmt ";" | discard | print_stmt | if_stmt | [ IDENT ":" ] loop_stmt | switch_stmt | jump_stmt | defer_stmt | assert_stmt | static_assert | reduce_stmt ; view_decl = ( "in" | "inout" ) type IDENT "=" expr ";" ; simple_stmt = place assign_op expr | place ( "++" | "--" ) | [ "try" ] call ; place = IDENT { "." IDENT | "[" index_list "]" } ; assign_op = "=" | "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/=" | "%=" | "<<=" | ">>=" | "&=" | "|=" | "^=" | "+%=" | "-%=" | "*%=" | "<<%=" | "+|=" | "-|=" | "*|=" ; discard = "_" "=" expr ";" ;

chunks.title: A.6 Statements (part 2)
A.7 Expressions
A.7 Expressions (part 2)
chunks.content:
primary       = literal
              | STRING { STRING }                        (* an argument for an `in U8[_]` parameter *)
              | IDENT
              | ( INT_TYPE | "Bool" | FIXED_TYPE ) [ "." IDENT ]
              | FIXED_TYPE "." "raw" "(" [ args ] ")"
              | "(" expr ")"
              | array_literal
              | "." IDENT ;
literal       = INT_LIT | CHAR_LIT | FRAC_LIT [ round_clause ] | bool_literal ;
bool_literal  = "false" | "true" ;
array_literal = "[" [ expr { "," expr } [ "," ] ] "]" ;
```

21. A `neg_literal` is formed whenever a `-` in the position of an operand is followed by an `INT_LIT`, `CHAR_LIT` or `FRAC_LIT` token, whatever white space or comments lie between them: `- 5` is the literal -5. A binary `-` is not affected [LS-302].
22. A `call` names its callee directly: a function, a built-in operation, a struct (a constructor), a kernel (a dispatch), after a module name a function, kernel or struct of that module or after the name of an arena or a pool one of its members (paragraph 28). An expression in parentheses, an indexed expression or the result of a call is not called [LS-302].
23. A `STRING` used as a value is an argument for a parameter of type `in U8[_]`, which receives its bytes. Its adjacent literals are one string, and it contains no hole (C1033) [LS-302].
24. `( INT_TYPE | "Bool" | FIXED_TYPE ) "." IDENT` names a property of the type, such as `I64.max`; the type alone is a type argument (A.8, paragraph 30) [LS-302].

chunks.title: A.8 Disambiguation and diagnosed forms
chunks.content: ### A.8 Disambiguation and diagnosed forms

chunks.title: A.8 Disambiguation and diagnosed forms (part 2)
chunks.content: 25. A statement that begins with a type followed by an identifier, or with `const`, `in` or `inout`, is a declaration. At module level, a result type, an identifier, then `(` or `[` begin a function declaration, and a `const_decl` or a `var_decl` is a `declaration`, not a `statement`, so it does not make the module a script (5.1.2). A `_` followed by `=` begins a `discard`. Any other statement that does not begin with a keyword or a string literal is a simple statement [LS-303]. 26. In a `case_item`, a conditional expression is in parentheses, so the `:` that ends the case is never read as part of it; `case_item` is an `or_expr` for this reason [LS-304]. 27. In `for x in a..b`, the `range` belongs to the `for` statement: `in` is never an expression operator, and `..` and `..=` appear only in an `index`, a `range` and a `case_item`, never as expression operators [LS-305]. 28. `a.f(args)`, where `a` is a name, is a `call` of `f` qualified by `a`. When `a` names an imported module, `f` is a function, kernel or struct of that module. When `a` names an arena, `f` is one of its members `alloc`, `alloc_result`, `child` and `reset`; when `a` names a pool, `f` is one of `insert`, `insert_result` and `remove` (6.14). A program does not declare members [LS-306]. 29. `a.f` without an argument list is a field of the struct `a`, the storage integer `a.raw` of a fixed-point value, or a name, constant or struct of the module `a` [LS-306]. 30. In an argument list, an argument that is a type name and not a value is a type argument; only the built-in operations take type arguments (7.1). The mode and operation positions of the built-in operations take a bare identifier (7.1) [LS-307]. 31. ## Annex B (informative) Codes and operation identifiers

This annex collects the codes that translation and execution report: the diagnostic codes of translation (B.1), the fault codes of execution (B.2) and the operation identifiers that name the operation in a fault record (B.3). Each diagnostic code and fault code is defined in the subclause that the tables name. B.3 is the exception: it states the form and the spelling of operation identifiers, and its paragraphs that carry clause identifiers are normative.

chunks.content:
### B.1 Diagnostic codes

Five codes, C5051, C6002, C9001, C9002 and C9102, are reported by cint and not by the reference. C9102 is both a refusal and the code of some constraints (4, paragraph 4). cint refuses some constructs with C9102 before it reaches their other rules, so it does not report every code of the table [LS-313].

### B.2 Fault codes

3. A fault code names the kind of fault. Its number is the code's value in the canonical encodings of SPEC-01P.2. The table of 5.2.3, paragraph 1 lists every fault code with its number and the operations that raise it.

chunks.title: B.3 Operation identifiers
B.3 Operation identifiers (part 2)
chunks.content: 5. `form` is the form of the operator: `checked` for a checked operation, `wrap` and `sat` for the wrapping and saturating forms, and `result` for the result forms. `add` and `mul` occur only as the operation folded by `fold_checked` [IM-131]. 6. The first `op_type` is the operand type. A second `op_type` is present when the result type differs from the operand type: for a conversion, the source and then the target. `sum`, `dot` and `muldiv` always write the operand or element type and then the result type, even when the two are equal; `qmul` writes the types of its two operands and then of its result, and `mul_int` the fixed-point type and then the integer type [IM-132]. 7. `mode` is present exactly when the operation rounds, whether the mode was written or is the default. It names the mode the operation used [IM-133]. 8. A record holds the identifier of an operation that faulted. The wrapping, saturating and result forms of arithmetic never fault, so `sat` and `result` appear in no record, and `wrap` only in `shl.wrap.t`, the form of `<<%`, whose count is checked. Operations that cannot fault, such as the two-operand `min` and `max` (7.2.1), `uabs`, `mul_full`, `sum_wrap`, `sum_sat` and `count`, likewise appear in no record [IM-131]. 9. The identifiers of the operations that can fault are these [IM-134]. In the table, `t` is the operand type, `s` and `t` the source and target of a conversion, `e` the element type, `r` the result type, `q`, `qa` and `qb` fixed-point types and `n` an integer type, each spelled as `op_type`:

chunks.title: Annex C (informative) Defined behavior and deliberate absences
chunks.content:
## Annex C (informative) Defined behavior and deliberate absences

This annex is for a reader who knows C. C leaves many behaviors undefined, unspecified or to the implementation, and a C program that meets one of them can do different things on different compilers, or on the same compiler with different options. Clause 4, paragraph 6, states that within the scope of this document cint has no such behavior. C.1 lists, kind by kind, what cint does where C leaves the outcome open, and where C defines a behavior that cint defines differently. C.2 lists the features of C and of other languages that cint leaves out, each with its reason and what a program writes instead.

chunks.title: C.1 Behavior that C leaves open
chunks.content: ### C.1 Behavior that C leaves open 1. Every operation of this document has a defined result or a defined fault for every input, and every program that is accepted has exactly one outcome for each set of semantic inputs (clause 4, paragraph 2). This claim is about the language. The claim that the C an implementation emits evaluates no C operation whose behavior C leaves undefined, and the assumptions that claim rests on, are stated in SPEC-09P.1; this annex adds nothing to that scope [IM-128]. 2. The tables below follow the lists of Annex J of the C standard, ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17). The first column names the C17 subclause that sets the behavior. The last column names the subclause of this document that defines what cint does.

chunks.content:

|---|---|---|---|

| 6.5.5 | Division or remainder by zero | `/` and `%` fault `E_DIV_ZERO` | 6.7.7 |
| 6.5.5 | `INT_MIN / -1` and `INT_MIN % -1` | `MIN(T) / -1` faults `E_OVERFLOW`; `MIN(T) % -1` is 0 | 6.7.7 |

chunks.content:
| C17 | Defined in C | In cint | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6.2.5 | Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N | Unsigned arithmetic is checked like signed arithmetic. `+%`, `-%` and `*%` wrap where the program writes them | 6.7.6, 6.7.7 |

| 6.5.5 | `/` truncates toward 0: `-7 / 2` is -3 and `-7 % 2` is -1 | `/` rounds toward negative infinity, and a remainder other than 0 has the sign of the divisor: `-7 / 2` is -4 and `-7 % 2` is 1 | 6.7.7 |
| 6.5.10 | `x & 1 == 0` is `x & (1 == 0)` | The bitwise operators bind tighter than the comparisons: `x & 1 == 0` is `(x & 1) == 0` | 6.7.1 |

| 6.5.16 | An assignment is an expression, so `if (x = 0)` compiles | An assignment is a statement; one written as a condition is C1041 | 6.7.14 |

**Examples**

4. This example shows floor division and the arithmetic right shift. A C compiler prints `-3 -1` for the first two values; the third is implementation-defined in C:

```cint c_division.ci

I64 b = 2;
"{a / b} {a % b} {a >> 1}\n";
```

```text
-4 1 -4
```

5. `I64.min % -1` is 0. `I64.min / -1` has the exact result 2^63, one more than `I64.max`, so it faults:

```cint c_min_div.ci
I64 m = I64.min;
I64 d = -1;
"{m % d}\n";
I64 q = m / d;
"{q}\n";
```

chunks.content:
13. C does not address what happens when deep recursion or large local arrays exhaust the stack, and on most hosts the process ends with a signal. In cint each entry has a call-depth limit and a frame arena, and passing either faults at the same operation on every implementation (5.2.5, 5.2.6).
14. The scope of the claim excludes code reached through the host interface, defects in an implementation or in the C compiler that builds its output, hardware faults, and host resources an implementation cannot detect running out (clause 4, paragraph 6).

chunks.content: ### C.2 Deliberate absences 1. The features in the table below are absent from `cint-core-1`, and an implementation shall not add them [LS-271].

|---|---|---|

Annex D (informative) cint for C and Python programmers
chunks.content:
## Annex D (informative) cint for C and Python programmers

This annex lists the habits of each language that carry over and those that do not, and points each to the clause that holds the rule. Annex C lists the features that cint leaves out and gives the reasons. The Python spellings are those of the Python Language Reference and the Python Standard Library. The C spellings are those of ISO/IEC 9899:2018, except the case range `case 1 ... 5:`, which is a GCC extension.

chunks.title: D.1 For Python programmers
chunks.content:
### D.1 For Python programmers

1. The habits in this table carry over with the change shown:

| Python habit | cint spelling | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `for i in range(n):` | `for i in 0..n { }` | Half-open, as in Python. `0..=n` includes `n` (6.10.4). |
| `1_000_000` | `1_000_000` | As in PEP 515, except that `_` does not follow a base prefix: `0x_FF` is C1021 (6.4.5). |
| `print(f"x={x}")` | `"x={x}\n";` | A string literal on its own is a print statement. No newline is added (6.10.10). |
| `f"{x=}"` | `"{x=}\n";` | The same debug form (7.5.1). |
| `a // b`, `a % b` | `a / b`, `a % b` | Floor division and its remainder, as in Python (6.7.7). |
| `0 <= i < n` | `0 <= i && i < n` | A chained comparison is C2102 (6.7.2). |
| `a[-1]` | `a[len(a) - 1]` | There are no negative indices: `a[-1]` faults with `E_BOUNDS` (6.12.2). |
| `try: ... except E:` | `f() catch (e) { ... }` | For errors only. A fault is not caught (6.11.4). |
| `with x:`, cleanup | `defer { ... }` | Runs when the block exits, by any path, and not after a fault (6.10.7). |
| `assert x == y` with pytest | `assert(x == y);` inside `test "name" { }` | Both compared values are reported when the assertion fails (6.10.9, 6.15.3). |
| `float` | none | Fixed point, such as `Q32.32` (6.3.2), or scaled integers, printed with a scale such as `{v:/100}` (7.5.3). |

2. A Python `int` has no bound. Each cint integer type has a range, and every plain operator is checked: an operation whose exact result is outside the range faults (6.7). The forms `+%` and `+|` wrap and saturate where that is the intent (6.7.6).

**Examples**

3. This example shows a loop over a half-open range, the debug form of a hole and floor division:

```cint py_loop.ci
I64 total = 0;
for i in 0..5 {
    total += i;
}
"{total=} {-7 / 2} {-7 % 2}\n";
```

```text
total=10 -4 1
```

chunks.title: D.2 For C programmers
chunks.content:
### D.2 For C programmers

1. The habits in this table carry over with the change shown:

| C habit | cint spelling | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int64_t x = 0;` | `I64 x = 0;` | A variable of an integer, fixed-point, `Bool` or error-set type always has an initializer (6.9.1). |
| `(int32_t)x` | `x as I32` | Checked: `E_NARROW` when the value does not fit. `x as% I32` wraps (6.6). |
| `x + y` with signed overflow | `x + y` | Faults with `E_OVERFLOW`, for signed and unsigned types alike. `x +% y` wraps and `x +| y` saturates (6.7.6). |
| `switch` with fallthrough | `switch` without fallthrough | `fallthrough;` is written where it is meant. An empty case body is C4023 (6.10.5). |
| `case 1 ... 5:` (GCC) | `case 1..=5:` | Case ranges are inclusive. `case 1..5:` is C4022 (6.10.5). |
| `#include`, `#define` | `import name;`, `const` | There is no preprocessor (6.15.1, 6.9.2). |
| `printf("%d\n", x)` | `"{x}\n";` | Holes in a string literal (6.10.10, 7.5). |
| `if (x)` with an integer `x` | `if (x != 0) { ... }` | A condition is `Bool` (C2002), and braces are required (C1043) (6.10.2). |
| `(a & b) == c` | `a & b == c` | Bitwise operators bind more tightly than comparisons, so the parentheses that C needs can be left out (6.7.1). |
| `int *p; p + 1` | views and indices | There are no pointers in source (6.12). |

2. C leaves signed overflow, an index outside an array and a read of an uninitialized variable undefined. cint defines each: the first two fault, and the third cannot be written. Annex C goes through each kind of behavior that C leaves undefined, unspecified or implementation-defined.

**Examples**

3. Signed overflow is a fault, and its record holds the operands, the exact result and the bound it crossed:

```cint c_overflow.ci
I32 x = 2_147_483_647;
I32 y = x + 1;
"{y}\n";
```

Annex E (informative) Open questions
chunks.content:
## Annex E (informative) Open questions

This annex lists a question about a rule of this edition that the edition leaves open. Questions are numbered within each edition. Where this edition settles a question, the rule states the outcome, and the question is not listed here.

1. **Checking a handle at a call.** In this edition a call does not check its handle arguments when it begins. Passing a stale handle does not fault, and the first use of it in the callee faults `E_STALE_HANDLE` (6.9.5, 6.14.4). The open question is whether a call checks each handle argument when it begins; such a check reports the fault at the caller's line. A caller that needs the fault at its own line uses the handle before the call.

chunks.title: SPEC-06P.1
chunks.content:
# SPEC-06P.1: The cint tools

SPEC-06P.1, edition 1 of the specification of the cint tools, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

This edition specifies the command lines, outputs and exit statuses of the tools of cint 0.2.0. The language they run is specified by SPEC-04P.2, and the byte encodings of the files they read and write by SPEC-01P.2.

chunks.title: Foreword
chunks.content:
## Foreword

This document specifies the cint tools as cint 0.2.0 provides them: the `cint` command and the tools it starts, the interpreter `cint interp`, the workbench `cint workbench`, `cint explain` and `cint debug`.

Rules are numbered paragraphs within each section and are cited by section and paragraph, such as 5.4, paragraph 3. A rule that applies a clause of another cint specification ends with that clause's identifier in brackets, after the name of the edition that states the clause, such as [SPEC-04P.2 LS-234]. An identifier names one rule in every edition and document; section numbers belong to this edition only.

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.content:
## Introduction

cint is a C-family language whose every value is an integer of a declared type, or is built from such integers, and in which every plain operator is checked. Its tools turn a source file into a running program, and they also explain, record, replay and compare runs, so that a reader can find out why a program did what it did.

The first tool is `cint`. It compiles a program to C, builds it with the host C compiler, and runs it:

```console
$ cint run hello.ci
hello, world
answer=42
$ echo $?
0
```

The other tools work beside it. `cint interp` runs the same program from its intermediate representation without a C compiler, and records runs. `cint workbench` is an interactive session: each line typed at its prompt is compiled and run, and the session can show any value exactly, keep checkpoints and go back to an earlier state by replay. `cint explain` prints what the compiler knows about a function without running it. `cint debug` opens a recording, replays it, compares two executors on it and locates the boundary at which a run faulted.

In the source tree, `python3 tools/cint_bootstrap.py --leg LEG` builds `cint` with the C compiler `LEG`, one of `gcc`, `clang`, `apple-clang` and `msvc`. `python3 tools/cint_tools.py --leg LEG` then builds `cint-debug`, `cint-explain`, `cint-workbench`, `cint-repl` and `cint-interp` beside it.

chunks.title: How this document is organized
chunks.content:
### How this document is organized

Clauses 1 to 4 state the scope, the documents this one relies on, its terms and what conformance means for a tool. Clause 5 specifies the `cint` command, its four subcommands, and how it starts the other tools. Clause 6 lists the identities the tools print, and clause 7 the text and machine forms of diagnostics, fault reports and other messages. Clause 8 covers the interpreter, clause 9 the workbench and `cint explain`, and clause 10 `cint debug`. Clause 11 describes checkpoints, recordings and cases and clause 12 the receipts the tools write. Clause 13 lists directions beyond this edition. Annex A holds longer transcripts.

Examples of programs are written in `cint` blocks, each followed by the exact output of `cint run`. Transcripts of the tools are written in `console` blocks. A line that starts with `$ ` is a command, and the lines after it are what the command wrote to standard output and standard error, in the order a terminal shows them. In a session, the text after a prompt `ci[1]> ` or `..> ` is what was typed. `$ echo $?` prints the exit status of the command before it. A line `...` stands for lines left out.

Every transcript was produced by the tools of cint 0.2.0. A digest in a transcript, such as a 64-digit revision identity (clause 6), is the value the tools printed for that file with that build; the text says what each digest is. Digests change when the source, the compiler or the runtime changes and timings change from run to run.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols
chunks.content: ## 3 Terms, definitions and symbols For the purposes of this document, the terms of SPEC-04P.2 clause 3 apply, among them value, fault, fault record, operation identifier, diagnostic, refusal, the reference, executor, entry, fuel, call depth, frame arena, semantic input, module, script and revision. The following terms also apply. **3.1 tool**: the `cint` command, or one of the commands that it starts: `cint interp`, `cint workbench`, `cint repl`, `cint explain` and `cint debug` (5.1). **3.2 exit status**: the integer a tool returns to the operating system when it ends, from the table of 5.2. **3.3 tool error**: the refusal by a tool of its command line or its environment, such as an unknown option or an unreadable file. A tool error is not an outcome of a program, and a tool that reports one runs no program. **3.4 text form, machine form**: the two forms of a message. The *text form* is written for a person to read. The *machine form* is one JSON object, named by its `schema` key, written when the tool is given `--json`. **3.5 output set**: the files that `cint emit-c` writes for a program: the C of each module and of the program, the intermediate representation of each module as text, and a manifest of their digests (5.7). **3.6 project directory**: a directory that holds a program's modules, either directly or in a subdirectory `src`, with the root module `main.ci` (5.5). **3.7 boundary**: a point of a run at which the state of its context is defined and its state hash is taken, such as the end of an entry that ran (SPEC-01P.2, 3.16).

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 2)
chunks.content: **3.8 recording**: a file that holds a program, a checkpoint (3.10) of a context when recording began and the events that followed, from which the run can be replayed (SPEC-01P.2, 3.14). **3.9 case**: a recording that also holds the source text of every module of its program (SPEC-01P.2, 3.15). **3.10 checkpoint**: the canonical bytes of a state, taken between entries, from which a context can be restored (SPEC-01P.2, 3.11). **3.11 replay**: running the entries of a recording again from its initial state with the recorded inputs, and comparing each boundary with the recording. **3.12 receipt**: a canonical JSON file that records one run of a tool: its inputs, its outcome and what it observed (SPEC-09P.1, 3.14). **3.13 session**: one run of the workbench: a sequence of entries and commands typed at its prompt, with the state they produce. **3.14 identity**: a SHA-256 digest, written as 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, that names a program, a file or a state (clause 6).

chunks.title: 4 Conformance
chunks.content:
## 4 Conformance

1. In this document, "shall" states a requirement on a tool and "may" a permission.
2. A conforming tool accepts the command lines this document specifies, writes the outputs it specifies to the channels it specifies, and ends with the exit status it specifies.
3. The tools that run programs are implementations in the sense of SPEC-04P.2 clause 4. A program has one outcome for each set of semantic inputs: the same output bytes, the same fault record and the same fuel consumed under `cint run`, `cint test`, `cint interp` and the workbench.
4. A text form is written for reading, and its wording may change from one release to the next, except for the layouts of diagnostics and fault reports, which 7.1 and 7.3 fix. A machine form names its format and version in its `schema` key, and a reader locates every field by its key, never by its position.
5. A tool that cannot do what its command line asks reports a tool error, with exit status 4, 5 or 7, and the rules of the other statuses do not apply to it.
6. Transcripts and Notes are informative. Where a transcript and a rule differ, the rule governs.

chunks.title: 5 The `cint` command
chunks.content: ## 5 The `cint` command

chunks.title: 5.1 Command line
chunks.content:
### 5.1 Command line

`cint` translates and runs programs, and it starts the other tools. Each use names one subcommand: `run` runs a program, `build` writes an executable or a library, `test` runs the tests of a module, and `emit-c` writes the C and the intermediate representation of a program without compiling them. The other tools are started as `cint NAME`.

```text
cint [--json] run [--receipt PATH] [--root DIR] [--toolchain FILE] [--cache DIR] FILE.ci
cint [--json] build [--receipt PATH] [--root DIR] [--out DIR] [--lib] [--toolchain FILE] [--cache DIR] [FILE.ci | DIR]
cint [--json] test [--receipt PATH] [--root DIR] [--toolchain FILE] [--cache DIR] [FILE.ci | DIR]
cint [--json] emit-c --root DIR --out DIR [--toolchain FILE] MODULE.ci...
cint NAME ARGUMENTS...
```

chunks.title: 5.1 Command line (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. `cint --help` and `cint help` write the usage to standard output and exit with status 0. `cint` with no subcommand writes it to standard error and exits with status 4, and so does an unknown subcommand.
2. `cint NAME` runs the executable `cint-NAME` (`cint-NAME.exe` on Windows) from the directory that holds `cint`, with every other argument in order, a `--json` written before `NAME` included, on the same standard input, standard output and standard error, so that `cint workbench` is interactive in a terminal; `cint` exits with that tool's exit status. A tool finds the `cint` beside it, so `cint` passes it no option of its own. The tools of 0.2.0 are `interp`, `workbench`, `repl`, `explain` and `debug`. A `NAME` is 1 to 64 lowercase letters, digits and `-`, and does not begin with `-`. A `NAME` outside that rule, or one with no executable `cint-NAME` beside `cint`, is an unknown subcommand, exit status 4, and an executable that `cint` cannot start gives exit status 5. Clauses 8 to 10 specify the arguments of each tool, and this document names each tool by its command: `cint debug` is the executable `cint-debug`.
3. For `run`, `build`, `test` and `emit-c`, `--json` may appear anywhere on the command line. It selects the machine forms of clause 7 for everything the tool writes to standard error.
4. The options and the file may appear in any order after the subcommand. Each option other than `--json` and `--lib` takes one value, and each may be given at most once; otherwise the exit status is 4, with the message "an option needs one value and is given at most once".
5. An option that the subcommand does not take is a usage error, exit status 4. `--out` belongs to `build` and `emit-c`, `--lib` to `build` and `--receipt` and `--cache` to `run`, `build` and `test`.
6. A program takes no arguments. `cint run` given more than one file exits with status 4, with the message "

chunks.title: 5.1 Command line (part 3)
chunks.content:
The options:

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--json` | Write the machine forms of clause 7 to standard error. |
| `--receipt PATH` | Write a receipt of the run, the build or the tests to `PATH` (clause 12). |
| `--root DIR` | The directory that module paths are relative to (5.3). |
| `--toolchain FILE` | The toolchain file that names the host C compiler and its flags, in place of `cint.toolchain` beside `cint` (SPEC-09P.1). |
| `--cache DIR` | The directory for the files of each build (5.3), in place of the one the toolchain file names. |
| `--out DIR` | Where `build` writes its executable or library, or where `emit-c` writes its output set. |
| `--lib` | `build` writes a shared library in place of an executable. |

chunks.title: 5.2 Exit statuses
chunks.content:
### 5.2 Exit statuses

Every tool ends with one of eight exit statuses. A status says which kind of outcome the tool reached, so that a script can tell a program's fault from a failed check or a tool error.

| Status | Meaning | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Success: the program ended normally, the build was written, every test passed, or the check found what it looked for. | every tool |
| 1 | The program stopped with a fault. Standard output holds what it wrote before the fault. | `cint run`, `cint interp run` |
| 2 | Translation rejected the program with a diagnostic, or refused it. Nothing ran. | `cint run`, `build`, `test`, `emit-c` |
| 3 | A check failed: a test failed, a replay diverged or was refused, a comparison found a difference, a locate found no target, or a file is not a complete recording or checkpoint. | `cint test`, `cint interp`, `cint debug` |
| 4 | Usage error: the command line is wrong. | every tool |
| 5 | Environment error: a file cannot be read or written, or a tool or the host C compiler cannot be found. | every tool |
| 6 | `main` returned an error. Standard error names the error set, the value and its tag. | `cint run`, `cint interp run` |
| 7 | Internal error: the compiler faulted, the host C compiler rejected or warned on the emitted C, or the program process ended without a cint status. | every tool |

1. A program that faults ends with status 1 and a program whose `main` returns an error with status 6; neither is a tool error. `main` returning an error is not a fault: the run completed and its result is an error value [SPEC-04P.2 LS-221].
2. A tool error ends with status 4, 5 or 7, and its message is the only thing the tool writes to standard error.

chunks.title: 5.3 What every subcommand does
chunks.content: ### 5.3 What every subcommand does

chunks.title: 5.3 What every subcommand does (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. *Channels.* Standard output carries only the bytes that the program's print statements write, byte for byte, and `cint` flushes it before it reports a fault. Everything else goes to standard error: diagnostics, the fault report, the error result of `main`, the line `built: PATH` of `cint build`, the line `receipt: PATH` when a receipt is written, and tool errors. Under `--json`, the lines `built:` and `receipt:` are not written, and every other line on standard error is one machine-form object (clause 7).
2. *Module paths.* The root of a program is the directory of `FILE.ci`, or `--root DIR` when it is given; then `FILE.ci` is a path under that root. A module path is relative to the root: it is one or more segments separated by `/`, each made of ASCII letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`, with no empty segment and no segment `.` or `..`. Each segment, with `.ci` removed from the last one, is an identifier, so `import util.money;` names the file `util/money.ci` under the root. When the path of `FILE.ci` is outside this grammar, or the file is missing, a symbolic link, unreadable or larger than 4 MiB, `cint` exits with status 5. An imported module that is missing, a symbolic link, unreadable or larger than 4 MiB is the diagnostic C3009, and one whose path breaks the rule of SPEC-09P.1 7.1 is the diagnostic C3030, each with exit status 2 [SPEC-09P.1 CINTC-12].
3. *The program process.* `cint run` and `cint test` build the program into a fresh directory of the cache, `CACHE/DIGEST/run-N`, where `DIGEST` is the SHA-256 digest of the root path and the source, and `N` counts the runs of that source. A build reuses nothing from earlier runs. The program runs as a child process whose standard input is the null device. Before it starts the host C compiler, `cint` removes the environment variables `CL`, `_CL_`, `LINK`, `_LINK_` and `CCC_OVERRIDE_OPTIONS`, which would change the

chunks.title: 5.3 What every subcommand does (part 3)
chunks.content:
| Subcommand | Fuel allowance | Call-depth limit | Frame arena | Executor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cint run` | none | 256 | 2,097,152 elements | `cpu-c17` |
| `cint test` | 1,000,000,000 per test | 256 | 2,097,152 elements | `cpu-c17` |

5. *Receipts.* With `--receipt PATH`, `cint` writes a receipt to `PATH` after the run, the build or the tests, and, without `--json`, writes the line `receipt: PATH` to standard error. Without `--receipt` no receipt is written; there is no default destination. A receipt is written for the exit statuses 0, 1, 2, 3 and 6.

```console
$ cint run --receipt hello.json hello.ci
hello, world
answer=42
receipt: hello.json
$ cint run --json --receipt hello.json hello.ci
hello, world
answer=42
```

chunks.title: 5.4 `cint run`
chunks.content:
### 5.4 `cint run`

`cint run FILE.ci` translates the program whose root module is `FILE.ci`, with every module it imports, builds it with the host C compiler, and runs it once on the executor `cpu-c17`.

1. The root module shall have a program: top-level statements, which make it a script, or a function `main`. The script's statements, or `main`, run as one entry with the defaults of 5.3.
2. A root module with neither is an importable module, and it has no program to run. `cint run` translates it, reports a usage error that names `cint test`, and exits with status 4; nothing runs.
3. When the program ends normally, standard output holds what it printed and the exit status is 0.
4. When the program faults, standard output holds the bytes it wrote before the fault, with no byte added, standard error holds the fault report of 7.3, and the exit status is 1.
5. When translation rejects the program, standard error holds the diagnostics of 7.1, nothing runs, standard output is empty, and the exit status is 2.
6. When `main` returns an error, standard output holds what the program printed, standard error holds one line `error: SET.VALUE (tag N)` (7.5), and the exit status is 6 [SPEC-04P.2 LS-221].
7. `cint run` takes one file. A project directory is not a program for `cint run`; `cint build` (5.5) builds one.

Examples

8. A program that ends normally:

```cint hello.ci
"hello, world\n";
I64 answer = 6 * 7;
"answer={answer}\n";
```

```text
hello, world
answer=42
```

9. A program that faults after it printed one line. Its report names the operation, both operands, the exact result and the bound it crossed:

```cint partial.ci
I64 big = I64.max;
"partial: big={big}\n";
I64 r = big + 1;
"{r}\n";
```

chunks.title: 5.4 `cint run` (part 2)
chunks.content:
```text
partial: big=9223372036854775807
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> partial.ci:3:13
   |
 3 | I64 r = big + 1;
   |             ^ add.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 9223372036854775807
   = operand: I64 1
   = exact:   9223372036854775808
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   ...
```

10. The same program as a transcript, with its exit status:

```console
$ cint run partial.ci
partial: big=9223372036854775807
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> partial.ci:3:13
   |
 3 | I64 r = big + 1;
   |             ^ add.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 9223372036854775807
   = operand: I64 1
   = exact:   9223372036854775808
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   = revision: 2a5d25c827694f7bef7e0477ec0d760c95a7be976beaf854285a43555aeedef8
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 0
   = fuel-consumed: 1 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
$ echo $?
1
```

11. A `main` that returns an error:

```console
$ cat ledger.ci
error LedgerError { overdrawn, frozen }

LedgerError!I64 withdraw(I64 balance, I64 amount) {
    if (amount > balance) {
        return .overdrawn;
    }
    return balance - amount;
}

LedgerError!void main() {
    I64 b = try withdraw(100, 30);
    "left: {b}\n";
    I64 c = try withdraw(b, 500);
    "left: {c}\n";
}
$ cint run ledger.ci
left: 70
error: ledger.LedgerError.overdrawn (tag 1)
$ echo $?
6
```

12. A module without a program, and a command line without a file:

chunks.title: 5.4 `cint run` (part 3)
chunks.content:
```console
$ cint run prices.ci
...
cint: error: the root module has no main and no script statements, so there is no program; `cint test` runs its tests
$ echo $?
4
$ cint --json run
{"category":"usage","exit_status":4,"message":"no FILE.ci given","schema":"CINT-TOOL-1"}
$ echo $?
4
```

Note

13. The fault report after a run of `cint` is written by `cint` from the fault record that the program process hands back; the program process itself writes no report. An executable written by `cint build` (5.5) therefore stops with exit status 1 and writes only what the program printed.

chunks.title: 5.5 `cint build`
chunks.content:
### 5.5 `cint build`

`cint build` translates a program and writes it as an executable, or with `--lib` as a shared library, that runs without `cint`.

1. `cint build FILE.ci` writes an executable named after the root module, without `.ci`, into `--out DIR`, by default the directory `build` under the root. On the `msvc` toolchain its name ends in `.exe`. The tool writes `built: PATH` to standard error.
2. `cint build DIR` builds the project in the directory `DIR`: its root is `DIR/src` when that directory exists, and `DIR` otherwise, and its root module is `main.ci` there. `--out` defaults to `DIR/build`. A project directory takes no `--root`. `cint build` with no file or directory builds the project in the current directory.
3. With `--lib`, the root module shall be an importable module, with no `main` and no top-level statements, and the tool writes a shared library, `lib<name>.so` on Linux, `lib<name>.dylib` on macOS and `<name>.dll` on Windows. `--lib` on a script or a module with `main` is a usage error, exit status 4. Without `--lib`, a root module with no program is the usage error of 5.4, paragraph 2.
4. An executable built by `cint build` runs the program as `cint run` does, with the same defaults, and exits with status 0, 1 or 6. It writes no fault report (5.4, paragraph 13).
5. The exit status of `cint build` is 0 when the file was written, 2 for a diagnostic and 4, 5 or 7 for a tool error.

Example

6. A script, a project with an imported module and a library:

```console
$ cint build hello.ci
built: ./build/hello
$ ./build/hello
hello, world
answer=42
$ cint build shop
built: shop/build/main
$ shop/build/main
300 cents
$ cint build --lib --out lib shop/src/util/money.ci
built: lib/libmoney.so
```

The project `shop` holds `src/main.ci`, which imports `util.money` and calls `money.cents(3)`, and `src/util/money.ci`, which exports `cents`.

chunks.title: 5.6 `cint test`
chunks.content:
### 5.6 `cint test`

`cint test` runs the `test` blocks of a module and reports which passed. Tests are part of the language, and SPEC-04P.2 specifies what passes and what fails; this section specifies how the tool runs them and what it prints.

chunks.title: 5.6 `cint test` (part 2)
chunks.content:
1. `cint test FILE.ci` runs the tests of `FILE.ci` and of every module it imports. `cint test DIR` runs those of the project in `DIR`, as 5.5 locates it. Modules are taken in the byte order of their paths, and the tests of a module in source order [SPEC-04P.2 LS-234].
2. Each test runs in a process of its own, from a fresh context with fresh module state, with a fuel allowance of 1,000,000,000 and the other defaults of 5.3. The top-level statements of a script do not run under `cint test` [SPEC-04P.2 LS-234, LS-239].
3. A test without `expect_fault` passes when its body completes. It fails on a fault, including a failed `assert`, and when an error leaves it through `try` [SPEC-04P.2 LS-235, LS-315].
4. A test with the header `expect_fault CODE` passes only when its body faults with the fault code `CODE`. With `expect_fault CODE at LINE`, the fault shall also be on line `LINE`. The test fails when the body completes, when an error leaves it, or when it faults with another code or on another line [SPEC-04P.2 LS-236, LS-240].
5. For each test, standard output receives one line, `test FILE:LINE "NAME" ... ok` or `... FAILED`, where `LINE` is the line of the `test` keyword. After the last test, one line gives the count, `K of N tests passed`.
6. The reason for each failure goes to standard error after the test's line: the fault report of 7.3, whose `state` line reads "the test stopped; its output is not shown"; for an expected fault that did not come, `  expected fault CODE; the test completed`; for a fault with another code or on another line, the report and then `  expected fault CODE at line LINE`; and for an error that left the test, the line of 7.5 [SPEC-04P.2 LS-315]. A test's own prints are not shown.
7. The exit status is 0 when every test passed, 3 when any failed and 2 when translation rejected a module.
8. With `--json`, standard output receives one `CINT-TEST-1

chunks.title: 5.7 `cint emit-c`
chunks.content:
### 5.7 `cint emit-c`

`cint emit-c` writes the output set of a program: the C that `cint run` would compile, and the intermediate representation that `cint interp` runs. It compiles nothing and runs nothing.

1. `cint emit-c --root DIR --out OUT MODULE.ci...` takes the module paths of the program under `DIR`, each module after every module it imports, with the root module last. It does not follow imports itself: a module named before a module it imports is rejected with a diagnostic, exit status 2. `--root` and `--out` are required, and `--receipt` and `--cache` are not taken.
2. The output set goes into a new directory `OUT.stage-N`, where `N` is 0 for the first output set and goes up by one with each output set after it; the directory of the last output set is then removed. `OUT` itself receives one file, `MANIFEST.ref`, a line with the name of the current output set's directory and the SHA-256 digest of its manifest.
3. The output set holds, for each module `M.ci`, the C file `M.c` and the text `M.sites`, which is the module's semantic intermediate representation (SIR) as text, with its table of source positions; the program's C, `cint-program.c`, and its list of modules, `cint-program.sites`; and `MANIFEST`. The manifest's first line is `cint-manifest-1`, and each further line gives a file's SHA-256 digest, its size in bytes and its name.
4. `cint emit-c` writes nothing to standard output. Its exit status is 0, 2 for a diagnostic or 4, 5 or 7.

Example

5. Two output sets of the same program:

```console
$ cint emit-c --root . --out partial-out partial.ci
$ ls partial-out partial-out.stage-0
partial-out:
MANIFEST.ref

chunks.content:
