chunks.title: SPEC-09P.1
chunks.content:
# SPEC-09P.1: Toolchain and conformance

SPEC-09P.1, edition 1 of the toolchain and conformance specification, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

chunks.title: Foreword
chunks.content:
## Foreword

This document specifies how the cint toolchain of cint 0.2.0 is built and checked: the intermediate representation that its compiler produces, the C that the compiler emits and the runtime that C calls, what two implementations of cint must agree on, the conformance suite that measures that agreement, the bootstrap of the compiler from a hand-written C program, and the receipts from which a reader reruns a published figure.

Each rule ends with one or more clause identifiers in brackets, such as [SIR-09] or [EMIT-03]. An identifier names one rule across editions: a rule keeps its identifier when its text moves to another section or another document, and an identifier is not reused. Code comments, test files and receipts cite rules by these identifiers. Section numbers belong to this edition only.

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.content:
## Introduction

cint has one specification of meaning, SPEC-04P.2, and several implementations of it. A program compiled to C, the same program run by the interpreter, and a program whose kernels run on a GPU must give the same output bytes, the same fault record and the same count of fuel. A separate implementation written in Python, the reference, runs each program from its source text and gives the expected results. This document says how these implementations are built, what they must agree on, and how that agreement is measured and recorded.

A small program shows what agreement means. It prints a sum of squares and then narrows the sum to a type too small for it.

```cint agree.ci
I64 total = 0;
for i in 1..=10 {
    total += i * i;
}
"{total}\n";
I8 small = total as I8;
"{small}\n";
```

```text
385
fault[E_NARROW]: the value does not fit the destination type
  --> agree.ci:6:18
   |
 6 | I8 small = total as I8;
   |                  ^ as.checked.i64.i8
   |
   = operation: as.checked.i64.i8
   = operand-count: 1
   = operand: I64 385
   = exact:   385
   = limit:   I8 127
...
```

`cint run` compiled the program to C, built it and ran it. The reference shares no code with the compiler (5.4). It reads the same source and prints the outcome as the text that the conformance suite stores (9.3):

```console
$ python3 -m cint_ref run agree.ci
case agree
source reference
outcome fault
stdout-bytes 4
stdout-sha256 5476dba1f4bd59f1444ca1fd0770c1db808311b772f7685b3ff60ad7956418a8
fuel-consumed 11
fault.code E_NARROW
fault.operation as.checked.i64.i8
fault.operand I64 385
fault.exact 385
fault.limit I8 127
fault.position agree.ci:6:18
fault.revision self
fault.address none
fault.stack-depth 0
```

chunks.title: Introduction (part 2)
chunks.content: The two agree. Both wrote the same 4 bytes, `385` and a line feed, whose SHA-256 digest is the `stdout-sha256` line. Both stopped at the conversion at `agree.ci:6:18`, with the same operation, operand, exact result and limit. Both consumed 11 units of fuel: 1 for the entry and 1 for each of the 10 loop iterations. The line `fault.revision self` stands for the revision of the program under test, which the reference does not compute (6.5).

chunks.title: How this document is organized
chunks.content:
### How this document is organized

Clauses 1 to 4 state what the document covers, the documents it relies on, its terms and what conformance means. Clause 5 describes the architecture: one front end, one intermediate representation, three executors and the reference. Clause 6 defines that intermediate representation, SIR, and its text form. Clause 7 defines the C that the compiler emits and the runtime contract it relies on. Clause 8 says what two implementations must agree on and how a case that is not compared is reported. Clause 9 describes the conformance suite and how to run one case. Clause 10 describes the bootstrap of the compiler and what its self-hosting fixpoint shows and does not show. Clause 11 describes receipts and how a reader reruns a published figure. Clause 12 lists the constructs that the tools of cint 0.2.0 refuse. Clause 13 names two future directions. Annex A gives the measured figures of the release, and the Bibliography lists the works cited for information.

Every example in this document was run with the tools of cint 0.2.0. A `cint` block is a complete program, and the `text` block after it is its output exactly as `cint run` prints it. A `console` block is a tool session: a line that begins `$ ` is a command, the lines after it are its output exactly as printed, and a line `...` stands for lines left out. Commands that name a file of the source tree, such as `tools/cint_check.py`, are run from the root of the tree. The others are run from a directory that holds the example's files. In every session the tree's `ref/` directory is on `PYTHONPATH`, so that `python3 -m cint_ref` runs the reference, and the `cint` command is on `PATH`. Digests in the output change when the sources change, so the text says what each digest is, not its value.

chunks.title: 1 Scope
2 Normative references
chunks.content:
## 2 Normative references

The following documents are referred to in the text in such a way that some or all of their content constitutes requirements of this document. For dated references, only the edition cited applies.

- ISO/IEC 9899:2018, *Information technology: Programming languages: C* (C17). Used for the language of emitted C and for the behaviors that clause 7 avoids.
- D. Crocker, editor and P. Overell. *Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF*. RFC 5234 (STD 68), January 2008. Used for the grammar of 9.3.
- P. Kyzivat. *Case-Sensitive String Support in ABNF*. RFC 7405, December 2014. Used for the `%s"..."` strings of 9.3.
- A. Rundgren, B. Jordan and S. Erdtman. *JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)*. RFC 8785, June 2020. Used for the bytes of a receipt, with the departure in the escaping of strings that 11.2 states.
- T. Bray, editor. *The I-JSON Message Format*. RFC 7493, March 2015. Used for the integer range of a receipt.
- National Institute of Standards and Technology. *Secure Hash Standard (SHS)*. FIPS PUB 180-4, August 2015. Used for SHA-256.
- F. Yergeau. *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*. RFC 3629 (STD 63), November 2003.
- The Unicode Consortium. *The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0.0*, 2025. Used for the term Unicode scalar value (8.1).

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols
chunks.content: ## 3 Terms, definitions and symbols The terms of SPEC-04P.2 clause 3 apply, among them diagnostic, refusal, implementation, the reference, executor, entry, fuel, semantic input and revision. The following terms are added. Other terms are defined where they first appear, in italic type. **3.1 toolchain**: the programs of cint 0.2.0 that translate, run and check cint programs: the compiler `cintc`, the `cint` command and its subcommands, the interpreter `cint-interp`, the runtime and the conformance tools under `tools/` and `conformance/tools/`. **3.2 front end**: the part of the compiler that reads source text, checks it and produces SIR. **3.3 SIR**: the semantic intermediate representation, the form of a checked program that every executor of the toolchain runs (clause 6). **3.4 node**: one operation of SIR, such as one checked addition or one call. **3.5 site**: a node that can fault, identified by its module and its ordinal within the module, with the source position and the operation identifier that a fault record reports for it. **3.6 emitted C**: the C17 source text that the compiler writes for a program. **3.7 runtime**: the C code declared in `rt/cint_rt.h` and `rt/cint_rt_host.h` and built as the library `cint_rt`, which emitted C and the interpreter `cint-interp` call for checked arithmetic, fuel, call depth and fault records (SPEC-03P.1, 3.3). Its interface is the runtime contract of 7.10. **3.8 helper**: a function of the runtime that performs one operation of one type and reports its fault, such as `cint_add_i64`.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 2)
chunks.content: **3.9 capability**: a set of SIR node families, forms and types that an executor carries out with their exact meaning. An executor's *capability table* lists, for every family, form and type, whether it is supported. **3.10 conformance case**: a program, or one operation, together with its expected outcome. **3.11 expectation**: the expected outcome of a conformance case, written in the `.expect` format of 9.3. A *frozen* expectation is one that is part of the suite and is not edited in place (9.1). **3.12 canonical outcome**: what implementations compare for one entry: the output bytes, the kind of outcome, the returned value, the fuel consumed and the fault record, or, for a rejected program, the diagnostic code and position. **3.13 agreement**: the relation between two implementations whose canonical outcomes for a program and the same semantic inputs are equal in the sense of 8.1. **3.14 receipt**: a canonical JSON file (11.2) that records one run of a tool: its inputs, its outcome and what it observed. A bootstrap, a fixpoint run and a conformance run each write one, and so do the tools of SPEC-06P.1 that take `--receipt` (SPEC-06P.1 12). **3.15 receipt identity**: the SHA-256 digest of the canonical bytes of a receipt's inputs and outcome (11.2). Two runs with the same receipt identity had the same inputs and the same outcome. **3.16 configuration**: one choice of C toolchain, optimization level, helper mode (7.3) and sanitizers under which the toolchain and the programs it compiles are built.

chunks.title: 3 Terms, definitions and symbols (part 3)
chunks.content: **3.17 compiler source identity**: the SHA-256 digest of the source manifest of the compiler's source files (11.2). **3.18 bootstrap**: the building of the compiler from its source text and a C toolchain, with no cint compiler built earlier. **3.19 fixpoint**: the state in which the compiler, built from the C that it emitted for its own source, emits that same C again.

chunks.title: 4 Conformance
chunks.content:
## 4 Conformance

1. In this document, a rule is stated in the present tense, as a fact about a conforming implementation or tool, and ends with its clause identifiers (Foreword). "May" states a permission.
2. Clauses 6 and 7 apply to the toolchain and to any other implementation that produces SIR or emits C for the runtime of 7.10. Clauses 8 to 11 apply to every implementation that claims agreement with the reference.
3. A conformance run is evidence of agreement for the cases it runs, in the configurations it runs. It does not define the language: where an implementation and SPEC-04P.2 differ, SPEC-04P.2 governs, and the difference is a defect of the implementation or an ambiguity in the text.
4. Clause 12, Annex A, the examples and the notes are informative.

chunks.title: 5 Architecture
chunks.content:
## 5 Architecture

The toolchain turns a program's source text into one checked representation and runs that representation in several ways. Each way of running it is held to the same expected results, which a separately written implementation computes from the source text alone.

chunks.title: 5.1 Overview
chunks.content:
### 5.1 Overview

1. The figure shows the parts and how outcomes are compared.

```text
                     source text (.ci)
                            |
             +--------------+---------------+
             |                              |
     cintc front end                 the reference
             |                       (cint_ref, Python,
            SIR                       reads the source itself)
             |                              |
   +---------+-----------+                  |
   |         |           |                  |
 cpu-c17  cpu-sir-interp gpu-cuda           |
 emitted  cint-interp    cpu-c17 plus       |
 C and    runs the SIR   PTX for the        |
 runtime  text           work-item bodies   |
   |         |           |                  |
   +---------+-----------+--------+---------+
                                  |
                 canonical outcomes, compared (clause 8)
```

chunks.title: 5.2 One front end
chunks.content: ### 5.2 One front end The compiler `cintc` is written in cint and is the only front end of the toolchain. **Semantics** 1. One front end produces the SIR of a program, and every path that runs or describes the program takes that SIR: `cint run`, `cint build`, `cint test`, `cint emit-c`, the interpreter and the debugging tools `cint-explain` and `cint-workbench`. Arithmetic is carried out in these places only, each held to the conformance suite: the helpers of the runtime (7.10), the constant evaluation of the front end (held by the constant and run-time category of 9.4), each executor on its capability table, and the reference. The interpreter calls the runtime helper for every arithmetic, conversion and built-in node, the same helper that emitted C calls for that node, so it adds no arithmetic of its own [ARCH-01].

chunks.title: 5.3 Executors
chunks.content:
### 5.3 Executors

An executor runs the SIR of a program. cint 0.2.0 has three: `cpu-c17`, `cpu-sir-interp` and `gpu-cuda`.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 5.3 Executors (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The executor `cpu-c17` runs a program as C17 that the compiler emits (clause 7), compiled by a C toolchain and linked with the runtime. It runs the work-items of a kernel dispatch one at a time, in canonical order, stages the outputs and publishes them only when the dispatch ends without a fault. 2. `cpu-c17` is the reference implementation of the language on a CPU and the oracle against which other executors are compared. Where it and SPEC-04P.2 differ, SPEC-04P.2 governs (clause 4, paragraph 3). Every other executor is admitted by comparing its outcomes with those of `cpu-c17` and of the reference on the conformance suite [BACK-03]. 3. An executor that writes files is a module of `cintc`, compiled into it. The compiler loads no executor code when it runs, because such code would lie outside the compiler source identity [BACK-01]. 4. The executor `cpu-sir-interp` is the interpreter `cint-interp`, a C17 program outside `cintc`. It reads the SIR text that `cintc` writes for each module (6.2) and the program file `cint-program.sites` that lists the modules. Before it runs a program it checks the verifier rules it relies on (each temporary defined once and before it is used, the operand types, and a site on every node that can fault) and recomputes the revision identity (6.5); a text that fails these checks is reported with its position and is not run. It needs neither `cintc` nor a C compiler at run time. It calls the runtime helper for each arithmetic, conversion and built-in node and uses the `cint_rt` library for contexts, fault records and output. It executes the structured control flow of SIR as written, keeps frames under the depth limit, counts local arrays against the frame-arena capacity in elements, charges fuel only where SIR charges it (6.1), and runs the work-items of a dispatch one at a time i

chunks.title: 5.3 Executors (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Notes**

7. SPEC-02P.1 specifies how each executor carries out a dispatch so that its outcome is the sequential one.

chunks.title: 5.4 The reference
chunks.content:
### 5.4 The reference

The reference `cint_ref` is a Python program that runs cint source directly. Its results are the expected results of the conformance suite.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 5.4 The reference (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The reference is written in Python with the standard library only. It reads `.ci` source, parses it with its own parser, and executes it on Python integers, which have no fixed width, with an explicit range check after every operation that can overflow. It shares no code, tables, grammar files or generated files with the compiler or the runtime: it does not import, generate from or read any file of `cintc`, of the bootstrap compiler (10.2) or of `rt/cint_rt.h`. It enforces the call-depth limit itself, faulting `E_DEPTH`, so the recursion limit of Python is not reached first [ARCH-02, REF-01]. 2. The reference shares no code with the compiler, but it is not independent of it in a stronger sense. Both were written from the same specification text, so an ambiguity in the text can reach both. The check on such shared errors is the set of anchor cases (9.2), each derived by hand with its derivation written beside it [REF-02]. 3. The reference runs the work-items of a kernel dispatch one at a time in canonical order, stages the outputs and publishes them only on success. It reports each fault with the full fault record except the revision, which it does not compute [REF-03]. 4. Speed is not a requirement of the reference [REF-04]. 5. Anyone may run the reference directly on a program in its scope, from its command line or inside another Python runtime. A direct run is not a conformance run and writes no receipt. The reference does not define the meaning of a program: this specification does, and the reference is held to it [REF-08]. 6. The reference runs one `test` block of a module as its entry, in a fresh context, with `python3 -m cint_ref run FILE.ci --test NAME`, where `NAME` is the test's name. The outcome of the test body gives the v

chunks.title: 5.5 Capabilities and refusal
5.5 Capabilities and refusal (part 2)
chunks.content:
The capability table of `gpu-cuda` lists saturating arithmetic as `unsupported`. The emitted C carries the refusal inside the block that only a `gpu-cuda` build compiles:

```console
$ cint emit-c --root . --out out sat.ci
$ grep '#error' out.stage-0/sat.c
#error "gpu-cuda: E_UNSUPPORTED: kernel sat.k needs capability sat, node 35, at 2:17 (SPEC-09 BACK-05)"
```

A `gpu-cuda` build compiles this file with the macro `CINT_GPU_CUDA` defined, so it stops at the `#error`, which names the kernel, the capability, the SIR node and the position `2:17` of the `+|`. A `cpu-c17` build of the same file does not define the macro and runs the program.

chunks.title: 5.6 The compiler
chunks.content: ### 5.6 The compiler The compiler is a checked cint program. It keeps all its state in tables whose sizes it computes before it starts, and a host program drives it. **Semantics** 1. The source of the compiler is the import closure of `compiler/main.ci`. In cint 0.2.0 it is 14 modules: `back_c`, `back_ptx`, `check`, `decl`, `emit`, `fold`, `limits`, `lowering`, `main`, `parse`, `resolve`, `scan`, `sha256` and `verify`, each a file `compiler/.ci`. 2. All compiler state lives in tables of fixed capacity. The capacity of each table is a formula of the sizes of the inputs, capped by a hard limit. An input that exceeds a capacity is reported with the diagnostic C9001, naming the table, the limit and the source position; it does not crash the compiler and is not cut short silently [CINTC-01]. 3. Blocks nest at most 256 deep, not counting the body of a function or a test, and the `{` of a block 257 deep is the diagnostic C9004; the arms of an `else if` chain or a `switch` do not nest (paragraph 4). An expression nests as deep as the parser's stack holds, and beyond that is also C9004. The `cint` command reads at most 2,048 modules for one program, and stops a program of more with a tool error and exit status 5; 12 states what it does with a source file beyond the limit below. For a module of `n` source bytes, whose number of tokens, `tokens`, is at most `n + 1`, the tables have these capacities and hard limits; each division rounds down [CINTC-02]:

chunks.title: 5.6 The compiler (part 2)
chunks.content:
| Table | Capacity | Hard limit |
|---|---|---|
| Source | `n` bytes | 4,194,304 bytes per module, 67,108,864 bytes per program |
| Modules | the modules of the build | 4,096 per program |
| Syntax nodes | `2 * tokens + 16` | set by the source limit |
| Symbols | `tokens / 2 + 64` | 1,048,576 per module |
| Functions | `tokens / 4 + 1` | 65,536 per module |
| Types | `256 + tokens / 8` | 65,536 per module |
| SIR nodes | `4 * tokens + 16` | set by the source limit |
| Parser stack | `512 + tokens / 32` frames | 131,072 frames |
| Declarations seen across modules | 1, plus `n / 4 + n / 32 + 1` for each module | 1,048,576 per program |
| Output | the bytes that `measure` counts | 268,435,456 bytes per module |
| Retained diagnostics | 100 per module | 100 per module |

chunks.title: 5.6 The compiler (part 3)
chunks.content: 4. A chain of `else if` arms, and the arms of a `switch`, are one node with an ordered list of arms, and every pass of the compiler walks the list iteratively. A chain of 1,000 arms therefore uses the same stack depth as a chain of 2 [CINTC-03]. 5. The compiler uses no heap allocator and requests no memory during a call. A host program, the bridge (`rt/cint_bridge.c` and `rt/cint_build.c`), drives it through four exported calls: `plan`, which computes the size of every table from the sizes of the inputs; `compile`, which reads the source of a module into the tables and produces its SIR or its diagnostics; `measure`, which counts the bytes of each output file of a module; and `emit`, which writes them. The bridge allocates the tables after `plan` and the output buffers after `measure` [CINTC-05]. 6. `measure` and `emit` run over the same SIR in separate calls. The bridge allocates exactly the number of bytes `measure` counted, and `emit` writes exactly that many; a different count is an internal compiler error [CINTC-04]. 7. The compiler performs no input or output of its own. 7.1 describes how the bridge reads its inputs and commits its outputs. 8. A fault inside the compiler, such as an index outside a table, is reported as an internal compiler error with the full fault record, the compiler source identity and the identity of the compiler's inputs [CINTC-10]. **Notes** 9. Because the compiler is a checked program, a fault inside it stops it instead of corrupting memory. A logic error that produces wrong output without a fault, such as lowering `+` to `+%`, is found only by the conformance suite and the fixpoint (10.4).

chunks.title: 6 SIR
chunks.content:
## 6 SIR

SIR is the program after it has been checked: every value has its type, every intermediate value has a name, control flow is structured, and every point where the program can fault is marked with its source position. Every executor of the toolchain runs SIR, and `cint-explain` prints it.

chunks.title: 6.1 Design rules
chunks.content:
### 6.1 Design rules

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 6.1 Design rules (part 2)
chunks.clauses: SIR-01 SIR-02 SIR-03 SIR-04 SIR-05 SIR-06 SIR-07 SIR-15 SIR-16
chunks.content: 1. SIR is typed. Every temporary, local, parameter and result has exactly one cint type, `Bool` for comparisons and conditions. There is no implicit conversion: every change of width or signedness is an `as` node [SIR-01]. 2. Every node that produces a value defines a new temporary, `%t0`, `%t1` and so on, exactly once. A variable of the source is a *slot*, read by `load.local` and written by `store.local`. Nodes are evaluated in the order they are written; nothing in SIR is unordered [SIR-02]. 3. A checked operation is one node, such as `add.checked.i64`, not an addition followed by a test. An executor lowers the node as a unit and cannot separate the check from the operation [SIR-03]. 4. Every node that can fault, including a fuel charge and a call, is a site: it carries its module, line, column and operation identifier. Sites are numbered from 1 in each module, in node order; the number 0 means no site [SIR-04]. 5. Control flow is structured: blocks, `if`, `loop`, `switch`, `break`, `continue`, `return` and the fault exit. There is no arbitrary jump. `&&` and `||` become an `if` that evaluates the right operand only when it is needed. A chain of `else if` arms is one `if` node with an ordered list of arms. The interpreter runs this structure as it is written and lowers nothing itself [SIR-05]. 6. The front end resolves every default of the language before it writes SIR. A fixed-point multiplication carries its intermediate width and its rounding mode even when the source used the default, and a reduction carries the width of its accumulator. An executor does not supply a default [SIR-06]. 7. Every fuel charge is explicit in SIR, so every executor charges at the same points. An entry's charge and a loop iteration's charge are `fuel.cha

chunks.title: 6.2 The text form
chunks.content: ### 6.2 The text form SIR has one text form. The compiler writes it for every module, the interpreter reads it, and `cint-explain` prints it. **Semantics** 1. The text form is ASCII with LF line endings and one node per line. Temporaries are numbered from `%t0` in each function, in the order they are defined. A node that is a site ends with its ordinal and position, `# @::`, where `` is the module-relative path. A node is indented two spaces for each level of structure that encloses it, up to 16 levels and 32 spaces at any deeper level, so the size of the text stays linear in the number of nodes; braces carry the structure [SIR-09]. 2. The text of a module is, in order: a line `module ` with the module's dotted name; the `sites` line, `sites ` followed by one item `:::` for each site in node order; one `struct` line for each struct type of the module, in declaration order; one `global` line for each module-level variable, in declaration order; and the functions, kernels, script body and test blocks of the module. In the `sites` line, the operation of a call's site is `call.enter`, that of a print statement's site is `print`, and that of any other site is the node's own operation identifier. On a node line, a site's annotation begins at the 50th character, or after it when the node text is longer, with at least one space before it. A parameter is written `%`, a slot `$.`, a module-level variable `@` and a structure that `break` or `continue` names `L`; these numbers count from 0, and site ordinals from 1. Values are decimal, and printed text is written in double quotes with `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t` and `\x` for other bytes outside printable ASCII [SIR-09a]. 3. The main forms are these.

: , ...) -> {` | A function; `-> ` is absent when it has no result, and the line begins `export ` for an exported function. | | `kernel @.(%

`cint emit-c` writes the SIR text of each module into a file named after the module with the extension `.sites`, beside its C file (7.1):

```console
$ cint emit-c --root . --out out add.ci
$ cat out.stage-0/add.sites
module add
sites add.ci 1:2:14:add.checked.i64 2:2:18:add.checked.i64 3:4:1:fuel.charge 4:4:3:call.enter 5:4:1:print
func @add.add3(%a: I64, %b: I64, %c: I64) -> I64 {
  %t0 = add.checked.i64 %a, %b                   #1 @add.ci:2:14
  %t1 = add.checked.i64 %t0, %c                  #2 @add.ci:2:18
  return %t1
}
script @add {
  fuel.charge 1                                  #3 @add.ci:4:1
  %t0 = const I64 1
  %t1 = const I64 2
  %t2 = const I64 3
  %t3 = call @add.add3(%t0, %t1, %t2)            #4 @add.ci:4:3
  print.begin                                    #5 @add.ci:4:1
  print.value I64 %t3
  print.bytes "\n"
  print.end
}
```

The two additions of `a + b + c` are sites 1 and 2, at the two `+` signs. The script charges 1 unit when its entry begins (site 3). The call charges its unit at the call's site (site 4, `call.enter`), where a call that would exceed the depth limit also faults. The function `add3` has no `fuel.charge` of its own, because it is entered only by calls.

5. `cint-explain` prints the fault sites of a function and its SIR:

    add3#2  add.ci:2:18  add.checked.i64  E_OVERFLOW possible
...

chunks.title: 6.2 The text form (part 4)
chunks.content: The first line gives the revision identity of the program (6.5). SPEC-06P.1 describes the other lines.

chunks.title: 6.3 Verifier
chunks.content: ### 6.3 Verifier **Constraints** 1. Before any executor runs, the verifier checks that every temporary is defined exactly once and before it is used; that the types of the operands match the node's signature exactly; that every node that can fault has a site; that every write goes to a view with write permission or carries the run-time `E_ALIAS` check; that kernel bodies meet the restrictions of SPEC-04P.2 6.13; and that the outputs of each dispatch are covered by one alias check over all its writable bindings. A failure is an internal compiler error that names the node, not a warning. The interpreter checks again, when it reads a SIR text, the rules it relies on (5.3) [SIR-10]. 2. The verifier computes the capabilities that each function and kernel needs. The executor's admission of a program compares this set with its capability table (5.5) [SIR-11].

chunks.title: 6.4 Transformations
chunks.content: ### 6.4 Transformations **Constraints** 1. A transformation of SIR is admissible only if, for every input, it keeps the output bytes, whether a fault occurs, the full fault record (code, operation, operands, exact result, position and address, including the step ordinal), every effect that comes before the fault, and the fuel charged up to any point that can be observed [SIR-12].

chunks.title: 6.5 Revision identity
chunks.content: ### 6.5 Revision identity The revision identity is a digest of a program's SIR with the source positions taken out. Fault records, checkpoints and receipts name a program by it. **Semantics** 1. The *hashed encoding* of a module is its SIR text (6.2) with the `sites` line removed and, on every node line, the text ` @::` after the site ordinal removed. The ordinals `#` stay, and so do the spaces before them; no line or column remains. The revision identity is the SHA-256 digest of these bytes, in order [SIR-17]: - the domain `cint-core-1/revision/v1`, the profile name `cint-core-1` and the runtime contract version (7.10), each as a 32-bit little-endian length followed by its ASCII bytes; - the number of modules, as a 32-bit little-endian integer; - for each module, in byte order of its module-relative path: the path, as a 32-bit little-endian length followed by its UTF-8 bytes, then the hashed encoding, as a 64-bit little-endian length followed by its bytes.

chunks.title: 6.5 Revision identity (part 2)
chunks.content:
The fuel model is not an input of the revision identity. A separate *source-map digest* is the SHA-256 digest of the domain `cint-core-1/source-map/v1`, as a 32-bit little-endian length followed by its ASCII bytes; the number of modules, as a 32-bit little-endian integer; and for each module, in the same order, its path, as a 32-bit little-endian length followed by its UTF-8 bytes, its number of sites, as a 32-bit little-endian integer, and for each item of its `sites` line, in the line's order, the ordinal, line and column, as 32-bit little-endian integers, and the operation, as a 32-bit little-endian length followed by its ASCII bytes. Both are recorded with a program. Fault positions are read through the source map recorded with the revision. The interpreter recomputes the revision identity from the text it reads, so a checkpoint, a recording or a case runs on it only with the revision it names.
**Examples**

2. For `add.ci` of 6.2, the hashed encoding of the module `add.ci` is the text of `add.sites` without its second line, with each ` @add.ci:<line>:<column>` removed. Its revision identity is the digest that `cint-explain` printed in 6.2, and the same 32 bytes are the array `cg_revision` of the emitted `cint-program.c`. A copy of the module with a blank line added before it keeps the same revision, while its sites move to line 3:

```console
$ mkdir moved
$ { echo; cat add.ci; } > moved/add.ci
$ cint-explain --root moved add.ci:add3
module add.ci   revision bc1faa5409ed570368f6f2ed815f89623096edcce3fcde135d6a1db89a37a2f2

function add3   add.sites:3   pure
  signature  (in a: I64, in b: I64, in c: I64) -> I64
  fault sites (2): 2 possible, 0 statically excluded
    add3#1  add.ci:3:14  add.checked.i64  E_OVERFLOW possible
    add3#2  add.ci:3:18  add.checked.i64  E_OVERFLOW possible
...
```

**Notes**

chunks.title: 6.5 Revision identity (part 3)
chunks.content:
3. A blank line added to a module, or a function moved down, changes the source map but not the revision identity, so a checkpoint of a context that has not faulted still restores. Reordering two statements, or adding an operation that can fault, changes the site ordinals and so the revision identity.
4. A checkpoint of a context that holds a fault keeps the position of its fault, and a restore maps that position back to a site by its line and column. After an edit that moves the faulting line, such a checkpoint is refused even though the revision identity has not changed.

chunks.title: 7 Emitted-C contract
chunks.content:
## 7 Emitted-C contract

The compiler emits C17 that is defined for every input that reaches it: each check comes before the operation it guards, and the C compiler is given nothing it may treat as undefined. The emitted C calls the runtime for checked operations, fuel, call depth and fault records. This clause states what the emitted C and the runtime promise each other.

chunks.title: 7.1 The output set
chunks.content: ### 7.1 The output set The compiler writes the files of a program as one set, which a reader sees complete or not at all. **Semantics** 1. The compiler performs no input or output. The bridge reads the files named in the build manifest, in manifest order and not by listing a directory, and passes each module's path relative to the source root, with `/` separators. Outputs are committed as one set [CINTC-06]: 1. All output files are written into a new sibling directory `.stage-`, where `N` is the first unused decimal integer, created exclusively. Each module's files are written as its `emit` call completes, and the program file after the last module. A diagnostic, a fault or a failed write in any module abandons that directory: the committed set stays as it was, byte for byte, and no new file is visible to a reader. 2. The bridge writes the file `MANIFEST` into that directory. Its first line is `cint-manifest-1`, and each following line is ` ` for one output file, in byte order of path. The bridge flushes every file to stable storage. 3. The commit is one atomic replacement of the single file `/MANIFEST.ref`, which holds the name of the new directory and the SHA-256 digest of its `MANIFEST`: `rename` on POSIX systems, and `MoveFileExW` with `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING` and `MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH` on Windows. These are the only platform calls of the bridge. 4. Readers trust only the files that the `MANIFEST` named by `MANIFEST.ref` lists, after checking each file's digest. Directories left by earlier builds are removed after a commit when possible; their presence does not change what a reader sees.

chunks.title: 7.1 The output set (part 2)
chunks.content: A reader that runs while a build commits sees `MANIFEST.ref` name either the complete old set or the complete new one. No claim is made for single files, or for durability after a crash or a power loss, which depends on the file system. 2. A module-relative path is one or more segments separated by `/`. Each segment is made of ASCII letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`, and is not empty, `.` or `..`. A path has no leading `/`, no drive letter, no `\` and no `:`. No segment names a Windows device (`CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM1` to `COM9`, `LPT1` to `LPT9`, in any case) before its first `.`, and no segment ends in `.`. All the paths of one build differ under ASCII case folding. With the final `.ci` removed, every segment is an identifier, so a dotted module name and its path correspond one to one. Any other path is the diagnostic C3030, naming the path and the rule it breaks. The bridge opens every file relative to the source root and refuses symbolic links and other reparse points [CINTC-12]. **Examples** 3. The build of `add.ci` from 6.2: ```console $ cint emit-c --root . --out out add.ci $ ls out out.stage-0 out: MANIFEST.ref out.stage-0: MANIFEST add.c add.sites cint-program.c cint-program.sites $ cat out/MANIFEST.ref out.stage-0 06d38f20f86a9e377eca47c7cd7eebc5c8fd7154ee06e93498ed881a63395424 $ cat out.stage-0/MANIFEST cint-manifest-1 1a4f0c8f856d921cbfa7f478970c9926c77ce455ee776711033781b195708d34 2358 add.c d83a256fcde82d46d7b00eaa2de7c6e491dc1ac747e3f4f10244d35b758887f5 634 add.sites 2a7330a85849fd42f62eb7f4643131da96de92dc9f2cec08ffeb2a36285b141b 1318 cint-program.c ce55c32dc70f577c08198ce999ba084cbbf8e0e291a2a4828d6933b052ca778d 16 cint-program.sites $ sha256sum out.stage-0/MANIFEST 06d38f20f86a9e377eca47c7cd7eebc5c8fd7154ee06e93498ed881a63395424 out.stage-0/MANIFEST ```

chunks.title: 7.1 The output set (part 3)
chunks.content:
`add.c` is the module's C, `add.sites` its SIR text, `cint-program.c` the program file that ties the modules together and holds the revision, and `cint-program.sites` the list of modules that the interpreter reads. The digest in `MANIFEST.ref` is the SHA-256 digest of `MANIFEST`, as an external tool computes it.

**Notes**

4. Microsoft does not document the replacement by `MoveFileExW` as atomic, so on Windows the property of paragraph 1, that a reader sees the complete old set or the complete new one, rests on a test that stops the bridge after each file and checks what a reader sees.

chunks.title: 7.2 Language level and headers
chunks.content:
### 7.2 Language level and headers

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 7.2 Language level and headers (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. Emitted C is C17: GCC and Clang compile it with `-std=c17`, and MSVC with `/std:c17`. It includes only ``, ``, ``, ``, `` and `cint_rt.h`. It does not include `` or ``, and it contains no `float`, `double` or `long double` token. The C sources of the runtime, the bridge, the harness, the `cint` command, the interpreter and the bootstrap compiler contain no floating-point type, literal or header either; `python3 tools/cint_lint.py` checks each of these sources for them [EMIT-01, RT-2]. 2. Emitted C relies only on behavior that C17 defines for every input that reaches it, and on these properties of the C implementation, each checked when `cint_rt.h` is compiled: `CHAR_BIT` is 8 (a static assertion); `int8_t` to `int64_t` and `uint8_t` to `uint64_t` exist, which in C17 makes the signed exact-width types two's complement (an `#error` otherwise); `size_t` has at least 32 bits (a static assertion); and pointers have 64 bits, so the runtime supports 64-bit hosts only (a static assertion). External identifiers must be significant to at least 247 characters, which no source check can test; a generated symbol longer than 247 bytes is the diagnostic C9002 (7.7). No string literal of emitted C, after adjacent literals are joined, is longer than 4,095 characters, the minimum that C17 5.2.4.1 requires an implementation to accept: the literal text of a print statement reaches the runtime in pieces of at most 1,024 bytes, each written as adjacent literals of at most 64 bytes, and the PTX of a module's kernels is an array of literals, one per line [EMIT-02]. 3. Emitted C is ASCII with LF line endings, a final LF, no trailing space, no tab and four-space indentation. Its first line is the comment `/* cint-core-1, cint-rt-3, emitted by cintc

chunks.title: 7.3 Checks before operations
chunks.content:
### 7.3 Checks before operations

In C, a signed overflow, a division by zero and a shift by the width of the type are undefined. Emitted C performs the check that cint requires before the operation, so the undefined case is never evaluated, and it computes the defined result with operations that C defines for all inputs.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.3 Checks before operations (part 2)
chunks.clauses: EMIT-03 EMIT-04 EMIT-05 EMIT-07 EMIT-08 EMIT-09 EMIT-10
chunks.content: 1. No emitted operation is evaluated when its C result would be undefined. Either the check comes first, or the operation is one that C defines for all inputs: unsigned arithmetic, or a checked builtin. Computing a signed result that overflows and testing it afterward is forbidden. Every helper of the runtime computes a defined C result before it reports any fault [EMIT-03, RT-9]. 2. Emitted C performs a checked operation by calling a helper `bool cint__(cint_ctx *ctx, cint_site site, ..., T *out)`, such as `cint_add_i64(ctx, site, a, b, &out)`. A helper writes `*out` and returns `true` when the exact result is in range. Otherwise it writes the full fault record into the context, if the context holds none yet, and returns `false` without writing `*out`. A wrapping helper that cannot fault takes no context; a wrapping left shift takes the context and the site, because it still faults `E_SHIFT` for a bad count. The checked add, subtract and multiply have two *helper modes*. With `CINT_RT_HELPERS_BUILTIN`, they use `__builtin_add_overflow`, `__builtin_sub_overflow` and `__builtin_mul_overflow` on GCC and Clang, and the intrinsics `_mul128` and `_umul128` for the multiply on MSVC for x64. With `CINT_RT_HELPERS_PORTABLE`, which `CINT_RT_PORTABLE=1` also selects, they use range tests in `int64_t` and `uint64_t` before the operation. Defining both macros is an `#error`. With neither defined, `cint_rt.h` selects the builtin mode on GCC and Clang and the portable mode elsewhere. The two modes give identical outcomes, and the conformance suite runs in both [EMIT-04, EMIT-05, RT-8, RT-12]. 3. A wrapping operation (`+%`, `-%`, `*%`, `<<%`) is computed in the unsigned type of the same width, or in `uint64_t` for widths below 64, and the result

chunks.title: 7.4 Memory
chunks.content: ### 7.4 Memory **Semantics** 1. Index and slice checks are computed on integer offsets before any pointer is formed. No emitted expression forms a pointer outside an object or more than one element past its end [EMIT-13]. 2. The bytes of a buffer are reinterpreted only with `memcpy` or through `unsigned char`. No pointer is cast between distinct object types, so the aliasing rules of C17 6.5 are neither relied on nor broken [EMIT-14]. 3. Every scalar local is initialized where it is declared, and every array is zeroed where the language says it is. A wide temporary may be left uninitialized at its declaration when the node that defines it comes before every use on every path, which the emitter reads from the structured control flow of SIR [EMIT-15].

chunks.title: 7.5 The shape of the code
chunks.content:
### 7.5 The shape of the code

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.5 The shape of the code (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. Each SIR node becomes one C statement, with two exceptions: an index check that the emitter shows cannot fail becomes none, and a *counted loop* is emitted twice. A counted loop is a loop whose `I64` counter is compared by `<` with a bound that the loop does not change, is stepped once per iteration by a constant of at least 1, and whose body holds only loads, stores, element and field accesses, arithmetic, conversions, comparisons, built-ins and checks. Before it, one test enters a copy of the loop that charges no fuel per iteration, when the context holds no fault and the fuel left covers every iteration the counter allows; otherwise the loop runs as written. Each exit of the copy first sets the fuel consumed to the count the loop as written would have reached, so the outcome, fault record and fuel are those of the loop as written. No emitted C expression contains more than one operation that can fault or has a side effect, so C's unspecified order of evaluation of operands and arguments never matters [EMIT-16]. 2. Scalar temporaries are C locals, such as `int64_t t3`, not slots in memory managed by the runtime [EMIT-17]. 3. Faults do not use `setjmp`, `longjmp` or signals. A function emitted for a cint function follows the convention of the runtime's helpers [EMIT-18]: - It returns `bool`: `true` on success, and `false` after the runtime has written the fault record. A function that returns a value writes it through a final `T *result` parameter, and only when it returns `true`. - A checked operation calls a helper with a `cint_site`, the pair of the module's index in the program and the site ordinal. When the helper returns `false`, the function jumps to its single fault exit. - A call of a cint function is preceded by `cint_rt_call_enter(ctx, site)`, which checks the depth limit, charges the

chunks.title: 7.5 The shape of the code (part 3)
7.6 Independence from the C compiler's options
chunks.content: ### 7.6 Independence from the C compiler's options **Semantics** 1. The observable behavior of emitted C does not depend on the optimization level, on `-fwrapv`, `-ftrapv` or `-fno-strict-aliasing` or on MSVC's `/O1`, `/O2` or `/Od`, for a program that does not exhaust the C stack. The conformance suite runs at `-O0` and `-O2` (`/Od` and `/O2`) and requires identical outcomes [EMIT-19]. 2. With GCC and Clang, the conformance suite also runs under `-fsanitize=undefined,address`, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and AddressSanitizer, and requires that they report nothing. A sanitized build is a conformance build only [EMIT-20]. **Notes** 3. The sanitized runs are evidence for 7.3 paragraph 1 over the programs run, not a proof for all programs (11.4).

chunks.title: 7.7 Deterministic output
chunks.content:
### 7.7 Deterministic output

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.7 Deterministic output (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. Emitted C is a function of these inputs only: the bytes of the declared input files and their module-relative paths, the compiler source identity, the language profile and the executor and its options. It contains no time, date, host name, user name, absolute path, environment value, random value or digest of the compiler's executable. The C toolchain that built the compiler is not an input [EMIT-21]. 2. Emitting the same program twice, from different working directories, with different environment variables and on different hosts, gives byte-identical C [EMIT-25]. 3. Every file that an executor writes, PTX text included, follows paragraphs 1 and 2: LF line endings, stable numbering and no time or path [BACK-02]. 4. Symbol names are built with an encoding that is injective, so two different names never give the same symbol, and self-delimiting, so a symbol splits back into its parts in one way only. A component `s` is encoded as `E(s)`: each byte in `[A-Za-z0-9]` is copied, and every other byte, `_` included, becomes `_x` and two uppercase hexadecimal digits. A component is written C(s), which is `__`, where `` is the decimal length of `E(s)` in bytes. Every symbol encodes the module-relative path `P` without `.ci`, with `/` separators, never the dotted module name. There are four families: `ci` for user functions, `ci` + C(P) + C(name); `cg` for generated internal names, `cg` + C(P) followed by a generated name; `cx` for the public wrapper of an exported function, `cx` + C(P) + C(name); and `cm` for the public descriptor of a module, `cm` + C(P). The program file also exports `cint_program_abi`, `cint_observer_desc` and `cint_library_desc`. A symbol longer than 247 bytes is the diagnostic C9002, naming the symbol. A `cx` or `cm` symbol that contains `__` is the diagnostic C

chunks.title: 7.7 Deterministic output (part 3)
chunks.content: | Module | Name | Symbol | | --- | --- | --- | | `add` | `add3` | `ci_3_add_4_add3` | | `ab` | `x_c_d` | `ci_2_ab_11_x_x5Fc_x5Fd` | | `ab_c` | `x_d` | `ci_7_ab_x5Fc_6_x_x5Fd` | | `arith/add` | `f` | `ci_12_arith_x2Fadd_1_f` | | `add` | `add3`, public wrapper | `cx_3_add_4_add3` | | `a/b_c` | `f`, public wrapper | `cx_11_a_x2Fb_x5Fc_1_f` | | `a_b/c` | `f`, public wrapper | `cx_11_a_x5Fb_x2Fc_1_f` | 5. Sites are numbered from 1 in each module, in SIR node order, and 0 means no site. A site is the pair `cint_site { uint32_t module; uint32_t index; }`. The C of each module holds one constant site table, whose row `k` gives the line, column and operation identifier of site `k`, and one module descriptor that holds the module-relative path and the table. A helper that faults receives the site and resolves it into the record's position and operation; emitted code does not format a position itself. No hash-table order or address enters the numbering, so two compilations of one program give identical site tables [EMIT-23, RT-6, RT-7]. **Examples** 6. The same program emitted from two directories, with different time zones, locales and `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`: ```console $ mkdir a b $ cp add.ci a/ && cp add.ci b/ $ (cd a && TZ=UTC LANG=C cint emit-c --root . --out out add.ci) $ (cd b && TZ=Asia/Tokyo LANG=C.UTF-8 SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=1 cint emit-c --root . --out out add.ci) $ diff -r a/out.stage-0 b/out.stage-0 && echo identical identical ```

chunks.content: ### 7.8 Warnings **Constraints** 1. Emitted C, `cint_rt.h`, the `cint_rt` library, the bridge, the harness and the bootstrap compiler compile with no warning under these flags [EMIT-26]: | Toolchain | Flags | | --- | --- | | GCC | `-std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Wshadow -Wpedantic -Werror` | | Clang | the GCC flags and `-Wimplicit-int-conversion` | | MSVC | `/std:c17 /W4 /WX` |

chunks.title: 7.9 Symbol audit
chunks.content: ### 7.9 Symbol audit **Constraints** 1. Every generated object is audited at both optimization levels of the conformance suite. The audit fails on an exported symbol other than the `cx_` and `cm_` symbols, `cint_library_desc`, `cint_program_abi` and `cint_observer_desc`; on an external definition that is not exported, other than the `ci_` and `cg_` symbols of the program's own modules; and on any undefined symbol outside this list [EMIT-31]: | Class | Symbols | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | Runtime | `cint_rt_` and the other `cint_` functions of `rt/cint_rt.h` | the runtime contract | | Same build | `ci_` and `cg_` symbols of another module, or of the program file, of the same build | imports and site tables | | C support | `memcpy`, `memset`, `memmove`, `memcmp` | emitted by 7.4, and inserted by GCC, Clang and MSVC for large copies and zeroing | | MSVC x64 and ARM64 | `__chkstk`, `__security_cookie`, `__security_check_cookie`, `__GSHandlerCheck`, `__report_rangecheckfailure`, `__isa_available` | stack probes for frames over one page; the `/GS` checks, the MSVC default; the CPU feature level that code built with `/O2` reads | | GCC and Clang | `__stack_chk_fail`, `__stack_chk_guard` | `-fstack-protector-strong` | | Apple Clang, macOS | `__chkstk_darwin`, `___chkstk_darwin`, `bzero` | the stack probe on AArch64 and x86-64; the zeroing of a large local array at `-O0` | A row for a target applies to that target only. A library build (`cint build --lib`) also exports the host functions of the runtime, which carry `CINT_RT_EXPORT` in such a build, and the audit of its export table admits exactly those. The list may shrink when a build removes the stack protector with `-fno-stack-protector` or `/GS-`; such a build records the flag in its receipt.

chunks.title: 7.10 The runtime contract
chunks.content:
### 7.10 The runtime contract

The runtime is the header `rt/cint_rt.h` and the library `cint_rt`. The header is the normative statement of the contract; this subclause explains it.

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 7.10 The runtime contract (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The *runtime contract version* is a string `cint-rt-` that names the interface and meaning of `cint_rt.h` and the `cint_rt` library on which emitted code depends: the names and signatures of the helpers, the layout of the fault record and the layout of the site table. It changes when any of these changes incompatibly, and it is an input of the revision identity (6.5). In cint 0.2.0 it is `cint-rt-3`, and the header defines the interface version `CINT_ABI_VERSION` as `0x00030002`. A checkpoint binds to the revision identity; the compiler source identity is recorded beside it for identification only, so a new compiler that leaves the SIR and the runtime contract unchanged does not invalidate checkpoints [RCPT-08]. 2. Every symbol that the runtime exports is in the `cint_` namespace. The helpers are `static inline` and add no undefined symbol to a generated object [RT-3]. 3. A context, `cint_ctx`, is an opaque object that holds one instance of a program's state from its creation to its destruction. Emitted code passes the pointer to helpers and does not read its fields. For each entry it holds the fuel budget and the fuel consumed, the depth limit and the current depth, and the stack of call sites. Across entries it holds module state, registered buffers, arenas and the fault record [RT-4]. 4. Faults are sticky. The first fault of an entry writes the fault record once. A later helper call on a context that holds a fault returns `false` and changes nothing. Emitted code tests every helper result and leaves through the function's single fault exit. Only the host clears the record, with `cint_ctx_clear_fault`, which changes no other state [RT-10]. 5. A call checks the depth limit first, faulting `E_DEPTH` without a fuel charge, then charges one unit of fuel, then records its call

chunks.title: 7.10 The runtime contract (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Notes**

8. The status values of `rt/cint_rt.h` are `CINT_OK` (0), `CINT_FAULT` (1), `CINT_REFUSED` (2), `CINT_BUSY` (3), `CINT_FAULTED` (4) and `CINT_RESOURCE` (5). SPEC-03P.1 specifies what each means to a host program.

chunks.title: 8 Agreement
chunks.content:
## 8 Agreement

Two implementations of cint agree on a program when every observable part of its outcome is the same. This clause says what is compared, what is not, and how a case that is not compared is reported, so that a refusal is never counted as agreement.

chunks.title: 8.1 What is compared
chunks.content:
### 8.1 What is compared

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 8.1 What is compared (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A program is in the scope of both the reference and a compiler when the reference runs it and the compiler builds it without a diagnostic whose code begins with `C9`. For such a program and the same semantic inputs, the two agree as a conformance case does: the same bytes on standard output; the same kind of outcome; the same returned value; the same fuel consumed; and the same fault record in every field except the revision and the source-map digest, which the reference does not compute. For a program that both reject, they agree when they report the same diagnostic code at the same position. A disagreement is a defect of one of them or an ambiguity in the text; it is not settled by choosing one. The program, reduced to a case, joins the suite. Agreement on one program is a measurement of that program and shows nothing about another [REF-06]. 2. A position, in a diagnostic, a fault record, SIR text or an `.expect` file, is written `::`. `` is the module-relative path, `.ci` included, with `/` separators. Lines count from 1. Columns count from 1 in Unicode scalar values, not bytes [DIAG-01]. 3. Codes have two separate sets of names. A fault code is one of the `E_` names of SPEC-04P.2 5.2.3. A diagnostic code is `C` and four digits, listed in Annex B of SPEC-04P.2. A constant expression whose evaluation meets a fault condition is the diagnostic C6001, which carries the fault code, and C6002 when it runs out of compile-time fuel. A diagnostic that reports a limit of an implementation has a code that begins with `C9`: C9001 for a capacity or an output size, C9002 for a generated symbol longer than 247 bytes, C9003 for a local array over the frame limit, and C9004 for nesting beyond the implementation's limit [DIAG-02]. 4. These are not compared: the message text of a diagnostic, the r

chunks.content:
**Examples**
