chunks.title: 8.2 Categories of a case
chunks.content: ### 8.2 Categories of a case **Semantics** 1. A conformance run reports each case in exactly one category. The category depends only on the case, its frozen expectation and the compiler under test, not on the C toolchain, so it belongs in the outcome part of the receipt [CONF-14]: 1. *Compared.* The implementation produced an outcome and it was compared with the frozen expectation. An expected diagnostic is compared too: the frozen outcome is a compile error, and the compiler reports the same code at the same position. 2. *Unsupported by this implementation.* The frozen outcome is a value, a fault or a compile error with another code or position; the compiler reports a `C9` code under a documented limit; and the file `conformance/unsupported.txt` lists that case, compiler, code and limit. For `gpu-cuda`, the refusal `E_UNSUPPORTED` of 5.5 takes the place of the `C9` code. An unsupported case is a named gap, not agreement. 3. *Held.* The file `conformance/held.txt` lists the case, which has no frozen expectation. 4. *Outside the subset.* The compiler under test accepts only a subset of the language (10.2), the case is outside it and the compiler reports the diagnostic for that. 5. *Not applicable.* An operation fixture whose operation has no operator form in the subset that the compiler accepts, so that no program exists for it.

chunks.title: 8.2 Categories of a case (part 2)
chunks.content:
Any other result is a disagreement: a `C9` code that `conformance/unsupported.txt` does not list, a refusal by a subset compiler of a case inside its subset, or a compile error whose code or position differs from the frozen expectation. A case that the list names as unsupported and that the compiler accepts is also a disagreement, until the list is corrected.
2. Each line of `conformance/unsupported.txt` is `<case> <compiler> <code> <limit> <reason>`. For `gpu-cuda` the compiler is `cintc/gpu-cuda`, the code is `E_UNSUPPORTED`, and the limit is `BACK-05 capability <name>`, where `<name>` is the capability that the refusal names; a refusal that names another capability is a disagreement. For example, the line `control/nest_blocks_200 cint-seed C9004 SEED-15 the seed compiles at most 199 nested blocks` lists a case that the seed refuses under its nesting limit (10.2, paragraph 8).

chunks.title: 8.3 Disagreement
chunks.content: ### 8.3 Disagreement **Semantics** 1. Any disagreement fails the run. A disagreement between the reference and a hand-derived anchor expectation is a defect of the reference, and it also fails the run until the reference is fixed or the expectation is corrected by an erratum (9.5) [CONF-04].

chunks.title: 8.4 The run matrix
chunks.content: ### 8.4 The run matrix **Semantics** 1. A conformance run executes every case on the reference and on every build in this matrix, and requires identical canonical outcomes across all of them [CONF-03]: | Axis | Values | | --- | --- | | C toolchain | GCC on Linux x86-64; Clang on Linux x86-64 and Apple Clang on macOS AArch64; MSVC on Windows x86-64 | | Optimization | `-O0` and `-O2` (`/Od` and `/O2`) | | Helper mode | `CINT_RT_HELPERS_BUILTIN` and `CINT_RT_HELPERS_PORTABLE` | | Compiler | the `cintc` built by the bootstrap (10.3), and the bootstrap compiler on the cases of its subset (10.2) | | Executor | `cpu-c17` on every case; `cpu-sir-interp` on every case; `gpu-cuda` on the cases its capability table supports, the others producing `E_UNSUPPORTED` at translation |

chunks.title: 8.5 Parallel executors
chunks.content: ### 8.5 Parallel executors An executor may run the work-items of a dispatch in parallel, but its outcome is the one of running them one at a time in canonical order. **Semantics** 1. The canonical outcome of a dispatch, fuel included, is the outcome of running its work-items one at a time in canonical order, as `cpu-c17` does. The dispatch first charges `N`, the number of its work-items. A parallel executor computes the outcome as follows, where `F` is the fuel left when the first work-item starts, `c(i, s)` is the fuel that item `i` has charged through its step `s`, and `C(i)` is the total charge of item `i` when it runs to its end or to its first fault other than `E_FUEL` [BACK-09]: - `k_fault` is the least item with a fault other than `E_FUEL`, and `s_fault` the step of that fault. - `k_fuel` is the least item `i` with a charge point `s` such that `C(0) + ... + C(i - 1) + c(i, s) > F`, and `s_fuel` is the first such `s`. Without a budget there is no `k_fuel`. - The canonical fault is the lesser of (`k_fault`, `s_fault`) and (`k_fuel`, `s_fuel`) in work-item, then step, order; the second is `E_FUEL`. - The fuel consumed by the dispatch is `N` plus the charges of items 0 to `k - 1` plus the charges of item `k` before its faulting step, where `k` is the item of the canonical fault; a charge that faults `E_FUEL` is not consumed. Without a fault it is `N` plus the sum of all `C(i)`. Which work-item failed first on the hardware cannot be observed. 2. The outputs of a dispatch that faults are not published [BACK-10]. 3. Running a work-item again to find or describe the canonical fault charges no fuel. The canonical fuel is computed once, by paragraph 1 [BACK-12]. **Examples**

chunks.title: 8.5 Parallel executors (part 2)
9 The conformance suite
chunks.content:
## 9 The conformance suite

The conformance suite, in `conformance/`, holds the cases on which every implementation must agree, with their expected outcomes. Most expectations come from the reference, and the boundary cases are derived by hand.

chunks.title: 9.1 Case files
chunks.content:
### 9.1 Case files

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 9.1 Case files (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. There are two kinds of case, with one rule of agreement (8.1). An *operation fixture* is one operation on given operands, in a CIF-1 file under `conformance/integer-machine/`, one JSON object per line. A *program case* is a `.ci` file and its `.expect` file, for whole programs: control flow, views, kernels, diagnostics and fuel. Each operation fixture is also run through generated *table programs*, `conformance/tables/.ci` with the list of calls `.cases`, so both kinds run on every implementation. A program case begins with a header comment of lines `// case: `, `// clause: ` and `// entry: ; args: [; fuel ][; depth ]`; without an `entry` line, the case runs its script, else its function `main`, else its only test. A case with several entries has one file `..expect` for each. The `.expect` file is canonical text in the grammar of 9.3 [CONF-01]. 2. An expectation comes from one of three sources, which its `source` line states: `anchor`, derived by hand, with the derivation written beside it, and used for boundary cases and to check the reference itself; `reference`, written by the reference with `conformance/tools/gen_expect.py` and then frozen; or `compile-error`, the expected diagnostic code and position. A frozen expectation is not edited in place. It changes in one of three ways [CONF-02]: - A change of meaning (a value, a fault code or content, a fuel count or a diagnostic code or position) comes with a new language profile, which has its own frozen expectations. A change of encoding with the same content comes with a new version of that encoding: a new domain string, a new runtime contract version (7.10) or a new `.expect` format (9.3). Frozen files of the old version stay valid and are read in their own format. - A `reference` expectation found wrong

chunks.title: 9.2 Operation fixtures and coverage
chunks.content: ### 9.2 Operation fixtures and coverage **Semantics** 1. A CIF-1 line is one JSON object with the keys `id`, `status`, `op`, `args` and `expect`, in that order. `op` is an operation identifier, `args` a list of typed values `{"t": , "v": }`, and `expect` holds either a `value` or a `fault` with its code and, where the record has them, its exact result and limit. Every integer is a JSON string of decimal digits, so no JSON reader loses precision. A hand-derived anchor adds a key `derivation` that shows the arithmetic. 2. The suite holds these fixtures: `anchors.cif1.jsonl`, the anchors; `exh8/`, every operand pair of the 14 binary operator forms (`+ - * / % << >> +% -% *% <<% +| -| *|`) on `I8` and `U8`, 1,835,008 records; `bnd64/`, the `I64` boundary matrix of the 16 values `MIN`, `MIN + 1`, -2^32, -2^31, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 2^31 - 1, 2^31, 2^32, 3037000499, 3037000500, `MAX - 1` and `MAX` for each form (3037000499 and 3037000500 bracket the square root of 2^63); and `bnd128/` to `bnd1024/`, the boundary matrices of the wide types. 3. Every implementation that evaluates constants is also run on the *constant and run-time category*: each boundary-matrix and exhaustive 8-bit expression is evaluated as a constant expression and at run time from variables, and the two must give the same value, or the same fault code, operation and operands, which the constant program reports as the diagnostic C6001. If the front end folded `I8` `100 +| 100` to anything other than 127, the two programs would disagree [CONF-08]. **Examples** 4. The reference checks the anchors against their hand-derived values: ```console $ python3 -m cint_ref cif1 conformance/integer-machine/anchors.cif1.jsonl cif1: 300 records, 300 agree, 0 disagree, 0 unsupported, 0 invalid ```

chunks.title: 9.3 The `.expect` format
chunks.content: ### 9.3 The `.expect` format The `.expect` format is the canonical text of an outcome: one field per line, in a fixed order, with every integer in exact decimal. **Syntax** 1. An `.expect` file is the text that this grammar derives. The notation is ABNF (RFC 5234) with the case-sensitive strings `%s"..."` of RFC 7405; `ALPHA`, `DIGIT`, `SP`, `LF` and `VCHAR` are the core rules of RFC 5234. A file whose third line is `format 2`, `format 3`, `format 4` or `format 5` is a file of that format. A file without that line is a format 1 file, stays valid and is compared in format 1. Keys appear in this order: `case`, `clause`, `format`, `source`, `outcome`, `stdout-bytes`, `stdout-sha256`, `return`, `fuel-consumed`, the `error.` keys, the `fault.` keys, the `diagnostic.` keys, `refused.reason` and `state.global` [CONF-11]. ```abnf expect-file = case-line clause-line [ format-line ] ( run-case / compile-case / refused-case ) format-line = %s"format 2" LF ; absent: format 1 case-line = %s"case" SP case-name LF case-name = segment *( "/" segment ) segment = 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" / "-" / "." ) clause-line = %s"clause" SP text LF text = VCHAR *( *SP VCHAR ) ; printable ASCII, no edge space

chunks.title: 9.3 The `.expect` format (part 2)
chunks.content:
run-case         = %s"source" SP ( %s"anchor" / %s"reference" ) LF
                   ( value-body / fault-body ) *state-line   ; state-line: format 2
state-line       = %s"state.global" SP module-name SP name SP typed-value LF
value-body       = %s"outcome value" LF output-lines [ return-line ] fuel-line
fault-body       = %s"outcome fault" LF output-lines fuel-line fault-record
output-lines     = %s"stdout-bytes" SP count LF
                   [ %s"stdout-sha256" SP 64lhex LF ]
return-line      = %s"return" SP typed-value LF
fuel-line        = %s"fuel-consumed" SP count LF
fault-record     = %s"fault.code" SP fault-code LF
                   %s"fault.operation" SP op-id LF
                   *( %s"fault.operand" SP typed-value LF )
                   %s"fault.exact" SP ( int / %s"none" ) LF
                   %s"fault.limit" SP ( typed-value / %s"none" ) LF
                   %s"fault.position" SP position LF
                   %s"fault.revision self" LF
                   [ %s"fault.source-map self" LF ]      ; format 2
                   %s"fault.address" SP ( %s"none" / address ) LF
                   %s"fault.stack-depth" SP count LF
                   *( %s"fault.stack" SP position LF )   ; format 2

compile-case     = %s"source compile-error" LF %s"outcome compile-error" LF
                   %s"diagnostic.code" SP c-code LF
                   %s"diagnostic.position" SP position LF
                   [ diagnostic-fault ]
diagnostic-fault = %s"diagnostic.fault.code" SP fault-code LF
                   %s"diagnostic.fault.operation" SP op-id LF
                   *( %s"diagnostic.fault.operand" SP typed-value LF )
                   %s"diagnostic.fault.exact" SP ( int / %s"none" ) LF
                   %s"diagnostic.fault.limit" SP ( typed-value / %s"none" ) LF

chunks.title: 9.3 The `.expect` format (part 3)
chunks.content:
refused-case     = %s"source reference" LF %s"outcome refused" LF
                   %s"refused.reason" SP text LF

typed-value      = int-type SP int / %s"Bool" SP ( %s"true" / %s"false" )
                   / %s"Z" SP int
int-type         = %s"I" ( "8" / "16" / "32" / "64" / "128" / "256" / "512" / "1024" )
                   / %s"U" ( "8" / "16" / "32" / "64" )
fault-code       = %s"E_" 1*( %x41-5A / "_" )
op-id            = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "_" / "." )
c-code           = %s"C" 4DIGIT
position         = segment *( "/" segment ) ":" pos-int ":" pos-int
address          = count SP count SP count         ; dispatch, work-item, step
int              = [ "-" ] count
count            = "0" / %x31-39 *DIGIT
pos-int          = %x31-39 *DIGIT
lhex             = DIGIT / %x61-66                 ; lowercase hexadecimal digit
module-name      = name *( "." name )
name             = ( ALPHA / "_" ) *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" )
```

2. Format 3 adds the outcome `error`, for an entry that returns an error, by incremental alternatives (`=/`), so the rules above are unchanged:

```abnf
format-line      =/ %s"format 3" LF
run-case         =/ %s"source" SP ( %s"anchor" / %s"reference" ) LF
                    error-body *state-line
error-body       = %s"outcome error" LF output-lines fuel-line error-value
error-value      = %s"error.set" SP [ module-name "." ] name LF
                   %s"error.value" SP [ name "." ] name LF
                   %s"error.tag" SP uint-type SP pos-int LF
uint-type        = %s"U" ( "8" / "16" / "32" / "64" )
```

3. Format 4 adds the fault record of a kernel dispatch:

chunks.title: 9.3 The `.expect` format (part 4)
chunks.content:
```abnf
format-line      =/ %s"format 4" LF
fault-record     =/ %s"fault.code" SP fault-code LF
                    %s"fault.operation" SP op-id LF
                    *( %s"fault.operand" SP typed-value LF )
                    *( %s"fault.descriptor" SP descriptor LF )
                    %s"fault.exact" SP ( int / %s"none" ) LF
                    %s"fault.limit" SP ( typed-value / %s"none" ) LF
                    %s"fault.position" SP position LF
                    %s"fault.revision self" LF
                    %s"fault.source-map self" LF
                    %s"fault.phase" SP phase LF
                    %s"fault.kernel" SP kernel-name LF
                    %s"fault.address" SP kernel-address LF
                    %s"fault.stack-depth" SP count LF
                    *( %s"fault.stack" SP position LF )
kernel-address   = count SP ( count SP count / %s"none none" )
                                                   ; dispatch, then work-item and step
phase            = %s"entry" / %s"work-item" / %s"epilogue"
kernel-name      = module-name "." name
descriptor       = elem-type SP ( count SP count / %s"none" ) SP count SP int
                   1*( SP count SP int SP int ) SP ( %s"read" / %s"write" )
elem-type        = int-type
```

4. Format 5 adds fixed-point values, the unsigned wide types and fixed-point element types:

```abnf
format-line      =/ %s"format 5" LF
typed-value      =/ q-type SP %s"raw" SP int
int-type         =/ %s"U" ( "128" / "256" / "512" )
elem-type        =/ q-type
q-type           = %s"Q" pos-int "." count          ; i + f is 8, 16, 32 or 64
```

**Constraints**

chunks.title: 9.3 The `.expect` format (part 5)
chunks.content:
5. These rules hold in addition to the grammar:
   1. The file is ASCII with an LF after every line, the last included. It contains no CR, no tab and no trailing space.
   2. `stdout-sha256` is present exactly when `stdout-bytes` is not 0, and is the SHA-256 digest of the output bytes.
   3. `return` is present exactly when the entry returns a value. A `void` function, a test block and a script have no `return` line.
   4. There is one `fault.operand` line for each operand of the record, in the record's order. `fault.exact` and `fault.limit` are `none` when the record has no such field.
   5. `fault.revision self` means that the record's revision must equal the revision identity of the program under test, and `fault.source-map self` the same for the source-map digest; both are compared only between builds of `cintc`. `fault.address` gives the dispatch, the work-item as one linear index and the step. `fault.stack-depth` is the number of positions in the record's stack. A format 2 file writes `fault.source-map self` in every fault record and one `fault.stack` line per position, outermost first; a format 1 file writes neither.
   6. `diagnostic-fault` is present exactly when the code is C6001 or C6002. The message text of the diagnostic is not part of the file.
   7. The outcome `refused` means that the host interface refused the entry before it started, for example for a fuel budget below 0. No execution exists, so the file has no output or fuel line. The `refused.reason` text is informative and is not compared. An implementation that cannot decide a case does not produce a frozen expectation for it.
   8. The `clause` value is free text. A case cites the rules it exercises by their clause identifiers, with `;` between documents.
   9. Two `.expect` texts agree when they are equal byte for byte, except the `refused.reason` line and the `fault.revision` and `fault.source

chunks.title: 9.3 The `.expect` format (part 6)
chunks.content:
A file of a later format may use every line of the earlier formats, and files of earlier formats are not rewritten. `conformance/tools/check_expect_abnf.py` checks every `.expect` file of the suite against this grammar and the rules that a single file can show.

**Examples**

6. The expectation of the case `arith/add_i64_overflow` is in format 1:

```console
$ cat conformance/arith/add_i64_overflow.expect
case arith/add_i64_overflow
clause SPEC-01 IM-30, IM-32, IM-106, IM-107
source reference
outcome fault
stdout-bytes 0
fuel-consumed 1
fault.code E_OVERFLOW
fault.operation add.checked.i64
fault.operand I64 9223372036854775807
fault.operand I64 1
fault.exact 9223372036854775808
fault.limit I64 9223372036854775807
fault.position arith/add_i64_overflow.ci:5:15
fault.revision self
fault.address none
fault.stack-depth 0
```

The case is a test block, which is its entry and charges 1 unit. The fault is in the entry's own body, so the stack is empty. The print after the addition does not run, so no byte was written. The program is lines 2 to 7 of `conformance/arith/add_i64_overflow.ci`, after its header comment:

```cint
test "add overflow at I64 max" {
    I64 a = 9223372036854775807;
    I64 b = 1;
    I64 c = a + b;
    "c={c}\n";
}
```

chunks.title: 9.4 Lists of the suite
chunks.content:
### 9.4 Lists of the suite

**Semantics**

1. `conformance/held.txt` lists, one per line, the program cases that have no frozen expectation, each with its reason. A held case is not compared.
2. `conformance/unsupported.txt` lists the cases that an implementation refuses under a documented limit, in the line format of 8.2.
3. `conformance/errata/` holds the errata of 9.1.

chunks.title: 9.5 Required case lists
chunks.content: ### 9.5 Required case lists **Semantics** 1. A *required case list* is a file `conformance/required/.txt` with one line ` ` for each case and compiler, where the category is one of 8.2 and, where the category needs one, the line adds the limit. The compiler column names the executor as well: `cintc` for the compiler's C on `cpu-c17`, `cintc/cpu-sir-interp` for its SIR text on the interpreter, and `cintc/gpu-cuda` for `gpu-cuda`. `python3 tools/cint_check.py --required FILE` fails a run when a listed case is absent, a case of the suite is not listed, a case's category differs from the list, a compile error's code or position differs from the frozen expectation, or a case has no `.expect` file and is not held [CONF-15].

chunks.title: 9.6 Observing compiled programs
chunks.content: ### 9.6 Observing compiled programs **Semantics** 1. A compiled conformance program is observed through `cint-harness`, a C17 program. It reads a *case list*, one call per line, ` `, and calls each exported function through its observer entry with a fresh context and the case's fuel budget. It writes the canonical outcome (the returned value, or the full fault record from the context, and the fuel consumed) in `.expect` syntax. The reference evaluates the same calls. The same harness serves every compiler under test, so all are compared through the same path [CONF-10]. 2. The interpreter is observed the same way: `cint-interp observe` takes the command line of `cint-harness`, with a directory of SIR text in place of a program library, and writes the same text. `tools/cint_check.py --interp` runs it on every compared case [CONF-10a]. 3. A case list is the text that this grammar derives, with the core rules of 9.3. Line `n` is call `n`, and each call runs in a fresh context [CONF-12]: ```abnf case-list = *call-line call-line = module-name SP name *( SP typed-value ) LF ```

chunks.title: 9.6 Observing compiled programs (part 2)
chunks.content: 4. A program built for the harness follows the observer interface `cint-observe-1` [CONF-13]: - It is one shared library built from the C of all its modules, the program file and the `cint_rt` library of the same version as the harness. Its exported symbols have C linkage and carry `CINT_RT_EXPORT`. The harness resolves the program's path before it loads it. - It exports exactly two observer symbols, both defined in the program file: `const uint32_t cint_program_abi = CINT_ABI_VERSION;` and `const cint_observer cint_observer_desc;`. The descriptor names the program (every module's site table, the root module first) and lists one entry for every exported function of every module whose parameters and result are scalars, in module order and then declaration order. The harness does not call a program whose `cint_program_abi` differs from its own. - Each entry carries its module index, its name, a type signature of its result and at most 16 parameters (the tags of `I8` to `I64`, `U8` to `U64` and `Bool`) and its function, of type `cint_status (*)(cint_ctx *ctx, int64_t fuel, int64_t depth, const uint64_t *args, uint64_t *result)`. An argument is a 64-bit pattern: sign-extended for a signed type, zero-extended for an unsigned type, 0 or 1 for `Bool`. The function calls `cint_rt_entry_begin(ctx, , fuel, depth)`, returns that status unless it is `CINT_OK`, then runs the body and returns `cint_rt_entry_end(ctx)`. It writes `*result` only when there is a result and the status is `CINT_OK`. - Entry functions are `static`, named `cg` + C(P) + `_o`, with type signatures `cg` + C(P) + `_t`, numbered in each module in declaration order (7.7). Each module's C file defines its observer table `cg` + C(P) + `_obs` and its site table with external linkage, not exported, so that the program file can name them.

chunks.title: 9.6 Observing compiled programs (part 3)
chunks.content: A change to this interface is a new version, `cint-observe-2`. The layouts of `cint_observer` and `cint_observer_entry` are declared in `rt/cint_rt.h`, which governs where it and this paragraph differ.

chunks.title: 9.7 Further checks of a run
chunks.content:
### 9.7 Further checks of a run **Semantics** 1. For each conformance program, the compiler is run twice: from two different working directories, with the source tree at two different absolute paths, and with different values of `TZ`, `LANG` and `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`. The two sets of emitted C are compared byte for byte, and a difference fails the run [CONF-05]. 2. The reference writes the canonical type signature of each export (SPEC-03P.1), and `tools/cint_check.py` compares it, for every export of the suite that has a public wrapper, with the bytes that the compiler under test writes into the program's reflection table. A difference fails the run as an outcome difference does [CONF-16]. 3. A conformance run on `gpu-cuda` uses the same frozen expectations. Each compared case runs at two block sizes, 32 and 256 work-items (`tools/cint_check.py --backend gpu-cuda --block 32` and `--block 256`), on the device. The boundary matrices of `bnd64/` also run as kernels, through the kernel tables `conformance/tables/kernel__
_i64.ci`: one dispatch over the rows that do not fault, and one dispatch for each row that faults, with expectations in format 4. A case that the capability table of `gpu-cuda` does not support is unsupported, with its line in `conformance/unsupported.txt` naming the capability (8.2) [CONF-17].

chunks.title: 9.8 Running one case
chunks.content:
### 9.8 Running one case

**Examples**

1. The reference checks one case against its frozen expectation. It prints nothing and exits with status 0 when they agree, and names the first line that differs otherwise:

```console
$ python3 -m cint_ref check conformance/arith/add_i64_overflow.ci conformance/arith/add_i64_overflow.expect
$ echo $?
0
$ sed 's/^fuel-consumed 1$/fuel-consumed 2/' conformance/arith/add_i64_overflow.expect > wrong.expect
$ python3 -m cint_ref check conformance/arith/add_i64_overflow.ci wrong.expect
wrong.expect: line 6 differs
  expected: fuel-consumed 2
  actual:   fuel-consumed 1
$ echo $?
1
```

2. `tools/cint_check.py` runs cases through a compiler and compares them with their frozen expectations and with the reference. `--only` selects the cases whose name contains its argument, and `--quick` leaves out the table programs. `--compiler b1 --cint "$BOOT/cint"` tests the compiler inside the `cint` command that the bootstrap of 10.3 wrote into the directory `$BOOT`; without `--cint`, the tool first runs that bootstrap itself. `--leg`, `--opt` and `--helpers` choose the configuration and `--no-receipt` writes no receipt (11.3 writes them):

chunks.title: 9.8 Running one case (part 2)
chunks.content:
```console
$ python3 tools/cint_check.py --leg gcc --opt 0 --helpers portable --quick --compiler b1 --cint "$BOOT/cint" --only arith/add_i64_overflow --no-receipt
inventory: 1 programs, 1 records, 0 cases classified without compiling; cint_ref against the frozen .expect files: 0 differ (23 ms)
...
runtime symbol audit: 131 defined external symbols, 0 outside cint_
gcc-0-portable-quick: 1 programs compiled, 1 records compared, 0 disagree, 0 sanitizer reports, 0 nondeterministic, 0 symbol audit findings, 0 type signatures compared, 0 type signature disagreements, 8 s; suite 5ccd378e30da7e1917bb03176f68a388d770da998075a10160043635f6e89d79
not compared: held 0, not_applicable 0, outside_subset 0, unsupported 0; disagreements before compiling: 0
...
```

The first line reports that the reference agrees with the frozen expectation. The runtime's own symbols are audited (7.10). The case was compiled twice (9.7) and compared, and no case fell in another category of 8.2. The digest after `suite` is the SHA-256 digest of the suite's files, which identifies the version of the suite.

chunks.title: 10 Bootstrap
chunks.content:
## 10 Bootstrap

The compiler is written in cint, so building it needs a cint compiler. cint 0.2.0 breaks this circle with a C17 program written by hand, which compiles the compiler's source once. Every later compiler is built from that one. This clause describes that program, how the compiler is built from it, the check that the compiler reproduces itself, and what that check does not show.

chunks.title: 10.1 Names
chunks.content:
### 10.1 Names

1. These names are used in this clause only:
   - *C0*: the C toolchain of a configuration.
   - *the seed*: the bootstrap compiler `cint-seed`, built by C0 from `seed/`.
   - *the seed's C*: the C that the seed emits for the compiler's source.
   - *the first compiler*: the compiler that C0 builds from the seed's C, the runtime and the bridge. The `cint` command contains the same compiler objects as the first compiler.
   - *the first emitted C*: the C that the first compiler emits for the compiler's source.
   - *the second compiler*: the compiler that C0 builds from the first emitted C.
   - *the second emitted C*: the C that the second compiler emits for the compiler's source.

chunks.title: 10.2 The seed
chunks.content:
### 10.2 The seed

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 10.2 The seed (part 2)
chunks.clauses: SEED-01 SEED-02 SEED-03 SEED-04 SEED-05 SEED-13 SEED-15 SEED-16
chunks.content: 1. The seed compiles the compiler's source into the seed's C, and, for its own conformance, programs of the boot subset of paragraph 7. It is not a compiler for users and is not installed [SEED-01]. 2. The seed is written by hand in C17. It is not generated from cint, and no generated C file is an input of the bootstrap [SEED-02]. 3. The seed depends only on the C17 standard library, `cint_rt.h`, the `cint_rt` library and the bridge. Its platform calls are confined to the bridge [SEED-03]. 4. The seed shares no code with `cintc` other than the runtime and the bridge. It translates its parse tree directly into C and builds no SIR [SEED-04]. 5. The seed performs every run-time check of the boot subset and produces the full fault record, field for field identical to the one `cintc` produces, except the revision, which it reports as absent because it builds no SIR [SEED-05]. 6. The seed performs no optimization. It does not remove, merge or reorder run-time checks; it folds no expression that is not a constant expression; it does not inline functions, eliminate common subexpressions, hoist loop invariants or unroll loops; it does not choose a representation for a value from the value; and it relies on no extension of the C compiler other than those that `cint_rt.h` selects. The C compiler that compiles the seed's C may optimize [SEED-13]. 7. The *boot subset*, `cint-boot-1`, is the part of the language that the seed accepts: the integer types `I8` to `I64` and `U8` to `U64`, `Bool`, the checked, wrapping and bitwise operators, `as` and `as%`, structs, local arrays of constant extent, rank-1 views as parameters, constants, functions, `if`, `while`, the C form and the range form of `for`, `switch`, and `import` and `

chunks.title: 10.2 The seed (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Notes**

10. The root of trust that the seed adds is a set of files a reader can read. The C toolchain that compiles it stays trusted, and 10.5 says what checks it.
11. Two translators of different structure that agree, such as the seed and `cintc`, are stronger evidence than one translator checked against itself.

chunks.title: 10.3 Building the compiler
chunks.content:
### 10.3 Building the compiler

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 10.3 Building the compiler (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The compiler's own source keeps these design rules: no call cycle; no print statement or other input or output; no module-level variable or statement, since state outside the tables that the bridge allocates would outlive a module; no call of a program function in a constant, a static assertion or an extent; and ASCII bytes only. In cint 0.2.0 the compiler's source is inside the boot subset, so the seed compiles it directly [BOOT-03]. 2. The compiler's sources, the seed, the runtime, the bridge and the harness use LF line endings, and the bootstrap refuses a CR byte in them [CINTC-07]. 3. `python3 tools/cint_bootstrap.py --leg gcc --out "$BOOT"` builds the compiler with GCC into the directory `$BOOT`, which must lie outside the source tree. It builds, in order: the runtime objects; the seed, from `seed/*.c`, `rt/cint_rt.c` and `rt/cint_bridge.c`; the seed's C, by running the seed on `compiler/main.ci` in `compiler/`, one C file for the whole compiler; the first compiler, from the seed's C, `compiler/tests/golden_host.c`, the runtime and the bridge; and the `cint` command, from `cli/` and the same compiler objects. It then writes `cint`, two toolchain files and the receipt `bootstrap.json` into `$BOOT`. `cint.toolchain` is the configuration with which `cint run` and `cint build` compile programs, `-O2` with the builtin helpers, and `cint-bootstrap.toolchain` the one with which the first compiler and `cint` were built, `-O0` with the portable helpers. 4. Digests are computed twice: by the `digest` export of `compiler/sha256.ci` in the first compiler, and by an external SHA-256 implementation. The bootstrap tool computes in the first compiler the digests of the source manifests, of the seed's C, of `cint` and of the runtime sources, compares each with Python's `hashlib` and fails on any difference. The recei

chunks.title: 10.3 Building the compiler (part 3)
chunks.content:
**Examples**

5. The receipt of a bootstrap:

```console
$ jq -r '.schema, .identity.profile, .identity.runtime_contract_version, .outcome.source_digest_verification' "$BOOT/bootstrap.json"
cint-bootstrap-receipt-1
cint-core-1
cint-rt-3
pass
$ jq -r '.identity.compiler_sources[].path' "$BOOT/bootstrap.json"
compiler/back_c.ci
compiler/back_ptx.ci
compiler/check.ci
compiler/decl.ci
compiler/emit.ci
compiler/fold.ci
compiler/limits.ci
compiler/lowering.ci
compiler/main.ci
compiler/parse.ci
compiler/resolve.ci
compiler/scan.ci
compiler/sha256.ci
compiler/verify.ci
$ jq -cS '{identity, outcome}' "$BOOT/bootstrap.json" | tr -d '\n' | sha256sum
2b4859c123ecdced8c3bb8ec5e6eee55c1de5fb55b5e53eb014dee1daf9d0cfc  -
$ jq -r .identity_sha256 "$BOOT/bootstrap.json"
2b4859c123ecdced8c3bb8ec5e6eee55c1de5fb55b5e53eb014dee1daf9d0cfc
```

The identity names the 14 source files of the compiler with their digests, the runtime sources and the seed's source identity. The last two commands recompute the receipt identity (11.2) with external tools and show the value the receipt records.

chunks.title: 10.4 The fixpoint
chunks.content:
### 10.4 The fixpoint

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 10.4 The fixpoint (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. The first compiler compiles the compiler's source into the first emitted C, one C file for each module and a `MANIFEST`; C0 builds the second compiler from it; and the second compiler compiles the same source into the second emitted C. The first and the second emitted C are byte-identical, file by file, the `MANIFEST` included. The seed's C is not compared with them, because the seed is a separate translator that does not optimize, and its C differs from that of `cintc` [FIX-01]. 2. The fixpoint is checked by comparing bytes and by comparing the SHA-256 digest of each file, and both results are recorded in the receipt. The report of a difference names the first differing file, its byte offset and its line [FIX-02]. 3. The first and the second compiler emit byte-identical C for every program of the corpus: every `.ci` program under `conformance/`, `examples/` and `compiler/tests/`. This extends the fixpoint from one program, the compiler, to all of them [FIX-03]. 4. The digests of the executables of the seed and of the first and second compilers are recorded as observations, outside every identity. They differ between toolchains and may differ between two builds with one toolchain; for example, an MSVC link without `/Brepro` writes a time stamp into the executable. No claim is made that executables are byte-identical [FIX-05]. 5. `python3 tools/cint_fixpoint.py --leg gcc --receipt FILE` builds the seed, the two compilers and the two emitted C in one configuration and checks paragraphs 1 to 3; `--opt` and `--helpers` choose the configuration, `--sanitize` adds the sanitizers of 7.6 and `--no-corpus` checks paragraphs 1 and 2 only. The receipt's identity holds the input digests and the digest of the first emitted C, and no path, time or executable digest.

chunks.title: 10.5 What the fixpoint does not show
chunks.content: ### 10.5 What the fixpoint does not show **Semantics** 1. *Cross-toolchain bootstrap agreement*: the first emitted C is byte-identical whichever toolchain of the run matrix (8.4) is C0, at every optimization level. `python3 tools/cint_fixpoint.py --compare RECEIPT ...` checks that a set of fixpoint receipts has one identity. Different C compilers produce different executables of the seed and of the first compiler, so a miscompilation that changed the compiler's emitted C would have to occur identically in every C compiler of the matrix to go undetected. The check shows that the compiler's emitted C does not depend on which toolchain of the matrix built the compiler. It does not show that any distributed executable corresponds to the compiler's source (10.4 paragraph 4); that the shared inputs, the compiler's source, the seed, the runtime and the bridge, are free of defects, since every toolchain compiles the same ones; or that the toolchains share no code or design [FIX-04]. **Notes** 2. The idea of rebuilding a compiler with a diverse second compiler and comparing the result comes from Wheeler's diverse double-compiling. That technique makes a different claim: under its stated assumptions, the equality of the final executable with the distributed one shows that source and executable correspond. The check of paragraph 1 designates no trusted compiler and compares emitted C, so it makes no claim about executables and is not diverse double-compiling.

chunks.title: 10.6 Reproducing the bootstrap
chunks.content:
### 10.6 Reproducing the bootstrap

**Examples**

1. A reader with a C17 toolchain, Python 3 and the source tree reproduces the bootstrap and the fixpoint with two commands, each on one configuration:

```text
python3 tools/cint_bootstrap.py --leg gcc --out "$BOOT"
python3 tools/cint_fixpoint.py --leg gcc --receipt fixpoint-gcc-0-portable.json
```

`--leg` is `gcc`, `clang` or `apple-clang` on Linux and macOS, and `msvc` on Windows. The fixpoint receipt's identity is then compared with the published one (11.3).

chunks.title: 11 Receipts and reproduction
chunks.content:
## 11 Receipts and reproduction

A receipt records what a run read, what it concluded and what it observed of the machine. Its identity covers only the first two, so two machines that ran the same inputs to the same outcome produce the same identity. A published figure is rerun by producing a receipt and comparing its identity.

chunks.title: 11.1 Identities
chunks.content: ### 11.1 Identities **Semantics** 1. Each kind of output has its own identity [RCPT-01]: | Identity | Inputs | What it determines | | --- | --- | --- | | Build identity of emitted text | the sources and their module-relative paths, the compiler source identity, the language profile, the executor and its options | emitted C and PTX, byte for byte; C0 is not an input (7.7) | | Executable observation | the above and C0 | executables and objects, recorded and not claimed identical (10.4) | | Revision identity | 6.5 | the meaning of a program, shared by every build of it against one runtime contract version | | Execution identity | the revision and the semantic inputs | the output bytes, the fault record and the fuel | An x86-64 executable and a GPU kernel do not share a digest; built against one runtime contract version, they share the revision identity and the canonical outcomes.

chunks.title: 11.2 Receipt content
chunks.content:
### 11.2 Receipt content

**Semantics**

chunks.title: 11.2 Receipt content (part 2)
chunks.content: 1. A bootstrap, a fixpoint run and a conformance run each write a receipt. A receipt file is the receipt object followed by one LF, written as the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785) writes it, with keys sorted and no white space outside strings, except in the escaping of strings. That departure is this: a receipt holds ASCII characters only, so a character outside ASCII is written `\u` with four lowercase hexadecimal digits, and a character above U+FFFF as its UTF-16 surrogate pair, where RFC 8785 writes the character itself. The tools of this clause write a receipt with Python's `json.dumps` and the arguments `sort_keys=True`, `separators=(",", ":")` and `ensure_ascii=True`. They refuse a string outside ASCII, and they write U+007F as `\u007f`, where RFC 8785 and the tools of SPEC-06P.1 12.1 write it as itself. A receipt holds integers only, each within the I-JSON range of plus or minus 2^53 - 1; larger values and all digests are strings, and digests are 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Arrays of files are in byte order of path. The key `schema` names the format of the receipt and its version, such as `cint-bootstrap-receipt-1` or `cint-conformance-receipt-2`. A new version is written to a new file, and a receipt of an earlier version is not edited or regenerated; it stays valid for the sources it names. `identity.encodings` records each encoding version that the receipt relies on, such as the `.expect` formats and the fault record version [RCPT-02]. 2. A receipt has three parts: `identity`, the inputs and the digests of emitted text; `outcome`, the result of each check; and `observations`, the timings, the host, the C toolchain, the digests of executables and the counts of executions. The receipt identity is the SHA-256 digest of the bytes of the object `{"identity": ..., "outcome": ...}`, written as paragraph 1 state

chunks.title: 11.3 Rerunning a published figure
chunks.content:
### 11.3 Rerunning a published figure

**Examples**

1. A published figure of agreement is a set of receipts. To rerun one, a reader builds `cint` with the bootstrap of 10.3, runs `tools/cint_check.py` with the same arguments, writes the receipt with `--receipt` and compares its identity with the published one. Two configurations of the same tree and the same suite have the same identity, because nothing in it depends on the configuration:

chunks.title: 11.3 Rerunning a published figure (part 2)
chunks.content:
```console
$ python3 tools/cint_check.py --leg gcc --opt 0 --helpers portable --quick --compiler b1 --cint "$BOOT/cint" --only arith/add_i64_overflow --receipt rc/receipt-gcc-0-portable.json
...
receipt written

chunks.title: 11.4 Claims
chunks.content: ### 11.4 Claims **Semantics** 1. A published claim about cint is backed by material that a reader can obtain, normally a receipt. No claim of compliance with MISRA C, the SEI CERT C Coding Standard or another standard is made without a documented assessment against named editions and rules. Citations are to published material [DISC-02]. 2. The statement that emitted C has no undefined behavior is made only in this form [DISC-03]: | Part | Content | | --- | --- | | Claim | Emitted C, `cint_rt.h` and the `cint_rt` library do not evaluate an operation whose C17 behavior is undefined, for programs that `cintc` accepts. | | Design rules | 7.3 and 7.4. | | Evidence | The conformance programs compiled and run under UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and AddressSanitizer on the toolchains and versions that the receipts record, with no report. These sanitizers do not detect violations of the aliasing rules, unsequenced modifications or every lifetime error, so the evidence covers the programs run, not every accepted program. | | Assumptions | A correct bootstrap compiler (10.2), `cintc`, runtime and bridge; the properties of 7.2 paragraph 2; a correct C toolchain for the constructs used (none of the toolchains of the matrix claims full C17 conformance); no foreign code; buffers from the host that meet the contract of SPEC-03P.1. | | Exclusions | Exhaustion of the C stack; foreign functions; buffers from the host that break the contract. | 3. A performance number is published only with its workload, machine, toolchain, flags and method of measurement [DISC-04].

## 12 Refusals of the cint tools in 0.2.0

This clause is informative. It lists the constructs that the reference runs and that a tool of cint 0.2.0 refuses, by construct, with the tool and the diagnostic, and the limits of the tools that are below the minimums of SPEC-04P.2. A refused program is not run with another meaning (8.2), and on an implementation that runs it, its outcome is the one SPEC-04P.2 specifies. The interpreter runs the SIR text that `cint` writes, so a construct that `cint` refuses does not reach it.

1. The `cint` command (`cint run`, `cint build`, `cint test` and `cint emit-c`) refuses these constructs with the diagnostic C9102, or the one that the row names, at the position shown:

2. A program whose entry is a function `main`, rather than top-level statements, may declare struct types: the row of a struct declared in a script applies to scripts only. The `cint` command also reports C9102 for `==` between two arrays, which the reference rejects with the diagnostic C2013 at the same position, so both reject such a program. It reports C9102 for a fraction literal given to an integer type, as in `I64 x = 1.5;`, which the reference rejects with the diagnostic C2004 at the same position. In the same way it reports C9102, at the print statement, for the conversion `!ratio` of an integer, as in `"{x!ratio}\n";` with `I64 x`. SPEC-04P.2 7.5.4 makes that conversion C1037, and the reference reports C1037 at the value of the hole. The C3005 of a kernel called after a module's name is not a refusal in the sense of SPEC-04P.2 4, paragraph 4, whose codes begin with `C9`: the `cint` command rejects that conforming program as it rejects an undefined name.
3. In one case the direction is reversed, and the reference refuses a run that the `cint` command carries out. For `clamp(x, lo, hi)` with `lo` greater than `hi` at run time, `cint run` faults `E_DOMAIN` with the operation `clamp.checked.<t>`, such as `clamp.checked.i64`, and the operands `x`, `lo` and `hi`, with no exact result and no limit, as SPEC-04P.2 7.2.1 states. The reference reports the outcome `refused` for that run.
4. A `gpu-cuda` build refuses a kernel whose body needs a capability that the `gpu-cuda` table lists as unsupported, with `E_UNSUPPORTED`, naming the kernel, the capability, the SIR node and the position (5.5). The `cpu-c17` build of the same program runs it.

chunks.title: 13 Future directions
chunks.content:
## 13 Future directions

This clause is informative. It names work that cint 0.2.0 does not include.

1. *Reproducible executables.* The executables of a bootstrap differ between toolchains and may differ between two builds with one toolchain, so receipts record their digests as observations only (10.4). Byte-identical executables, built with options such as `-ffile-prefix-map` for GCC and Clang and `/Brepro` for MSVC, let a receipt identify the executable as well as the C it was built from.
2. *Diverse double-compiling.* In Wheeler's technique, the compiler's source is compiled by a second compiler that is trusted, and the resulting executable is compared with the distributed one; equality shows that the source and the executable correspond. It needs reproducible executables and a designated trusted compiler, and it extends the agreement of 10.5 from emitted C to executables.

# GLOSSARY-P.2: Glossary

GLOSSARY-P.2, edition 2 of the glossary of the cint specification, cint v0.2.0, 2026-10-11.

This edition replaces GLOSSARY-P.1. It is a reference to the rules of the other editions: where an entry and the section it points to differ, the section governs. Its text does not change after its release; a correction that changes no meaning is listed in [ERRATA.md](ERRATA.md), and a change of meaning is published as a new edition.

Section 1 explains, in plain words, the ideas a first reading meets. Section 2 lists the types and operators. chunks.title: How to read an entry
chunks.content:
## How to read an entry

- An entry gives the author or organization, the title, the date and a stable identifier: a standard number, an RFC number, a FIPS number, a DOI, an arXiv identifier, an ISBN or the official documentation URL. Titles of whole works are in italics; titles of parts (articles, chapters, pages, sections) are in quotation marks.
- "Read 2026-10-10" marks a web page with no version of its own; the page may change after that date. Where a locator serves the newest version of a versioned document, the entry says so.
- Where an edition names a work without its edition, version or revision, the entry gives the one read on 2026-10-10 and says so.
- In a "Cited by" note, "2" is the citing edition's clause 2, Normative references, and "Bibliography" is its list of other works. Any other number is a section of that edition, followed where it helps by a note, a paragraph or an item.

Each entry gives the erratum's name, the section and clause, the text as published, the corrected text, and the release that lists it.

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-00: welcome This is lesson 101-00 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will run your first program, change it and run it again.*

chunks.title: what a program is
chunks.content:
## what a program is

A program is a list of instructions that a computer carries out in order. A programming language is a way of writing those instructions down so that both you and the computer can read them. cint is a programming language about whole numbers, which programmers call integers. It makes one promise about its plain arithmetic signs, such as `+` and `*`: each answer is exact, or the program stops and tells you where and why.

You can run every program in this course in two places:

- **In your browser**: each program on these pages has a **Run** button, and there is nothing to install.
- **On your computer**: [set up cint](../setup.md) once, with an editor to write programs in and a terminal to run them. Then save a program in a file, and in the terminal type `cint run` and the file's name.

Use whichever you like. What a program prints is the same in both, down to the last character; only the messages about mistakes are laid out differently in the browser.

chunks.title: your first program
chunks.content:
## your first program

```ci
"Hello, world\n";
```

Run it. cint prints:

```text
Hello, world
```

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

The program is one line, and that line is one **statement**: one instruction to the computer.

- Text between double quotes, on its own, is printed. Programmers call printed text **output**.
- `\n` does not print a backslash and an n. It means "end the line here", so that whatever comes next starts on a new line.
- The semicolon `;` ends the statement, the way a period ends a sentence.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

Change the program, then run it again. Guess what it will print before you run it.

1. Print your own name instead of "world".
2. Print two lines: put a second statement under the first, such as `"Goodbye, world\n";`.
3. In the two-line program, delete the `\n` from the first line only.

<details>
<summary>what the third change prints</summary>

```text
Hello, worldGoodbye, world
```

Without `\n`, the first line never ends, so the second statement's text follows it on the same line. If you printed your own name in step 1, it appears in place of the first "world".
</details>

chunks.title: what cint 0.2.0 does not do
chunks.content:
## what cint 0.2.0 does not do

Many first programs ask for your name and greet you, or roll dice. cint 0.2.0 cannot do either: it has no way to read what you type, no way to keep a piece of text in the program's memory and no random numbers. It does not draw pictures.

So every program in this course carries its numbers and text inside it. To try different text or a different number, you change the program and run it again, as you just did. Lesson 101-01 shows how much you can still draw with plain characters.

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-01: printing This is lesson 101-01 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will draw a picture with characters one line at a time and meet your first error message.*

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**The first line is a comment.** Everything from `//` to the end of the line is for people. cint skips it. Comments say what a program is for, or why a line is there.

**Each other line is one statement**, and each prints one line of the picture. The computer carries them out from top to bottom, so the roof comes out first.

**Spaces inside the quotes are printed.** The spaces before `/\` push the top of the roof to the right, so it sits in the middle.

**A backslash is written twice.** Inside quotes, a backslash starts an **escape code**: you met `\n`, which ends a line. Because of that, a backslash on its own would be read as the start of an escape code. To print one backslash, you write two: `\\`. So the first statement holds `/\\\n`: a slash, a backslash written as `\\`, then `\n` to end the line.

Four escape codes are all this course needs:

| You write | cint prints |
|---|---|
| `\n` | the end of a line |
| `\\` | one backslash |
| `\"` | a double quote, without ending the text |
| `\t` | a tab, a wide space for lining things up |

For example, `"She said \"hi\"\n";` prints `She said "hi"`.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Add a chimney to the roof. You will need to change two lines, and add a backslash or two.
2. Draw the first letter of your name, five lines tall.
3. Print a line with a quote in it, such as `The sign said "open"`.

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

Leave out the closing quote on the first line of a program:

```ci
"Hello, world\n;
```

cint does not run anything. It prints:

```text
error[C1034]: invalid character or string literal
  --> hello.ci:1:1
   |
 1 | "Hello, world\n;
   | ^
   |
```

Read an error message from the top:

- **`error`** means cint found a problem before running the program, so nothing ran.
- **`C1034`** is the error's code. Each kind of mistake has its own code, and the [list of messages]({{DIAGNOSTICS}}) explains each one.
- **The rest of the first line** says what kind of problem it is. A **string literal** is a piece of text in quotes, so this one says the text in quotes is not right.
- **`--> hello.ci:1:1`** is the **source position**: `hello.ci`, the file the program was saved in, then line 1, character 1, counting characters from the left of the line.
- **The picture below it** shows that line, with `^` under the place where cint found the problem.

In your browser the same message is laid out differently, with the same code and position.

Here the `^` points at the opening quote, the start of a piece of text that never ends. Put the closing quote back, after `\n`, and the program runs.

Every lesson from here on ends with one mistake like this, so that you meet each of these messages first in a lesson.

chunks.content:
## new words

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-02: arithmetic This is lesson 101-02 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will have the computer do arithmetic inside printed text, and find out what it does with a remainder.*

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**Braces make a hole in the text.** cint works out what is inside `{` and `}` and prints the answer in its place. Outside the braces, `2 + 3 * 4` is printed just as it is written; inside them, it is worked out.

**These signs are called operators.** `+` adds, `-` subtracts and `*` multiplies. `/` divides and `%` gives the remainder of a division.

**Multiplying and dividing come before adding and subtracting**, as in school arithmetic. So `2 + 3 * 4` is `2 + 12`, which is 14. Parentheses go first, so `(2 + 3) * 4` is `5 * 4`, which is 20.

**Division gives a whole number.** cint works with whole numbers only, so `17 / 5` is 3, not 3.4. `%` gives what is left over: 17 is three 5s and 2 more.

**Division rounds down.** The last line divides a negative number. On a number line, -17 divided by 5 is -3.4, and "down" means toward the left, so the answer is -4, not -3. The remainder is then 3, because five times -4 is -20, and -20 plus 3 is -17. For every division that gives an answer, the answer times the number you divided by, plus the remainder, gives back the number you started with.

```text
   -5     -4     -3     -2     -1      0
    |------|------|------|------|------|
               ^
             -3.4 rounds down to -4
```

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Print how many hours are in a year of 365 days.
2. Print how many days old you are, roughly: your age times 365.
3. What is `100 / 7`, and what is `100 % 7`? Check the rule from above: the answer times 7, plus the remainder, is 100.

<details>
<summary>answers</summary>

```text
hours in a year: 8760
```

`100 / 7` is 14 and `100 % 7` is 2: 14 times 7 is 98, and 98 plus 2 is 100.
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

In school, many people write `x` for times. Try it:

```ci
"minutes in a week: {7 x 24 x 60}\n";
```

```text
error[C1035]: invalid character or string literal
  --> minutes.ci:1:22
   |
 1 | "minutes in a week: {7 x 24 x 60}\n";
   |                      ^
   |
```

The `^` points into the hole: what is inside the braces is not something cint can work out, because `x` is not an operator. Write `*` for times.

chunks.title: new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[operator]({{GLOSSARY}}#operator), [remainder]({{GLOSSARY}}#remainder), [rounding down]({{GLOSSARY}}#floor)

Next: [lesson 101-03, names for values](03-names.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-03: names for values This is lesson 101-03 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will give a number a name, change it as the program runs and count money exactly.*

chunks.title: the program
what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**`I64 jar = 0;` makes a variable.** A **variable** is a named place that holds a number. This line does three things: `I64` says what kind of number the place holds, `jar` is its name and `= 0` puts 0 in it to start. Until lesson 101-04 explains it, read `I64` as "a whole number, which may be negative".

**A variable's number can change.** `jar += 125;` means "add 125 to what `jar` holds". After it, `jar` holds 125. `jar -= 15;` takes 15 away. You can also write the long form, `jar = jar + 125;`: work out the right side, then put the answer in the variable on the left. This is called an **assignment**, and the `=` sign here means "put", not "is equal to".

**A name in a hole prints its number.** `{jar}` prints whatever `jar` holds at that moment, so the same hole prints 125, then 365, then 350 as the program runs.

**Money is counted in cents.** The jar holds 350 cents, not 3.50 dollars, because cint counts in whole numbers. Lesson 101-02's `/` and `%` turn cents into dollars and cents: 350 divided by 100 is 3, with 50 left over. Many programs that handle money count this way, in the smallest unit, because a whole number of cents is always exact. Many other languages store an amount such as 0.10 as the nearest fraction a computer can hold, which is close to 0.10 but not equal to it.

**Names are yours to choose.** A name starts with a letter and may hold letters, digits and the underscore `_`. Pick names that say what the number is: `jar`, `dollars`, `cents`.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Start the jar at 1000 cents instead of 0. What does the last line print?
2. Add a line that puts in 99 more cents, and a line after it that prints the jar.
3. Add a variable `quarters` that holds how many whole quarters (25 cents each) the jar could be changed into.

<details>
<summary>what the last line prints after the first change</summary>

```text
that is 13 dollars and 50 cents
```
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

Names must match exactly, capital letters included. Here the last line says `Jar` instead of `jar`:

```ci
I64 jar = 0;
jar = jar + 10;
"{jar}\n";
"{Jar}\n";
```

```text
error[C3005]: undefined or unusable name
  --> jar.ci:4:3
   |
 4 | "{Jar}\n";
   |   ^
   |
```

To cint, `Jar` and `jar` are two different names, and no variable is called `Jar`. You get the same message if you use a name before the line that makes it, or leave out the `I64` in that line.

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-04: numbers have sizes This is lesson 101-04 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will meet cint's eight kinds of whole number, see how large each can be and watch cint refuse a number that does not fit.*

chunks.title: the program
what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**A computer keeps a number in a box of bits.** A **bit** is a single 0 or 1. Eight bits can be set in 256 different ways, so a box of 8 bits can hold 256 different numbers. A box of 16 bits can hold 65,536 different numbers, and every extra bit doubles the count.

**The name of a type says the size of its box.** The kind of number a variable holds is called its **type**. In cint, a type's name says two things: `U` for numbers that are never negative (unsigned), or `I` for numbers that may be negative (signed: an integer with a sign), then the number of bits.

| Type | Smallest | Largest |
|---|---|---|
| `U8` | 0 | 255 |
| `U16` | 0 | 65535 |
| `U32` | 0 | 4294967295 |
| `U64` | 0 | 18446744073709551615 |
| `I8` | -128 | 127 |
| `I16` | -32768 | 32767 |
| `I32` | -2147483648 | 2147483647 |
| `I64` | -9223372036854775808 | 9223372036854775807 |

You never need to learn these by heart: `U8.min` and `U8.max` give them, as the program shows, and the same works for every type.

**Pick the type that fits the job.** A pixel's brightness runs from 0 to 255, so it fits a `U8`, and a picture with millions of pixels takes a quarter of the memory it would as `I32`. When in doubt, use `I64`: it holds any whole number from about minus nine billion billion to about nine billion billion.

**Underscores make long numbers readable.** `2_000_000_000` is two billion. cint ignores the `_`; it is there for your eyes.

**cint checks that a number fits its box.** Write a number that cannot fit, and cint refuses the program before it runs. This lesson's mistake shows it.

**cint never moves a number to another type on its own.** Even when the number would fit, you say so:

```ci
U8 b = 200;
I64 wide = b as I64;
"{wide}\n";
```

chunks.title: what happened (part 2)
chunks.content: This prints `200`. Without `as I64`, cint refuses the line. `as` is a checked **conversion**: cint checks that the number fits the new type, and lesson 101-05 shows what happens when it does not. Keeping each number in the type you chose means you always know which box it is in.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Print the largest `U16`.
2. Put `-1` in a `U8`. What does cint say?
3. Make a `U8` that holds 200 and add it to an `I64` that holds 100, using `as`. The answer, 300, would not fit in a `U8`.

<details>
<summary>one way to write the third change</summary>

```ci
U8 a = 200;
I64 total = (a as I64) + 100;
"{total}\n";
```

This prints `300`.
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

```ci
U8 brightness = 256;
```

```text
error[C2003]: literal does not fit its type
  --> brightness.ci:1:17
   |
 1 | U8 brightness = 256;
   |                 ^
   |
```

A **literal** is a value written out in the program, like `256` or text in quotes. The largest `U8` is 255, so 256 does not fit, and cint says so before anything runs. Change the type to `U16`, or the number to 255.

chunks.content:
