chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-05: when a number runs out This is lesson 101-05 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will double a number until it no longer fits its box, watch cint stop at that exact step and read the report it prints.*

chunks.title: the program
chunks.content:
## the program

```ci
// Double a number until it no longer fits in a U8.
U8 x = 1;
for step in 1..=10 {
    "step {step}: {x}\n";
    x *= 2;
}
```

The program has two new parts. `for step in 1..=10 { ... }` is a **loop**: it runs the lines between the braces ten times, with `step` counting 1, 2, 3 and so on up to 10. Lesson 101-07 is all about loops. `x *= 2;` doubles `x`, the way `+=` added in lesson 101-03.

Run it:

```text
step 1: 1
step 2: 2
step 3: 4
step 4: 8
step 5: 16
step 6: 32
step 7: 64
step 8: 128
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> doubling.ci:5:7
   |
 5 |     x *= 2;
   |       ^ mul.checked.u8
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.u8
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: U8 128
   = operand: U8 2
   = exact:   256
   = limit:   U8 255
   = revision: 8efe88d0637573b3291746f4096933013c3e869ecc8be5ae436c45314575f6f4
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 0
   = fuel-consumed: 9 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

Eight lines printed. At step 8, `x` held 128, and the next doubling would make 256. The largest `U8` is 255. There is no right answer that fits, so cint stopped the program at that multiplication and told you what happened. This is called a **fault**. Lesson 101-01's errors stop a program before it runs; a fault stops it while it runs, at the exact step that went wrong.

chunks.title: reading the fault report
chunks.content:
## reading the fault report

The report is long, but five parts of it explain the fault:

| Line | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range` | What kind of fault. **Overflow** means the true answer is too large (or too small) for the type. |
| `--> doubling.ci:5:7` and the picture | Where: line 5, character 7, the `*=`. |
| `operation: mul.checked.u8` | What was being done: a checked multiplication (`mul`) of two `U8` numbers. |
| `operand: U8 128` and `operand: U8 2` | The numbers it was working on. **Operands** are the numbers an operation takes. |
| `exact: 256` and `limit: U8 255` | The true answer, and the most the type can hold. |

The other lines are there for tools that read faults, and you can skip them. `revision` is a fingerprint of the program's operations. `fuel-consumed` counts the steps the program took to run, which are not the loop's `step`. `stack-depth` (lesson 101-11 uses it), `source-map` and `address` matter in larger programs.

Notice what did not happen: the program did not print a wrong number. Everything it printed before the fault is true.

chunks.title: the same fault, every time
chunks.content:
## the same fault, every time

Run the program again, and again. You get the same eight lines and the same report, with the same numbers in it, every time. Run it on another computer and the output is the same down to the last character. In your browser the report is laid out differently, but it names the same fault, the same operation and the same numbers.

A mistake that shows up every time, at the same place, with the numbers that caused it written down, is a mistake you can find and fix. It also means that you can run the old and new versions of a changed program and compare them line by line. Any difference then comes from your change.

chunks.title: fix it
chunks.content:
## fix it

There are two ways to fix a program that runs out, and each one means something different:

1. **A bigger box**: change `U8` to `U16` in the line `U8 x = 1;`. Now all ten steps fit.
2. **Fewer steps**: the doubling at the end of step 8 is the one that does not fit. If the program only needs the first seven numbers, change `1..=10` to `1..=7`. The last doubling is then 64 times 2, and 128 fits.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Make the box `U16` and the loop `1..=20`, and delete the comment line. Before you run it: at which step will it stop, and what will `exact` and `limit` say?
2. Triple instead of double, with `x *= 3;`. Which step stops a `U8` now?

<details>
<summary>where the U16 version stops</summary>

```text
step 16: 32768
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> doubling.ci:4:7
   ...
   = operand: U16 32768
   = operand: U16 2
   = exact:   65536
   = limit:   U16 65535
```

(The line number is 4 because the comment line is gone.)
</details>

Two other programming languages, C and Python, behave differently. The same loop in C, with an 8-bit unsigned `x`, built with GCC 13.3 on Linux with no options, prints `step 9: 0` and `step 10: 0` and gives no sign that anything went wrong. Python's whole numbers have no fixed limit, so it prints 256 and 512.

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

Lesson 101-04's `as` is checked the same way. Moving 300 into a `U8`:

```ci
I64 big = 300;
U8 small = big as U8;
```

stops with a different fault:

```text
fault[E_NARROW]: the value does not fit the destination type
  --> narrow.ci:2:16
   |
 2 | U8 small = big as U8;
   |                ^ as.checked.i64.u8
   |
   = operation: as.checked.i64.u8
   = operand-count: 1
   = operand: I64 300
   = exact:   300
   = limit:   U8 255
   ...
```

**Narrow** means moving a number into a smaller type. The same five parts describe the fault: what kind of fault, where, which operation, the number it had and the limit it hit.

chunks.title: new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[fault]({{GLOSSARY}}#fault), [overflow]({{GLOSSARY}}#overflow), [operand]({{GLOSSARY}}#operand), [fault report]({{GLOSSARY}}#fault-record), [loop]({{GLOSSARY}}#loop)

Next: [lesson 101-06, true or false](06-true-or-false.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-06: true or false This is lesson 101-06 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will ask questions whose answer is true or false, and make a program do one thing or another depending on the answer.*

chunks.title: the program
what happened
change it
when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

One `=` where two were meant is a common slip. cint stops it before the program runs:

```ci
I64 x = 5;
if (x = 3) { "three\n"; }
```

```text
error[C1041]: assignment in a condition
  --> assign.ci:2:5
   |
 2 | if (x = 3) { "three\n"; }
   |     ^
   |
```

A condition must be a `Bool`, too. A number on its own is not a question:

```ci
I64 year = 2024;
if (year) {
    "yes\n";
}
```

```text
error[C2002]: condition is not `Bool`
  --> ifnum.ci:2:5
   |
 2 | if (year) {
   |     ^
   |
```

Some other languages, such as C and Python, take any number that is not 0 to mean true. In cint, a condition must be true or false, so a test on a number is written out, such as `year != 0`.

chunks.title: new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[Bool]({{GLOSSARY}}#bool), [comparison]({{GLOSSARY}}#comparison), [condition]({{GLOSSARY}}#condition)

Next: [lesson 101-07, counting loops](07-counting-loops.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-07: counting loops This is lesson 101-07 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will repeat lines a set number of times, put one loop inside another and line up numbers in rows.*

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**A `for` loop counts.** Lesson 101-05 met the loop: `for row in 1..=9 { ... }` runs the lines between the braces once for each number from 1 to 9, and `row` holds that number. Each time through the lines is called a **pass**.

**A range says where to start and stop.** There are two ways to write one:

- `1..=9` means 1 up to 9, including 9.
- `1..9` means 1 up to 9, leaving 9 out: 1 to 8.

The second kind is useful when counting starts at 0, as it does for lists in lesson 101-12. `0..7` gives seven numbers, 0 to 6.

**A loop can hold another loop.** For each `row`, the inner loop runs through `col` from 1 to 9. The line `"{row * col:>3}";` runs 9 times 9, which is 81 times, once for each number in the table.

**A print without `\n` stays on the same line.** The inner loop prints nine numbers side by side. After it ends, `"\n";` ends the line, and the outer loop goes on to the next row.

**`:>3` sets a width.** `{row * col:>3}` prints the number in 3 characters, with spaces in front to fill them, so `4` prints as two spaces and a 4. This keeps the numbers lined up under each other. The `>` means the number goes at the right of its space.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Change `1..=9` to `1..9` in both loops. Which row disappears, and which number disappears from each row?
2. Make the table go up to 12 in both loops. Look at the last rows: what goes wrong, and what width fixes it?
3. Print only the squares, 1, 4, 9 and so on up to 81, one on each line. You need only one loop.

<details>
<summary>the last rows of the 12 table</summary>

```text
  9 18 27 36 45 54 63 72 81 90 99108
 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 90100110120
 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88 99110121132
 12 24 36 48 60 72 84 96108120132144
```

From row 9 on, numbers with three digits fill all 3 characters and run together. A width of 4 leaves a space between them.
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[width]({{GLOSSARY}}#width), [range]({{GLOSSARY}}#range), [pass]({{GLOSSARY}}#pass)

Next: [lesson 101-08, loops that wait](08-loops-that-wait.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-08: loops that wait This is lesson 101-08 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will write a loop that runs until something becomes true, however many passes that takes. You will also stop a loop early or skip a pass.*

chunks.title: the program
what happened
stopping early, skipping a pass
change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Set `start` to 7. How many steps does it take, and how high does it climb?
2. Set `start` to 97. Which takes more steps, 27 or 97?
3. Change the countdown to count down from 10 in twos: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.

<details>
<summary>what 7 prints</summary>

```text
7 reaches 1 in 16 steps, climbing as high as 52
```
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

Leave out the halving by mistake, so that every pass triples and adds one:

```ci
I64 n = 27;
I64 steps = 0;
while (n != 1) {
    n = 3 * n + 1;
    steps += 1;
}
```

`n` only grows, so it never reaches 1. The same loop written in Python 3.13 ran until it was stopped after 10 seconds, because Python's numbers can grow until the computer runs out of memory. In cint, the number runs out of room on pass 37 and the program stops with a fault:

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> runaway.ci:4:11
   |
 4 |     n = 3 * n + 1;
   |           ^ mul.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 3
   = operand: I64 4127602470667475827
   = exact:   12382807412002427481
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   ...
```

A loop that starts with a true condition, never changes anything its condition reads and has no `break` runs forever. To stop a program running in a terminal, press **Ctrl+C**. To stop one running in the browser, reload the page.

chunks.title: new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[while loop]({{GLOSSARY}}#while), [break]({{GLOSSARY}}#break), [continue]({{GLOSSARY}}#continue)

Next: [lesson 101-09, choosing among many](09-choosing-among-many.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-09: choosing among many This is lesson 101-09 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will sort a number into one of several groups with `switch`, using ranges of numbers, and make sure every number lands somewhere.*

chunks.title: the program
what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**The loop makes the scores.** `tens` counts from 4 to 10, and `score` is ten times `tens`: 40, 50 and so on up to 100. A range in cint 0.2.0 counts by ones only, so a loop that needs steps of ten counts by ones and multiplies.

**`switch` sorts one number into cases.** `switch (score)` looks at `score` once and runs the lines of the case that holds it. Each **case** names a number or a range of numbers:

- `case 90..=100:` holds every score from 90 to 100.
- `case 80..=89:` holds 80 to 89, `case 70..=79:` holds 70 to 79 and `case 60..=69:` holds 60 to 69.
- `default:` holds every number no other case holds.

**Only one case runs.** When the lines of a case are done, the `switch` is done, and the program goes on after its closing brace. Here each case prints one letter and the line ends.

**Every number must have a place.** A `switch` without `default` must have a case for every possible value. With `default` at the end, every number has somewhere to go.

**A `switch` can do what `else if` does.** This program could be written as a chain of `if` and `else if`, as in lesson 101-06. A `switch` is shorter when every question is about the same number, and cint checks that its ranges do not overlap.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Make the loop count from 0 to 10 instead. What do scores 0 to 30 get?
2. Add a grade `E` for scores from 50 to 59.
3. Give exactly 100 the grade `A+`. What else must change, and why?

<details>
<summary>what 3 needs</summary>

`case 100: "A+\n";` added above the A case is refused, because 100 is already in `case 90..=100:` and two cases cannot hold the same number. cint points at the range in the A case that overlaps the new one:

```text
error[C4021]: `switch` rule
  --> aplus.ci:6:14
   |
 6 |         case 90..=100: "A\n";
   |              ^
   |
```

Change the A range to `90..=99` as well.
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[switch]({{GLOSSARY}}#switch), [case]({{GLOSSARY}}#case), [default]({{GLOSSARY}}#default)

Next: [lesson 101-10, functions](10-functions.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-10: functions This is lesson 101-10 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will give a calculation a name, use it as often as you like with different numbers and start a program from a function called `main`.*

chunks.title: the program
what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**A function is a calculation with a name.** The first three lines make a **function** called `area`. Read its first line from left to right:

- `I64` is the type of the answer it gives back.
- `area` is its name.
- `(I64 width, I64 height)` are its **parameters**: the numbers it needs, each with a type and a name.

The lines in the braces are its body. `return width * height;` works out the answer and gives it back.

**Calling a function runs it.** `area(4, 3)` runs `area` with `width` set to 4 and `height` set to 3, and the call is replaced by the answer, 12. The numbers in a call are its **arguments**, and they fill the parameters in order. `area(5, 4)` runs the same lines again with different numbers. A function is written once and used as often as you need.

**A function can make choices.** `larger` returns `a` if it is bigger and `b` otherwise. A `return` ends the function at once, so when `a > b`, the last line never runs.

**`main` is where the program starts.** Until now, every program ran from its first line to its last. A program can instead start from a function called `main`, and cint runs `main` when the program starts. `void` in front of `main` means it gives back no answer. From lesson 101-12 on, programs start from `main`, because in cint 0.2.0 a list of numbers can only be made inside a function.

**Each function has its own names.** `width` and `height` exist only inside `area`, and `kitchen` exists only inside `main`. Two functions can use the same name for different things without mixing them up.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Add a room `hall` that is 6 by 2, and print its area.
2. Write a function `perimeter` that gives back the distance around a room: twice the width plus twice the height. Print the kitchen's perimeter.
3. Use `larger` twice in one line to print the largest of three rooms.

<details>
<summary>one way to write perimeter</summary>

```ci
I64 perimeter(I64 width, I64 height) {
    return 2 * width + 2 * height;
}
```

`"{perimeter(4, 3)}\n";` prints 14. A program that has functions but no `main` runs its other lines from the top, so this line can sit below the function.
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[function]({{GLOSSARY}}#function), [parameter]({{GLOSSARY}}#parameter), [argument]({{GLOSSARY}}#argument), [return]({{GLOSSARY}}#return)

Next: [lesson 101-11, functions that call themselves](11-functions-that-call-themselves.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-11: functions that call themselves This is lesson 101-11 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will write a function that uses itself to get its answer. You will watch it reach the edge of `I64` and read where the fault report says the call came from.*

chunks.title: the program
chunks.content:
## the program

The factorial of a number multiplies every whole number from 1 up to it: the factorial of 4 is `1 * 2 * 3 * 4`, which is 24. Mathematicians write it as 4 followed by an exclamation mark. cint has no factorial sign, so in this program the mark is only text that the program prints.

```ci
I64 factorial(I64 n) {
    if (n <= 1) { return 1; }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

void main() {
    for n in 1..=25 {
        "{n:>2}! = {factorial(n)}\n";
    }
}
```

Run it:

```text
 1! = 1
 2! = 2
 3! = 6
 4! = 24
 5! = 120
 6! = 720
 7! = 5040
 8! = 40320
 9! = 362880
10! = 3628800
11! = 39916800
12! = 479001600
13! = 6227020800
14! = 87178291200
15! = 1307674368000
16! = 20922789888000
17! = 355687428096000
18! = 6402373705728000
19! = 121645100408832000
20! = 2432902008176640000
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> factorial.ci:3:14
   |
 3 |     return n * factorial(n - 1);
   |              ^ mul.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 21
   = operand: I64 2432902008176640000
   = exact:   51090942171709440000
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   = revision: c0baa23c76db8b75f2ee6e08b38a56964c2051f06b6e45554fefca759b36e4ba
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: factorial.ci:8:21
   = fuel-consumed: 253 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**A function may call itself.** The factorial of 4 is 4 times the factorial of 3, and the factorial of 3 is 3 times the factorial of 2. The second line of `factorial` says exactly that: the factorial of `n` is `n` times the factorial of `n - 1`. A function that calls itself is called **recursive**.

**It needs a place to stop.** `if (n <= 1) { return 1; }` answers the smallest case right away, without calling `factorial` again. Follow `factorial(3)`:

1. `factorial(3)` needs `3 * factorial(2)`, so it calls `factorial(2)` and waits.
2. `factorial(2)` needs `2 * factorial(1)`, so it calls `factorial(1)` and waits.
3. `factorial(1)` returns 1 at once.
4. `factorial(2)` can now finish: `2 * 1` is 2.
5. `factorial(3)` can now finish: `3 * 2` is 6.

**Factorials grow fast.** The factorial of 20 is 2432902008176640000, which still fits in an `I64`. The factorial of 21 is 21 times that, 51090942171709440000, more than five times the largest `I64`. So the multiplication for 21 faulted, and the program printed 20 lines and stopped.

**The report says where the call came from.** `--> factorial.ci:3:14` is where the fault happened: the `*` in `factorial`. `called from: factorial.ci:8:21` is the line that called `factorial`: line 8, in `main`, at the `factorial(n)` in the print. The calls in progress at any moment are called the **call stack**. `stack-depth: 1` counts the calls in progress besides `main`: here only `factorial(21)`, the call that faulted. The calls for 20, 19 and the rest had already returned their answers.

chunks.title: change it
chunks.content:
## change it

1. Make the loop stop at 20. Does the program finish now?
2. Write a recursive function `sum_to(n)` that adds 1 + 2 + ... + n, and print `sum_to(100)`.
3. The largest `U64` is 18446744073709551615, about twice the largest `I64`. Would the factorial of 21 fit in a `U64`? Work it out from the numbers in the report.

<details>
<summary>what sum_to(100) prints</summary>

It prints 5050. One way to write it:

```ci
I64 sum_to(I64 n) {
    if (n == 0) { return 0; }
    return n + sum_to(n - 1);
}
```
</details>

chunks.title: when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

Leave out the stopping line, and `factorial` calls itself for 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1 and on without end:

```ci
I64 factorial(I64 n) {
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}
void main() {
    "{factorial(5)}\n";
}
```

A program may have at most 256 calls in progress at once, and `main` counts as one of them. This program passes that limit and stops with a different fault:

```text
fault[E_DEPTH]: call depth limit exceeded
  --> nobase.ci:2:16
   |
 2 |     return n * factorial(n - 1);
   |                ^ call.enter
   |
   = operation: call.enter
   = operand-count: 0
   = exact:   none
   = limit:   I64 256
   ...
   = stack-depth: 255
```

The full report lists 255 `called from` lines, one for each call in progress besides `main`. A recursive function needs a stopping case that every call eventually reaches.

chunks.title: new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[recursion]({{GLOSSARY}}#recursion), [call stack]({{GLOSSARY}}#call-stack)

Next: [lesson 101-12, lists](12-lists.md).

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content: # 101-12: lists This is lesson 101-12 of CU-101.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will keep a week of numbers under one name, reach each one by its position and see what cint does when a position does not exist.*

chunks.title: the program
chunks.content:
## the program

```ci
void main() {
    I64[7] temps = [12, 15, 11, 18, 21, 19, 16];
    "there are {len(temps)} days\n";
    "Monday was {temps[0]}, Sunday was {temps[6]}\n";
    temps[2] = 13;
    "Wednesday, corrected: {temps[2]}\n";
    "the day after Sunday: {temps[7]}\n";
}
```

Run it:

```text
there are 7 days
Monday was 12, Sunday was 16
Wednesday, corrected: 13
fault[E_BOUNDS]: index out of bounds
  --> temps.ci:7:34
   |
 7 |     "the day after Sunday: {temps[7]}\n";
   |                                  ^ index.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: index.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 1
   = operand: I64 7
   = exact:   none
   = limit:   I64 7
   = revision: 9eb95af35c842e3f063ac00a7cb32e13cd838a461e5eb04b6d46c5eaf40c8c4b
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 0
   = fuel-consumed: 1 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**A list holds several numbers under one name.** `I64[7] temps` makes a list of seven `I64` numbers called `temps`. In cint a list of a fixed length is called an **array**. The `[12, 15, 11, 18, 21, 19, 16]` after the `=` gives the seven numbers to start with, in order: a week of noon temperatures in degrees Celsius, from Monday to Sunday.

**Positions count from 0.** `temps[0]` is the first number, 12, and `temps[6]` is the seventh and last, 16. The number in the square brackets is called the **index**. Other programming languages, such as C and Python, count positions from 0 too. An array of 7 has the indexes 0 to 6.

**`len` gives the length.** `len(temps)` is 7. A loop over `0..len(temps)` visits every index, 0 to 6, as lesson 101-07 explained for `..`.

**One number can change.** `temps[2] = 13;` replaces the third number, Wednesday's 11, with 13. The rest stay as they were.

**There is no eighth day.** `temps[7]` asks for an index the array does not have. cint stopped the program with an **index out of bounds** fault at line 7, at `temps[7]`. The report says the index was 7 and the limit is 7, meaning the index must be less than 7. The three lines before it printed, and nothing after it did.

chunks.title: change it
when it goes wrong
chunks.content:
## when it goes wrong

The index can come from a variable, and cint checks it the same way when the program runs:

```ci
void main() {
    I64[7] temps = [12, 15, 11, 18, 21, 19, 16];
    I64 day = 7;
    "the day after Sunday: {temps[day]}\n";
}
```

```text
fault[E_BOUNDS]: index out of bounds
  --> index.ci:4:34
   |
 4 |     "the day after Sunday: {temps[day]}\n";
   |                                  ^ index.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: index.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 1
   = operand: I64 7
   ...
```

In C, reading past the end of an array is undefined behavior: the program can quietly give back whatever number is stored next to it, or crash. In cint, every index is checked.

The starting numbers must match the length. `I64[7] temps = [12, 15];` gives two numbers for seven places, and cint refuses it with error C2011. In cint 0.2.0 an array can only be made inside a function, so this lesson's program starts from `main`, as lesson 101-10 explained.

chunks.title: new words
chunks.content:
## new words

[array]({{GLOSSARY}}#array), [index]({{GLOSSARY}}#index), [out of bounds]({{GLOSSARY}}#bounds)

chunks.title: CU-101.2
chunks.content:
# 101: first programs

This page is CU-101.2, edition 2 of 101: first programs, checked against cint 0.2.0 and released on {{RELEASE_DATE}}.

This edition is current. Every program in it was run on cint 0.2.0 with each of four C compilers (GCC, Clang, MSVC and Apple Clang), and every output comes from those runs. The text of this edition does not change after its release. Corrections that change nothing a reader would see are listed in [ERRATA.md](../ERRATA.md). A new edition is published when a release changes what a lesson shows or when lessons are added. Lesson identifiers are the same in every edition and are never reused.

101 is for people who have never written a program. It needs a browser and nothing else. To run the programs on your own computer as well, [set up cint](../setup.md). A new word is explained where it first appears and linked to the [glossary]({{GLOSSARY}}).

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-00: start here This is lesson 201-00 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will set up cint, meet its four commands and see the C it emits from a small program.* This course is for readers who already program in C, Python or a language like them. If you have never programmed, start with [101](../101/00-welcome.md) instead.

chunks.title: what cint is
chunks.content:
## what cint is

cint is a language for whole numbers. Its signed integer types run from 8 to 1024 bits and its unsigned ones from 8 to 512. It has fixed-point types for fractions and no floating point. Every plain operator is checked. When `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, a shift or a conversion has no exact result in its type, the program stops with a fault that names the operation, the operands, the exact result and the limit. Where wrapping or saturating is what a program means, it says so with a wrapping operator such as `+%` or a saturating one such as `+|`, and those never fault.

Three tools run cint programs:

- **`cint`**, the command you build in the next section. It translates a program to C17, compiles that with your C compiler (GCC, Clang, MSVC or Apple Clang) and runs it. The compiler inside it, `cintc`, is written in cint and compiles itself.
- **The reference**, an implementation of the language in Python that defines what every program means. On a four-core Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, finding the number below 1,000,000 with the longest Collatz path did not finish in five minutes on the reference, while `cint run` took under one second. The browser workspace on [integerc.dev](https://integerc.dev) runs it.
- **The interpreter**, which runs the same programs without a C compiler. [Lesson 201-06](06-workbench.md) uses it.

For every program in this course, all three print the same bytes. If they ever disagree, the reference decides.

chunks.content:

Lessons 201-01 to 201-04 cover the arithmetic at the core of the language in four steps: checked arithmetic and the fault record; the integer types and conversions; the wrapping and saturating operators; division and rounding. The [labs](../401/README.md) build complete programs on top.

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-01: numbers that hold This is lesson 201-01 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will run a program in your browser and with `cint run`, watch it stop at the one multiplication that does not fit and read the fault record.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run chessboard.ci
square  1:                    1   total                    1
square  2:                    2   total                    3
square  3:                    4   total                    7
...
square 62:  2305843009213693952   total  4611686018427387903
square 63:  4611686018427387904   total  9223372036854775807
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> chessboard.ci:9:16
   |
 9 |         grains *= 2;
   |                ^ mul.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 4611686018427387904
   = operand: I64 2
   = exact:   9223372036854775808
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   = revision: 20867626996cb61a47e788e74f82b7226550f13626a9d9494bb161d07f294382
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 0
   = fuel-consumed: 64 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

After square 63 the total is 9223372036854775807, which is `I64.max` exactly. The doubling that follows has no `I64` result, so the program stops at it. Every line it printed before the fault is correct; no wrong number reached the output.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The same loop was run in other languages on 2026-10-10:

| Language | What it printed |
|---|---|
| Python 3.13 | The exact total, 18446744073709551615: `int` has no fixed size. |
| JavaScript, Node 22.22.0 | At square 54, a total of 18014398509481984, one more than the exact 18014398509481983, with no error. Numbers are doubles, which hold every integer only up to 2<sup>53</sup>. Square 64 printed 18446744073709552000. |
| NumPy 2.5.3, `int64` scalars | At square 64, grains -9223372036854775808 and total -1, with `RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in scalar multiply`. |
| NumPy 2.5.3, `int64` arrays | `(2 ** np.arange(64, dtype=np.int64)).sum()` gives -1, with no warning. |
| C, GCC 13.3, `-O2` | Signed overflow is undefined behavior. This build printed grains -9223372036854775808 and total -1. Built with `-fsanitize=undefined`, it also reports `signed integer overflow: 4611686018427387904 * 2 cannot be represented in type 'long int'` and keeps going. |

Python computes the exact total because its integers grow without a fixed size. JavaScript, NumPy and C give no correct result for square 64; only the NumPy scalar warning and the C sanitizer build show that something went wrong. cint keeps fixed-size integers and checks every plain operator instead.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**Types come first.** `I64 grains = 1;` declares a signed 64-bit integer. Every variable has a type, and nothing changes it silently: [201-02](02-types-and-conversions.md) covers conversions.

**`for square in 1..=64`** counts from 1 to 64 inclusive. `0..n` excludes `n`, as Python's `range` does.

**Printing** happens when a string literal stands on its own as a statement. `{grains:>20}` prints `grains` right-aligned in 20 characters.

**The multiplication is checked.** For `grains *= 2`, cint computes the exact product, 9223372036854775808, compares it with the type's range and stops because it does not fit. [201-00](00-start-here.md) shows the call this becomes in the emitted C.

chunks.title: reading the fault record
chunks.content:
## reading the fault record

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `fault[E_OVERFLOW]` | The fault code. `E_OVERFLOW` means an exact result outside the type's range. |
| `-->` and the caret | The source position of the operation, here line 9, character 16. |
| `operation` | The operation by name: a checked (`checked`) multiply (`mul`) on `i64`. Each kind of checked operation has its own name. |
| `operand-count`, `operand` | The inputs, each with its type. |
| `exact` | The mathematically exact result. |
| `limit` | The bound it crossed. |
| `revision` | A digest of the program's operations, without their source positions. It is the same on every compiler for the same program and cint release. It stays the same when you only add blank lines or comments and changes when an operation changes. |
| `source-map` | A separate digest of the source positions. cint 0.2.0 prints `none`. |
| `address` | For a fault inside a kernel, the element it was working on; `none` elsewhere. |
| `stack-depth` | How many calls deep the operation was. A fault inside a function adds a `called from` line for each caller. |
| `fuel-consumed` | How many counted steps the program ran before the fault. It is not part of the record, but it is the same on every compiler, so a change in it means the program took a different path. |

The record is the same on every compiler cint supports, field for field, and so is everything the program printed before it. That is what lets you compare two runs of a program, on two machines or before and after a change, and trust that any difference comes from the program. [201-07](07-debugging-by-comparison.md) builds a way of debugging on it.

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-02: types and conversions This is lesson 201-02 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will meet the integer types, see that cint never converts a value implicitly and choose what happens at each edge of a conversion.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run downlink.ci
low:     32767
wrapped: -32768
handled: 32767
fault[E_NARROW]: the value does not fit the destination type
  --> downlink.ci:15:27
   |
15 |     I16 checked = high_dm as I16;
   |                           ^ as.checked.i64.i16
   |
   = operation: as.checked.i64.i16
   = operand-count: 1
   = operand: I64 32768
   = exact:   32768
   = limit:   I16 32767
   ...
```

3276700 mm is 32767 dm, `I16.max`, and fits. 3276800 mm is 32768 dm, one past `I16.max`. The program converts that value three ways, and each line says what it wants at the edge.

chunks.title: the three conversions
chunks.content:
## the three conversions

| Form | When the value fits | When it does not |
|---|---|---|
| `x as T` | the value | fault `E_NARROW` |
| `x as% T` | the value | wraps: the low bits of `x`, read as `T` |
| `x as? T catch v` | the value | `v`, chosen by the program |

`as` is the default. `as%` is for formats and hashes where only the low bits matter. `as?` turns the out-of-range case into an ordinary error, and `catch` gives the value to use instead.

chunks.title: no implicit conversions
chunks.content:
## no implicit conversions

cint never converts between types on its own, not even to a wider type:

```ci
I64 big = 40_000;
I16 small = big;
```

```text
error[C2001]: type mismatch
  --> narrow_error.ci:2:13
   |
 2 | I16 small = big;
   |             ^
   |
```

The same message comes from `I64 wide = b;` when `b` is a `U8`, although every `U8` fits an `I64`. Each conversion is written, so each one is a place you can see and search for.

chunks.title: literals take their type from where they are used
chunks.content:
## literals take their type from where they are used

A literal has no type until its context gives it one. That includes the arithmetic around it:

```ci
I16 seconds_per_day = 24 * 60 * 60;
```

```text
error[C6001]: fault during constant evaluation
  --> fold_error.ci:1:31
   |
 1 | I16 seconds_per_day = 24 * 60 * 60;
   |                               ^
   |
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> fold_error.ci:1:31
   ...
   = operation: mul.checked.i16
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I16 1440
   = operand: I16 60
   = exact:   86400
   = limit:   I16 32767
   ...
```

The multiplication is done in `I16` because that is the destination, and the compiler evaluates constant expressions with the same checks as the running program. The error comes before anything runs, although the full report still ends with "the program stopped".

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

These results were measured on 2026-10-10, on Ubuntu 24.04 for x86-64:

| Language | `32768` into 16 bits | `int16 x = 24 * 60 * 60` |
|---|---|---|
| C, GCC 13.3, `-O2 -Wall` | `(int16_t)32768` gives -32768 | compiles with the warning `changes value from '86400' to '20864'` and prints 20864 |
| NumPy 2.5.3 | `np.array([32768]).astype(np.int16)` gives `[-32768]`; `np.int16(32768)` raises `OverflowError` | not applicable: Python has no typed variable declarations |

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-03: operators at the edge This is lesson 201-03 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will see that the plain operators are checked, and write the wrapping or saturating spelling only where that is what the program means.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run fnv.ci
hello -> 4f9f2cab
hellp -> 5c9f4122
```

Both values match a Python implementation of the published algorithm, which masks each product with `& 0xffffffff`.

chunks.title: the same hash with a plain `*`
chunks.content:
## the same hash with a plain `*`

Change `*%` to `*` and the first multiply faults:

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> fnv_checked.ci:10:15
   |
10 |         h = h * FNV_PRIME;
   |               ^ mul.checked.u32
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.u32
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: U32 2166136237
   = operand: U32 16777619
   = exact:   36342608486479703
   = limit:   U32 4294967295
   ...
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: fnv_checked.ci:16:13
```

`called from` gives the line in `main` that called `fnv1a`. In C, `uint32_t` arithmetic wraps by definition, so C versions of the two programs would read the same. In cint, the wrap is written where it is wanted, and every other multiply in a program stays checked.

chunks.title: three families of operators
saturating pixels
elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

On 2026-10-10, the same six pixels were brightened by 40 in other languages:

| Language | Result |
|---|---|
| cint, `+|` | `40 104 168 232 255 255` |
| NumPy 2.5.3, `uint8` array `+ np.uint8(40)` | `[ 40 104 168 232  14  39]`, with no warning |
| C, GCC 13.3 `-O2`, `uint8_t` with `+=` | `40 104 168 232 14 39` |

The two bright pixels turn dark. A plain `+` in cint would fault on 230 + 40 instead; `+|` gives the answer the program wants.

chunks.title: shifts are checked too
chunks.content:
## shifts are checked too

```ci
I32 one = 1;
I32 x = one << 31;
"x={x}\n";
```

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> p29_shift_overflow.ci:2:13
   |
 2 | I32 x = one << 31;
   |             ^ shl.checked.i32
   |
   = operation: shl.checked.i32
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I32 1
   = operand: I64 31
   = exact:   2147483648
   = limit:   I32 2147483647
   ...
```

A left shift is a multiply by a power of two, and it is checked the same way. In C, `1 << 31` on a 32-bit `int` is undefined behavior.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**Why checked is the default.** Most arithmetic in a program is not meant to wrap. Making the plain operators checked turns every unintended overflow in a plain operator into a fault at the operation that caused it. Intended wrapping and saturating stay visible as the `%` of `+%` and the `|` of `+|`.

**Bitwise operators** `&`, `|` and `^` take two integers of one type, and `~` takes one. Unlike the operands of these, a shift's count can be of another integer type. `h ^ (bytes[i] as U32)` converts the byte first, because cint does not convert implicitly.

**`in U8[n] bytes`** is a read-only view of `n` bytes, and `n` is a size parameter filled in at the call. A string literal passed to it is viewed as its bytes.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. Write a 64-bit FNV-1a with offset 14695981039346656037 and prime 1099511628211. What does it give for "hello"?
2. Darken the pixels by 40 with `-|`. What do the first two become?

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-04: division and rounding This is lesson 201-04 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will split a bill so the parts add up to the cent, and name the rounding rule wherever a result is not a whole number.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run bill.ci
bill 100.00, tip 18.00, total 118.00
person 1 pays 39.34
person 2 pays 39.33
person 3 pays 39.33
```

The three shares add up to 118.00 exactly. The cent that does not divide evenly goes to the first person, and the program says so in one line.

chunks.title: division in cint
`muldiv`
chunks.content:
## `muldiv`

`muldiv(I64, bill, 18, 100, half_even)` computes `bill * 18 / 100` with the product held exactly, rounds the quotient once by the mode and checks that the result fits `I64`. Writing `bill * 18 / 100` instead would round down and would fault if the product overflows even when the final result fits.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The same division and the same ties were evaluated in other languages on 2026-10-10:

| Language | `-7 / 2` | `-7 % 2` | rounding -3.5 | rounding 2.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cint | -4 | 1 | named: `half_even` gives -4, `half_up` gives -3 | named |
| C, GCC 13.3 | -3 | -1 | `round(-3.5)` is -4, `rint(-3.5)` is -4 | `round(2.5)` is 3, `rint(2.5)` is 2 |
| Python 3.13 | `-7 // 2` is -4 | 1 | `round(-3.5)` is -4 | `round(2.5)` is 2 |
| JavaScript, Node 22.22.0 | `Math.trunc(-7 / 2)` is -3 | -1 | `Math.round(-3.5)` is -3 | `Math.round(2.5)` is 3 |

Python's `round` rounds ties to even, and JavaScript's `Math.round` rounds them up. C's `round` rounds them away from zero, while `rint` follows a rounding mode set elsewhere in the program, by default to even. None of them names its rule at the call. In cint, a `div_round` or `muldiv` call carries the rule.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**Money in cents.** The bill is 10000 cents, an `I64`. Every amount stays an exact whole number of cents, and the only rounding, the tip's, is named in the call.

**`{bill:/100}`** prints a value divided by 100 with two decimal places: 10000 prints as `100.00`. Only the printing divides; the value is unchanged.

**The leftover cent.** `total % people` is 1, so one person pays one more cent. Any rule for who pays it is fine, as long as the program states it and the shares add up.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. Split 100.00 seven ways. How many people pay an extra cent?
2. Make the tip 15 percent of 99.99. Round it with `half_even`, then with `floor`, then with `ceil`. Which ones differ?

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-05: tests and goldens This is lesson 201-05 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will write tests beside the code they check and save a golden of a run you have checked. Then you will see which mistakes each one catches.*

chunks.title: the program
run it, then test it
chunks.content:
## run it, then test it

```text
$ cint run split.ci
bill 100.00, tip 18.00, total 118.00
person 1 pays 39.34
person 2 pays 39.33
person 3 pays 39.33
$ cint test split.ci
test split.ci:27 "the shares add up to the total" ... ok
test split.ci:37 "a tip of half a cent rounds to even" ... ok
test split.ci:42 "nobody to split among is a fault" ... ok
3 of 3 tests passed
```

`cint run` runs `main` and ignores the tests. `cint test` runs each test and ignores `main`.

chunks.title: tests
chunks.content:
## tests

A `test` block is a function with a name in quotes and no parameters, written in the same file as the code it checks. Each test starts from the program's initial state, so one test cannot change what another sees.

- **`assert(condition)`** stops the test with a fault when the condition is false.
- **`expect_fault CODE`** after the name turns the test around: it passes only when its body faults with that code. The third test passes because `share(100, 0, 1)` divides by zero.

Change `tip` to the plain division `return bill * 18 / 100;` and test again:

```text
$ cint test split.ci
test split.ci:27 "the shares add up to the total" ... ok
test split.ci:37 "a tip of half a cent rounds to even" ... FAILED
fault[E_ASSERT]: assertion failed
  --> split.ci:39:12
   |
39 |     assert(tip(75) == 14);      // 13.5 cents rounds to 14
   |            ^ assert.checked.bool
   |
   = operation: assert.checked.bool
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 13
   = operand: I64 14
   ...
test split.ci:42 "nobody to split among is a fault" ... ok
2 of 3 tests passed
```

A failed assertion is a fault, with a fault report like any other. For a comparison, its two operands are the values of the two sides: `tip(75)` returned 13 where the test wanted 14. The first assertion in the same test still passed, because 4.5 rounds down to 4 under both rules. `cint test` exits with status 3 when a test fails, so a script or a build can stop on it.

chunks.title: goldens
chunks.content:
## goldens

A test checks a case you chose. A **golden** checks a whole run: it is the saved output of a run that you checked by hand, and every run after it must match it byte for byte. Three rules govern a golden:

1. Check the output by hand before you save it.
2. Never edit a golden by hand.
3. When a change is meant to alter the output, check the new output by hand. Save it as the new golden in a separate step, so the change and the new golden stay apart.

cint supports two kinds of golden.

chunks.title: the output of a run
chunks.content:
### the output of a run

The output of `cint run`, saved to a file, is the simplest golden:

```text
$ cint run split.ci > split.golden
```

After a change, run again into another file and compare the two. A difference shows exactly which lines changed; [401-01](../401/01-ledger.md) works through an example.

In Windows PowerShell, `>` saves text in a different encoding from the one cint writes. Both files are saved the same way, so VS Code's **Select for Compare** still shows the lines that differ, and `fc.exe /b split.golden after.txt` still says whether the files match. Type `fc.exe` in full, since `fc` alone is the PowerShell alias for `Format-Custom`.

chunks.title: the reference's record
chunks.content:
### the reference's record

The reference, the Python program that defines what every cint program means, writes a record of a run. It is in the `ref` folder of the cint source. Point Python at that folder once per terminal, replacing `SOURCE` with the folder you unpacked cint into:

On macOS and Linux, type this:

```text
$ export PYTHONPATH="SOURCE/ref"
```

In Windows PowerShell, type this:

```text
PS> $env:PYTHONPATH = "SOURCE\ref"
```

Then save the record:

```text
$ python3 -m cint_ref run split.ci > split.expect
$ cat split.expect
case split
source reference
outcome value
stdout-bytes 97
stdout-sha256 266f03fdb752d2d04bc11f2ee54c21d60e281857c78c96ccaa0fadd181a1b439
fuel-consumed 9
```

In Windows PowerShell, write the first command of that block as `cmd /c "python -m cint_ref run split.ci > split.expect"`, so the record is saved byte for byte.

The record holds how the run ended (`outcome value`: it finished) and the size and SHA-256 digest of everything it printed. It also holds `fuel-consumed`, a count charged at each call and at each pass through a loop, which comes out the same on the reference and on the compilers. For a run that faults, the record also holds every field of the fault report. `check` runs the program again and compares:

```text
$ python3 -m cint_ref check split.ci split.expect
$ echo $?
0
```

Silence and status 0 mean the run matches the record. In PowerShell, `$LASTEXITCODE` shows the status.

chunks.title: a change only the record notices
chunks.content:
## a change only the record notices

Now compute the tip once and keep it in a variable. This change keeps the output the same but removes a call.

```ci
    I64 t = tip(bill);
    I64 total = bill + t;
    I64 people = 3;
    "bill {bill:/100}, tip {t:/100}, total {total:/100}\n";
```

Run it and compare with `split.golden`: the files match. The record disagrees:

```text
$ python3 -m cint_ref check split.ci split.expect
split.expect: line 6 differs
  expected: fuel-consumed 9
  actual:   fuel-consumed 8
```

The output is the same, byte for byte, but the fuel is 1 lower, because `tip` is called once instead of twice. A change in fuel means the program took a different path. Here a new path was the point of the change, so the record is out of date: check the output, then save a new record in a step of its own. When you did not mean to change the path, the same line warns that the program now takes a different path.

chunks.title: which to use
chunks.content:
## which to use

| | Catches | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| A test | a wrong answer for a case you chose: an edge, a tie, a fault | which assertion failed, with both sides |
| The output of a run | any change in what the program prints | which lines changed |
| The reference's record | any change in the output, in how the run ended, in a field of a fault or in the path it took | the first line of the record that differs |

A program you intend to keep has tests for its hard cases and a golden of its main run, and both live beside it in version control.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

Saved-output tests exist in most languages, as golden files, snapshot tests or approval tests. They are harder to keep where output is not the same from run to run. On 2026-10-10, running `python3 -c "print({'apple', 'banana', 'cherry'})"` five times with Python 3.13 on Ubuntu 24.04 printed the set in four different orders, because Python changes how it hashes strings each time it starts. A cint program has no such source of variation. One program, built by one release, prints the same bytes on every run and with each of the four C compilers used to check these lessons.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`for people in 1..=12`** inside a test checks twelve cases in one test. A test is ordinary code, so loops and helper functions work in it.

**`paid`, not `sum`.** `sum` is a built-in function, and a local variable cannot take its name; the compiler says `error[C3001]: duplicate name`. `count`, `min` and `max` are taken the same way.

**`_ = share(100, 0, 1);`** calls the function and discards its result. The test exists only for the fault.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. Add a test that splitting 1 cent among 3 people gives 1, 0 and 0.
2. Change `main` to split among 4 people. Which goldens fail, and what does each one show?
3. Save a record of a run that faults: set `bill` to `I64.max` in `main` and run the reference. Which fields does the record add, and which line of the program does it name?

chunks.content:

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-06: the workbench This is lesson 201-06 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will open a session on a module and ask it questions. Then you will run a year of interest in one command. You will find the first day the balance reached 1040.00 and walk through the operations of an entry that faulted.* This lesson needs cint on your own computer, with the debugging tools from [setup](../setup.md).

chunks.title: the module
open a session
chunks.content:
## open a session

In VS Code, open the folder that holds `savings.ci` and choose **Terminal > New Terminal**. Any other terminal in that folder works the same way. Type:

```text
$ cint workbench savings.ci
cint workbench   profile cint-core-1   backend cpu-sir-interp   new session
loaded savings (savings.ci)
ci[2]>
```

`cint repl` opens the same session. The first line says where entries run: `cpu-sir-interp` is the interpreter. The prompt counts **entries**, the things you type that run; loading the module was entry 1.

chunks.title: ask it questions
chunks.content:
## ask it questions

Type an expression and the workbench answers with its exact value and its type:

```text
ci[2]> savings.balance
= 100000 : I64
ci[3]> :inspect savings.balance /scale 100
savings.balance : I64   shown with scale 100
  exact   1000.0
  raw     100000
ci[3]> savings.daily_interest(1, 2)
error[C3008]: undefined or unusable name
  --> entry 3:1:9
   |
 1 | savings.daily_interest(1, 2)
   |         ^
   |
ci[4]>
```

- A name from the module is written with the module's name in front: `savings.balance`.
- A line that starts with a colon is a **command**. Commands are not entries, so the count stays at 3. `:inspect` shows a value in other forms. `/scale 100` divides it by 100, so cents read as dollars, and `/all` adds hexadecimal, binary and the bytes in memory.
- The session sees only what the module exports. `daily_interest` is not exported, so the third entry is an error, and an entry with an error still counts. A position inside an entry reads `entry 3:1:9`: entry 3, line 1, character 9.

chunks.title: run a year
chunks.content:
## run a year

A statement changes the module's state. Save the state first, then pay one day of interest:

```text
ci[4]> :checkpoint start
checkpoint start   #1   revisions: savings@r1
ci[4]> savings.day(450);
ci[5]> savings.balance
= 100012 : I64
```

A **checkpoint** is a saved copy of the state, under a name you choose, and `#1` is its number. `savings@r1` names the revision of the module it holds. Each time a module's code changes in a session, its revision number goes up. One day at 4.50 percent adds 12 cents.

To run the other 364 days, declare a function in the session and run it with `:run`:

```text
ci[6]> export void d() { savings.day(450); }
d : () -> void   revision session@r1
ci[7]> :run d() 364
ci[371]> savings.balance
= 104629 : I64
ci[372]> :checkpoint year
checkpoint year   #2   revisions: session@r1, savings@r1
```

`:run` calls an exported function of the session, here `d`, as many times as you say, and each call is one entry. The session's own code has revisions too, so `d` is `session@r1`. The year ends at 1046.29. Day 1 was entry 4, and days 2 to 365 are entries 7 to 370, so from day 2 on, the entry number is 5 more than the day.

chunks.title: compare two states
chunks.content:
## compare two states

`:diff` compares the current state with a checkpoint, one name at a time:

```text
ci[372]> :diff start
binding           status      differing   first canonical difference
savings.balance   differs     1           104629 here, 100000 in start
```

A **binding** is a name with its value. Only `balance` changed.

chunks.title: find the first day
chunks.content:
## find the first day

To find the day the balance first reached 1040.00, run `:replay` with `--when`:

```text
ci[372]> :replay start --when savings.balance >= 104_000
savings.balance >= 104_000 first holds at entry 322
bisection: 11 probes over 367 boundaries; PRED is taken as monotone
```

Entry 322 is day 317. A **boundary** is the point after an entry, where the workbench can compare or test the state, and there are 367 of them since `start`. The workbench did not test the condition at every one. It replayed from the checkpoint to the middle, tested there and halved the range, 11 probes in all. This is called bisection. It works only when the condition stays true once it holds. That is what `PRED is taken as monotone` means. Here it does, because the balance only grows. For a condition that can turn false again, the answer may not be the first entry where it holds.

chunks.title: a fault in the session
chunks.content:
## a fault in the session

Put the balance near the largest `I64` and pay a day of interest:

```text
ci[372]> savings.balance = I64.max - 100;
ci[373]> savings.day(450);
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> savings.ci:11:13
   |
11 |     balance += daily_interest(balance, basis_points);
   |             ^ add.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 9223372036854775707
   = operand: I64 1137128059338260
   = exact:   9224509164914113967
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   = revision: 03b315aa3c24f675b5fd489839960d132c9a000f478a1cb8310eee016fb5609f
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: entry 373:1:9
   = fuel-consumed: 3 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: no store completed in this entry; context reset
   = noncanonical: not part of the fault record
   = stack-source: entry 373:1:9
   |
 1 | savings.day(450);
   |         ^
   |
   = workbench-position: entry 373
   = site: day#5
   = backend: cpu-sir-interp
ci[374]> savings.balance
= 9223372036854775707 : I64
```

This is the layout that `cint run` prints. The lines from `operation` to `stack-depth` are the fault record, and every way of running the program reports the same values in them. The lines after `= noncanonical` are not part of the record. They say where the workbench found the fault: the source of each call, the entry, the operation's place in `day` and where the entry ran.

The interest was computed, but adding it to the balance went past the limit. `no store completed in this entry` means the entry changed nothing: `balance` still holds the value from before it. `context reset` means the session cleared the fault so that the next entry can run.

chunks.title: a fault in the session (part 2)
chunks.content:
`:trace` replays an entry and lists every counted operation it made, in order. `:trace fault` picks the last entry that faulted:

```text
ci[375]> :trace fault
entry 373   savings.day(450);   evaluator cpu-sir-interp, by replay
  ord  position           operation              operands                 value
    0  entry 373:1:9      call                   450
    1  savings.ci:11:16   call                   9223372036854775707, 450
    2  savings.ci:6:52    mul.checked.i64        10000, 365               3650000
    3  savings.ci:6:12    muldiv.checked.i64.i64.half_even 9223372036854775707, 450, 3650000 1137128059338260
    -  savings.ci:11:16   return                                          1137128059338260
    4  savings.ci:11:13   add.checked.i64        9223372036854775707, 1137128059338260 E_OVERFLOW
```

Read it from the top: the call to `day`, the call to `daily_interest`, the multiplication `10_000 * 365`, the `muldiv`, the return and the addition that faulted. Each row holds the operands the operation saw and the value it gave. The row marked `-` is the return, which is listed but not counted. Every plain operator is checked, including the multiplication `10_000 * 365`.

chunks.title: go back
chunks.content:
## go back

`:restore` makes a checkpoint the current state again:

```text
ci[375]> :restore year
saved current state as auto-1
restored year   #2
ci[375]> savings.balance
= 104629 : I64
```

Before it restores `year`, the workbench saves the current state as a checkpoint named `auto-1`, which you can restore in turn.

`:undo` goes back one entry:

```text
ci[376]> savings.balance = 0;
ci[377]> :undo
saved current state as auto-2
back to the state before entry 376
ci[377]> savings.balance
= 104629 : I64
```

chunks.title: check the interpreter against C
chunks.content:
## check the interpreter against C

The session runs entries in the interpreter. `--check cpu-c17` runs each call a second time in your C compiler's build of the module and compares the two:

```text
ci[378]> :run d() 3 --check cpu-c17
check: cpu-sir-interp and cpu-c17 agree at 3 boundaries
ci[381]> savings.balance
= 104668 : I64
```

After each of the 3 calls, the interpreter and the compiled C held the same state. The first `--check` of a module also prints a line as it builds the module with your C compiler, and later sessions reuse that build. If they ever differ, `:run` stops at the first call where they do. Such a difference is a defect in cint. Report it with the session.

chunks.title: go to any entry
chunks.content:
## go to any entry

`:goto` makes the state at the end of any entry current, by replay:

```text
ci[382]> :goto 322
saved current state as auto-3
at the end of entry 322, reached by replay
later entries go on branch entry-322, from auto-4
ci[382]> savings.balance
= 104005 : I64
ci[383]> :goto 321
saved current state as auto-5
at the end of entry 321, reached by replay
later entries go on branch entry-321, from auto-6
ci[383]> savings.balance
= 103992 : I64
```

At the end of day 316 the balance was 1039.92, and at the end of day 317 it was 1040.05, which agrees with the answer of `--when`. Each `:goto` saves two checkpoints: the state you left, as `auto-3`, and the state it reached, as `auto-4`. An entry typed now starts a **branch**, a second line of entries from this point, and the entries of the year stay as they were. Entry numbers keep counting across branches, so the prompt still says 382. `:goto fault` goes to the end of the last entry that faulted.

To leave, type `:quit --yes`. A plain `:quit` warns you first, because an unsaved session is lost when it ends. A second `:quit` ends it. `:save FOLDER` keeps a session to reopen with `:open FOLDER`.

chunks.title: why it can go back
chunks.content:
## why it can go back

Every entry gives the same result each time it runs: the same values, the same output, the same fault at the same operation. The workbench therefore does not record what the machine did. It keeps the checkpoints and the entries typed since, and it reaches any point by replaying from the nearest checkpoint. The checks in this lesson rest on the same fact: replaying entry 373 for `:trace` faulted at the same operation with the same operands, and so will every replay of it.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

In C, going back takes a debugger that records the run as it goes, such as GDB's `record` command, rr on Linux or Time Travel Debugging in WinDbg on Windows. GDB's `checkpoint` command can also save a copy of the running process to return to. Python's debugger, pdb, has no way to run backward.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`export void d() { savings.day(450); }`** is declared in the session, not in `savings.ci`. The session is a module of its own, and `:run` calls its exports.

**`10_000 * 365`** turns a yearly rate into one day's interest. A rate in basis points is a share of 10,000, and a year has 365 days, so `muldiv` multiplies the balance by the rate and divides by both at once. It rounds a tie to even and cannot overflow in between.

**`I64.max - 100`** is 9223372036854775707, the largest `I64` less 100.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. After `:run d() 364`, ask `:replay start --changed savings.balance`, which names the last entry since `start` that changed `balance`. Which entry does it name, and why that one?
2. Find the first day the balance reaches 1045.00, then check it with two `:goto` commands.
3. Type `:restore start`, declare `d` again with 9000 basis points (90 percent a year) and run it 365 times. The year at 4.50 percent gained 46.29. Is the gain at 90 percent more or less than twenty times that, and why?

chunks.title: reference
chunks.content:
## reference

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-07: debugging by comparison This is lesson 201-07 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will compare runs to find a bug. You will make one change at a time against a golden, read two fault reports side by side and check three ways of running one program against each other.*

chunks.title: the method
chunks.content:
## the method

A cint program run twice by one release prints the same bytes and, when it faults, the same fault report. So a run is a fixed thing you can compare, and a difference between two runs points at a cause. The steps run in this order:

| Step | What you do | With |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reproduce: run the program twice and compare. | `cint run` and `diff` |
| 2 | Keep a golden of a run you checked. | the output, and the reference's record ([201-05](05-tests-and-goldens.md)) |
| 3 | Change one thing, run again and compare with the golden. | `diff` |
| 4 | Read the first difference; the ones after it often follow from it. | `diff` |
| 5 | Read two fault reports as data. | the fault report |
| 6 | Read the lines that identify the run: `revision` and `fuel-consumed`. | the fault report and the record |
| 7 | Check that the ways of running the program agree. | `cint run`, `cint debug` and the reference |
| 8 | Locate the operation that faulted and keep the case. | `cint debug locate --save-case` |

When the code is a module, the workbench of [201-06](06-workbench.md) adds rewinding and bisection to steps 4 and 8.

chunks.title: the program
steps 1 and 2: reproduce, then keep a golden
chunks.content:
## steps 1 and 2: reproduce, then keep a golden

```text
$ cint run adler.ci > run1.txt
$ cint run adler.ci > run2.txt
$ diff run1.txt run2.txt
$ cint run adler.ci > golden.txt
$ python3 -m cint_ref run adler.ci > adler.expect
```

`diff` prints nothing: the two runs are the same, byte for byte. If two runs of one program by one release ever differ, that is a defect in cint. Check the three values by hand, here against zlib, and save the golden and the reference's record. In PowerShell on Windows, compare the two files with `fc.exe /b run1.txt run2.txt`, which says `no differences encountered` when they match. Save the record with `cmd /c`, as in [201-05](05-tests-and-goldens.md). Type `fc.exe` in full, since `fc` alone is the PowerShell alias for `Format-Custom`. To see which lines differ, use VS Code's **Select for Compare**, as in [401-01](../401/01-ledger.md).

chunks.title: step 3: one change
step 4: a second change, and the first difference
chunks.content:
## step 4: a second change, and the first difference

Now raise `BLOCK` to `8_192` and leave the comment as it was. Run and compare again:

```text
$ cint run adler.ci > after.txt
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> adler.ci:20:15
   |
20 |             b += a;
   |               ^ add.checked.u32
   |
   = operation: add.checked.u32
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: U32 4294283833
   = operand: U32 1480021
   = exact:   4295763854
   = limit:   U32 4294967295
   = revision: 4d94cdfe0404d5729f9866a699d45a763db38646e80ce3f71a1a3132eb1b6099
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: adler.ci:40:13
   = fuel-consumed: 45822 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
$ diff golden.txt after.txt
3d2
< 20000 x 255   9f51d664
```

The fault report appears in the terminal and not in `after.txt`, because cint writes it to a separate stream, standard error. The output stops after line 2, so the first difference is line 3: the third message never finished. The report says why. Adding `a` to `b` at line 20 went past the largest `U32`, 4294967295, while the call at line 40 computed the checksum of the third message.

The operands say where in the message. `a` started at 1 and grows by 255 with each byte, so `a` = 1480021 = 1 + 255 × 5804: the sum broke on byte 5804 of the third message, in its first block. A block of 8192 bytes of 255 is more than `b` can hold.

chunks.title: step 5: two fault reports as data
chunks.content:
## step 5: two fault reports as data

Change the third message to 20,000 bytes of 200 (`high[i] = 200;`) and run again. The report starts the same way:

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> adler.ci:20:15
   |
20 |             b += a;
   |               ^ add.checked.u32
   |
   = operation: add.checked.u32
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: U32 4294842753
   = operand: U32 1310801
   = exact:   4296153554
   ...
```

The code, the operation and the position are the same, and the operands are new. Now `a` = 1310801 = 1 + 200 × 6554, so the smaller bytes took 6554 of them to break the sum. Read two reports this way:

| Two reports with | Mean |
|---|---|
| the same code, operation, position and operands | the same fault, reproduced |
| the same position and new operands | the same bug, reached by new data |
| a new position | a new fault, to read on its own |

Put the 255 back.

chunks.title: step 6: the lines that identify a run
chunks.content:
## step 6: the lines that identify a run

Add a comment line at the top of `adler.ci` and run again:

```text
  --> adler.ci:21:15
   ...
   = revision: 4d94cdfe0404d5729f9866a699d45a763db38646e80ce3f71a1a3132eb1b6099
   ...
   = called from: adler.ci:41:13
   = fuel-consumed: 45822 (not part of the fault record)
```

Every position moved down one line, and the `revision` stayed the same. The revision is a digest of the compiled program. A comment or a blank line does not change it, while renaming a variable or changing a value does. The module's name is part of it too, so keep editing `adler.ci` instead of saving copies under new names. When a report moves, the revision says whether the code changed or only moved. The fuel is the same too: the run took the same path to the same fault.

chunks.title: step 7: three ways to run it
chunks.content:
## step 7: three ways to run it

`cint run` compiles the program to C and runs it with your C compiler. `cint debug locate`, in step 8, runs it in the interpreter. The reference runs it in Python. All three must agree, and here they do. This is the reference's record of the faulting run:

```text
$ python3 -m cint_ref run adler.ci > fault.expect
$ cat fault.expect
case adler
source reference
outcome fault
stdout-bytes 46
stdout-sha256 5f8d699b8acfd3a2c790a21a2df45c68e91fab8e3482b95125864a5490a056b5
fuel-consumed 45822
fault.code E_OVERFLOW
fault.operation add.checked.u32
fault.operand U32 4294283833
fault.operand U32 1480021
fault.exact 4295763854
fault.limit U32 4294967295
fault.position adler.ci:20:15
fault.revision self
fault.address none
fault.stack-depth 1
```

It holds the same code, operation, operands, position and fuel as the compiled run. The reference writes `self` where the compiled run prints the revision's digest. If two of the three ever disagree, the program is not the problem: that is a defect in cint, and the case of step 8 is what to report.

For code you run in the workbench, `cint debug diff` makes the same check from the terminal. It takes a case of calls to exported functions, like one saved in a session, and refuses a case of a whole program such as `overflow.case`. In the session of 201-06, `:checkpoint s`, then `:run d() 3`, then `:save-case three.case` saves the three calls as a case. `cint debug diff` runs it in your C compiler's build and in the interpreter and compares the two after every entry:

```text
$ cint debug diff three.case
case       three.case   3 boundaries   density entry
reference  cpu-c17
candidate  cpu-sir-interp
boundaries 3 of 3 compared
outcome    agree
```

chunks.title: step 7: three ways to run it (part 2)
chunks.content: In this output, `reference` names the side the other is compared against, here the C build, and not the Python reference. `cint debug diff` exits with status 0 when the two agree and 3 when they do not.

chunks.title: step 8: locate the operation and keep the case
chunks.content:
## step 8: locate the operation and keep the case

`cint debug locate` runs the program in the interpreter, replays it to the fault and lists the last operations before it. `--save-case` keeps the run. The first lines say what it searched. A whole program is one entry, so its run has one boundary, at its end, and the fault is there. The count of trace events is every operation the interpreter replayed, and the workbench's `:trace` lists them all.

```text
$ cint debug locate adler.ci --save-case overflow.case
program    adler.ci   evaluator cpu-sir-interp, recorded as the case overflow.case
target     boundary 1 of 1, the program entry: the first fault, reproduced by replay
bracket    the initial state; then boundary 1
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> adler.ci:20:15
   ...
the last 20 counted operations of boundary 1, of 189084 trace events (:trace shows them all)
  ord  position           operation              operands                 value
   ...
189072                     add.wrap.i64           5801, 1                  5802
189073  adler.ci:19:22     index.checked.u8       5802
189074  adler.ci:19:26     as.checked.u8.u32      255                      255
189075  adler.ci:19:15     add.checked.u32        1479511, 255             1479766
189076  adler.ci:20:15     add.checked.u32        4292804067, 1479766      4294283833
189077                     add.wrap.i64           5802, 1                  5803
189078  adler.ci:19:22     index.checked.u8       5803
189079  adler.ci:19:26     as.checked.u8.u32      255                      255
189080  adler.ci:19:15     add.checked.u32        1479766, 255             1480021
189081  adler.ci:20:15     add.checked.u32        4294283833, 1480021      E_OVERFLOW
```

chunks.title: step 8: locate the operation and keep the case (part 2)
chunks.content:
Each byte is five rows. The loop counts `i` up by one in the rows with no position. Then it reads `data[i]`, widens it to `U32` and adds it to `a`, and last it adds `a` to `b`. `b` climbs toward the limit, 4292804067, then 4294283833, and the next addition faults. The index is 5803, counted from 0, which is byte 5804, as step 4 worked out from the operands.

`overflow.case` holds the program's source and its run. Copy it to another folder and `cint debug locate overflow.case` reproduces the same fault from the case alone, without `adler.ci`. It is the file to attach to a bug report.

chunks.title: the fix
chunks.content:
## the fix

Put `BLOCK` back to `5_552`, run and compare with the golden: the output matches. zlib's source gives 5_552 as the largest block length *n* for which 255*n*(*n* + 1)/2 + (*n* + 1)(65,521 - 1) is at most 2<sup>32</sup> - 1. The expression is the largest `b` can reach after a block of bytes of 255 when `a` and `b` start just below 65,521.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The same function in C, with `uint32_t` sums and a block of 8192, built with GCC 13.3 and `-O2 -Wall -Wextra` on Ubuntu 24.04 for x86-64, gives no warning and exits with status 0. It prints `9caed664` for the third message where Adler-32 is `9f51d664`, because `uint32_t` arithmetic wraps. Clang has a check for this, `-fsanitize=unsigned-integer-overflow`, which is off unless a build turns it on. Built with Clang 18.1 and that check in its trapping form, the program stopped at the third message. Without such a check, only a golden or a test against a known value catches the wrong checksum. Written in Python, the same function gives the right checksum with a block of any size, because Python's integers have no fixed size.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`data[i] as U32`** widens a byte to `U32`. Widening never fails, and the trace shows it as its own operation, `as.checked.u8.u32`.

**`(b << 16) | a`** puts `b` in the top 16 bits and `a` in the bottom 16. Both are below 65,521 at this point, so the shift cannot overflow.

**`while (start < n)`** walks the data a block at a time. The `if` shortens the last block, so `end` never passes `n`.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. With `BLOCK` at `8_192`, change `b += a;` to `b +%= a;`, which wraps as C does. The program runs to the end. Which line of the golden differs, and which line of the record?
2. Find the largest `BLOCK` for which this program runs without a fault. Is it safe for every message? Compare it with 5552.
3. Run `cint debug locate` on the version with bytes of 200 and compare its last operations with the version with 255.
