chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-08: control flow This is lesson 201-08 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will write cint's loops and branches and see where they differ from C: braces are required, `switch` never falls through by accident and a loop counter faults instead of wrapping.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run collatz.ci
   1 takes 0 steps
  10 takes 6 steps
 100 takes 25 steps
1000 takes 111 steps
below 1000: 133 quick, 618 middling, 248 slow
first past 100000: 703, first goes over 100000 at 148444
```

The same rule written in Python 3.13 on Ubuntu 24.04 prints the same six lines.

chunks.title: `if` and `while`
two kinds of `for`
chunks.content:
## two kinds of `for`

The range form counts through a range of `I64` values:

- `for i in 0..n` runs `i` from 0 up to n - 1.
- `for i in 1..=n` runs `i` from 1 up to n, including n.

The bounds are computed once, before the first pass, and the body cannot assign to `i` (error C2052). An empty range, such as `5..5`, runs the body no times. cint 0.2.0 does not support a step on the range form, so any other step needs the C form:

```ci
for (I64 start = 1; start <= 1_000; start *= 10) {
```

The C form has the three parts C has: a declaration, a condition and an update. The update can be any statement without a block, such as `start *= 10`. Its variable can be assigned in the body.

Because `++` is checked, a C-form loop cannot run past the end of its type:

```ci
void main() {
    I64 steps = 0;
    for (I8 i = 0; i <= 127; i++) {
        steps++;
    }
    "{steps}\n";
}
```

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> i8loop.ci:3:31
   |
 3 |     for (I8 i = 0; i <= 127; i++) {
   |                               ^ add.checked.i8
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i8
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I8 127
   = operand: I8 1
   = exact:   128
   = limit:   I8 127
   ...
```

`i <= 127` is always true for an `I8`, so this loop can never end on its condition. In cint it faults when `i++` tries to step past 127, after 128 passes.

chunks.title: `switch`
labels
chunks.content:
## labels

To leave more than one loop at once, label the outer loop and name the label:

```ci
starts: for start in 1..1_000 {
    ...
            break starts;
```

`break starts;` leaves the `for` loop and the `while` loop inside it, so the search stops at 703. `continue starts;` would go on to the next start. Without a label, `break` and `continue` apply to the innermost loop. cint has no `goto`.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The same `int8_t` loop in C, built with GCC 13.3 and `-O2 -Wall -Wextra` on Ubuntu 24.04 for x86-64, warns that `i <= 127` is always true. Built with `-Wall` alone it gives no warning. Either way the program ran until it was stopped after 10 seconds, because `i++` wraps to -128 and the condition never fails.

In C, a `case` with no `break` falls into the next one, and missing a `break` is a common mistake. GCC and Clang can warn about it with `-Wimplicit-fallthrough`. In cint, falling through is something you write.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`I64 next(I64 n)`** returns early with `return n / 2;` for an even number, so the last line handles only odd ones.

**`3 * n + 1`** is checked, as every plain operator is. No start below 1000 climbs anywhere near the limit of `I64`, but a path that did would fault instead of wrapping into a wrong path.

**`{start:>4}`** prints `start` right-aligned in four characters, which lines up the first four rows.

**`I64 taken`** cannot be named `count`, because `count` is a built-in function and a local variable cannot take its name.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. Change the first loop to start at 1 and multiply by 3 up to 2187. How many steps does 2187 take?
2. Change the `switch` so that starts taking exactly 111 steps count in a fourth counter. Does it matter where the new case goes? Why?
3. Change `break starts;` to `break;`. What does the program print now, and why?

chunks.title: CU-201.2
chunks.content: # 201-09: functions This is lesson 201-09 of CU-201.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will pass numbers and arrays to functions, write a recursive function, read the call stack in a fault report and meet the limit on how deep calls can go.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run harmonic.ci
gcd(1071, 462) = 21
H(10) = 7381/2520
H(20) = 55835135/15519504
H(30) = 9304682830147/2329089562800
H(40) = 2078178381193813/485721041551200
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> harmonic.ci:13:20
   |
13 |     I64 num = f[0] * k + f[1];
   |                    ^ mul.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 532145396070491417
   = operand: I64 44
   = exact:   23414397427101622348
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   = revision: 32960ad2bbac044b12ed41dcf78b45746985bc46b3eb99160afef5baf46c7225
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: harmonic.ci:26:9
   = fuel-consumed: 920 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

The four fractions agree with `fractions.Fraction` in Python 3.13 on Ubuntu 24.04. Then the program stopped while adding 1/44.

chunks.title: reading the call stack
chunks.content:
## reading the call stack

The fault happened inside `add_unit`, at line 13. `stack-depth: 1` says one call was in progress below `main`, and `called from: harmonic.ci:26:9` says where it was made: the line `add_unit(h, k);` in `main`. When calls are nested deeper, the report has one `called from` line for each call, starting from the call made in `main`.

The operands tell the rest. The first is the numerator of H(43), 532145396070491417, and the second is 44. Their product, 23414397427101622348, is more than twice the largest `I64`, so `f[0] * k` could not be computed.

chunks.title: parameters
chunks.content:
## parameters

A number passed to a function is copied. When `gcd` calls itself with `gcd(b, a % b)`, its new `a` and `b` are new copies, and the caller's variables are unchanged.

An array is passed as a **view** of the caller's array, with a mode that says what the function may do with it:

- `in I64[2] f` lets the function read the array but not write it; a write is error C2060.
- `inout I64[2] f` lets it read and write the caller's array. `add_unit` writes the new fraction into `h` this way.

A number cannot be passed `inout`: `void exchange(inout I64 a, inout I64 b)` is error C2064. To give back one number, return it. To give back several, pass an array `inout` or return a struct, as lab [401-01](../401/01-ledger.md) does.

A function's name cannot be the name of a built-in function. `swap` is a built-in function, so a function called `swap` is error C3001, like a variable called `sum`.

chunks.title: a smaller way to add
recursion and the depth limit
elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The first version of the program in C, with `int64_t`, built with GCC 13.3 and `-O2 -Wall -Wextra` on Ubuntu 24.04 for x86-64, gave no warning and exited with status 0. Its last line was `H(50) = -396549522021549939/211166340108011552`: a negative sum of positive fractions. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so the C standard places no requirement on what the program does next.

`fractions.Fraction` in Python 3.13 on Ubuntu 24.04 has integers of any size, so it computes H(50) exactly. Python limits recursion instead: `sum_to(100_000)` written in Python stopped with `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`. C has no depth limit of its own. A recursion deep enough to use up the stack can crash the program, unless the compiler turns the recursion into a loop. With GCC 13.3 or Clang 18.1 on the same machine, `sum_to(100000000)` in C crashed with a segmentation fault at `-O0` and printed 5000000050000000 at `-O2`.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`if (b == 0) { return a; }`** is the case that stops the recursion. Every recursive function needs one, and every chain of calls must reach it.

**`I64[2] h;`** declares an array of two numbers, both 0. `h[0] = 0;` changes nothing and is there so the starting fraction reads plainly, and `h[1] = 1;` makes it 0/1.

**`f[1] / gcd(f[1], k) * k`** divides before it multiplies. Written as `f[1] * k / gcd(f[1], k)`, the product would overflow sooner.

**`num` and `den`** are local to each call of `add_unit`, so each call starts with its own `num` and `den`.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. Print every H(k) instead of every tenth one. What is the last harmonic number each version of `add_unit` prints?
2. Write `lcm(a, b)` as a function that calls `gcd`, and use it in `add_unit`.
3. Rewrite `sum_to` with a loop and check that it gives 5050 for 100 and 5000050000 for 100,000.

chunks.title: CU-301.1
chunks.content: # 301-01: when 64 bits are not enough This is lesson 301-01 of CU-301.1, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will watch a product of two 64-bit numbers outgrow `I64`, compute it exactly in `I128` with `mul_full` and meet the integer types that go up to 1024 bits.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run fermat.ci
         1000000007: remainder 1
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> fermat.ci:6:14
   |
 6 |     return a * b % m;
   |              ^ mul.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 4294967296
   = operand: I64 4294967296
   = exact:   18446744073709551616
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   = revision: c9b0d558c225959442c702c2a4e5015ffb1547a735342e30e49711666e8e56f3
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 2
   = called from: fermat.ci:28:30
   = called from: fermat.ci:18:13
   = fuel-consumed: 97 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

The first test passes. For 1000000007, every product of two numbers below it is about 10<sup>18</sup> at most, far below `I64.max`. The second test squares `b` again and again: 2, 4, 16, 256, 65536, 4294967296. The next square is 2<sup>64</sup>, and the fault record shows it as the exact result. A number below 2<sup>61</sup> times another can need up to 122 bits, and `I64` has 63 bits for the value and one for the sign.

chunks.title: the fix: an exact 128-bit product
chunks.content:
## the fix: an exact 128-bit product

`mul_full` multiplies two `I64` values and returns the exact product as an `I128`, which can never overflow. The remainder is then small enough to convert back:

```ci
// a * b % m, for a and b below m, through the exact 128-bit product.
I64 mul_mod(I64 a, I64 b, I64 m) {
    I128 product = mul_full(a, b);
    return (product % (m as I128)) as I64;
}
```

Nothing else in the program changes:

```text
$ cint run fermat.ci
         1000000007: remainder 1
2305843009213693951: remainder 1
2305843009213693953: remainder 4
```

Both primes leave 1. The remainder 4 proves that 2305843009213693953 is not prime, as expected, since 3 divides it. A remainder of 1 does not by itself prove a number prime, because some composite numbers also leave 1. The smallest is 341, which is 11 times 31. Programs that need certainty use a stronger test, such as Miller-Rabin with a fixed set of bases, and it needs this same exact product.

chunks.title: the wide integer types
chunks.content:
## the wide integer types

cint 0.2.0 has signed integers in eight sizes, from `I8` up. This table shows `I64` and the wider ones. Each wider type holds every value of the narrower ones:

| Type | Largest value | Digits in the largest value |
|---|---|---|
| `I64` | 9223372036854775807 | 19 |
| `I128` | 170141183460469231731687303715884105727 | 39 |
| `I256` | 5789604461865809771... | 77 |
| `I512` | 6703903964971298549... | 154 |
| `I1024` | 8988465674311579538... | 308 |

Each `T.max` above was printed by cint. `I128` to `I1024` are called the wide types. They take the same operators as `I64`, and every plain operator on them is checked the same way.

cint 0.2.0 also has the unsigned wide types `U128`, `U256` and `U512`. `mul_full` of two `U64` values gives a `U128`:

```ci
void main() {
    U64 a = U64.max;
    U128 square = mul_full(a, a);
    "{a} squared is {square}\n";
    "U128 runs up to {U128.max}\n";
}
```

```text
18446744073709551615 squared is 340282366920938463426481119284349108225
U128 runs up to 340282366920938463463374607431768211455
```

chunks.title: widths never mix silently
chunks.content:
## widths never mix silently

An `I64` value does not become an `I128` on its own. Each of these lines is refused with error C2001, type mismatch:

```ci
I128 product = a * a;      // a * a is an I64 product, and it may already have overflowed
"{product % m}\n";         // product is I128 and m is I64
```

Convert a value with `as` to widen it. `(a as I128) * (a as I128)` computes the same exact product as `mul_full(a, a)`. Widening never fails, since every `I64` value is an `I128` value.

Narrowing can fail, and `as` checks it. Converting an `I128` that holds 2<sup>63</sup> to `I64` faults:

```text
fault[E_NARROW]: the value does not fit the destination type
  --> narrow.ci:5:11
   |
 5 |     "{big as I64}\n";
   |           ^ as.checked.i128.i64
   |
   = operation: as.checked.i128.i64
   = operand-count: 1
   = operand: I128 9223372036854775808
   = exact:   9223372036854775808
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   ...
```

In `mul_mod`, `(product % (m as I128)) as I64` cannot fault, because a remainder after dividing by m is always less than m, and m is an `I64`.

chunks.title: a wider type moves the edge
chunks.content:
## a wider type moves the edge

`I128` has an edge of its own. Doubling 1 in an `I128` faults at the 127th doubling:

```text
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> over128.ci:4:16
   |
 4 |         grains *= 2;
   |                ^ mul.checked.i128
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i128
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I128 85070591730234615865843651857942052864
   = operand: I128 2
   = exact:   170141183460469231731687303715884105728
   = limit:   I128 170141183460469231731687303715884105727
   ...
```

Pick the narrowest type that holds every value the program can reach, as `mul_mod` does: its inputs stay in `I64`, and only the product needs `I128`. A wide value takes more memory and each operation on it does more work.

chunks.title: refused on wide types in 0.2.0
chunks.content:
## refused on wide types in 0.2.0

A few forms that work on `I64` are refused on the wide types in cint 0.2.0, with error C9102, not yet supported:

- A `switch` cannot test a wide value.
- `as?`, the conversion that returns an error instead of faulting, cannot convert from a wide type.
- The built-ins that return an error instead of faulting, such as `add_result`, do not take wide values.
- `muldiv` cannot give a wide result from narrow operands.

In place of a `switch`, compare with `if` and `else if`. In place of the others, convert a value that is known to fit to `I64` first, or widen the operands with `as`.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The same test was written in C with `uint64_t` and `a * b % m`. It was built with GCC 13.3 and with Clang 18.1, using `-O2 -Wall -Wextra` on Ubuntu 24.04 for x86-64. Neither gave a warning, and both builds printed:

```text
         1000000007: remainder 1
2305843009213693951: remainder 0
2305843009213693953: remainder 0
```

Unsigned arithmetic in C wraps without an error, so the products lost their high bits. A remainder of 0 would mean m divides a power of 2, which no odd number above 1 does. The program called a prime composite, and nothing signaled it. Computing the product as `unsigned __int128`, an extension that GCC and Clang provide on 64-bit targets, printed 1, 1 and 4, as cint does.

`__int128` is signed and unchecked. A C program that doubled an `__int128` 128 times, built with the same compilers, printed that the result was zero at `-O0` and positive at `-O2`, with no warning at either. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so the C standard places no requirement on what the program does. C23 adds `_BitInt(N)` for integers of a chosen width. Clang 18.1 built a `_BitInt(256)` program, and GCC 13.3 did not recognize `_BitInt`. GCC's release notes list it as new in GCC 14.

Python's `int` has no fixed size. `pow(2, m - 1, m)` in Python 3.13 on the same machine printed 1, 1 and 4.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`mul_full(a, b)`** takes two values of the same type and returns their exact product in the type twice as wide: `I64` to `I128`, `I128` to `I256`, `I256` to `I512` and `I512` to `I1024`.

**`m as I128`** widens `m` so that `%` has two operands of one type.

**`e % 2 == 1`** tests the lowest bit of the exponent. Repeated squaring multiplies `result` by `b` for each 1 bit, so about 120 multiplications cover an exponent near 2<sup>61</sup>.

**`I64[3] tests`** is declared inside `main`, since an array cannot be declared at the top level of a program in cint 0.2.0.

chunks.title: try this
chunks.content:
## try this

1. Add 9223372036854775783, the largest prime below 2<sup>63</sup>, to `tests` in the version with `mul_full`. The array and the loop then need a length of 4. Does the product still fit, and what does the new line print?
2. Replace `mul_full(a, b)` with `(a as I128) * (b as I128)`. Does any output change?
3. The first version is safe for every m up to some size. What is the largest such m, and why?

<details>
<summary>answer to 3</summary>

Every product in the program multiplies two numbers below m, so the largest is (m - 1)<sup>2</sup>. It fits in an `I64` while m - 1 is at most 3037000499, the integer square root of `I64.max`. So the first version is safe for every m up to 3037000500.
</details>

chunks.title: CU-301.1
chunks.content: # 301-04: big exact numbers This is lesson 301-04 of CU-301.1, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will compute 100 factorial and a binomial coefficient to the last digit in `I1024`, see why each conversion is written where the value is used and find the first factorial that does not fit.*

chunks.title: the program
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run bignum.ci
100! = 93326215443944152681699238856266700490715968264381621468592963895217599993229915608941463976156518286253697920827223758251185210916864000000000000000000000000
100! has 158 digits
52 choose 5 = 2598960
100 choose 50 = 100891344545564193334812497256
170! has 307 digits
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> bignum.ci:7:11
   |
 7 |         f *= k as I1024;
   |           ^ mul.checked.i1024
   |
   = operation: mul.checked.i1024
   = operand-count: 2
   ...
   = operand: I1024 171
   ...
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: bignum.ci:39:23
   = fuel-consumed: 969 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
```

The first `...` stands for three lines that hold numbers of more than 300 digits: `170!`, the exact `171!` and `I1024.max`. The second stands for the revision, source-map and address lines. Each value printed above agrees with `math.factorial` and `math.comb` in Python 3.13 on Ubuntu 24.04, digit for digit.

chunks.title: what happened
chunks.content:
## what happened

**`I1024` holds numbers up to about 8.99 times 10<sup>307</sup>.** `100!` has 158 digits, so it fits. `170!` has 307 digits and still fits. `171!` is 171 times larger, with 310 digits, and the multiplication that makes it faults. The record names the operands, `170!` and 171, both as `I1024` values, and gives the exact product in full.

**The conversion is written at the multiplication.** `f` is an `I1024` and `k` is an `I64`, and cint never mixes two widths on its own. Leave out the conversion and the program is refused before it runs:

```text
error[C2001]: type mismatch
  --> noas.ci:4:14
   |
 4 |         f *= k;
   |              ^
   |
```

`k as I1024` widens `k` at the one place it meets `f`. The conversion is visible on the line where the two widths meet, so a reader does not have to look elsewhere to find it.

**`choose` divides exactly at every step.** After step i, `c` holds (n - k + i) choose i, which is a whole number. So the multiplication comes first, and the division that follows leaves no remainder. Dividing first, as in `c * ((n - k + i) / i)`, would round away part of the answer at most steps.

**`digits` works on a local variable.** A parameter cannot be assigned in cint, so `x /= 10` inside `digits` is error C2060. The function puts `x` into the local `rest` and divides that.

chunks.title: carrying the harmonic sum further
chunks.content:
## carrying the harmonic sum further

Lesson [201-09](../201/09-functions.md) added 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 and so on as an exact fraction in `I64`. Its second version, which adds over the least common denominator, stopped at 1/47, because the denominator of H(47) is 63245806209101973600, too large for `I64`. The second version goes on to 100 with `I256` in place of `I64` in `gcd`, `add_unit` and `h`, and with `k as I256` at the call:

```text
$ cint run harmonic256.ci
H(47) = 280682601097106968469/63245806209101973600
H(100) = 14466636279520351160221518043104131447711/2788815009188499086581352357412492142272
```

The denominator of H(100) has 40 digits. Run on, the same program prints H(170) and faults while adding 1/179, when a denominator times 179 passes `I256.max`.

chunks.title: elsewhere
chunks.content:
## elsewhere

The same factorial loop in C with `double`, built with GCC 13.3 and `-O2 -Wall -Wextra` on Ubuntu 24.04 for x86-64, printed `100!` as a number of 158 digits whose first 15 digits are right. The exact `100!` ends in 24 zeros, and the `double` version ends in 813248. `171!` printed as `inf`. The same `double` loop for 100 choose 50 printed 100891344545564219663900999680, right in its first 15 digits and wrong after them. A `double` holds 53 binary digits, which is about 16 decimal digits, so most larger whole numbers in it are rounded.

Python's `int` grows to any size, so `math.factorial(171)` and much larger values are exact. It has no fault for a value outside a chosen type, because it has no fixed types. In cint the program states a fixed width, and every plain operator is checked against it.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`I1024 factorial(I64 n)`** takes a small count and returns a large value. A function's parameter and return types need not match.

**`f *= k as I1024`** is the same as `f = f * (k as I1024)`. The conversion applies to `k` alone, and the result is then multiplied into `f`, so no parentheses are needed.

**`while (rest > 0)`** compares an `I1024` with the literal 0. The literal takes the type of `rest`, so no conversion is written.

**`{f}`** prints all 158 digits. Printing works the same for every integer type.

chunks.title: CU-401.2
chunks.content: # 401-01: an exact ledger This is lab 401-01 of CU-401.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will keep a bank ledger in whole cents, pay a day of interest rounded by a stated rule, refuse an overdraft as an error and stop on an overflow. Then you will save a checked copy of the ledger's output, called a golden. The golden catches a mistake the tests miss, and the tests catch a mistake the golden misses.* Take it after [201-04](../201/04-division-and-rounding.md). The walk-through explains the parts of the language the program uses that 201-00 to 201-04 do not cover.

chunks.title: the program
the program (part 2)
run it
chunks.content:
## run it

```text
$ cint run ledger.ci
0: deposit    125000 -> 1250.00
1: withdraw    40050 -> 849.50
2: interest      450 -> 849.60
3: rejected, overdrawn
4: deposit        99 -> 850.59
final balance: 850.59
```

One day of interest on 849.50 (84950 cents) at 4.50 percent a year is 84950 × 450 / 3650000 cents, about 10.47 cents. `half_even` rounds it to 10, and the balance becomes 849.60. Entry 3 asks for 2000.00 from a balance of 849.60, so `apply` returns the error `overdrawn`. The loop prints a line and moves on, and the balance does not change.

chunks.title: test it
chunks.content:
## test it

```text
$ cint test ledger.ci
test ledger.ci:71 "interest ties round to even" ... ok
test ledger.ci:76 "an overdraft is an error" ... ok
test ledger.ci:81 "an overflow is a fault" ... ok
3 of 3 tests passed
```

The first test checks two ties, where a rounding rule matters: an exact half cent rounds to the even neighbor, 0, and an exact cent and a half rounds to 2. The third test passes because the deposit faults: `expect_fault E_OVERFLOW` says a fault with that code is the expected result.

chunks.title: errors and faults
chunks.content:
## errors and faults

The ledger has two different ways to fail.

- **An overdraft is an error.** It is something a ledger expects: a customer asks for more than the balance. `apply` returns it as a value of type `LedgerError!I64`, and the caller decides what to do with it, here with `catch`.
- **An overflow is a fault.** A balance past `I64.max`, about 92 quadrillion dollars, means the program is wrong. No caller can catch it. The program stops at the operation and prints a fault report.

chunks.title: keep a golden
chunks.content:
## keep a golden

A *golden* is a saved output that you have checked by hand and that later runs must match byte for byte. The output above is right: you checked the interest and the rejected entry. Save it:

```text
$ cint run ledger.ci > golden.txt
```

Now make a mistake. Change the interest entry's rate from `450` to `45` and run again into a second file:

```text
$ cint run ledger.ci > after.txt
```

Compare the two files. In VS Code, right-click `golden.txt` in the Explorer and choose **Select for Compare**, then right-click `after.txt` and choose **Compare with Selected**. In a terminal on macOS or Linux, use `diff`:

```text
$ diff golden.txt after.txt
3c3
< 2: interest      450 -> 849.60
---
> 2: interest       45 -> 849.51
5,6c5,6
< 4: deposit        99 -> 850.59
< final balance: 850.59
---
> 4: deposit        99 -> 850.50
> final balance: 850.50
```

In PowerShell on Windows, `fc.exe /b golden.txt after.txt` says whether the two files match, and VS Code's compare shows the lines that differ. Type `fc.exe` in full, since `fc` alone means something else in PowerShell.

**Read the first line that differs.** Line 3 is the first difference, and it names entry 2. Every later difference follows from it: the balance after entry 2 is 9 cents short, so every balance after it is too. The first differing line points at the change; the lines after it are consequences.

The tests still pass with the typo, because none of them reads `book`. That is one thing a golden is for: it checks the whole run, including data no test looks at.

Put `450` back and check that the run matches the golden again. `diff` prints nothing when the files are the same.

chunks.title: a mistake only the tests catch
chunks.content:
## a mistake only the tests catch

Now make a different change. Replace the body of `daily_interest` with a plain division that looks as if it does the same thing:

```ci
    return balance * basis_points / (10_000 * 365);
```

Run it and compare with the golden. There is no difference: 10.47 cents rounds down to 10, the same result as rounding to the nearest cent. The tests disagree:

```text
$ cint test ledger.ci
test ledger.ci:71 "interest ties round to even" ... FAILED
fault[E_ASSERT]: assertion failed
  --> ledger.ci:73:12
   |
73 |     assert(daily_interest(5_475_000, 1) == 2);  // exactly 1.5 cents: rounds to 2
   |            ^ assert.checked.bool
   |
   = operation: assert.checked.bool
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 1
   = operand: I64 2
   ...
test ledger.ci:76 "an overdraft is an error" ... ok
test ledger.ci:81 "an overflow is a fault" ... ok
2 of 3 tests passed
```

The two operands are the two sides of the comparison: the function returned 1 where the test wanted 2, because `/` rounds down. A golden holds what one run printed; a test holds a case chosen because it is hard. A program you intend to keep needs both. Put `muldiv` back.

chunks.title: when it faults
chunks.content:
## when it faults

Change the last entry to deposit the largest `I64`:

```ci
    book[4] = Entry(DEPOSIT, I64.max);
```

```text
$ cint run ledger.ci
0: deposit    125000 -> 1250.00
1: withdraw    40050 -> 849.50
2: interest      450 -> 849.60
3: rejected, overdrawn
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> ledger.ci:24:28
   |
24 |             return balance + e.cents;
   |                            ^ add.checked.i64
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i64
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I64 84960
   = operand: I64 9223372036854775807
   = exact:   9223372036854860767
   = limit:   I64 9223372036854775807
   ...
   = stack-depth: 1
   = called from: ledger.ci:56:20
```

The four lines before the fault are the program's output up to that point. The fault report goes to standard error, not standard output, so `cint run ledger.ci > after.txt` saves the four lines and the report still appears in the terminal. `cint run` exits with status 1.

Run it again. With the same cint release, the report is the same, byte for byte, every time and on every computer: the same operation, the same operands and the same line. That makes a fault report a golden too. Save it and fix the program. When a fault comes back after a later change, compare the new report with the saved one to see whether it is the same fault or a new one. [201-07](../201/07-debugging-by-comparison.md) builds this into a method.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`const U8 DEPOSIT = 0;`** gives each kind of entry a name with a type. `switch (e.kind)` matches against the names, and `default` takes any other value, which `apply` returns as `unknown_kind`.

**`Entry[5] book;`** declares five entries, all zero, and the lines after it fill them in.

**`catch (err) { ... continue; }`** handles the error where `apply` is called. `err` holds which error it was, and the `switch` prints a line for each. `continue` goes on to the next entry, so the line `I64 next = ...` never completes for a rejected entry.

**`apply(100, Entry(WITHDRAW, 101)) catch -1`** is the short form: if `apply` returns an error, the whole expression is -1.

**`{e.cents:>8}`** prints the amount right-aligned in 8 characters, and **`{balance:/100}`** prints cents as dollars with two decimal places.

**A basis point is a hundredth of a percent.** That makes 450 basis points 4.50 percent. Dividing by 10,000 turns basis points into a fraction, and by 365 a yearly rate into a daily one. `muldiv` multiplies before it divides, holds the product exactly and rounds once.

chunks.title: extend it
chunks.content:
## extend it

1. Add a `FEE` kind that takes a fixed 2.50 from the balance and is refused as `overdrawn` when the balance is smaller. Save a new golden only after you have checked the new output by hand.
2. Add a test for a withdrawal of exactly the balance. Should it be accepted?
3. Pay 365 days of interest on 1000.00 at 4.50 percent, compounding daily, and print the balance at the end. Then round each day with `floor` instead of `half_even`. How much less does the account earn in a year?

chunks.title: CU-401.2
chunks.content: # 401-02: hunting an overflow This is lab 401-02 of CU-401.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *You will summarize a month of temperature readings until a sum overflows two calls below `main`. Then you will find the reading where it broke and try three fixes. An exact check will show that the program's first output was wrong.* Take it after [201-09](../201/09-functions.md). It uses the method of [201-07](../201/07-debugging-by-comparison.md) from start to end.

chunks.title: the program
step 1: run it, and keep what it printed
chunks.content:
## step 1: run it, and keep what it printed

```text
$ cint run weather.ci > golden.txt
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
  --> weather.ci:25:15
   |
25 |         total += xs[i] * xs[i];
   |               ^ add.checked.i32
   |
   = operation: add.checked.i32
   = operand-count: 2
   = operand: I32 2146711192
   = operand: I32 1201216
   = exact:   2147912408
   = limit:   I32 2147483647
   = revision: c92d9c049c47774f269b91122ebc997629c7f7b431d5bd0b41b36a292759d57f
   = source-map: none
   = address: none
   = stack-depth: 2
   = called from: weather.ci:53:9
   = called from: weather.ci:46:20
   = fuel-consumed: 38831 (not part of the fault record)
   = state: the program stopped; stdout holds what it wrote before the fault
$ cat golden.txt
day  1: low 3.40, high 10.84, mean 7.52, spread 1.87
day  2: low 4.00, high 11.42, mean 8.12, spread 1.87
day  3: low 4.60, high 12.07, mean 8.72, spread 1.87
day  4: low 5.19, high 12.63, mean 9.32, spread 1.87
day  5: low 5.79, high 13.30, mean 9.91, spread 1.93
day  6: low 6.39, high 13.86, mean 10.52, spread 1.87
day  7: low 6.98, high 14.42, mean 11.12, spread 1.88
day  8: low 7.58, high 15.09, mean 11.71, spread 1.93
```

A golden should be checked by hand before it is saved. The lows, highs and means are easy to check against `reading`. The spreads are not, so this lab saves them unchecked, to show what that costs.

chunks.title: step 2: read the call stack
chunks.content:
## step 2: read the call stack

The report names three places, from the outside in:

1. `called from: weather.ci:53:9` is `summarize(d);` in `main`.
2. `called from: weather.ci:46:20` is the call to `sum_of_squares` in `summarize`.
3. `--> weather.ci:25:15` is the `+=` inside `sum_of_squares`, where the fault happened.

`stack-depth: 2` counts the two calls below `main`. The output stops after day 8, so the fault came while summarizing day 9. The first operand is the running total of squares, 2146711192, and the second is one more square, 1201216, which is 1096 × 1096. Together they pass the largest `I32`, 2147483647.

chunks.title: step 3: locate the reading
chunks.content:
## step 3: locate the reading

The report says which addition broke, but not at which minute. `cint debug locate` replays the run and shows the operations before the fault:

```text
$ cint debug locate weather.ci --save-case hot.case
program    weather.ci   evaluator cpu-sir-interp, recorded as the case hot.case
target     boundary 1 of 1, the program entry: the first fault, reproduced by replay
bracket    the initial state; then boundary 1
fault[E_OVERFLOW]: the exact result is outside the type's range
   ...
the last 20 counted operations of boundary 1, of 357848 trace events (:trace shows them all)
  ord  position           operation              operands                 value
   ...
344862                     add.wrap.i64           1360, 1                  1361
344863  weather.ci:25:20   index.checked.i32      1361
344864  weather.ci:25:28   index.checked.i32      1361
344865  weather.ci:25:24   mul.checked.i32        1108, 1108               1227664
344866  weather.ci:25:15   add.checked.i32        2145483528, 1227664      2146711192
344867                     add.wrap.i64           1361, 1                  1362
344868  weather.ci:25:20   index.checked.i32      1362
344869  weather.ci:25:28   index.checked.i32      1362
344870  weather.ci:25:24   mul.checked.i32        1096, 1096               1201216
344871  weather.ci:25:15   add.checked.i32        2146711192, 1201216      E_OVERFLOW
```

The lines with no position are the `for` loop moving `i` to the next index. The loop stops at its bound long before `i` could leave `I64`, so that step is recorded as a wrapping addition that cannot fault.

chunks.title: step 3: locate the reading (part 2)
chunks.content: The index is 1362, so the reading that broke the sum was minute 1362 of day 9, at 10:42 PM: 10.96 degrees. There is nothing odd about it. The squares of day 9's readings average about 1.55 million, and 1,440 of them add up to more than an `I32` holds. The fault is where the total crossed the limit, not where the data was unusual. Keep `hot.case` for exercise 3 of extend it.

chunks.title: step 4: three fixes
chunks.content: ## step 4: three fixes

chunks.title: fix 1: a wider total
fix 2: subtract the mean first
which spread is right
chunks.content:
### which spread is right

Neither `cint run` nor the reference can say which formula is right, because each computes exactly what its program says. So check with exact arithmetic outside cint. `fractions.Fraction` in Python 3.13 on Ubuntu 24.04 computes each day's variance with no rounding at all. Its square root, rounded down to hundredths as `isqrt` rounds, is 1.87 on all 30 days.

So fix 2 is right on every day. Fix 1 is wrong on 20 of the 30, and the first program was already wrong on days 5, 7 and 8. The cause is the formula. `mean` is rounded down to a whole hundredth, and the formula squares it: an error of less than 1 in `mean` becomes an error of up to about 2 × `mean` in `mean * mean`. As the days warm, the error grows. Subtracting the mean first keeps every number small, so the sum stays inside `I32`. It also changes what the rounding costs. With the distances from the rounded `mean`, the rounding adds only its own square to the variance, and that square is less than 1.

The golden was wrong from the start, and that went unnoticed because the spreads were never checked. Now that fix 2 is checked, save a new golden from it as a separate change.

chunks.title: fix 3: report instead of stopping
what each fix changes
chunks.content:
## what each fix changes

The reference's record of each version shows what it changed:

| | Outcome | Output | Fuel | Spreads right |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The first program | fault on day 9 | 8 days | 38831 | 5 of 8 |
| Fix 1, a wider total | value | 30 days | 129691 | 10 of 30 |
| Fix 2, the mean first | value | 30 days | 129691 | 30 of 30 |
| Fix 3, an error | value | 8 days and 22 refusals | 114436 | 5 of 8 |

Fixes 1 and 2 have the same fuel, because they make the same calls and the same passes through their loops. Fuel follows the path a run takes, not the arithmetic on it. The outputs differ, and only the exact check showed which was right.

chunks.title: walk-through
chunks.content:
## walk-through

**`I32 reading(I64 d, I64 m)`** computes in `I64` and converts once at the end with `as I32`. If a reading ever left the range of `I32`, that conversion would fault there.

**`from_peak * 600 / 720`** multiplies before it divides. Dividing first would make `600 / 720` zero, and the swing would disappear: every minute would read as if it were 2 PM.

**`isqrt(variance)`** is the integer square root, rounded down. It takes an integer and returns one of the same type.

**`ArithError!I32`** is the type of a value that is either an `I32` or an `ArithError`. A **result form** is a built-in such as `add_result`, `sub_result` or `mul_result` that returns its answer or an `ArithError` where the plain operator would fault.

**`try add_result(...)`** returns the error from `sum_of_squares` at once, when there is one, and otherwise gives the sum.

**`catch (err) { ... return; }`** runs its block when `sum_of_squares` returns an error. The block prints a line and leaves `summarize` early, so the day gets no summary and the month goes on.

chunks.title: extend it
chunks.content:
## extend it

1. Store the readings as `I16`, as many sensors send them, and change the types to match. Which fixes need a wider type for the squares, and why?
2. Change `reading` so that each day swings twice as far. Does fix 2 still fit in `I32`? Work out the largest distance from the mean before you run it.
3. Copy `hot.case` to a folder without `weather.ci` and run `cint debug locate hot.case` there. Does it reproduce the fault, and do its last operations match step 3?

chunks.content: # cint for C programmers This page is part of CU-000.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *Read this before [201](201/README.md) if you know C. It lists what carries over, what changes and the lesson that shows each change running.*

chunks.title: what carries over
chunks.content:
## what carries over

Much of cint reads like C. Functions are declared with the return type first, statements end with a semicolon and blocks are in braces. `if`, `else`, `while`, `break`, `continue` and `return` keep their meaning, and so does the C form of `for`. `switch` looks the same and differs in the ways listed below. Comments are written with `//`. Integer types say their width in the name: `I8` to `I1024` are signed and `U8` to `U512` are unsigned. `I32` is C's `int32_t` and `U8` is `uint8_t`. cint compiles a program to C17, and [201-00](201/00-start-here.md) shows the C it makes.

chunks.title: what changes
chunks.content: ## what changes

chunks.title: what changes (part 2)
chunks.content:
| In C | In cint | Shown in |
|---|---|---|
| Signed overflow is undefined behavior. | Every plain operator is checked. A result that does not fit stops the program with a fault that names the operation, the operands and the exact result. | [201-01](201/01-numbers-that-hold.md) |
| Unsigned arithmetic wraps without a sign of it. | Plain unsigned operators are checked too. Wrapping is written as an operator of its own, such as `+%`, and saturating as `+|`. | [201-03](201/03-operators-at-the-edge.md) |
| A shift by the width of the type or more is undefined. | A shift that loses bits faults. | [201-03](201/03-operators-at-the-edge.md) |
| Integer promotion and implicit conversions happen everywhere. | No conversion happens on its own, not even to a wider type. `as` converts and faults if the value does not fit. `as%` keeps the low bits and `as?` hands the failure to the program. | [201-02](201/02-types-and-conversions.md) |
| `/` rounds toward zero, and `%` takes the sign of the dividend. | `/` rounds toward negative infinity, and `%` takes the sign of the divisor, as in Python. `div_trunc` and `rem_trunc` give C's results. | [201-04](201/04-division-and-rounding.md) |
| A rounding rule is set somewhere else, or implied. | Each rounded division names its rule, such as `div_round(a, b, half_even)`. | [201-04](201/04-division-and-rounding.md) |
| An array index is not checked. | Every index is checked, and one past the end faults with `E_BOUNDS`. | [101-12](101/12-lists.md) |
| A function takes a pointer and a length. | A function takes a view of an array, `in I64[n]` to read it or `inout I64[n]` to change it, and the length travels with it. | [201-07](201/07-debugging-by-comparison.md), [201-09](201/09-functions.md) |
| A deep recursion can crash when the stack runs out, unless the compiler turns it into a loop. The depth depends on the machine. | At most 256 calls can b

chunks.title: the same program on every compiler
chunks.content:
## the same program on every compiler

A C program that overflows can print one thing at `-O0` and another at `-O2`, and [301-01](301/01-when-64-bits-are-not-enough.md) shows one doing exactly that. A cint program prints the same bytes on GCC, Clang, MSVC and Apple Clang. When it faults, it prints the same fault record on each of them, field for field. So one saved output checks a run on any of those compilers, as [201-05](201/05-tests-and-goldens.md) shows.

chunks.title: where to start
chunks.content:
## where to start

Start with [201-00](201/00-start-here.md). It sets up cint and shows the four commands and the C that a small program becomes.

chunks.content: # cint for Python and NumPy programmers This page is part of CU-000.2, checked against cint 0.2.0. *Read this before [201](201/README.md) if you know Python. It lists what carries over, what changes and the lesson that shows each change running.*

chunks.title: what carries over
chunks.content:
## what carries over

`for i in 0..n` counts from 0 to n - 1, as `for i in range(n)` does. `/` on integers rounds toward negative infinity and `%` takes the sign of the divisor, which is Python's rule for `//` and `%`. A string with `{name}` inside prints the value of `name`, much as an f-string does. Tests can live in the same file as the code, and `cint test` runs them.

chunks.title: what changes
chunks.content: ## what changes

chunks.title: what changes (part 2)
chunks.content:
| In Python or NumPy | In cint | Shown in |
|---|---|---|
| `int` grows to any size. | Every integer has a fixed width, from `I8` to `I1024`. A result that does not fit stops the program with a fault that names the operation, the operands and the exact result. | [201-01](201/01-numbers-that-hold.md), [301-01](301/01-when-64-bits-are-not-enough.md) |
| A NumPy `int64` array wraps without a warning, and an `int64` scalar warns and carries on with the wrapped value. | Arrays and single values are checked the same way. Wrapping is written as an operator of its own, such as `+%`. | [201-01](201/01-numbers-that-hold.md), [201-03](201/03-operators-at-the-edge.md) |
| `astype(np.int16)` keeps the low bits of a value that does not fit. | `as I16` faults when the value does not fit. `as% I16` keeps the low bits when that is the intent. | [201-02](201/02-types-and-conversions.md) |
| A variable takes whatever type is assigned to it. | Each variable is declared with its type, and no value changes type on its own. | [201-02](201/02-types-and-conversions.md) |
| `round` rounds ties to even, without saying so at the call. | Each rounded division names its rule, such as `div_round(a, b, half_even)`. | [201-04](201/04-division-and-rounding.md) |
| `float` is the default for fractions. | There is no floating-point type. Every value in these courses is an integer. | |
| Indentation marks a block. | Braces mark a block, and every body needs them. | [201-08](201/08-control-flow.md) |
| A deep recursion stops with `RecursionError`. | At most 256 calls can be in progress at once, counting `main`, and one more faults with `E_DEPTH`. | [201-09](201/09-functions.md) |
| A list grows and shrinks. | An array has a fixed length, and every index is checked. | [101-12](101/12-lists.md) |
| A function can change a list it is given. | A function says what it may do with an array: `in` to read it, `in

chunks.title: why the fixed widths
chunks.content:
## why the fixed widths

Python's integers never run out of room, so a sum or product of them is never cut short. A fixed width matches the data that sensors, files, images and network packets carry. In NumPy the price of a fixed width is a wrong answer when a value outgrows it, with a warning for a single value and none for an array. In cint the price is a fault at the exact operation, with the numbers that caused it. When a program needs more room, a wider type such as `I128` or `I1024` holds it. It needs an `as` wherever it meets a narrower value, as [301-04](301/04-big-exact-numbers.md) shows with 100 factorial.

chunks.title: the same output on every compiler
chunks.content:
## the same output on every compiler

A cint program prints the same bytes on every compiler cint supports, and a fault prints the same record on each of them. [201-05](201/05-tests-and-goldens.md) builds a way of testing on this: save a program's output once and compare every run after it against the saved copy.

chunks.title: where to start
chunks.content:
## where to start

Start with [201-00](201/00-start-here.md). It sets up cint and shows its four commands.

# cint university

cint university teaches the cint language through short lessons, each built around one program that runs in your browser or on your computer. Every output in a lesson was printed by the cint release named at the top of that lesson.

chunks.title: courses
chunks.content:
## courses

| Course | For | Edition | Checked against |
|---|---|---|---|
| [101: first programs](101/README.md) | People who have never programmed | CU-101.2 | cint 0.2.0 |
| [201: cint for programmers](201/README.md) | People who program in C, Python or a language like them | CU-201.2 | cint 0.2.0 |
| [301: wider numbers](301/README.md) | Readers who finished 201 up to 201-09 | CU-301.1 | cint 0.2.0 |
| [401: labs](401/README.md) | Graduates of 101 or 201 | CU-401.2 | cint 0.2.0 |

A newcomer starts with 101 and a programmer with 201. A programmer who knows C or Python can first read [cint for C programmers](from-c.md) or [cint for Python and NumPy programmers](from-python.md). These pages list what changes and where each change is shown. Each lab lists the lessons it builds on. To run programs outside the browser, first [set up cint on your computer](setup.md).

chunks.title: editions
chunks.content:
## editions

The courses are published in editions, the same way the cint specification is.

- **Names.** An edition is named `CU-NNN.E`: `CU` for cint university, the course number `NNN` and the edition number `E`. `CU-101.1` is the first edition of 101. This page, the setup page and the two pages for programmers form course 000, whose current edition is `CU-000.2`.
- **Tied to a release.** Each edition names the cint release it was checked against. Every program in it was run on that release with each of GCC, Clang, MSVC and Apple Clang. Every output block comes from those runs.
- **Frozen text.** Once released, an edition's text does not change. A correction that changes nothing a reader would see when running a program, such as a typo fixed or a sentence made clearer, is listed in [ERRATA.md](ERRATA.md). It is written `CU-101.1 E1`. The edition keeps its number.
- **New editions.** A course gets a new edition when a release changes a program's output, a message a lesson shows or a rule a lesson cites in that course. No other course does. A course that gains lessons also gets a new edition. Each edition is complete in itself: no lesson in it links to an unpublished lesson. Each new edition ends with a list of what changed since the edition before it, lesson by lesson. Earlier editions stay readable beside the new one.
- **Stable identifiers.** Each lesson has an identifier, such as `101-05`, and a named link anchor, both the same in every edition and never reused. A lesson's place in the course belongs to its edition and may change; its identifier does not. Link to a lesson by its identifier.

chunks.title: CU-000.2
chunks.content:
# set up cint on your computer

Every program in cint university runs in your browser at [integerc.dev](https://integerc.dev), with nothing to install. This page sets up the other way: cint on your own computer, an editor to write programs in and a terminal to run them.

You need three things:

- **Python 3.12 or later.** The build scripts are written in Python.
- **A C compiler.** cint turns your program into C, then uses this compiler to build it. On Windows that is Microsoft's C compiler (MSVC), on macOS it is Apple Clang and on Linux it is GCC or Clang.
- **The cint source**, downloaded from {{SOURCE_URL}} and unpacked into a folder.

chunks.title: build cint
chunks.content:
## build cint

Pick the steps for your system. Each one ends with the `cint` command and its debugging tools in a folder called `cint` in your home folder.

chunks.title: Windows
chunks.content:
### Windows

1. Install Python from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/). On the installer's first screen, select **Add python.exe to PATH**.
2. Install **Build Tools for Visual Studio** from [visualstudio.microsoft.com](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/downloads/). In the installer, choose the workload **Desktop development with C++**.
3. In File Explorer, right-click the folder where you unpacked cint and choose **Open in Terminal**. Then run these two commands:

   ```text
   python tools\cint_bootstrap.py --leg msvc --out "$HOME\cint"
   python tools\cint_tools.py --leg msvc --out "$HOME\cint"
   ```

4. Add the new folder to your PATH, so that `cint` works from any folder. Open the Start menu and search for **Edit environment variables for your account**. Select **Path** and choose **Edit**, then **New**. Type the folder's full path, for example `C:\Users\ada\cint`, then close and reopen any open terminals.

The build finds the C compiler on its own. You do not need a "Developer Command Prompt".

chunks.title: macOS
chunks.content:
### macOS

1. Open **Terminal** and install Apple's command line tools, which include Apple Clang:

   ```text
   xcode-select --install
   ```

2. Install Python 3.12 or later from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/). The command line tools include an older Python that is too old for the build.
3. In Terminal, go to the folder where you unpacked cint and run these two commands:

   ```text
   python3 tools/cint_bootstrap.py --leg apple-clang --out ~/cint
   python3 tools/cint_tools.py --leg apple-clang --out ~/cint
   ```

4. Add the folder to your PATH, then open a new Terminal window:

   ```text
   echo 'export PATH="$HOME/cint:$PATH"' >> ~/.zprofile
   ```

chunks.title: Linux
chunks.content:
### Linux

These commands are for Ubuntu 24.04 or later and Debian 13 or later; older releases come with a Python older than 3.12. Other distributions have the same packages under similar names.

1. Install the compiler and Python:

   ```text
   sudo apt install gcc python3
   ```

2. Go to the folder where you unpacked cint and run these two commands:

   ```text
   python3 tools/cint_bootstrap.py --leg gcc --out ~/cint
   python3 tools/cint_tools.py --leg gcc --out ~/cint
   ```

3. Add the folder to your PATH, then open a new terminal:

   ```text
   echo 'export PATH="$HOME/cint:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
   ```

The first command builds `cint`. It runs in three steps and prints a line for each. First, a small compiler written in C is built. That compiler translates the cint compiler, which is written in cint, into C. Then your C compiler builds that C into the `cint` command.

The second command builds five debugging tools into the same folder. Each one runs as a `cint` command:

- `cint workbench` opens an interactive session that can rewind a run. `cint repl` opens the same session.
- `cint debug` locates, replays and compares faults.
- `cint explain` shows what the compiler knows about each function.
- `cint interp` is the interpreter, which runs a program without a C compiler.

Timed once by the wall clock, on a four-core Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz running Ubuntu 24.04 with GCC 13.3, the first command took 45 seconds and the second 36 seconds.

chunks.title: write and run a program in VS Code
chunks.content:
## write and run a program in VS Code

[VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com) is a free editor for Windows, macOS and Linux, and it is the editor these lessons use in their steps.

1. Install VS Code and open it.
2. Choose **File > Open Folder**, make a new folder called `cint-programs` and open it.
3. Choose **File > New File**, name it `hello.ci` and type:

   ```ci
   "Hello, world\n";
   ```

   Save it with Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS).
4. Choose **Terminal > New Terminal**. A terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already in your folder. Type:

   ```text
   cint run hello.ci
   ```

   and press Enter. The terminal prints:

   ```text
   Hello, world
   ```

If the terminal says it cannot find `cint`, close VS Code and open it again, so that it reads the new PATH.

chunks.title: color for cint programs
chunks.content:
### color for cint programs

VS Code does not know cint, but cint looks enough like C that C's colors fit most of a program: comments, text in quotes, numbers and words such as `if`, `for` and `return`. Type names such as `I64` stay uncolored. To turn this on, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS), choose **Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)** and add this line inside the outer braces:

```json
"files.associations": { "*.ci": "c" }
```

chunks.title: run with one key
or use a text editor and a terminal
chunks.content:
## or use a text editor and a terminal

If you would rather not use VS Code, any plain text editor and a terminal will do. Programs were written this way long before editors had buttons. You type the program into a file and hand the file to the compiler, as programmers once did on teletypes, typewriters wired to a computer.

1. Open a plain text editor:
   - **Windows:** Notepad.
   - **macOS:** TextEdit. Choose **Format > Make Plain Text** and turn off **Edit > Substitutions > Smart Quotes**. Or use `nano` in Terminal.
   - **Linux:** your desktop's Text Editor, or `nano` in a terminal.
2. Type the program:

   ```ci
   "Hello, world\n";
   ```

3. Save it as `hello.ci` in a folder of your own. In Notepad, set **Save as type** to **All files** so the name does not become `hello.ci.txt`. Set **Encoding** to **UTF-8**.
4. Open a terminal, go to that folder with `cd` and run:

   ```text
   cint run hello.ci
   ```

Two editor settings cause trouble. Curly quotes, which some editors put in place of straight ones as you type, are not quotes to cint:

```text
error[C1013]: invalid name
  --> hello.ci:1:1
```

A file saved as "UTF-8 with BOM" starts with three invisible bytes that cint refuses:

```text
error[C1002]: invalid source bytes
  --> hello.ci:1:1
```

Either message on the first line of a file you just typed means the editor changed what you typed. Fix the setting and save the file again.

chunks.title: what you have now
chunks.content:
## what you have now

- `cint run FILE.ci` builds a program and runs it.
- `cint test FILE.ci` runs the tests in a file.
- `cint build FILE.ci` writes a program you can run without cint, into a folder called `build` next to the file.
- `cint emit-c --root DIR --out DIR FILE.ci` writes the C that cint makes from your program.

Each lesson tells you which of these it uses.
